Groa, speaking from the grave, asks what troubles her only son, then acknowledges the length of his journey and the power of love. At Svipdag’s request she chants nine protective charms to guard him against various dangers: inner afflictions, aimless wandering, deadly streams, enemies on the gallows-road, fetters, storms at sea, killing frost on high crags, curses from a dead Christian woman, and a verbal contest with a warlike giant. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10069-l10184","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LAYS OF THE HEROES / VLUNDARKVITHA / THE LAY OF VLUND / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10069-10184","start":"10069","end":"10184","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly introductory prose explains the manuscript situation and transmission of the Vlundarkvitha, noting its position in Codex Regius and an incomplete copy in the Arnamagnan Codex, and stating that the underlying Weland/Wayland smith legend likely came north from Saxon regions, with parallels to the Old English poem Deor and to wider Teutonic traditions. It describes how the main story of the smith Weland’s laming by King Nithuth and his revenge is combined with a separate swan-maiden/Valkyrie legend, itself part of a broader German folktale tradition, perhaps adapted to Norse myth by identifying the maidens as Valkyries. The note discusses prose narrative links in the poem. A prose introduction then outlines the story: King Nithuth of Sweden has two sons and a daughter Bothvild. Three brothers, Slagfith, Egil, and Vlund, sons of a king of the Finns, travel on snowshoes, hunt, and settle in Ulfdalir by a lake, Ulfsjar. One morning they find three women on the shore, spinning flax near their swan-garments; the women are Valkyries: Hlathguth the Swan-White and Hervor the All-Wise, daughters of King Hlothver, and Olrun, daughter of Kjar from Valland. The brothers bring them home; Egil takes Olrun, Slagfith takes Swan-White, and Vlund takes All-Wise, and they live together seven winters. The Valkyries then fly away to seek battles and do not return. Egil and Slagfith depart on snowshoes to follow their maidens, while Vlund remains in Ulfdalir, famed as a highly skillful man, until King Nithuth has him seized by force. The first stanza of the poem proper depicts fair young maidens flying from the south through Myrkwood, resting by the sea shore and spinning flax as they follow their content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l817-l899","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAIMERS / HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD; lines 817-899","start":"817","end":"899","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage recounts the reign of the legendary king Jemshd, renowned for wisdom and credited with introducing armor, fine garments, agriculture, and building techniques. With the aid of demons he constructs a splendid palace using bricks made from water and clay and commands them to raise his jeweled throne into the air so he can travel instantly. He establishes the N-rz New Year feast, where mortals and various spirits celebrate together, and his seven-hundred-year government is depicted as a golden age without sickness or death. After many years Jemshd becomes proud, accepts flattery that no king equals him, and claims that all science and prosperity come from him alone. God punishes this impiety by casting him down from power, and a moral voice explains his fall as the result of neglecting the worship of God.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Jemshd is described as eminently distinguished for learning and wisdom.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Armor such as coats of mail, cuirasses, swords, and various kinds of armor are said to have been invented and manufactured in Jemshd's time.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Garments of silk are said to have been made and worn by Jemshd's people.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Guided by Jemshd's skill, people make helmets, swords, silks, linen, and robes of fur and ermine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Desert lands are cultivated during Jemshd's reign.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Jemshd fixes the habitations of his people wherever streams or rivulets wander and the soil is good, and there they plough and reap.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In Jemshd's age all people labor and none are allowed to remain in sloth and idleness, which is viewed as destructive to even the best resolutions.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Jemshd commands his Demons to construct a splendid palace and directs his people how to make its foundations strong.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Jemshd teaches the \"unholy Demon-train\" to mix water and clay into bricks used to build walls, high turrets, towers, balconies, and roofs that keep out rain, cold, and sunshine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The narrative states that every art was known to Jemshd and that he was without equal in the world.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Jemshd makes vessels for travel on the sea and the river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Jemshd erects a magnificent throne embellished with pearls and precious stones.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Seated upon his throne, Jemshd commands his Demons to raise him up into the air so that he can transport himself in a moment wherever he chooses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Jemshd names the first day of the year N-rz and holds a royal feast on every N-rz.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Under Jemshd's hospitable roof at N-rz, mortals, Genii, Demons, and Peris are equally regaled with wine and music and are described as delighted and happy.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Jemshd's government is said to have continued for seven hundred years.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"During Jemshd's seven-hundred-year rule none of his subjects suffer death or disease; man seems immortal, sickness is unknown, and life is full of happiness and joy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"After seven hundred years, inordinate ambition inflames Jemshd's heart.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Jemshd assembles all the illustrious personages and learned men in his dominions and asks whether there exists or ever existed a king as magnificent and powerful as he is.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The assembled men reply that Jemshd alone is the mightiest and most victorious king and that there is no equal to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"God sees Jemshd's pride and vanity with displeasure and punishes him by casting him from the government of an empire into utter degradation and misery.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"People look upon the throne and see only Jemshd as king, absorbing every thought and adoration in him and forgetting the worship of the great Creator.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Jemshd tells his nobles that he is unequalled, that the earth owes all its science and benefits to him, that his sovereignty has driven disease and want from the land, and that he is the only monarch of the world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"As soon as Jemshd utters these impious words, his earthly grandeur fades, tongues grow clamorous and bold, and his day passes into gloom with his brightness obscured.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"A speaker identified as the Moralist says that when Jemshd was king his subjects were obedient, but whoever neglects the worship of his God brings desolation on his house and home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Seeing the insolence of his people, Jemshd realizes that Heaven's wrath has been provoked and is overcome by content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l392-l462","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Persian Literature, Volume 1 / PERSIAN LITERATURE / SPECIAL INTRODUCTION; lines 392-462","start":"392","end":"462","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"The ascetic is the serpent of his age\" and \"Open my grave when I am dead...\" are cited amid images of wine, love, Paradise, the willow-tree, and a grave emitting fire and smoke.","summary":"The passage surveys Persian lyric poetry focused on love, wine, youth, and nature. It highlights Rudagi and poets of sentiment from the Samanid era, notes Firdusi’s lyrical joy in some minor poems, and presents Shams al-Din Mohammed Hafiz as the greatest Persian lyric poet. Hafiz is described as unaffected by surrounding wars, content to live and sing, rooted in Shiraz with little inclination to travel, adopting the garb of a Dervish yet criticizing asceticism with the saying \"The ascetic is the serpent of his age.\" His poetry is characterized by melody, rich imagery, delicate rhythm, and boisterous joy without anything base, and he is quoted as preferring the shade of the willow-tree and fruitful field over the Garden of Paradise. The author stresses Hafiz’s deep ethical humanity and his thorough Sufi orientation; Shah Shuja remarks that Hafiz writes of wine, Sufism, and his beloved in the same song. Sufism is described as a mystic philosophy that reconciled old Persian tradition with conquering Islam by veiling transcendental meanings in everyday images, making it hard to distinguish literal from mystical bodies, wine, and love in Hafiz’s verse. Hafiz is quoted as saying that after his death, opening his grave will reveal smoke from a fire still burning in his heart, igniting his shroud. Persians cherish Hafiz as the poet of their joyous moments and the companion of their feasts. The passage concludes by listing Firdusi, Omar, Sa'di, Hafiz, and Jami as unmatched giants of Persian poetry, noting unsuccessful later revivals under Shah Abbas and Akbar, and attributing the lack of a new literary \"spring\" to Persia’s political decline, followed by Richard Gottheil’s signature and date.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Persian poetry is said to have forms beyond the heroic and didactic, including lyric poems that celebrate love, wine, youth, and nature without aiming to draw a moral or illustrate a tale.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"From the times of Rudagi and the poets.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"War and strife surrounded Hafiz’s country and disturbed his native place, yet his poems show no trace of these events, as if he were removed from them while observing the actual things of life.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hafiz is described as apparently unconcerned by external content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l12875-l12984","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HELGAKVITHA HUNDINGSBANA II / THE SECOND LAY OF HELGI HUNDINGSBANE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 12875-12984","start":"12875","end":"12984","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial prose notes to Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II describe manuscript issues, interpolations, and parallels with other poems. They highlight the naming of Hogni’s sons Bragi and Dag, Dag’s puzzling appearance, and Sigrun’s reference to oaths her brother swore to Helgi. The notes gloss various mythic places and beings: Sevafjoll (Wet Mountain) where giantesses ride wolves; an ambiguous term translated “maid” that may mean valkyrie or “wise”; the Norns; and Dag’s habit of blaming a murder on Othin. A stanza about Hlebjorg (Sea-Mountain), Styrkleifar (Battle-Cliffs), and Starkath is likely from another poem, paralleling Saxo’s story where Starkath’s severed head bites the ground. Another section covers a quarrel between Gothmund and Sinfjotli that closely matches a longer version in Helgakvitha Hundingsbana I, including details of a war-banner and a “battle-light” perhaps meaning the northern lights. The commentator explains obscure references such as a “realm of the fishes” (probably the sea), the place Fjoturlund (Fetter-Wood) where Helgi dies at Dag’s hands using Othin’s victory-bringing spear, the river Leipt, Uth the daughter of the sea-god Ægir and her sacred stone, and purely mythical sites like Vandil’s Shrine and Battle-Dale. Helgi’s horse Vigblær is named. A final prose note mentions a tradition that Helgi shares Othin’s rule in Valhall, which the editor considers a late development.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The notes state that the only new features in the introductory prose are the names of Hogni’s sons Bragi and Dag, and that Dag’s name does not actually appear in the verse, leaving its source unknown.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The prose note introduces a new section of the poem that deals with Helgi’s death at the hands of Dag, Sigrun’s brother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The commentator says that Sigrun refers to oaths her brother had sworn to Helgi, and elsewhere notes that Dag’s life was spared because he swore loyalty to Helgi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sevafjoll, glossed as Wet Mountain, is mentioned only in this poem.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"“Giant-steeds” are explained as wolves, described as the usual steeds of giantesses.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The word rendered “maid” is described as doubtful and may specifically mean a valkyrie or simply “wise.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The notes connect the stanza mentioning the maid with the Norns and remark that in stanza 33 Dag similarly lays the blame for the murder he has committed on Othin.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hlebjorg (Sea-Mountain) and Styrkleifar (Battle-Cliffs) are identified as place names not mentioned elsewhere, and nothing further is known of Hrollaug’s sons who appear with them.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The editor cites Saxo Grammaticus’s account of the Swedish hero Starkath, son of Storverk, whose severed head bit the ground in anger.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The commentary judges that the stanza containing Starkath most probably comes from an entirely different poem about the Starkath story and that identifying this hero as a third son of Granmar lacks foundation.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The dispute between Gothmund and Sinfjotli in this lay is said to appear at much greater length in Helgakvitha Hundingsbana I, with some stanzas, notably Helgi’s rebuke, nearly identical, suggesting direct borrowing from the older version.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The note explains that in this version a banner (gunnfani) serves as the signal for war, whereas in Helgakvitha Hundingsbana I a red shield fills that role.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"“Battle-light” is glossed as perhaps referring to the northern lights.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In stanza 23, the “realm of the fishes” is interpreted as meaning the sea, though the underlying word translated “fishes” is obscure and may instead be a proper name “Fjorsungs.”","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The new prose section notes Helgi’s death at Fjoturlund and comments that the annotator likely introduced the reference to Othin’s spear, described as a weapon that made victory certain, based on Dag’s statement that Othin was responsible for Helgi’s death.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Fjoturlund (Fetter-Wood) is mentioned only in the prose note and stanza 28 as the location associated with Helgi’s death.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Leipt is identified as a river; Uth is described as a daughter of the sea-god Ægir who possesses a sacred stone, about which nothing further is known.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"According to the annotator’s explanation, Dag’s life was spared because he swore loyalty to Helgi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Vandilsve (Vandil’s Shrine) and Vigdalir (Battle-Dale) are said to be purely mythical places, and nothing is known about Vandil himself.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Vigblær (Battle-Breather) is identified as Helgi’s horse.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"A prose note reports a notion that Helgi shares Othin’s rule in Valhall, which the commentator considers unlikely for the earlier Helgi poems and probably a late development from a time when Othin was no longer taken seriously.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Helgi","description":"Hero whose oaths with Sigrun’s brother are mentioned, who dies at Dag’s content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l13064-l13143","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / FRA DAUTHA SINFJOTLA / OF SINFJOTLIS DEATH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 13064-13143","start":"13064","end":"13143","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The introductory note explains how the Helgi tradition, originally Danish, became associated with the Volsung tradition of German/Frankish origin through genealogical links, particularly by making Helgi a son of Sigmund Volsungsson. Sinfjotli, another son of Sigmund, appears only briefly in the Helgi lays, where he engages in a verbal quarrel with Gothmund Granmarsson. The note then summarizes Sinfjotli’s backstory from the Volsungasaga: Signy, twin sister of Sigmund, marries Siggeir, who hates Sigmund over Odin’s sword. Siggeir treacherously kills Volsung and imprisons his sons. A wolf, possibly Siggeir’s mother, devours one son each night until only Sigmund survives, aided by Signy, who helps him escape and kill the wolf. Sigmund vows vengeance, and Signy, believing he needs a helper of his own blood, exchanges forms with a witch and unknowingly sleeps with Sigmund. She bears Sinfjotli and sends him to Sigmund. Father and son live in the woods, sometimes as wolves. When grown, Sinfjotli joins Sigmund in an attack on Siggeir, but they are betrayed by Signy and Siggeir’s young sons, whom Sinfjotli kills. Siggeir has Sigmund and Sinfjotli buried alive, but Signy smuggles Sigmund’s sword into the grave and they dig themselves out. The next night they burn Siggeir’s hall; Siggeir dies in the flames and Signy, refusing to abandon her husband out of belated loyalty, dies with him. The note observes that this story probably derives from a lost poem, though it survives in prose in Volsungasaga, which quotes two lines of verse. It states that the Volsung tradition underlies about fifteen Eddic poems, and distinguishes three parts: the Volsung-Sigmund-Sinfjotli story, the Helgi story, and the Sigurth story, which are only loosely connected genealogically and were probably originally distinct. Finally, the compiler of Codex Regius, lacking poems on the deaths of Sigmund and Sinfjotli, includes a short prose passage, 'Of Sinfjotli’s Death', after the second lay of Helgi Hundingsbane to relate their deaths and so bridge to the Sigurth poems.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Helgi tradition is described as originally coming from Denmark and becoming early associated with the Volsung tradition, which is said to be of German or Frankish origin.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The main link between the Helgi and Volsung stories is the identification of Helgi as a son of Sigmund Volsungsson.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Another son of Sigmund, Sinfjotli, appears in the Helgi poems only to engage in a wordy dispute with Gothmund Granmarsson.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sinfjotli’s detailed history is said to be told in the early chapters of the Volsungasaga.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Signy is identified as the twin sister of Sigmund Volsungsson and as the wife of Siggeir.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Siggeir is said to hate Sigmund because he desires a sword that belonged to Othin and had been won by Sigmund.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Siggeir treacherously invites Volsung and his ten sons, kills Volsung, and captures the sons, who are set in the stocks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Each night a wolf, which some men say was Siggeir’s mother, comes out of the woods and eats one of the captive brothers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"On the tenth night Sigmund is the only one of Volsung’s sons left alive.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On the tenth night Signy aids Sigmund in escaping, and Sigmund kills the wolf.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Sigmund vows vengeance on Siggeir, and Signy, who hates her husband, is determined to help him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Signy is described as being convinced that Sigmund must have a helper of his own race.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Signy exchanges forms with a witch and, in the witch’s likeness, spends three nights with Sigmund, who does not know who she is.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After these nights Signy gives birth to a boy she names Sinfjotli and sends him to Sigmund.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Sigmund and Sinfjotli live in the woods for a time and occasionally turn into wolves.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When Sinfjotli is fully grown, he and Sigmund go to Siggeir’s house but are seen and betrayed by the two young sons of Signy and Siggeir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Sinfjotli kills the two young sons of Signy and Siggeir after they betray him and Sigmund.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Siggeir has Sigmund and Sinfjotli buried alive after the killing of his sons.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Signy secretly smuggles Sigmund’s famous sword into the grave, and with it Sigmund and Sinfjotli dig their way These strands were linked so that Gundicarius became the Gunther of the Nibelungenlied and the Gunnar of the Eddic poems, while Attila became Etzel and Atli; Ermanarich was attached as the husband of Sigurth’s daughter Svanhild and appears as Jormunrek in some Eddic poems. After the legend reached Norway it was reshaped: names were Scandinavianized, new minor figures and northern local color added, and the early part of the story was connected to Norse mythology by making the Volsungs descendants of Othin and involving the gods with Fafnir’s treasure. Brynhild’s figure was altered into a Valkyrie sleeping on a flame-girt rock, yet she remained also the human daughter of Buthli whom Sigurth woos for Gunnar, producing a confused double character akin to the overlapping identities of Svava and Sigrun in the Helgi tradition. The editor stresses that the legend grew through accretions from the Danube to Iceland, so inconsistencies in the Sigurth story, like Helgi’s being reborn twice so three different men can kill him, result from conflicting traditions rather than from a coherent biography.\n\nAn introductory prose note to Gripir’s Prophecy (Gripisspo) then states that Gripir, son of Eylimi and brother of Hjordis, ruled lands and was the wisest and most foresighted of men. Sigurth rides alone to Gripir’s hall, where he meets a man named Geitir outside. After asking who owns the dwelling and who the people’s king is, Sigurth learns it is Gripir. Sigurth asks if the all-knowing king will speak with him, and identifies himself as Sigurth, son of Sigmund and Hjordis. Geitir conveys this to Gripir, who comes out, warmly welcomes Sigurth, and has Geitir take Grani. The two then converse, and Sigurth asks his mother’s brother Gripir to tell him what his life will be. Gripir prophesies that Sigurth will be the mightiest and most renowned of men, generous, brave, noble in appearance, and wise in speech. At Sigurth’s request for more detail, Gripir foretells that Sigurth will first avenge his father and Eylimi by slaying the hardy sons of Hunding and winning victory. When Sigurth asks if even greater deeds are foreseen, Gripir predicts that he will fight alone with a fiery dragon lying greedily at Gnitaheith and will be the slayer of both Regin and added.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Norse version links the earlier part of the story with Northern mythology by making the Volsungs direct descendants of Othin.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the Norse material the gods are closely concerned with Fafnir’s treasure.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Norse storytellers changed Brynhild by making her a Valkyrie sleeping on a flame-girt Slim accepts, descends from the fort, and is slain in single combat when Minchihr beheads him, leading to the rout of the enemy troops. The leading warriors of the defeated army seek Minchihr’s protection and help unite the forces of Slim and Tr under his command; Minchihr assigns ranks according to merit. After the victory, Minchihr visits the venerable monarch Feridn, shows humility by alighting and kissing the ground, and is honored in the palace. As Feridn’s end approaches, he entrusts Minchihr to the care of Sm and Narmn, declares his hour of departure, and directs that Minchihr be seated on the throne and crowned, filling his mind with wise counsel. After Feridn’s death, Minchihr succeeds to the empire, faithfully maintains his great grandfather’s laws, and orders his subjects to worship God. The army and people praise him, pray for his happiness and long life, and affirm their hearts’ loving loyalty to {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1262-l1382","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1262-1382","start":"1262","end":"1382","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An exiled king, Jemshd, weeps in the presence of a princess and her nurse, saying he pities the misfortunes of Jemshd, who has lost his throne and may have died in the wilderness. The nurse and princess suspect he is Jemshd himself, based on his voice, discourse, and likeness to a picture, and recall a prophecy that the princess will be united with Jemshd and bear him a son. Jemshd repeatedly denies his identity, citing fear of a powerful enemy and distrust of entrusting secrets to women. The princess dismisses her attendants, professes intense love and willingness to sacrifice her life, and weeps until Jemshd is moved to reveal his name and the story of his misfortunes. She joyfully takes him secretly to her chamber, and they marry according to her country’s custom, enjoying mutual bliss in a secret bower.

King Greng notices his daughter’s visits have become infrequent, sets spies on her, and discovers she has married without his permission. He becomes angry and rebukes her sharply, accusing her of casting away modesty and suggesting fair daughters are always false. The princess defends herself, saying she has never brought him shame and that Jemshd is her wedded lord. The Kabul nurse, described as having many spells, adds that a prophecy she had earlier communicated is being fulfilled: the Almighty and destiny have brought Jemshd into the king’s realm, and planetary influence indicates the princess will soon become a mother. The princess prostrates herself before her father, reminding him that he once granted her freedom to choose her husband and stating that she has united her fortunes with Jemshd, whom she calls the greatest king and most perfect of mankind.

With this explanation, King Greng outwardly expresses satisfaction, but his true joy comes from the opportunity to betray Jemshd. He plans to send Jemshd bound as a captive to Zohk, a powerful enemy king, expecting a magnificent reward. In verse, he declares that he blesses the day Jemshd came into his power and that by delivering this long-sought noble prize he will, on solemn oath, obtain a wealthy kingdom.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At the beginning of their friendship, the princess asks Jemshd why he is weeping and whether content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1633-l1743","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK / KAVAH, THE BLACKSMITH; lines 1633-1743","start":"1633","end":"1743","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The tyrant king Zohk, whose serpents are fed with the brains of youths, summons nobles and philosophers to plan a vast army of Men, Demons, and Peris, and orders a complete register of his subjects. Kavah, a strong and brave blacksmith with many children, protests when two of his sons are to be killed for the serpents, compelling Zohk to release them, but then tears up the royal register and leaves the court. Kavah publicly denounces the king’s injustices, rallies multitudes around a banner fashioned from his leather apron, and urges alliance with the young hero Feridn to overthrow Zohk’s oppression. When Kavah finds Feridn, the banner is richly adorned and becomes the revered flag of Kavah, later honored by all succeeding kings as a sacred sign of royalty. Guided by Kavah, Feridn sets out against Zohk with his mother’s blessing and his two elder brothers, armed with an iron mace shaped like a cow’s head. On his journey he visits a shrine, prays for divine aid, and is taught the mysteries of magic by a radiant figure, emerging visibly transformed. His jealous brothers then attempt to kill him by rolling a rock down a mountain while he sleeps, but he halts it with sorcery, sees through their pretense of innocence, and nevertheless forgives them, raising them to greater honor.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"King Zohk summons all the nobles and philosophers of the kingdom, speaks of a young enemy, and proposes raising a large army of Men, Demons, and Peris.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Zohk decrees that a register or muster-roll of all proceeds against Zohk, taking his two elder brothers with him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Feridn’s mother weeps at his departure and repeatedly implores God’s blessing upon him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Feridn has two elder brothers who accompany him on his journey against The Turanian champion Brmn offers single combat; despite his brother Krun’s pleas, the aged Persian leader Kobd accepts, after declaring that all men are destined to die. Brmn eventually kills Kobd, prompting Krun to lead a fierce counterattack in which many on both sides fall, including fifty thousand Persians, until night ends the fighting. After a second day of heavy battle in which Nauder duels Afrsiyb and the Persians fare worse, Nauder sorrowfully recalls Minchihr’s warning and sends his sons Ts and Gustahem, along with his household, back to Iran to take refuge on Mount Alberz so that some of Feridn’s line may survive the looming ruin. Following a two-day pause, a third day of battle brings a decisive Turanian victory and the death of the Persian champion Shahpr. Nauder and Krun retreat to the fortress of Dehstn. Afrsiyb then dispatches Karkhn with cavalry through the desert to seize Nauder’s household; Krun, defying Nauder’s wishes, marches out at midnight with volunteers, reaches the White Fort ruled by household.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Brazen drums on elephants are sounded as the signal for Afrsiyb’s army to depart, and the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1030-l1151","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1030-1151","start":"1030","end":"1151","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Zohak, dreaded for keeping two devouring serpents, gains the Persian crown as nobles abandon Jemshid and ally with Arab troops. Jemshid is defeated, wanders in exile through wilderness and mountains, and eventually takes refuge in Zabulistan. There King Greng\u0019s daughter is portrayed as extraordinarily beautiful, intellectually gifted, and trained in war; dressed in male armor, she defeats King Minuchihr\u0019s attack and saves her father\u0019s realm. Although many kings seek her hand, her father decrees she may marry only one she loves. Her nurse, a Kabul sorceress skilled in magic and astrology, foretells that she is destined to marry King Jemshid and bear him a beautiful son. In spring, when roses bloom in Greng\u0019s garden, the exiled Jemshid arrives but is barred from entering, and sits weary under a tree by the garden gate. A slave-girl sees him, hears of his lost fortunes and desire for wine, and describes his beauty to the princess. Delighted, the princess promises wine, music, and herself as mistress, goes gracefully to the gate, invites the stranger to rest and drink, and declares her father has given her freedom in matters of the heart. Jemshid hesitates but, captivated by her face, becomes enamoured; she takes his hand and leads him along the garden walks.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Zohak keeps near him two devouring serpents, and news of this causes alarm and terror among the people of Iran and Turan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Because of fear produced by Zohak\u0019s serpents, the nobles of Persia abandon their allegiance to Jemshid and ally with Arab troops against their own country.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Jemshid resists the combined forces for some time but is eventually defeated and becomes a wanderer upon the earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Zohak gains the imperial crown and erases Jemshid\u0019s name from all acts and deeds of royal importance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the government falls to the usurper, Zohak sends spies in all directions to capture Jemshid, but they fail; Jemshid suffers many misfortunes and ultimately takes refuge in Zabulistan.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Jemshid\u0019s wandering is described as flying from place to place through wilderness, wide plain, and mountain, veiled from human eyes, hungry and worn with fatigue and sorrow, until he reaches Zabul.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The king of Zabulistan, Greng, has a daughter of extreme beauty, remarkable mental endowments, and familiarity with warlike exercises.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Greng\u0019s daughter is described with wine-sipping lips, a mouth like sugar, dimpled smiling cheeks, and glow like a summer rose, and her look is said to remove sorrow from the aged.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The damsel habitually dresses in warlike male habiliments and combats with heroes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"At fifteen years of age she is so accomplished in valor, judgment, and discretion that King Minuchihr, who attacked her father, is forced to abandon his claims and submit to her gallantry, thereby saving her father\u0019s realm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Many kings seek the damsel as a bride, but Greng refuses their suits and agrees only that she may marry a sovereign whom she spontaneously loves.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Greng states that love alone must bind his daughter to another\u0019s throne and that the choice of husband belongs entirely to her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The daughter of Greng has a Kabul woman as her nurse, who is deeply skilled in magic and sorcery.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Kabul sorceress can draw fire from the watery element, kill a dragon by sealing its eyes with her magic breath, conjure dew from a flint-stone, knows the moon and seven stars, and can speak of things invisible to human sight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The sorceress had long before told the damsel that, according to her destiny ascertained from the motions of the heavenly bodies, she would one day marry King Jemshid and bear him a beautiful son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Both the damsel and her father are overjoyed at the prophecy, and in consequence the father continues to refuse every other suitor.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"In accordance with the prophecy, Jemshid arrives at Zabul in the spring season when roses are in bloom, and King Greng\u0019s garden lies in his path while the daughter is amusing herself inside it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The keepers of the garden refuse Jemshid entrance, so he sits, fatigued and dispirited, under the shade of a tree by the garden door.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A slave-girl comes out of the garden, sees the melancholy stranger, asks who he is, and hears him say that he once possessed wealth and affluence but is now abandoned by fortune and wishes for a few cups of wine to relieve his fatigue and affliction.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The slave-girl returns and tells the princess that a young, travel-wearied man sits at the gate and that his countenance is even lovelier than her mistress\u0019s, and that he requested wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"On hearing of the stranger\u0019s beauty and request, the damsel says she will give him not only wine but also music and a beautiful mistress.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The damsel, attended by her hand-maid, goes towards the gate with motion compared to a waving cypress, sees the stranger, thinks he is a warrior from Iran, and notes his pale visage like a pomegranate flower and his appearance like light in darkness.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Warm emotions rise in the damsel\u0019s heart and she invites the grief-stricken stranger to rest under the shady bowers, enter the pleasant garden, and drink wine to make him glad.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"When Jemshid hesitates, the damsel tells him she is permitted by her father to do as she pleases and that her heart is her own, explaining that her father is the mild monarch of Zabulistan and she his only child on whom his fond affection is centered.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Jemshid had previously heard of the character and renown of Greng\u0019s daughter but initially resists her entreaty; after contemplating her lovely face, his heart becomes enamoured, and she takes him by the hand and leads him along the beautiful garden walks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zohak (Zohk)","description":"Usurper who gains the Persian imperial crown and keeps two devouring The Simurgh, searching for food, finds the infant on a hard rock, chooses compassion over devouring him, carries him home, and raises him. A non-earthly voice in the mountain nest declares the child divinely protected, commands the Simurgh to foster him with paternal care, and foretells that a world champion will descend from Zal, while content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l14696-l14932","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / FAFNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF FAFNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 14696-14932","start":"14696","end":"14932","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this section of Fafnismol, the speaker reflects that someone will always hold Fafnir’s hoard until the destined day, while every person must eventually journey to Hel. Sigurth questions the dying Fafnir about the Norns and their diverse origins and about the future island where all the gods will battle the fire-being Surt when the bridge Bilrost breaks and horses must swim a flood. Fafnir describes wearing a fear-helm and breathing venom as he lay shining over his hoard, but warns Sigurth that the gold and rings will be his doom and that Regin will betray them both. Regin, who had stayed away during the fight, returns to praise Sigurth and argue over who deserves credit, while Sigurth insists that courage and gladness matter more than weapons and recalls that Regin urged him to seek Fafnir. Regin then cuts out Fafnir’s heart, drinks his blood, and tells Sigurth to roast the heart over a fire so Regin can eat it. As Sigurth cooks the heart and burns his finger, the dragon’s heart-blood touches his tongue, and he suddenly understands the speech of birds. A group of nut-hatches comments on his situation, urging him to eat the heart himself and warning that Regin plans to betray and kill him for the treasure, advising Sigurth to behead Regin so that he alone will possess the hoard.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker states that someone will always hold the hoard until a destined day comes, and that every man will in time journey to Hel.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fafnir says that the fate of the Norns is found before a headland and warns that one will drown if he rows against the wind, with danger lying close to death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigurth asks Fafnir who the Norns are, describing them as helpful in need and as bringing the baby from the mother.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fafnir replies that the Norns have many different births, that they are not of one race, and that some are kin to the gods, some to the elves, and some are Dvalin’s daughters.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sigurth asks for the name of the island where all the gods and Surt will mingle sword-sweat in battle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Fafnir names the island Oskopnir, says all the gods will seek the play of swords there, that the bridge Bilrost will break when they cross it, and that the steeds will have to swim in a flood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Fafnir says he wore a fear-helm to frighten mankind while he lay guarding his gold, and that he seemed mightier than any man.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sigurth responds that the fear-helm does not shield a man when he faces a valiant foe and that one often finds, when meeting an enemy, that he is not the bravest of all.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Fafnir says he breathed venom as he lay bright by the hoard his father had, that none was mighty enough to dare meet him, and that he feared neither weapons nor wiles.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sigurth calls Fafnir a glittering worm whose hissing was great and says that men have more hatred for the one who owns the fear-helm.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Fafnir advises Sigurth to heed his speech and ride home, warning that the sounding gold, glowing wealth, and rings will be Sigurth’s bane.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sigurth rejects Fafnir’s counsel, saying he will go to the gold hidden in the heather and telling Fafnir that he is fighting with death and will lie where Hel shall have him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Fafnir declares that Regin betrayed him and will also betray Sigurth, bringing both to death, and says that Sigurth was the mightier man.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"During Sigurth’s fight with Fafnir, Regin had gone some distance away and only returned after Fafnir was slain, while Sigurth was wiping blood from his sword.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Regin greets Sigurth, hails his victory over Fafnir, and calls him, in his opinion, the most fearless of all men on earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Sigurth replies that when all are together it is unknown who will seem the bravest, and notes that some men are valiant though they never redden a sword in an enemy’s blood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Regin says that Sigurth is glad of the battle gained as he cleans the sword Gram on the grass, that Sigurth has slain his fierce brother in fight, and that Regin himself did something to help.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Sigurth says that Regin went far away while he matched his strength with Fafnir and that Regin hid in the heather.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Regin replies that Sigurth would have let the hoary giant remain longer in the heather if the keen-edged weapon Regin forged had not proved effective.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Sigurth declares that a good heart is better than a mighty blade for one who must fight fiercely, that brave men are better than cowards in battle, and that a glad man is better than a gloomy one when facing what lies before him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Sigurth recalls that it was Regin’s advice that he ride over high mountains to fight the glittering worm, and says that Fafnir would still have his wealth and life if Regin had not mocked Sigurth’s might.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Regin goes up to Fafnir’s body, cuts out his heart with his sword Rithil, and drinks blood from Fafnir’s wounds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Regin tells Sigurth to sit while he sleeps and to hold Fafnir’s heart to the fire so that all of it will be eaten, saying that he has already drunk deeply of Fafnir’s blood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Sigurth takes Fafnir’s heart and cooks it on a spit over a fire until the blood foams out of the heart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"To test whether the heart is fully cooked, Sigurth touches it with his finger, burns himself, and then puts his finger in his mouth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"When Fafnir’s heart-blood touches Sigurth’s tongue, he understands the speech of birds and hears nut-hatches chattering in the thickets.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"One nut-hatch says that Sigurth sits sprinkled with blood cooking Fafnir’s heart over the fire, and that it would be wise for him, the ‘breaker of rings,’ to eat the bright life-muscles himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"A second nut-hatch says that Regin lies planning to betray the youth who trusts him, that he will speak lying words and use wiles, until he avenges his brother, the maker of mischief.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"A third nut-hatch says that Regin should go from there to Hel ‘less by a head,’ so that Sigurth alone can wield all the wealth that Fafnir guarded.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"A fourth nut-hatch, calling the birds sisters, urges that Sigurth would seem wise if he heeded their good counsel, mentions gladdening ravens with thought of killing, and says there is always a wolf where she sees its ears.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"A fifth nut-hatch says that Sigurth, the ‘tree of battle,’ would be less wise than she thought if he lets one brother go free when he has slain the other.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"The text notes that a sixth bird begins to speak, but its words are not given in this passage.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Human hero who slays Fafnir, debates about courage and weapons with Regin, cooks Fafnir’s heart, and gains the ability to understand bird speech after tasting the dragon’s heart-blood.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8","ev:10","ev:12","ev:14","ev:15","ev:19"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Fafnir","description":"Mighty, venom-breathing, glittering ‘worm’ who wore a fear-helm while lying bright by his father’s gold hoard, is slain by Sigurth, and in dying gives counsel about fate, gods, and Regin’s betrayal.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6","role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Regin","description":"Brother of Fafnir who forges Sigurth’s sword, gives him counsel to seek Fafnir, stays away during the fight, then returns to claim some credit, cuts out Fafnir’s heart, drinks his blood, and is said by Fafnir and the birds to be plotting to betray Sigurth.","role_refs":["role:3","role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8","ev:11","ev:13","ev:16","ev:17","ev:19"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Norns","description":"Supernatural beings associated with fate who are said to be of many different births and races, some kin to gods, some to elves, and some daughters of Dvalin, and who help in need and bring the babe from the mother.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"The gods","description":"Collective group ‘all the gods’ who are foretold to meet Surt in battle on the island Oskopnir, crossing the bridge Bilrost, which will break under them.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Elves","description":"Supernatural race to whom some of the Norns are said to be kin.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Dvalin","description":"Being named as the father of some Norns, whose daughters are among the fateful beings.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Dvalin’s daughters","description":"Daughters of Dvalin mentioned by Fafnir as among the Norns of diverse origins.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Surt","description":"Figure named as meeting all the gods in battle on the isle Oskopnir, where swords and sword-sweat will mingle.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Nut-hatch sisters (speaking birds)","description":"Group of nut-hatches whose speech Sigurth understands after tasting Fafnir’s heart-blood, who comment on his situation, urge him to eat the heart himself, and warn that Regin plans to betray him, advising that he kill Regin.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14","ev:15","ev:16","ev:17","ev:18","ev:19","ev:20"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Ravens","description":"Carrion birds mentioned by one deaths.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7","ev:17"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Dragon-slaying hero","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Sigurth matches his strength with serpent","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Fafnir is called a glittering ‘worm,’ breathes venom, lies by his father’s hoard, and wears a fear-helm to terrify men.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Traitorous brother and smith-mentor","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Fafnir calls Regin a betrayer of them both; Regin identifies Fafnir island Oskopnir to seek the play of swords with Surt.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"Fiery end-time adversary","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:9"],"basis":"Fafnir gives knowledge of intends to betray and kill him.","evidence_refs":["ev:14","ev:15","ev:16","ev:17","ev:18","ev:19"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"Underworld destination of the dead","assigned_to":["fig:13"],"basis":"The text states that every man must journey to Hel and that slain or condemned figures such as Fafnir and Regin are spoken of as going there.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7","ev:17"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"Carrion birds anticipating death","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"A bird speaks of gladdening ravens in connection with the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l3886-l3929","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"AFRSIYB MARCHES AGAINST NAUDER / AFRSIYB / GARSHSP / KAI-KOBD; lines 3886-3929","start":"3886","end":"3929","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"I yield the realm / Beyond the Jihn--let that river be / The boundary between us; but thy son, / Afrsiyb, must take his solemn oath / Never to cross that limit, or disturb / The Persian throne again.\"","summary":"Kai-kobd recalls earlier and recent fratricidal violence that has fueled conflict between Persia and Turan, including Tur's killing of his brother Iraj and Afrsiyab's invasion across the Jihun, murder of Nauder, and stabbing of his brother Aghriras. Declaring that he does not seek vengeance, he offers to cede the realm beyond the Jihun and to make the river the boundary between them, on condition that Afrsiyab swear never to cross it or attack the Persian throne again. A messenger carries these terms to Poshang, who accepts them and withdraws the Turanian army behind the agreed line. Rustem protests that peace is made at a moment favorable for war, but Kai-kobd values justice and tranquillity above continued fighting, concludes peace, and richly honors Rustem, Zal, and other warriors. Kai-kobd then rules from Istakhar and later Iran with benevolence and clemency, ensuring equal justice and preventing oppression while building towns and spreading prosperity over a hundred-year reign. As his death approaches, he appoints his eldest son Kai-Kaus as successor and solemnly instructs him to govern with integrity, justice, kindness, and mercy.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker reminds his interlocutor that the present war did not begin with him but began when Tur, the interlocutor's ancestor, slew his own brother Iraj.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker recounts that Afrsiyab, the interlocutor's son, crossed the Jihun river with a numerous force, invaded Persia, and caused Nauder's death by murder rather than in battle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker recalls that Afrsiyab later stabbed his brother Aghriras, who was deeply mourned by their father.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker declares that he does not thirst for vengeance or strife and offers to yield the realm beyond the Jihun river.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker proposes that the Jihun river be the boundary between the two sides and stipulates that Afrsiyab must take a solemn oath never to cross that limit or disturb the Persian throne again, in return for peace.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A messenger promptly conveys the king's peace terms to Poshang.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Upon receiving the message, Poshang withdraws the Turanian army within the agreed line of division.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rustem protests to the king against making peace at a time he considers most advantageous for war and when his victorious career has just begun.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Kai-kobd disagrees with Rustem, esteems justice and tranquillity above further warfare, and therefore concludes peace.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kai-kobd confers the highest honors on Rustem and Zal and generously rewards other warriors engaged in the conflict with his bounty and gratitude.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Kai-kobd moves toward Persia, establishes his throne at Istakhar, and administers his government with benevolence, clemency, and unceasing solicitude for the welfare of his subjects.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Under Kai-kobd's rule, every person is said to have an equal claim to consideration and justice, and the strong are described as lacking power to oppress the weak.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After ten years at Istakhar, Kai-kobd builds towns and cities, diffuses improvement and happiness over the land, and then removes his throne into Iran.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Kai-kobd's reign lasts one hundred years, characterized by continuous exercise of princely virtues and munificent liberality.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Kai-kobd has four sons named Kai-Kaus, Arish, Poshun, and Aramun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"As the time of his dissolution draws near, Kai-kobd appoints his eldest son as successor and solemnly enjoins him to pursue integrity and justice and to be kind and merciful in administering the empire.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Kai-kobd","description":"Persian king who proposes peace terms centered on the Jihun river, concludes the treaty, rewards his warriors, rules long with justice and benevolence from Istakhar and later Iran, and instructs his eldest son on just governance before his death.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Poshang","description":"Turanian king who receives the messenger's report of the peace offer, withdraws his army within the prescribed boundary, and is described as father of Afrsiyab and mourner of Aghriras.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Afrsiyab (Afrsiyb)","description":"Son of Poshang who crosses the Jihun with a numerous force to throne.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Tur (Tr)","description":"Ancestor of the Turanian king whose slaying of his own brother Iraj is cited as the He has a beloved son, Saimuk, while his only enemy is a hideous Demon whose fierce son resents the heavenly favor shown to the king and prince. Saimuk raises an army and fights the Demon's son but is killed, causing the royal army to retreat and Kaimers to grieve for a year. A mysterious voice then tells Kaimers to send another army for assured victory. Saimuk’s son Husheng, endowed with knowledge and goodness and especially loved by Kaimers, is made commander; under him, all beasts and birds obey, and with God’s blessing he kills the Demon and his son, while the army and animals destroy the enemy legions; after Kaimers’ death Husheng becomes king.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kaimers is said to be the first person to establish a code of laws and exercise the functions of a monarch in Persia.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Kaimers dwells among the mountains and wears garments made of the skins of beasts.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Kaimers reigns for thirty years and spreads the blessings of a paternal rule over the earth.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Wild animals are described as obedient to Kaimers’ will, assembling around his throne and doing him homage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Kaimers has a son named Saimuk, portrayed as handsome, brave in war, and the delight of his father who fears being parted from him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The narrative generalizes that parents dote on their offspring, using Kaimers’ love for Saimuk as an example.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kaimers has no enemy except a hideous Demon who envies his power and seeks his ruin; the Demon has a fierce and embittered son, while the favoring heavens smile on the monarch and his heir.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When Saimuk hears of the Demon's plan to overthrow him and his father, he is indignant, raises a martial force, and goes to war wearing a leopard-skin garment.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In battle, Saimuk and the Demon's son meet eagerly and exert their strength, but Saimuk falls lifeless from his enemy’s ‘dragon-grasp.’","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After Saimuk’s death, the army retreats and returns to Kaimers, who weeps bitterly and remains inconsolable for a long time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After a year, a mysterious voice addresses Kaimers, urging him to be patient and not despair, and instructs him to send another army against the Demons with the promise of triumph and rooted-out sorrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Saimuk leaves a son named Husheng, whom Kaimers loves even more than Saimuk and who is described as possessing eminent knowledge and goodness and inheriting his father’s dignity and station.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Kaimers appoints Husheng as leader of the army.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"During Husheng’s campaign, every species of animal, wild and tame, is said to be obedient to his command and to repose Sigurth declares that Regin will not live to tell of his death and that both Regin and Fafnir, as brothers, will soon die and go to Hel. Sigurth then cuts off Regin’s head, eats Fafnir’s heart, and drinks the blood of both Regin and Fafnir, after which he understands the words of a nuthatch. The bird tells him to bind the golden rings, to be fearless, and speaks of a beautiful, gold‑rich maid, the daughter of the king Gjuki, whom Sigurth may win as a bride. Another bird describes a high hall on the mountain Hindarfjoll, ringed with flames and made from flaming light of the flood, where a helmed battle‑maid lies asleep within a ring of fire. She has been struck with a thorn by Ygg as punishment for saving a warrior he wished to see slain, and the Norns have fixed the fate of her enchanted sleep and its connection with a hero’s son. Sigurth then follows Fafnir’s trail to his lair, an iron‑gated house dug into the earth, finds a great hoard of gold, fills two chests, and takes the fear‑helm, a golden mail‑coat, the sword Hrotti, and other treasures. He loads these on his horse Grani, who will not move until Sigurth mounts him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker says that a In the first, he travels rapidly, hunts a wild ass for food, sleeps in a forest wilderness, and his horse Rakush kills a lion that attacks; Rustem rebukes Rakush for fighting alone rather than warning him. In the second, Rustem and Rakush nearly die of thirst in a burning, waterless desert; Rustem prays to Heaven for protection and success in freeing Kai-ks and the Persian army from the demons, follows a sheep to a fountain of water, thanks God for his deliverance, kills a gor for food, and again instructs Rakush to warn him instead of battling lions or demons. In the third, a vast dragon-serpent repeatedly emerges at midnight to attack; Rakush wakes Rustem but the dragon vanishes into the darkness until providential light reveals it. Rustem and Rakush together slay the dragon, and Rustem attributes his survival from lions, demons, and the desert to the Back in Kabul, Mihrb’s wife Sndokht questions him about Zl and his stay with the Smrgh, and Mihrb praises Zl highly, including his unusual white hair. Listening, Rdbeh falls deeply in love with Zl, confides her feelings to her attendants, and persists despite their harsh objections to Zl’s non-human upbringing and appearance. Once her determination is clear, the attendants agree to help her and, in springtime, go to gather roses by a clear stream near Zl’s tent to attract his notice. Zl sees them, learns they come from the ‘moon of Kbulistn’ in Mihrb’s palace, shoots a bird that falls near them, and through his servant exchanges words with the damsels, who hint at the possibility of a union between Zl and Rdbeh. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l14293-l14373","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / REGINSMOL / THE BALLAD OF REGIN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 14293-14373","start":"14293","end":"14373","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"During a violent sea voyage, Sigurth and Regin encounter a mysterious man who gives several names for himself, including Hnikar and \"Man from the Mountain.\" After he boards their ship the storm subsides, and Sigurth asks him, as one who sees the fate of gods and men, about the best signs for battle. Hnikar lists favorable and unfavorable omens involving a black raven, two fighters, a howling wolf under an ash, seeing the enemy first, the setting of a celestial body, stumbling, battle formations, and personal preparation. Later Sigurth wins a great battle against Lyngvi son of Hunding and his brothers; Regin says a \"bloody eagle\" has been carved on the back of Sigmund's killer and praises the ferocity of that man's son. Sigurth returns to Hjalprek's house, where Regin urges him to fight Fafnir.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A violent storm at sea is described, with towering waves and wild waters where ships are metaphorically called Rvils steeds, sail-horses, sea-steeds, and roller-steeds, and someone is seen riding there.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Regin says that Sigurth and he are on the \"sea-trees\" (ships) in the stormy sea.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Regin states that the storm wind is driving them to their death, waves crash down on the forward deck, and the roller-steeds are sinking.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An unnamed man answers that he was once called Hnikar when Volsung gladdened the ravens and fought, and that he now can be called the Man from the Mountain, Feng, or Fjolnir, and he says he will travel with them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"They sail to land, the man comes on board the ship, and the storm subsides.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sigurth addresses the man as Hnikar, saying he sees the fate given to gods and men, and asks what sign is fairest for a fighter and best for the swinging of swords.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hnikar says that many signs are good for the swinging of swords and that it is favorable if a warrior meets a black raven on his road before battle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hnikar says another favorable sign is, when you are ready to go out, to see on the path before your house two fighters eager for fame.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hnikar says a third good sign is to hear a howling wolf under an ash tree and that fortune comes if you see your foe before the foe sees you.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hnikar advises that a man should not fight when he must face the \"moon’s bright sister\" setting late, and that the one who wins is he who can see well and arranges his men in a wedge-like formation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Hnikar says it is a foul sign if a warrior stumbles as She conceals his true parentage from Rustem, his father, even feigning that she bore a daughter. As Sohrab grows into an impressive athlete and warrior, he becomes increasingly troubled by his unknown lineage and demands that his mother reveal his father's identity, threatening her if she continues to conceal the truth. Tahmineh then discloses his illustrious ancestry, naming Sām, Zāl, and Rustem, and shows him Rustem's letter, jewels, and a protective bracelet charm sent from Persia. She warns him to keep his identity secret, fearing that Rustem's mortal enemy Afrasiab will strike at Sohrab, and that Rustem might one day claim his son, breaking her heart. Sohrab rejects caution, declaring that fate cannot be resisted; he vows to fight his father's foes, overthrow the Persian king Kai-Kaus, unite Turan under his own hand, and, together with Rustem, liberate mankind from tyranny, likening their combined glory to sun and moon outshining lesser stars. He insists on seeking his father and asks for a powerful and swift warhorse worthy of a prince. The stables are searched and ordinary horses prove inadequate until a destined steed, bred from Rakush, is found. Sohrab mounts it with ease and boasts that, with such a horse, Kai-Kaus will no longer reign. His fame spreads rapidly, thousands of warriors gather to his banner, and his grandfather generously supplies camels, horses, and gold. Armed in fine armor with a Grecian helmet, Sohrab stands as a formidable young leader. Afrasiab, hearing of this ambitious youth who has barely left infancy yet threatens war and destruction and has launched himself on a dangerous course away from his mother's protection, rejoices at the opportunity.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Tahmineh gives birth after nine months to a boy described as wondrous, whose presence Barz’s mother Shh-r, grieving over his imprisonment, travels to Iran and Sistan, enlists a singing-girl in Rustem’s service, and secretly sends Barz food containing a ring and later a file to cut his chains; with three swift horses prepared under the walls, Barz, his mother, and the singing-girl escape by night toward Turan. Rustem, hunting between Iran and Sistan, unexpectedly encounters the fugitives, fights them, and after they rest learns of Barz’s escape, which Barz attributes to the Almighty. Rustem then secretly attempts to poison Barz by sending him tainted food, but Barz’s mother warns him away from the dish; the loyal singing-girl eats some of the food and dies instantly, leading Barz The armies pause, then fight again, and the Persians are forced back to a mountain fortress at Hamwun, where Ts shelters the sick and wounded and withstands a siege thanks to wells of water and ample provisions. Informed of their situation, Khosru sends Rustem and Frburz, who are welcomed into the fort, and Rustem sits on a throne to deliberate with the Persian leaders. Prn-wsah writes to Afrsiyb claiming to have trapped the Persians and receives reinforcements: Shinkul of Sugsar, the Khakn of Chn, and Kms of Kushn, whose frown makes the air freezing and whose smile brings spring and flowers. Vast armies assemble; Rustem prays to the Creator and joins a ferocious battle described as darkened by dust and drenched in blood. He has four sons: Ardshr and Shydasp by the daughter of Kai-ks, and Gushtsp and Zarr by another woman. Gushtsp, described as intrepid and suited for sovereignty but disfavored by his father, rebels, gathers a large cavalry force, and marches toward Hindustan. Lohursp sends his brother Zarr with a smaller force to bring him back. Gushtsp laments that he and Zarr lack Kainian blood and have little claim to the throne compared to their half-brothers of Kai-ks’s line, and insists he will only return if named heir and treated with honor. Zarr persuades him to return, but Lohursp refuses to prefer Gushtsp over the other sons. Disgusted, Gushtsp flees alone toward Rum, and Zarr cannot find him. In Rum, Gushtsp lives in solitude until poverty forces him to seek employment: first as a scribe in the king’s establishment, then with the master of camel-drivers, who feeds him but has no work, and finally as a blacksmith’s assistant, where his first hammer blow breaks the anvil and he is angrily expelled. Broken-hearted, he leaves for other lands. He encounters a husbandman in a cornfield, who, seeing the strong youth in tears and hearing his story, pities him, brings him home, and feeds him. They discuss lineage: the husbandman claims descent from Feridn and membership in the Kainian tribe, while Gushtsp claims descent from Hsheng, ancestor of Feridn, showing a shared origin. His son Zohk possesses ten thousand horses. The Evil Spirit Iblis appears to Zohk in the guise of a virtuous man and wins his trust with eloquent speech. Demanding an oath of secrecy, Iblis then urges Zohk to kill his aged father and seize the throne, threatening him with death if he breaks the oath. Iblis secretly digs a pit on the path to Mirts’s house of prayer; Mirts falls in at night, is fatally injured, and dies, and Zohk usurps his pious father’s throne. Iblis continues to guide Zohk, promising him dominion over the seven climes. Gaining control of the royal kitchen, he introduces cooked meat dishes and eggs, which greatly please Zohk. In gratitude, Zohk vows to give Iblis whatever he desires. Iblis asks to kiss Zohk’s bare shoulder; when Zohk consents, Iblis kisses him and vanishes, and two black serpents spring from the shoulder. The serpents writhe as if seeking food; people search in vain for Iblis, and learned men and magicians cannot cure the affliction. Later Iblis returns disguised as a physician, claiming that the serpents are Zohk’s destiny and will remain with him for life. He advises that the only way to live with them is to feed them daily with human brains, which may eventually kill them. A pair of amorous ring-doves appear; an archery contest and wagers over shooting the birds become a coded exchange of marital intentions and display Jemshd's extraordinary prowess with a powerful bow. The princess, her nurse, and a previously cast horoscope all confirm that Jemshd is her destined spouse and that God will grant them a son who will conquer the world. A portrait of Jemshd is brought, and when he recognizes his own likeness he is overwhelmed by memories of his lost diadem and throne and weeps in anguish.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A richly adorned damsel moves with dignity and elegance, likened to a mountain partridge, with face.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The princess offers Jemshd more food because he has come a long journey, but he instead asks for more wine and remarks that
