doubles.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The picture of Jemshd is brought and found to resemble the stranger exactly; the princess gives it to Jemshd, who The nurse faithfully delivers the message. The youth, Byzun, rejoices and replies that he is not Saiwush but the son of Gw, who has come from Irn with the king's permission to exterminate a destructive herd of wild boars whose heads and tusks he has taken as trophies to send to Kai-Khosru so the king and warriors can appreciate his exploit. After hearing of Manjeh's beauty, he says, he forgot home and father and chose to follow his desire by coming to her. He offers the nurse gems and a gold coronet if she will introduce him to her mistress and expresses hope that Afrsiyb's daughter will hear his suit. The nurse relays the reply, and Manjeh eagerly consents, sending a message inviting the gallant youth to make her summer tent his home and declaring that she lives for him and that his love will protect her even under showers of arrows.

Byzun then proceeds secretly to the princess's tent. Manjeh embraces him, presses him to her bosom, removes his Kaini girdle so he may be comfortable, and asks him to recount his boar-hunting enterprise; he adds that, enraptured and impatient to see her charms, he left his companion Girgn behind. Manjeh has Byzun perfumed with musk and rose-water, serves him various refreshments, provides musicians and dark-eyed damsels to wait on him, and entertains him in a tent whose walls are lavishly adorned with amber, gold, and rubies, where old wine is drunk from crystal goblets. Their joyful feast lasts three nights and three days until Byzun, overcome by wine and happiness, falls asleep.

On the fourth day, when the time for departure arrives, the princess, unwilling to part from her lover, orders a narcotic draught to be administered to him. While he lies in a state of slumber and insensibility, he is secretly conveyed in disguise to Trn and even into the palace of Afrsiyb by Manjeh's emissaries and domestics, who alone know of his presence. He awakens from the trance in the palace, clasped in Manjeh's arms, suspects that he has been deceived by witchcraft, attempts to leave the seclusion, and fears a fatal outcome, but her blandishments persuade him to remain for a time, immersed in continual enjoyment of banquets and her attractions. Manjeh urges him not to grieve, saying there is a time for war and a time to soothe life's ills, and encourages him to drink the delightful ruby-colored wine instead of dwelling on care.

Eventually the princess's love for the Persian youth is discovered. The keepers and guards of the palace are terrified, expecting severe punishment for their negligence or treachery. Afrsiyb, the king and father of Manjeh, is seized with dreadful rage: he trembles like a reed, his color leaves his cheeks, and he groans as he declares that having a daughter is always a misfortune and that the grave is the best son-in-law. Isfendiyr plans an expedition to conquer the kingdom of Arjsp and free his captive sisters. He questions Kurugsar, a demon-guide who has sworn loyalty to the king after Isfendiyr interceded for his life, about the road to a brazen fortress. Kurugsar describes three routes: a safe three-month journey through pleasant lands; a less pleasant but still safe two-month road; and a seven-day route called the Heft-khan, where each stage contains deadly monsters and magical dangers. No king or army has dared to take this route. A poetic interlude elaborates on the horrors: wolves, dragons, and an enchantress with powerful spells. Despite repeated warnings, Isfendiyr, trusting in God and believing no man dies before his appointed time, resolves to take the Heft-khan. He entertains Kurugsar with wine, but even drunk the guide urges him to choose the safer road. When Kurugsar refuses to accompany him on the perilous path, Isfendiyr suspects his fidelity and has him bound in chains so he cannot flee. Isfendiyr justifies this as kindness, ensuring Kurugsar remains with him and is protected by the bonds. Finally, Isfendiyr receives his father Gushtsp's blessing, along with twelve thousand chosen horsemen and treasure, and sets out to subdue Arjsp's content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l19882-l19999","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ATLAMOL EN GRNLENZKU / THE GREENLAND BALLAD OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 19882-19999","start":"19882","end":"19999","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage consists of editorial notes to Bellows’s translation of *Atlamol en Gronlenzku* (“The Greenland Ballad of Atli”). The notes identify who is meant by certain terms in the poem (e.g., Atli, Gunnar, Hogni, Guthrun), explain that Atli plots and carries out the killing of his wife Guthrun’s brothers, which leads to his own death, and discuss the poem’s geography, including a sea and a fjord between Atli’s realm and that of the Gjukungs/Burgundians. The commentator describes Guthrun’s runic warning sent by messenger, Atli’s emissaries (including Vingi), and dialogues in which women (Kostbera and Glaumvor) relate ominous dreams that their men (Hogni and Gunnar) interpret in a matter-of-fact or optimistic way. Dream imagery includes an ice-bear, Atli’s spirit possibly in eagle form, ‘two roads’ as a sign of doubtful success, gallows, serpents, banners, bloody spears, and the phrase ‘Gods doom’ (ragna rok), which the editor notes is used unusually compared with its better-known sense in *Voluspo*. Several notes compare these elements to parallel material in other Eddic poems and the *Volsungasaga* and mention probable gaps or corruptions in the surviving text.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The word “men” in the poem refers to Atli and his advisers, who planned the death of Gjuki’s sons, Gunnar and Hogni.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poet introduces Atli abruptly without naming him and refers to Guthrun simply as “the woman” or “goddess of the house,” assuming the audience already knows the story.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The term “princes” refers to Atli, Gunnar, and Hogni, and Atli’s slaying of his wife’s brothers, who would have supported and defended him, is said to be the cause of his own death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In this version of the Atli story a sea separates Atli’s land from that of the Gjukungs, whereas the older Atlakvitha separates them only by a forest.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Guthrun sends a warning written in runes, and the note discusses two versions of this warning and the name of the messenger, here called Vingi, in connection with Drap Niflunga.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Limafjord mentioned in the poem is identified with the Limfjord of northern Jutland, and the commentator suggests the poet may have imagined the Burgundian kingdom as being located in Jutland or simply used the name for vividness.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kostbera (“The Giver of Food”) and Glaumvor (“The Merry”) are named women in the poem whom the commentator regards as likely creations of the poet.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Atli has two emissaries, one named Vingi and another unnamed in this passage, possibly called Knefrth, who are sent on his behalf.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"There is a dialogue between Kostbera and Hogni (covering several stanzas) in which Kostbera’s first dream is recounted; some lines may be missing but are not thought to alter the meaning significantly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kostbera’s warning dreams and Hogni’s matter-of-fact interpretations are explicitly compared with a similar sequence in Guthrunarkvitha II, stanzas 39–44.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A dream or image in stanza 17 includes an “ice-bear,” and the note observes that polar bears are common in Greenland but rarely found in Iceland and never in Norway, supporting the identification of Greenland as the home of the poem.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In stanza 18 the poem mentions “Atli’s spirit,” and the commentator suggests this is meant as a following-spirit (fylgja), though the word used is ‘hamr’ (“skin, shape”), which may imply that Atli has assumed the shape of an eagle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Grundtvig proposes an added line describing a figure whose feathers are black and covered with blood, connected with the scene of Atli’s spirit or eagle-form.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The phrase “two roads” in the corrupt passage of stanza 20 is interpreted by the commentator as probably meaning that the heroes’ way or success would be doubtful.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"There is a dialogue spanning stanzas 21–26 whose speakers are not named in the manuscript but are understood as a conversation involving Glaumvor and Gunnar about her dreams and his interpretations; some lines are thought to be lost.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Grundtvig suggests that Glaumvor dreamed of a gallows and of watching serpents, which Gunnar might interpret as gleaming banners and as wealth, respectively.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The poem uses the phrase “Gods doom” (ragna rok), which the commentator describes as an odd and apparently mistaken usage compared with its better-known meaning.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The concluding phrase of a line in stanza 23 may originally have been “bloody spears,” as in the Volsungasaga paraphrase, though the manuscript is uncertain.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Ruler who, with his advisers, plans the death of Gjuki’s sons Gunnar and Hogni; he is also counted among the princes and is later called “the king.”","role_refs":["role:1","role:3","role:4","role:7","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"Son of Gjuki, brother of Hogni and Guthrun, counted among the princes; he is invited by Atli, later killed by him, and interprets Glaumvor’s separated from Atli’s by either a forest or a sea in different versions of the story.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Vingi","description":"A messenger or emissary of Atli associated with carrying Guthrun’s runic warning; his name is discussed in relation to other versions of the story.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Unnamed emissary (possibly Knefrth)","description":"Second emissary of Atli mentioned alongside Vingi; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l9582-l9674","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU / AKWN DW; lines 9582-9674","start":"9582","end":"9674","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Kai-Khosru consoles a warrior (Gw) with a wondrous Cup that reveals everything hidden in the world and shows Byzun imprisoned in a cave with Manjeh sitting alone nearby. The king confirms his prophecy that Byzun lives and will be freed, then sends Gw to summon the champion Rustem. Rustem, who had intended to remain in peaceful retirement in Zabul, agrees to help because Byzun is his relative and prepares a covert mission: a caravan of a thousand camels laden with rich merchandise and a thousand warriors disguised as camel-drivers. Girgn is released from his bonds to join the party, while his children are held as hostages. When the caravan reaches the enemy territory near Byzun's prison, Manjeh comes to Rustem, asking if the Persian court knows of Byzun's captivity. Rustem, acting as a merchant, initially denies any knowledge and rebukes her, but after seeing her tears he gently asks the reason for her grief. Manjeh reveals that she is Afrasiyab's daughter, recounts her love for Byzun, her fall from royal status, and points out the pit where Byzun lies chained. She explains that she has been secretly feeding him bread and water through a fissure in the stone covering the pit. Rustem then hides his seal-ring inside a roasted fowl and sends it through Manjeh to Byzun. The captive hero discovers the ring bearing Rustem's name, learns that it came from the chief of the caravan, and smiles with joy. Manjeh, surprised by his joy, questions him. Byzun tells her he will explain if she keeps his secret, and she vows unwavering fidelity, recalling how she freely chose to be bound to him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The monarch tells a warrior that he will soon behold his son and that the Cup will bring dark things to light and quickly find what is lost.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The monarch holds up a bright Cup described as a mirror in which all things above and under ground, in ocean, stars, rock, or cavern, are clearly traced.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Cup is said to have first revealed concealed things to Jemshid.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Looking into the Cup, Kai-Khosru sees the extent of a province, including a dismal cave where Byzun sits bound on a demon-stone and Manjeh sits sad and alone.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Kai-Khosru smiles and tells Gw that his prophecy was true, that Byzun lives though bound in fetters, and will soon regain his liberty.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Kai-Khosru dispatches Gw to Rustem with an invitation, explaining the circumstances of Byzun's capture.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Rustem has resolved to live in peace and tranquillity in his Zabul principality and not to be drawn away by emergencies, but changes his purpose because of his near relative's distress and agrees to help free him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When asked what force he requires, Rustem says he does not need an army and prefers to go in disguise as a merchant.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A thousand camels are laden with jewels, brocades, and other merchandise, and a thousand warriors are dressed like camel-drivers to accompany Rustem.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Girgn prays to be released from his bonds and, through Rustem's intercession, is allowed to join the party, while his children remain in prison as hostages to guarantee his honorable conduct.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Rustem's caravan enters the enemy's territory near Byzun's prison, arousing loud clamor that an unprecedented caravan of merchandise from Iran has arrived.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Hearing of the caravan, Manjeh goes immediately to Rustem and asks whether Byzun's imprisonment is known at the Persian court.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Rustem, claiming to be a merchant, angrily replies that he is employed in traffic and knows nothing of such matters, denying acquaintance with the king or his warriors and sending Manjeh away.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Manjeh weeps bitterly at Rustem's reply, and her tears soften his heart so that he speaks soothingly and asks her to tell the cause of her grief.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Manjeh eventually tells Rustem that she is the daughter of Afrasiyab, recounts the story of her love and Byzun's misfortunes, and points out the pit where he is imprisoned and bound with heavy chains.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In verse, Manjeh laments that her love for Byzun has caused her fall from royal state, bower, and hall, leaving her pale and haggard, where a rosebud once bloomed but is now withered as she sits in unhelped solitude.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Rustem asks whether any food can be conveyed to Byzun, and Manjeh explains that she has been supplying him with bread and water through a fissure in the huge stone covering the mouth of the pit.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Rustem places his own seal-ring inside a roasted fowl and gives it to Manjeh to take to Byzun through the fissure.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Byzun receives the fowl, discovers the ring, asks who sent such a blessing, and is told it came from the chief of a caravan from Iran who showed great concern for him; he recognizes Rustem's name engraved on the ring and smiles with joy despite his captivity.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Manjeh is surprised to see Byzun smile in his melancholy situation; he tells her that if she will keep his secret he His followers gradually abandon him, and denied refuge anywhere, he hides alone in a cave. Nearby on a desert mountain lives Hm, a strong and brave man of Feridn's race, leading a religious, secluded life. One night Hm hears a Turkish lament from the cave, in which the speaker, calling himself king of Trn and Chn, mourns the loss of his power and wealth through Fortune. Recognizing Afrsiyb, Hm waits until dawn, then calls to him, claiming to have come from the invisible sphere to fulfill his desires. Afrsiyb, thinking it a spiritual summons, leaves the cave; Hm strikes him down, binds him, and confronts him with his past tyranny, including the sacrifice of many princes of Feridn's line. Hm explains that he has long prayed to God for Afrsiyb's ruin so he can return home, and that God has now delivered the king into his hands. Afrsiyb recounts his misfortunes and begs Hm to kill him immediately rather than take him to Kai-khosru, but Hm refuses and leads him to the Persian king. Kai-khosru exults on receiving Afrsiyb, rewards Hm, and recalls the basin and dagger used in the murder of Saiwush. He summons the treacherous Gerswaz so that he and Afrsiyb may share the same fate; the basin is brought, and both are beheaded like two goats. After this, Kai-khosru returns to Irn, while Rustem goes to his own principality. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l2689-l2810","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MINCHIHR / ZL, THE SON OF SM / THE DREAM OF SM / RDBEH; lines 2689-2810","start":"2689","end":"2810","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rudabeh’s attendants secretly arrange a nocturnal meeting between her and the warrior Zal at a secluded, richly decorated rural retreat. Rudabeh calls down to him from a balcony at dusk, then lets down her long hair for him to climb up into her chamber, where they admire each other and Zal vows, calling Heaven as witness, to be her affianced husband despite fearing his father Sam’s anger and King Minuchihr’s reproach. Afterwards Zal consults his counselors and Mobeds, praising marriage as a contract sealed by Heaven and revealing his love for Mihrab’s daughter, but they object because Mihrab is of the family of Zahhak the serpent-king and urge him to write to Sam. Sam consults astrologers, who predict that the union will be prosperous and produce a son of great strength who will conquer the world, so he secretly approves the marriage pending consultation with Minuchihr; Zal sends this good news to Rudabeh through a female emissary, who is discovered by Rudabeh’s mother Sindokht, arousing suspicion.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rudabeh’s attendants rejoice that their artifice has succeeded and say the lion has come into their toils, referring to Zal.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"There is a beautiful rural retreat in a sequestered situation, with apartments adorned with pictures of great men and splendid ornamentation.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Rudabeh retires to the rural retreat, dresses magnificently, and waits there for Zal.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rudabeh’s attendants invite Zal to the retreat after sunset, and he approaches as evening shadows fall.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"From her balcony Rudabeh addresses Zal, praising his lucid features that make the gloomy night clear as day and his perfume that scents the breeze.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hearing her sweet voice, Zal looks up, sees her bright face in the balcony, and replies that he had long hoped Heaven would display her charms in a secret place and now joyfully hears and sees her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Rudabeh’s hair is described as very luxuriant and long, so that when she casts it loose it flows down from the balcony.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rudabeh fastens the upper part of her hair to a ring, asks Zal to take hold of the other end and climb, and he kisses her tresses and ascends by them into the balcony.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Inside the chambers, the walls are embellished by a painter’s skill and decorated with sculpture and architectural ornament fit for a king.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Zal gazes with amazement at the artistic decorations but even more at Rudabeh’s beauty, including her tulip-like cheeks, musky locks, and glittering jewelry.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Zal’s appearance is majestic; he wears a ruby crown and a belted dagger near his breast.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rudabeh watches Zal with side-long glances, noting his noble aspect, fine proportions, strength, and beauty, and her enamoured heart causes her to blush and feel increasing transports.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Zal is compared to a gentle lion toying with his adventure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Zal calls the encounter a waking dream of rapture and vows, calling High Heaven as witness, that whoever may oppose his sacred vows he is Rudabeh’s, affianced to her for ever.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Rudabeh replies that Zal has won her heart, that kings may sue in vain, balcony, and hastens back to his tent.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Zal assembles his counselors and Mobeds as quickly as possible to seek their advice about sealed by Heaven and describes the warrior’s happiness among smiling children, whose sons succeed him and bear his rank, name, and renown.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Zal relates to his counselors his love and affection for the daughter of Mihrab.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The Mobeds know that Mihrab, chief of Kabul, is of the family of Zahhak, the serpent-king, and they do not approve the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l4804-l4910","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS; lines 4804-4910","start":"4804","end":"4910","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Kai-Kaus (Ks) and his heroes are freed from a mountain fortress and restored to power by Rustem, who reseats the king on his throne. The armies of several regions submit, swelling the Persian forces. Ks sends Afrasiyab a warning to withdraw from Iran and remember Rustem’s past victory over him. Afrasiyab angrily prepares for battle and promises his daughter and a kingdom to whoever captures Rustem alive, but in the ensuing battle those who seek the reward die first. Afrasiyab himself is beaten back by Rustem and flees in anguish to Turan, leaving Ks in possession of the kingdom. Ks governs again with justice and liberality, dispatches warriors to secure various provinces, and grants Rustem the title \"Champion of the World.\" At peace, Ks orders Demons to build lavish palaces and mansions on Mount Alberz, ornamented with gold, silver, and precious stones. Seeing the king’s vanity, Iblis persuades the Demons to help tempt him. One Demon, disguised as a servant, presents Ks with a nosegay and flatters him as lord of all beings, but points out that he cannot fly or know the motions of the heavens and the causes of cosmic order. This convinces Ks of his limitations and he becomes obsessed with ascending to the heavens without wings. His astrologers propose a device: they steal young eagles, rear them, and construct a wooden frame with javelins at its corners, each tipped with goat flesh, to which four eagles are tied. Ks sits in the center with a goblet of wine. When the hungry eagles strive for the meat, their upward flight lifts the frame into the sky and far beyond his land, but eventually their strength fails and the whole structure crashes down in a desolate region of Chin. Ks is left alone, hungry and despairing, until discovered by Demons sent by his anxious ministers to find him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ks and his illustrious heroes are released from their fetters and removed from a mountain-fortress where they had been confined; Rustem reseats Ks on his throne and gathers the valuables of three states that had submitted to Ks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Troops from Misser, Berberistn, and Hmvern declare allegiance to Ks, increasing his army to over three hundred thousand men; before marching toward Irn he sends a message to Afrsiyb commanding him to quit the invaded country and be content with Trn, reminding him of Rustem’s earlier victory over him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Afrsiyb receives Ks’s message with resentment, prepares his army for battle, and promises to give his daughter in marriage and a kingdom to whoever can take Rustem alive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When battle occurs, those who seek Afrsiyb’s offered reward are the first The chiefs, warriors, and people are distressed, fearing that an evil influence has turned him from worldly joys, and they appeal to Zāl and Rustem to restore him. When Zāl and Rustem visit, the king explains that he is weary of worldly deceit, loves heaven, and has heard a mysterious, possibly angelic voice in the night telling him that his time of departure is near and that he must prepare for his journey. Zāl initially calls death dreadful but then offers to retire with the king in prayer, while the king insists on seeking a solitary cell to resign his soul to heaven. The next day Kai-khosru publicly renounces the pageantry of the Kayanian throne, declares he has obtained what he sought, and vows to discharge his obligations to his faithful friends. He pitches tents in the desert, opens his treasury, holds a seven-day feast, and distributes food and money so that no indigent, widow, orphan, or destitute person remains in want. He rewards Rustem with lands and appoints Lohursp, his son-in-law, as successor, ordering the people and Friburz (son of a previous king) to obey him. The warriors murmur at the prince being placed under Lohursp, but Zāl and Kai-khosru justify Lohursp's rule by his enlightenment, mercy, and descent from the ancient king Husheng, and the warriors accept him. Kai-khosru then relates a dream of a fountain where, when he visits it, he will surrender his life to its Creator. He bids farewell, begins a journey toward this destiny, traveling by stages and pitching tents; he parts from Zāl and Rustem, who weep bitterly. The warriors lament that a man so great and brave seeks the tomb before his time, and the wise marvel that no mortal has taken the \"dim supernal way\" or, while living, seen the face of God.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kai-khosru becomes strongly attached to religious life, abandons the duties of sovereignty, and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l10107-l10213","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAI-KHOSRU / AKWN DW / BARZ, AND HIS CONFLICT WITH RUSTEM / SSEN AND AFRSIYB; lines 10107-10213","start":"10107","end":"10213","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After Afrsiyb returns defeated to Turan and laments the loss of Barz, a sorceress named Ssen offers to destroy Rustem and his family through magic instead of weapons. Afrsiyb supplies her with a warrior, Plsam, treasure, and attendants, and they travel toward Sistan, occupying a fort and establishing a lavish house of entertainment that hospitably feeds all travellers. Meanwhile Rustem holds a grand feast for heroes, including Ts (Tus), the king’s deputy, and Gdarz, whose long-standing hostility leads to a quarrel over noble ancestry; Ts boasts of descent from Nauder and Feridn and belittles Gdarz as the son of Kavah the blacksmith. Ts attempts violence but is restrained by Rehm, then angrily departs for Iran. Rustem, hearing of this, insists that a guest must be protected and treated as sacred as a king, and sends in succession Gdarz, Gw, Byzun, Fermurz, and finally Zl to reconcile Ts and bring him back. On his journey, Ts arrives at Ssen’s residence, sees many cooks preparing rich food for travellers, and enters to meet a strikingly beautiful woman. She tells him she is a singing-girl and widow of a wealthy Turanian merchant, persecuted by Afrsiyb, and that she has fled seeking refuge in Persia, professing a desire to serve Kai-Khosru, a true and gentle king.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Afrsiyb returns defeated to Turan and laments the misfortune which has deprived him of the assistance of Barz.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A woman named Ssen, deeply versed in magic and sorcery, comes to Afrsiyb and promises by her art to enable him to destroy Rustem and his whole family.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ssen declares that fighting brings disappointment, that weapons like sword and mace are useless, and that spells and charms will cause the mighty chief Rustem to bleed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Afrsiyb initially refuses to use Ssen’s power but, after she demonstrates her skill, consents to her proposal.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ssen requests that a distinguished warrior be sent with her, furnished with treasure, honorary tokens, and presents, so that no one will suspect her true employment.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Afrsiyb appoints Plsam as the warrior, supplies him, and sends him with Ssen on a journey toward Sistan, with people stationed along the road to hasten news of their success back to the king.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ssen and Plsam arrive at a fort, take possession of a commodious residence, deposit the wealth they brought there, and establish a house of entertainment where all travellers are hospitably and sumptuously fed with sparkling wine, rare viands, and mellow fruit.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rustem invites a large company of the most celebrated heroes of the kingdom to a magnificent feast at his palace in Sistan.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Among the guests is Ts, who has been deputed by the king to Rustem on important state affairs.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gdarz is also present at the feast, and due to habitual hostility between him and Ts, a dispute arises.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ts boasts that he is the son of Nauder and grandson of Feridn, and insults Gdarz by saying he is merely the son of Kavah the blacksmith, questioning why Gdarz puts himself on an equal footing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Gdarz replies with reproaches, accusing Ts of ignorance and folly, which further inflames Ts’s anger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ts becomes so enraged that he draws his dagger intending to punish Gdarz, but Rehm rises and prevents the intended bloodshed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ts, in serious displeasure, leaves the banquet and sets off on his return journey to Iran.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Rustem, who was not present at the altercation, becomes angry when he hears of it, stating that Gdarz is a relation of the family and Ts his guest, and that wrong has been done because a guest ought always to be protected.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Rustem declares that a guest should be held as sacred as the king, that heroes customarily treat guests with scrupulous respect, and that “a guest is the king of the feast.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Rustem asks Gdarz to follow Ts and, with fair words and proper excuses, persuade him to return to the feast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"After Gdarz departs, Gw says that Ts is almost mad and his own father is hasty, so he wishes to follow in order to prevent learns that the place is said to be occupied by the wife of a very wealthy merchant from Turan who sumptuously entertains every traveller passing that way.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Hungry and curious, Ts dismounts, leaves his horse with his attendants, and enters the principal apartment of the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l12968-l13018","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR / CAPTURE OF THE BRAZEN FORTRESS; lines 12968-13018","start":"12968","end":"13018","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this episode, the magical creature Smrgh turns to the grievously wounded champion Rustem, soothes him, removes the arrows from his body, sucks out the blood, and causes the wounds to close, restoring him to life and strength. Rustem asks for further help against the hero-prince Isfendiyr, but Smrgh laments that Isfendiyr is uniquely brave and perfect, favored by Heaven, and once slew a Smrgh during his Heft-khan trials; she warns that Rustem is safest at a distance from him. Zal intervenes, arguing that if Rustem retreats, his entire family will be enslaved and he will share their suffering. Hearing this, Smrgh thinks deeply, then instructs Rustem to mount his horse Rakush and follow her on a long journey, crossing a great river to a reed-covered place where the Kaz-tree grows abundantly. There she rubs one of her feathers on Rustem’s eyes and tells him to take a branch of the Kaz-tree, straighten it over a fire, fashion it into a forked arrow, and shoot it into Isfendiyr’s eyes. She predicts the arrow will only blind Isfendiyr, but warns that whoever spills his blood will suffer lifelong calamity; she adds that arrows made from the Kaz-tree never miss their intended target. Rustem gratefully accepts the guidance. Smrgh transports him back to his tent, affectionately kisses his face, and departs. Rustem prepares the arrow as instructed and, at dawn, rides to the battlefield. He finds Isfendiyr still sleeping and calls out for him to rise and face Rustem. Startled, Isfendiyr arms himself and tells Bashtan that he had thought Rustem would die of his wounds, but Rustem’s strong voice suggests full health; he sends Bashtan to inspect Rustem’s condition and his horse. Seeing Bashtan approach, Rustem declares loudly that he and Rakush are free from wounds thanks to an elixir that instantly heals severe flesh wounds, claiming that Isfendiyr’s arrows were like mere needles. Bashtan reports that Rustem looks fresher and stronger than before and, fearing Rustem’s likely victory in another combat, strongly advises Isfendiyr to seek reconciliation.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Smrgh turns to Rustem, soothes his grief, removes the arrows from his wounds, sucks out the blood, and the wounds close at her bidding, restoring Rustem to life and power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rustem is said to be reinvigorated by the magic Rewarded with honors, Gushtsp reveals his ambition to rule Irn and persuades the king of Rm to threaten Lohursp with war unless he yields half his kingdom. When Lohursp receives the letter, he laughs at the foreign king’s pride and asks how Khuz was taken. The messenger Kabs reports that a noble, invincible youth slew a wolf and a dragon and then overthrew Als; his name is Gushtsp and he resembles Zarr in Lohursp’s court, leading Lohursp to conclude the champion is his own son. Outwardly, Lohursp sends a defiant reply to Rm, but privately he instructs Zarr to go as ambassador, urge peace, and then ask Gushtsp’s forgiveness, inviting him to return home so Lohursp may, like Kai-khosru, withdraw from the world, devote himself to prayer, and make Gushtsp his successor. Zarr does as commanded, meets first the king of Rm and then Gushtsp, and conveys Lohursp’s repentance and promise of succession. Delighted and eager to return, Gushtsp sets out that very night with his wife Kitabn and Zarr for Irn. Near the city they are greeted by an honorary warrior delegation from the king. At court, Lohursp descends from his throne, embraces Gushtsp with tears of contrition, has a golden royal chair placed beside his own, and the people pledge allegiance to Gushtsp. Lohursp repeatedly declares that events were decreed by Fate and destined to end in Gushtsp’s sovereignty, then kisses the crown and gives it to his His daughter Kitabun, now of age, finds none of the invited youths suitable. She has repeated dreams of a youth from Iran to whom she is destined to be married, in which they exchange roses. She then proclaims that all royal youths, natives or strangers, should attend her father’s feast. Gushtasp, living in humble circumstances with a husbandman, comes to the city and attends the feast. Kitabun’s handmaid delays each youth at the door so her mistress can look upon him; Kitabun recognizes Gushtasp as the man from her dream and publicly chooses him by descending and giving him a bunch of roses. The king is enraged, thinking she has chosen a beggar or nameless stranger, and initially wants to kill her, but his people counsel him that fate governs all things and love cannot be restrained. The king orders inquiries into Gushtasp’s lineage and present condition, initially disbelieving the noble ancestry reported, but after hearing of his daughter’s dream, he grudgingly allows the marriage while driving the couple from his house without dowry or money. Gushtasp and Kitabun take refuge in a miserable cell. To support them, Gushtasp regularly crosses a river, hunts elk or wild ass in the forest, gives half of the animal to the ferryman for passage, and keeps half for food, so he and the ferryman become close through mutual benefit. A nobleman named Mabrin seeks the king’s second daughter, and another of rank, Ahrun, wants the third, but the king does not wish to part with them. After persistent entreaty, the king agrees to let Mabrin marry the second daughter if he can kill a monstrous wolf in the nearby forest that has long ravaged the king’s property and survived previous hunts. Mabrin sees this as an impossible condition. Hearing of his plight, the ferryman tells Mabrin about the remarkable strength of Gushtasp, the young man married to one of the king’s daughters who daily crosses the river carrying an elk on his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l11221-l11323","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF AFRSIYB / THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT; lines 11221-11323","start":"11221","end":"11323","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An invading force devastates the land with fire, uprooting trees and spreading unnatural gloom as King Gushtsp hastens to oppose them. Zerdusht tells Gushtsp to consult his vizir Jamsp about his horoscope; Jamsp foretells that many of Gushtsp's brothers, relations, and warriors will die, though he will ultimately win. Gushtsp laments but proceeds to battle. After prayers to Heaven, a fierce conflict ensues. Ardshr, son of Lohursp and descendant of Kai-ks, and his brother Shydasp are killed after fighting bravely. Bish, son of the vizir Jamsp, and the young prince Zarr perform great feats; Zarr cuts down demons and men and penetrates the enemy headquarters, alarming King Arjsp, who offers a rich reward to whoever kills him. The demon Bai-derafsh takes the offer and slays Zarr. Grief-stricken, Gushtsp calls for vengeance. His son Isfendiyr kisses the ground before him, asks to engage the demon, and is promised the crown and throne if he succeeds. Gushtsp gives Isfendiyr his famous black horse Behzd, a gift from Kai-khosru. As the Persian army despairs, Isfendiyr charges on Behzd, confronts Bai-derafsh wearing Zarr's mail, seizes the demon's dagger blow, kills him with a spear, and cuts off his head. He entrusts the severed head and Zarr's armor to Bish. Bish arms himself in his father's mail, fastens the demon's head to his horse, and, joined by the warrior Firshaid, advances with Isfendiyr to attack Arjsp. Arjsp retreats, his troops throw down their arms and ask for quarter, and many are taken prisoner. Gushtsp laments over Zarr's body, places him in a coffin, builds a lofty monument over him, and keeps lights burning around it day and night. He teaches the people fire worship and seeks to establish the religion of Zerdusht. Jamsp's officers count the dead: 30,000 Irnians, including 800 chiefs, and 900,000 enemies, including 1,163 chiefs. Gushtsp rejoices in the victory, orders drums sounded, increases his favor toward Zerdusht, and summons Isfendiyr. Isfendiyr appears in the royal court, holding a cow-headed mace, his manner expressing command and military pride. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l11737-l11850","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR; lines 11737-11850","start":"11737","end":"11850","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage narrates the first three stages of Isfendiyr’s journey. He travels with his bound demon-guide Kurugsar, his brother Bashtan, and warriors to the edge of the kingdom and into a desert wilderness. In the first stage they defeat two gigantic wolves near a forest and stream, and Isfendiyr credits Heaven’s favor for the victory. In the second stage he insists on fighting both a lion and a lioness himself to protect Bashtan, again triumphing and feasting afterward. Kurugsar then describes an enormous, poisonous dragon, prompting Isfendiyr to design a wheeled, weaponized apparatus drawn by horses. In the third stage he rides inside this machine toward the dragon despite his companions’ fears; the dragon tries to swallow the horses and car, but the device’s blades wound its jaws and lodge in its throat, causing convulsions and a flood of poison.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Isfendiyr travels with Kurugsar bound among his retinue, accompanied by his brother Bashtan and warriors, toward the uttermost limits of the kingdom and into a desert wilderness.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Kurugsar, though placed in bonds, acts as a guide and directs the party from time to time along their route.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Kurugsar warns that two monstrous wolves, as large as elephants with immense teeth, inhabit the region they are entering.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Isfendiyr instructs his people that when they see the wolves they must attack them immediately with arrows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"As day ends, the party reaches a forest and a murmuring stream, where the wolves appear.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Two enormous wolves suddenly rush toward the legions of Isfendiyr.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The warriors pour a shower of arrows onto the wolves, wounding them and exhausting them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Bashtan attacks one wolf and Isfendiyr the other, and their vigorous charge kills both monsters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After the wolves are killed, Isfendiyr declares that through the favor of Heaven the first obstacle has been easily extinguished.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kurugsar is amazed at the bravery and valor displayed by Isfendiyr.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Following the first stage, the warriors and party dismount, feast, drink wine, and rest until the next morning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"On the second stage, Isfendiyr asks what will oppose them next, and Kurugsar replies that the stage is infested by lions.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Isfendiyr responds that Kurugsar will see with what ease he can destroy the lions.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Near the close of the day, the party encounters a lion and a lioness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Bashtan suggests that Isfendiyr take one animal and he will engage the other, but Isfendiyr refuses and prefers to attack both himself so that his brother is not exposed to harm.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Isfendiyr first sallies forth against the lion and kills it with content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l4458-l4575","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GARSHSP / KAI-KOBD / KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM; lines 4458-4575","start":"4458","end":"4575","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rustem descends to a gloomy cavern at Mazindern and confronts the monstrous, mountain-like White Demon. After a brutal combat aided by Heaven, he kills the demon, tears out its heart, and later uses the heart’s blood to miraculously restore the sight of his blinded king Kai-ks and the warriors. The Persians then burn the enemy city and slaughter its magicians, while a proud refusal by the king of Mazindern to submit prompts Rustem to prepare a more forceful diplomatic challenge.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem advances to a cavern described as a gloomy place, \"dismal as hell,\" and at first sees no cursed, impious sorcerer in its depth.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Within the cavern Rustem perceives a monster with a \"mountain-form, covered with hair\" that fills all the space and is initially asleep.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Awakened by Rustem’s shouts, the monster seizes a huge millstone, comes forth, and accosts Rustem, warning him about invading the precincts of the demons and demanding his name before destroying him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem identifies himself as Rustem, sent by his father Zl, descended from the champion Sm Swr, and declares his purpose of avenging himself on the demon because the King of Persia is now a prisoner in Mazindern.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"On hearing the name Sm Swr, the demon writhes in agony \"like a serpent,\" then recovers strength and hurls the huge millstone at Rustem, who falls back and avoids the blow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem overcomes his alarm, attacks with his sword, pierces the demon’s thigh, cuts off the limb, and they grapple so fiercely that the cavern shakes, both are wounded, and their blood streams onto the earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"During the struggle Rustem thinks inwardly that if he survives the day his life must be immortal, while the White Demon inwardly despairs of life and of ever being welcomed again at Mazindern.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rustem gathers fresh power described as \"vouchsafed by favouring Heaven,\" lifts the gasping demon in his arms, dashes him to the ground so that he dies, and then promptly tears out the demon’s reeking heart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When Rustem tears out the White Demon’s heart, crowds of demons simultaneously fall as part of him and stain the earth with gore, while other demons tremble and flee from the scene of blood.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After leaving the cave, Rustem hastily removes his helmet, mail, and royal girdle, washes his face and body with water, chooses a pure place, and prays to praise his Maker as the giver of victory and the source of impregnable armor through divine grace.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"When his prayer is finished, Rustem resumes his war gear, goes to Ald, releases him from the tree where he was bound, and entrusts him with the heart of the White Demon as they set out back toward Kai-ks at Mazindern.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"On the journey Ald asks Rustem for a reward for his services, and Rustem again promises that Ald will be made governor of the country, adding that first the monarch of Mazindern, the Demon-king, must be subdued and cast into the yawning cavern and his legions of foul enchanters utterly destroyed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Upon returning to Mazindern, Rustem tells his sovereign what he has accomplished, especially that he has torn out and brought back the White Demon’s heart, whose blood is destined to restore Kai-ks and his warriors to sight; he applies this remedy, and as soon as the blood touches their eyes, their fearful blindness is completely cured.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Verses describe Rustem squeezing the blood from every part of the demon’s heart, dropping it onto the injured eyes so that everything becomes visible and bright and a \"magic gloom\" more dreadful than the tomb is dispelled in a moment.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After his sight is restored, the monarch ascends his throne surrounded by all his warriors, and they spend seven days in mutual congratulations and rejoicing; on the eighth day they mount again to complete the destruction of the enemy, burning the city to the ground and slaughtering the remaining magicians until streams of loathsome blood crimson the place.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Ks later sends Ferhd as an ambassador to the king of Mazindern, advising him to submit and citing the terrible fall of Arzang and of the White Demon with all his host as a warning against resisting Rustem’s valor.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The king of Mazindern responds with astonishment and pride, asserting that he surpasses Ks in all respects, has a larger empire and more numerous and brave warriors, possesses a hundred war-elephants while Ks has none, and therefore sees no reason to fear or submit to the sovereign of Persia.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ferhd is deeply impressed by the king’s haughty tone and quickly returns to tell Ks; Rustem, angered so that every hair on his body stands up like a spear, offers to go himself with a second, more urgent dispatch threatening to hang the enemy’s severed head on the walls of his own fort if he persists in refusing submission.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"The Persian champion, son of Zl and descendant of the champion Sm Swr, the king’s and warriors’ blindness, joins in burning the enemy city and slaughtering magicians, and volunteers to carry a second threatening dispatch to the king of His brother Bashtan and the troops revive him with rose-water and remedies; he bathes to purify himself from the monster's filth and prays in thanks to the merciful Creator, while his demon-guide Kurugsar secretly laments that the hero survived, since he must continue to accompany him through further arduous enterprises. Kurugsar then foretells that the next day Isfendiyr will meet an enchantress who can turn sea into dry land and land into ocean, attended by a gigantic ghoul, and Isfendiyr confidently predicts their defeat.

On the fourth day, the party travels on their destined journey and rests in a pleasant meadow by a clear rivulet, eating food and drinking wine. A beautiful, elegantly dressed enchantress appears with a sad, alluring expression, claiming to be the unhappy daughter of a distant king, seduced from her home by a monster, and begging Isfendiyr to free her and take her as his beloved. Isfendiyr invites her to sit, but seeing through her stratagems, he casts a lasso (kamund) over her and binds her despite her pleas. In extremity she transforms successively into a cat, a wolf, and a decrepit old man, but Isfendiyr detects her in each guise and finally cuts her into pieces.

A dark cloud of dust and vapor rises and then a black demon apparition with flames issuing from its mouth appears. Isfendiyr attacks; the flames burn his cloth armor and garments, yet he succeeds in cutting off the demon's head. He tells Kurugsar that, with Heaven's favor, the enchantress and ghoul as well as the wolves, lions, and dragon have been destroyed. Kurugsar acknowledges the prodigious labor but warns that tomorrow Isfendiyr will face the Smrgh (Simurgh), whose nest is on a lofty mountain and who has two gigantic young ones, each the size of an elephant, carried in her beak and claws. Isfendiyr replies that God will make the labor easy.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A dreadful dragon disgorges a wain, steeds, swords, and javelins before or during its combat with Isfendiyr.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Isfendiyr, described as a warrior-knight, leaps from his place of ambush, brandishes his blade, and splits the dragon's head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Venom issuing from the dragon's head is so overpowering that Isfendiyr is deprived of sense and falls staggering to the ground.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Bashtan and the troops, alarmed at Isfendiyr's condition, sprinkle rose-water on his face and administer other remedies to counteract the venom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After some time Isfendiyr recovers, bathes to purify victory.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Kurugsar grieves that Isfendiyr survived because Kurugsar will now have to accompany him through the remaining arduous loved and blessed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Isfendiyr calls the enchantress to him and asks her to sit down, which she does readily, expecting success from {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l3192-l3288","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DREAM OF SM / RDBEH / DEATH OF MINCHIHR / NAUDER; lines 3192-3288","start":"3192","end":"3288","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""...he who has a just estimate of the world, will never look upon it as his place of rest. It is but an inn, where all travellers meet on their way to eternity, but must not remain."

"...Death comes, and hurls the monarch from his throne,
His crown and sceptre scattering in the dust."

"The name
Of Feridn is honoured among men,
Whilst curses load the memory of Zohk."","summary":"After Minchihr's death, his son Nauder ascends the throne but quickly becomes a despotic and oppressive ruler, prompting widespread dissatisfaction among the people and anxiety among the courtiers. Anticipating revolt and invasion, Nauder summons the champion Sm from Mzindern. Sm has already heard the people's complaints; when he arrives, the people urge him to take the throne, but he refuses out of loyalty to Minchihr and fear of offending God. Acting as mediator, he counsels Nauder, delivering a speech that depicts the world as a temporary inn before eternity, stresses the suddenness of death, warns against attachment to earthly pomp, and contrasts the honored memory of the just king Feridn with the cursed memory of Zohk. This intercession leads Nauder to reform and promise to rule according to the principles of Hsheng, Feridn, and Minchihr, reconciling the chiefs and reuniting the kingdom. Meanwhile, in Trn, the ruler Poshang hears of Minchihr's death, Nauder's injustice, and the unrest in Persia. Seeing an opportunity to avenge the blood of Slim and Tr, he calls his heroic son Afrsiyb, praised in extravagant metaphors, to lead an army against Nauder. Afrsiyb's brother Aghrras urges caution, citing the continued presence of great Persian warriors Sm, Krun, and Garshsp, but Poshang insists that vengeance for ancestral blood is a grandson's duty and presses on with preparations for war.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the demise of Minchihr, Nauder ascends the throne and, within a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1514-l1602","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1514-1602","start":"1514","end":"1602","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"King Zohk has a terrifying dream in which three warriors attack him and the youngest strikes his head, binds him, and drags him before a crowd. His court wise men reluctantly interpret the dream as foretelling the end of his life and the future rule of Feridn, an as-yet-unborn son of Abtn whose father Zohk will kill. Zohk orders the seizure of Abtn’s kin; Abtn, long in hiding, is discovered and executed, and his wife Farnuk flees with their two‑month‑old son Feridn. Reaching a pasture, she feeds the child with milk from a charitable cow, Pur’mieh, then leaves him in the care of the pasture keeper and goes to the mountain Alberz. The keeper raises Feridn for three years, after which Farnuk secretly returns, reclaims her son, and—claiming divine inspiration—takes him toward the mountain. Zohk later discovers the pasture, kills the keeper, his tribe, and the cow, but does not find Feridn. King Minchihr, fearing political and moral chaos from an alliance with Zahhak’s line, consults the veteran champion Sam. Sam returns from campaigns in Karugsar and Mazanderan, recounting how he slew a monarch of Zahhak’s descent and routed a vast demon army. Pleased yet still vengeful, Minchihr orders Sam to destroy Kabul by fire and sword, especially Mihrab’s serpent-race house; Sam protests in vain. Alarm spreads in Kabul. He appoints Mihrab and Gustahem over the wings, Qaran (Krun) and Kishwad over the center, with Rustem in front and Zal and the king in the rear, under the standard of Kavah. Afrasiyab musters his Turanian forces with heroes such as Akbas, Wisah, Shimass, and Gersiwaz, and the two armies clash amid tremendous noise and confusion. Qaran kills Shimass in combat. Rustem asks Zal to point out Afrasiyab so he can fight him; Zal warns him of Afrasiyab’s terrible power, described with images of black armor and a steel mountain melting at his name. Rustem confidently declares that his heart, arm, and dagger are his castle and that Heaven aids him, claiming he can defeat dragon or demon. He charges on his horse Rakhsh toward the Turanian army. Afrasiyab learns that this is Rustem, son of Zal, bearing Sam’s battle-axe and seeking renown. In their encounter Rustem seizes Afrasiyab’s girdle, throws him from the saddle, and tries to drag him captive to Kai-Kobad so that his first great victory will be remembered, but the girdle breaks. Afrasiyab’s warriors rescue him, while Rustem carries off his crown and the broken girdle. A general battle follows in which Rustem, wielding a cow-headed mace and his sword, slaughters and captures many enemies, killing more than a thousand. The Turanians retreat in disarray toward the Jihun river, leaving the Persian “fire-worshippers” in possession of the field. The Persians return with prisoners, and Rustem is honored by Kai-Kobad. Afrasiyab reports the defeat to his father Poshang, marveling at Rustem’s strength and concluding that only peace can save their country. Poshang, noting their losses, sends Wisah with rich presents and a message to Kai-Kobad, recounting the chain of ancestral vengeance (Manuchehr avenging Iraj on Tur and Salm, Afrasiyab avenging them on Nauder) and proposing peace: both sides should accept what Feridun decreed, keeping to the empire allotted to Iraj and treating the Jihun as the boundary, since they are of one blood and should content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l4056-l4155","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"AFRSIYB / GARSHSP / KAI-KOBD / KAI-KS; lines 4056-4155","start":"4056","end":"4155","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Gw, a warrior in Kai-ks’s invading force, approaches the city of Mzindern and finds it extraordinarily splendid, full of beautiful women, treasure, and cattle. When this is reported, Kai-ks rejoices that Mzindern is a blessed, garden-like region. The invasion fills the king of Mzindern with grief, and he summons the gigantic White Demon to defend the land. Confident of victory, Kai-ks encamps near the city, but during the night a cloud brings pitch darkness and a devastating hailstorm upon the Persian host, killing many and scattering the rest. By morning Kai-ks is blind, his treasury taken, and his army destroyed or captured. For seven days he suffers, and on the eighth the White Demon mocks him as a barren willow-tree, pointing out that others wisely shrank from this enterprise and that he is now without an army. Twelve thousand demon-warriors are appointed to guard the Iranian captives, who are kept in bonds and barely fed. Arzang, a demon-leader, takes Kai-ks’s wealth, crown, and jewels and escorts the blind king and his troops to Mzindern, where they are handed over to the local monarch; the White Demon then returns home. Despite strict guard, Kai-ks sends a message to Zl (Zal), describing his blind helplessness, regretting he ignored Zal’s counsel, and begging for rescue. Zal is deeply vexed and privately tells his son Rustem that the sword must be unsheathed, that Kai-ks is captive in a dragon’s den, and that Rustem must take up the enterprise since Zal, being two centuries old, is unfit for war. He promises Rustem immortal fame if he frees the king. Rustem observes that the king took six months to reach Mzindern; Zal explains there are two roads, the long route Kai-ks took and a shorter one full of dangers—lions, demons, and sorcery—that could be traversed in seven days, if at all. Rustem accepts the challenge, saying that though it is said only desperate men willingly take the way to hell or rush into a tiger’s lair, he will gird himself and trust in God for victory. Terrified but dissembling before his army, Zohk dismisses the events as a prank by a \"gamesome guest,\" while Kandr mocks this by pointing out the violence done with a cow-headed mace and the liberation of the beauties Shahrnaz and Arnawaz. After rebuking Kandr for fleeing, Zohk turns to his army to regain power, but the soldiers and people, horrified by his cruelty in feeding serpents, revolt and embrace the cause of Feridn, the new king. Isolated, Zohk attempts alone to assassinate Feridn at night, spying him from a height as he dallies with Shahrnaz. Feridn awakens, strikes Zohk on the head with his cow-headed mace, and is about to kill him when a supernatural voice commands that Zohk instead be chained and taken to a deep, dark mountain cave to die slowly without comfort. Feridn, performing the work of heaven, purifies the world from sin and crime. A Fakr informs him that the fortress holds a hundred thousand veteran warriors, ample supplies, and pure water, making it seem impregnable. His officers urge retreat, but Isfendiyr refuses, trusting in God and deciding to take the fortress by stratagem rather than force. He devises a plan to enter as a merchant with rich wares, placing his brother Bashtan temporarily in charge of the army and arranging a signal: when a column of flame and smoke rises from within the fortress, Bashtan is to attack the gates. Isfendiyr prepares a caravan of one hundred dromedaries, some laden with fine cloths and jewels, others with chests each hiding two warriors, plus camel-drivers and servants. Posing as Persian merchants, they gain entry into the fortress, and Isfendiyr, calling himself Kherd, presents gifts to King Arjsp and is welcomed with repeated access to the palace. In conversation, Arjsp asks about Kurugsar and Isfendiyr, and the disguised hero reports hearing that Isfendiyr is marching by way of the Heft-khan toward the Brazen Fortress; Arjsp mocks this, saying the route is so dangerous that even birds fear it and that Isfendiyr would die many times attempting it. While trading, Isfendiyr discovers that two daughters of Gushtsp—his own sisters—are degraded to drawing and carrying water for Arjsp’s kitchen. They ask him, as a merchant from Irn, for news of their father and brother and lament that they toil bareheaded and barefoot while their family lives in peace, seemingly indifferent to their suffering. To avoid discovery, Isfendiyr hides his face and angrily denies knowing Gushtsp or Isfendiyr, but the elder sister recognizes his voice and secretly informs the younger. They clarify terms such as Goths and Niflungs, describing Niflungs as \"sons of the mist,\" originally a supernatural race owning a treasure and later a name for human dynasties. A ritual of blood-brotherhood between Gunnar and Sigurth is described, involving mingling blood in footprints. The prose note highlights two conflicting versions of Sigurth's death—slain in the forest versus slain in bed—records that Gotthorm kills Sigurth after being frightened by the hero's bright eyes, and cites German authorities and texts like the Nibelungenlied and Thithrekssaga as supporting the forest content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15721-l15838","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / BROT AF SIGURTHARKVITHU / FRAGMENT OF A SIGURTH LAY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 15721-15838","start":"15721","end":"15838","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial note on the fragment \"Brot af Sigurtharkvithu\" in Codex Regius. It explains the manuscript gap and argues that the surviving twenty stanzas are the end of a much longer \"Long Lay of Sigurth\" contrasted with a later \"Short Lay.\" The note discusses how Volsungasaga preserves the intervening narrative and quotes stanzas attributed to the Lay of Sigurth: Sigurth leaving a Valkyrie and visiting Heimir and Brynhild; Guthrun’s dream and Brynhild’s prophetic explanation; Grimhild’s magic draught making Sigurth forget Brynhild and marry Guthrun; Sigurth and Gunnar changing forms so Sigurth can ride through raging flames to win Brynhild; Sigurth’s three chaste nights with Brynhild with a sword between them; Brynhild’s marriage to Gunnar and her quarrel with Guthrun in which Sigurth’s dragon-slaying and flame-riding are recalled; and finally Sigurth’s grief so great that his iron mail-coat bursts, followed by Brynhild’s claim that she had given herself to Sigurth and Gunnar’s plotting of vengeance with Hogni, where the action of the Brot begins.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Codex Regius manuscript has a gap of eight leaves, after which a passage of twenty stanzas appears that seems to be the end of a longer poem; the next poem, Guthrunarkvitha I, has a clear heading marking where the fragment closes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The editor argues that the twenty surviving stanzas are the end of a poem titled Sigurtharkvitha or Long Lay of Sigurth, contrasting it with a relatively late and complete Sigurth lay called the Short Lay of Sigurth, about seventy stanzas long, and estimating that at least eighty to a hundred stanzas of the long lay are lost.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Volsungasaga gives in prose the narrative between the break in Sigrdrifumol and the start of the Brot and quotes four stanzas, one explicitly introduced as from the Lay of Sigurth; inconsistencies suggest several poetic sources, and the Long Lay of Sigurth probably occupied roughly the latter half of the lost manuscript section.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After leaving a Valkyrie, Sigurth goes to the dwelling of Heimir, Brynhild’s brother-in-law.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At Heimir’s home Sigurth meets Brynhild, and they renew their oaths of fidelity.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The narrative then shifts to the home of the Gjukungs, where Guthrun, daughter of Gjuki, experiences a terrifying dream.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Guthrun visits Brynhild to have her dream explained, and Brynhild interprets it by foretelling nearly everything that will happen.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Guthrun returns home, and Sigurth soon arrives at the Gjukungs’ dwelling, where he is enthusiastically welcomed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Grimhild, mother of Gunnar and Guthrun, gives Sigurth a magic draught that makes him forget Brynhild, and shortly afterward he marries Guthrun.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"An episode follows in which Brynhild is won for Gunnar; Volsungasaga reports that Gunnar fails to pass through flames and that Gunnar and Sigurth change forms so that Sigurth can make the attempt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"One quoted stanza describes fire raging and earth rocking, flames leaping up to heaven, and that few hardy heroes would dare to ride or leap the raging flames.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A second stanza shows Sigurth urging his horse Grani with his sword, the fire slackening before the hero, the flames sinking low for the fame-hungry rider, and armor flashing that Regin had fashioned.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After Sigurth has spent three nights with Brynhild, laying his sword between them, he and Gunnar return home; Brynhild goes to Heimir’s dwelling to prepare for her marriage with Gunnar and instructs Heimir to care for her daughter by Sigurth, Aslaug.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Brynhild and Gunnar’s wedding takes place, followed soon by a quarrel between Guthrun and Brynhild in which Guthrun reveals that it was Sigurth, not Gunnar, who rode through the flames, and Brynhild speaks contemptuously of Guthrun and her family.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A stanza quoted at this point says that Sigurth slew a dragon and that men will remember this while the world remains, and that Guthrun’s brother showed little boldness in riding or leaping the raging flames.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Gunnar and Sigurth both try unsuccessfully to appease Brynhild; after speaking with her, Sigurth leaves her hall without seeking further speech, with head bowed, and his grief is described as so great that his iron mail-coat bursts apart.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Brynhild tells Gunnar that she gave herself wholly to Sigurth before becoming Gunnar’s wife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Gunnar discusses plans of vengeance with his brother Hogni, and the editor notes that at this point the action of Brot Af Sigurtharkvithu begins.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sigurth","description":"Hero who leaves a Valkyrie, visits Heimir and Brynhild, is welcomed by the Gjukungs, drinks Grimhild’s magic draught and forgets Brynhild, marries Guthrun, changes forms with Gunnar to ride through raging flames, spends three nights with Brynhild with a sword between them, slays a dragon, and later grieves so deeply that his mail-coat bursts.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6","ev:7","ev:9","ev:10","ev:12","ev

He aids the brothers in wooing Brynhild, and, though he would have taken her himself, lies chastely beside her with a naked sword between them. Brynhild, once innocent of sorrow, becomes consumed with love for Sigurth, lamenting that he is Guthrun’s husband while she is Gunnar’s, and blaming the Norns for her ill fate. In her grief she wanders on glacier ice at evening while Guthrun shares the marriage bed with Sigurth. Brynhild feels joyless and mateless, and in wrath tells Gunnar he must lose her and her lands unless he dares Sigurth’s death; she threatens to return to her kin and ‘sleep her life away’, and urges that Sigurth’s son, called a ‘wolf-cub’, should also be killed to prevent vengeance.
