content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10801-l10847","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HELGAKVITHA HJORVARTHSSONAR / THE LAY OF HELGI THE SON OF HJORVARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10801-10847","start":"10801","end":"10847","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The note discusses the fragmentary and composite nature of the Helgakvitha Hjorvarthssonar: parts I, II, and IV may or may not derive from a single poem and are dated early, while the Hrimgertharmol (section III) is later. The poem has unusually many prose links, which contain most of the narrative, with verse mainly in dialogue. An anonymous composer appears to have tried clumsily to unify chaotic verse material through these prose passages. Bugge proposed that the prose sections were originally integral to the work, a view the editor finds inconsistent with the evidence. The note then sketches how the Helgi tradition, originating in Denmark, spread through Norse regions and became interwoven (though not essentially) with the southern Volsung hero cycle, generating many Helgi poems over time. In Iceland’s literary period, a zealous scribe is imagined to have written down and pieced together such poems and fragments, adding annotations. Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II is cited as explicitly acknowledging this patchwork process by referring to the Old Volsung Lay, the Karuljoth (Lay of Kara), and an earlier Helgakvitha. Finally, the author references Bugge’s major study on the origin and connections of the Helgi poems, available in English translation by W. H. Schofield, and emphasizes the complexity and importance of these issues for understanding Old Norse literature and for reading the Helgi poems intelligently.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Parts I, II, and IV of the work may or may not come from the same poem, and commentators generally date them no later than the first half of the tenth century.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Hrimgertharmol, designated as section III, is placed considerably later in date than the other parts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The question of when and by whom the fragments were pieced together involves examining the prose notes and links.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Helgakvitha Hjorvarthssonar has more prose notes and links than any other poem in the Edda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The prose links contain almost all of the narrative, while the verse is almost exclusively dialogue.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Whoever composed the prose links attempted to bring chaotic verse material into a semblance of unity but did so clumsily, with noticeable blunders and contradictions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Bugge proposed that the prose passages should be regarded as an original and necessary part of the work.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The editor states that Bugge’s theory about the prose passages does not agree well with the evidence.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Helgi tradition is said to have spread from its native Denmark through Norse regions of the North and West.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Helgi tradition became gradually interwoven, though not in essentials, with the southern Volsung hero cycle.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Many poems about Helgi were composed at different times and in different places, reflecting varied forms of the story.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After many generations, during Iceland’s literary period, a zealous scribe wrote down such Helgi poems or fragments as he knew, piecing them together and annotating them based on additional information.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The prose notes to Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II explicitly acknowledge a patchwork process, introducing four stanzas with the phrase “as is said in the Old Volsung Lay.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The final prose note of Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II cites an incident from the Karuljoth (Lay of Kara), and a two-line speech is quoted as previously written in the Helgakvitha.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Bugge’s study Helge-Digtene i den ldre Edda, Deres Hjem og Forbindelser examines in detail the origin, character, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15271-l15439","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / SIGRDRIFUMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE VICTORY-BRINGER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 15271-15439","start":"15271","end":"15439","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sigurth rides to the mountain Hindarfjoll and sees a fire-like glow reaching toward heaven around a shield-tower with a banner. Identified in the prose as the Valkyrie Sigrdrifa, she explains that Odin punished her with an enchanted sleep for slaying Hjalmgunnar, though he had promised that king victory, and decreed she would be wedded; she herself has vowed to marry only a man without fear. She gives Sigurth a horn of mead as a memory-draught, invokes day, night, gods, goddesses, and earth for wisdom and healing, and begins teaching him a series of runes for winning victory, securing ale from deceit, aiding childbirth, protecting ships at sea, healing wounds, ensuring just speech at judgments, and sharpening thought. Sigrdrifa recounts how Hropt devised, wrote, and mentally formed the runes from a draught that fell from Heithdraupnir's head and Hoddrofnir's horn, how Mim's head spoke truth to him on a mountain, and how he ordered runes inscribed on many notable beings and objects. The runes are shaved off, mixed into holy mead, and sent widely so that gods, elves, Wanes, and mortal men receive them; various specialized runes are said to aid those who know them rightly until the gods are gone. A final stanza, headed \"Brynhild spake,\" addresses Sigurth as \"tree of the biting blade,\" telling him he must choose speech or silence while their evil fate is already set.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigurth rides up on Hindarfjoll, turns toward the land of the Franks, and on the mountain sees a great light like fire, whose glow reaches up to heaven.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"On the mountain Sigurth finds a tower of shields with a banner above it, enters, and sees a fully armed figure lying asleep inside.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigurth removes the helm from the sleeper, discovers she is a woman whose mail-coat is stuck fast to her flesh, cuts the mail-coat open from the neck down and out to the arm-holes, takes it off, and she awakens, sits up, and sees him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Upon waking, the woman asks what cut through her byrnie, how her sleep was broken, and who freed her from her pale fetters; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16188-l16263","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / GUTHRUNARKVITHA I / THE FIRST LAY OF GUTHRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 16188-16263","start":"16188","end":"16263","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In stanzas 14–25 and a prose note, Guthrun, daughter of Gjuki, weeps intensely for her dead husband Sigurth, the \"hero\" and \"leader of men.\" Gollrond, her sister, comments on the greatness of Guthrun's love and her unhappiness whenever Sigurth was away. Guthrun praises Sigurth as surpassing Gjuki's sons, likening him to a spear-leek above the grass and a bright jewel worn by princes, and recalls feeling loftier than Herjan's maidens as his beloved. Now she feels as small as a leaf on a willow and blames Gjuki's sons for her grief. She curses Gunnar, predicting that his land will lose its people according to how he kept his oaths and that his gold rings, once linked to oaths sworn with Sigurth, will bring him no joy and become his slayers. The court was once happier when Sigurth saddled his horse Grani and went to win the hand of Brynhild, described as a bad woman. Brynhild, daughter of Buthli, curses an unnamed witch who used magic to loosen Guthrun's tears and make her speak. Gollrond rebukes Brynhild as a hated woman, bane of nobles, borne on an evil wave, bringer of sorrow to seven kings, and one who has made many women loveless. Brynhild then says that her brother Atli, son of Buthli, is guilty of all the sorrow, recalling an episode in the hall of the Hunnish race where the flames of a snakes' bed flashed around a hero, a sight that has caused her long suffering. Brynhild stands by pillars, gathers her strength, and when she sees Sigurth's wounds, fire burns in her eyes and she breathes venom. The prose note relates that Guthrun goes away to a forest in a desolate region and journeys to Denmark, where she lives seven half-years with Thora, daughter of Hokon. Brynhild refuses to live after Sigurth's death, has eight thralls and five serving-women killed, and then kills herself with a sword, as told in the Short Lay of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15003-l15124","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FAFNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF FAFNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 15003-15124","start":"15003","end":"15124","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes to Fafnismol explain manuscript features, missing or interpolated stanzas, and cross-references to other Eddic and saga texts. They summarize how Sigurth fears being harmed by Fafnir’s blood, is taunted by Regin, and receives disguised advice from Othin to dig trenches to divert the blood. The notes gloss references to Hjordis’s captivity while pregnant with Sigurth, the Norns and their role in fate and childbirth, Dvalin as chief of the dwarfs, Surt’s rule of the fire world and the final battle at Vigrith/Oskopnir where the rainbow bridge Bilrost/Bifrost breaks, Fafnir’s fear-helm, sword lore (Gram and Refil/Serpent), birds who speak proverbial stanzas, and kennings such as “wolf, etc.” (fire and smoke) and “tree of battle” (warrior). They also discuss probable interpolations from poems like Vafthruthnismol and Hovamol, and connections to texts such as Reginsmol, Volsungasaga, Voluspo, Grimnismol, and Sigrdrifumol.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigurth is described as being worried that the dragon’s blood pouring down on him could overcome him, and he asks Regin what would happen if this danger occurred.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Regin responds to Sigurth’s concern by taunting him with cowardice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigurth digs a trench before the encounter with Fafnir, following a plan to deal with the dragon’s blood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After Sigurth has dug his trench, an old man identified as Othin appears and advises him to dig additional trenches to carry off the dragon’s blood; Sigurth follows this advice and escapes harm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The note identifies Fafnir as Regin’s brother.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Fafnir is said to refer to Hjordis, mother of the still unborn Sigurth, being captured by Alf after Sigmund’s death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Stanzas 11–15 are described as probably interpolated from a poem similar to Vafthruthnismol and include a proverb about rounding the first headland, interpreted as disaster and the fate of the Norns awaiting at the beginning of life’s voyage, along with commentary on obstinate rashness.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:

{"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l5497-l5624","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HARBARTHSLJOTH / THE POEM OF HARBARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 5497-5624","start":"5497","end":"5624","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""Short now shall be our speech, for thou speakest in mockery only;
The passage thou gavest me not I shall pay thee if ever we meet."
...
"Get hence where every evil thing shall have thee!"","summary":"The close of Harbarthsljoth shows Thor ending a quarrel with the ferryman Harbarth, saying the other only mocks him, complaining about being refused passage, and threatening to repay him if they meet again; Harbarth replies by cursing him to a place where every evil thing will have him. Editorial notes then identify Harbarth with Othin and describe Thor as a wandering thunder-god whose many journeys, like those of Othin, often leave him temporarily worsted but ultimately victorious. The notes summarize related myths: Thor's Journey in the East where he meets the giant Skrymir and lifts a cat that is really Mithgarthsorm in Utgartha-Loki's house; Thor's legal vulnerability when among giants; his sons Meili and Magni (the latter, by the giantess Jarnsaxa, rescuing Thor from under the giant Hrungnir's foot as a three-day-old child and later inheriting Mjollnir with his brother Mothi); the duel with the giant Hrungnir and his stone body and dummy giant; the Norse idea of being doomed to die (feigr) and the custom of concealing one's name from enemies; Harbarth's overpowering success with seven sisters; witches riding wolves at night; the giant Thjazi's trick to seize the goddess Ithun and her apples, Loki's hawk-form rescue and transformation of Ithun into a nut, the gods' fire that burns Thjazi's eagle-wings and his death, and the compensatory marriage of his daughter Skathi to Njorth; the division of the giant Alvaldi's gold among his sons Thjazi, Ithi and Gang; a proverb about an oak expressing that the victor takes the spoils; and the clarification that Thor killed no giant women on his Journey in the East.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In stanza 59, Thor says their speech will now be short because the other speaker speaks only in mockery, complains that he was not given passage, and declares he will repay this if they ever meet.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In stanza 60, Harbarth tells Thor to get away to a place where every evil thing shall have him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The notes state that Harbarth (Gray-Beard) is Othin.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The notes describe Thor as the thunder-god whose journeys were almost as numerous as those of Othin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The notes compare Thor to the Robin Hood of the British ballads, saying that like Robin Hood he was often temporarily worsted but always managed to come out ahead in the end.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The notes mention that in Thor's Journey in the East he encountered the giant Skrymir, and in the house of Utgartha-Loki he lifted a cat that turned out to be Mithgarthsorm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A note glosses the phrase "Thy mother" as referring to Jorth (Earth).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The notes explain that when Thor is in the territory of his enemies, the giants, he is sekr, meaning he is outside the protection of any law.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The notes describe Meili as a practically unknown son of Othin, mentioned here only in the Edda.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The notes state that Magni is the son of Thor and the giantess Jarnsaxa; when Magni was three days old he alone of the gods was strong enough to lift the dead giant Hrungnir's foot from Thor's neck, thereby rescuing his father, and he remarked that he could have sent the giant to hell with his fist if he had arrived sooner. Magni and his brother Mothi inherit Thor's hammer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The notes explain that the Old Norse word feigr, meaning doomed to die, occurs frequently, and that belief in an inevitable but unknown fate was practically universal in the pre-Christian period.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The notes say that concealing one's name from enemies is a known practice, with a comparison to Fafnismol.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The notes recount that the giant Hrungnir wagered his head that his horse Gullfaxi was swifter than Othin's Sleipnir, lost the race, forced his way into the gods' home and became drunk there, was ejected by Thor, and challenged Thor to a duel. Hrungnir had a dummy giant made nine miles high and three miles broad, had a three-horned heart of stone, a head of stone, a shield of stone, and a grindstone as a weapon.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The notes state that Thor's servant Thjalfi told Hrungnir that Thor would attack him from underground, causing Hrungnir to lay down his shield and stand on it; Thor's hammer shattered both the grindstone and Hrungnir's head, though a piece of the grindstone knocked Thor down and Hrungnir fell with his foot on Thor's neck, while Thjalfi easily killed the dummy giant.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The notes suggest that Fjolvar is not otherwise mentioned in the poems and may be the father of the seven sisters referred to in stanza 18, while Algrn (The All-Green) is also otherwise unknown.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The notes interpret stanza 18 to mean that the women (seven sisters) were wise to give in cheerfully to Harbarth, because resistance to his power was as impossible as making ropes of sand or digging out the bottoms of valleys; nothing further is known of these seven sisters.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The notes remark that Thor is always eager for this sort of story, referring to Harbarth's tale about women.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The notes explain that the "riders by night" are witches, who were thought to ride on wolves in the dark, and that nothing further is known of this adventure.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The notes say that a proverb about an oak is found elsewhere, such as in Grettissaga, in nearly the same words, and that its meaning is similar to the saying "to the victor belong the spoils."","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The notes state that Thor killed no women of the giants' race on the Journey to the East described by Snorri and that his great giant-killing adventure is the one narrated in Thrymskvitha.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The notes explain that the giant Thjazi, by a trick, obtained possession of the goddess Ithun and her apples and carried her off into Jotunheim.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The notes recount that Loki, through whose fault Ithun had been betrayed, was sent by the gods to retrieve her; he used Freyja's hawks-dress, transformed Ithun into a nut, and flew back with her while Thjazi, in the form of an eagle, pursued him. The gods kindled a fire that burned the eagle's wings, after which they killed Thjazi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The notes say that Thjazi's daughter Skathi was allowed by the gods to marry Njorth as a recompense for her father's death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The notes state that Alvaldi, of whom little is known, was the father of Thjazi, Ithi, and Gang, who divided his wealth by each taking a mouthful of gold, and that it is not known which stars were called "Thjazi's Eyes."","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Thor","description":"The thunder-god engaged in a quarrel with Harbarth, a frequent journeyer who undertakes travels such as the Journey in the East, is sometimes temporarily worsted but ultimately prevails, is outlawed among giants, fights the giant Hrungnir, is rescued by his son Magni, and refrains from killing giant women on his eastern journey.","role_refs":["role:1","role:4","role:6","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4","ev:7","ev:9","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Harbarth","description":"A speaker who mocks Thor, refuses him passage, and curses him to go where every evil thing shall have him; identified in the notes as Othin under the name Gray-Beard and described as having irresistible power over women such as seven sisters.","role_refs":["role:2","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Othin","description":"High god identified in the notes as the true identity of Harbarth (Gray-Beard); his journeys are compared to Thor's, and he is the father of Meili. He races Hrungnir on the horse Sleipnir.","role_refs":["role:3","role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Robin Hood","description":"The Robin Hood of the British ballads, used in the notes as a comparison for Thor as a hero often temporarily worsted but ultimately victorious.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Skrymir","description":"A giant encountered by Thor during his Journey in the East.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Utgartha-Loki","description":"The figure in whose house Thor lifted a cat that turned out to be Mithgarthsorm.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Mithgarthsorm","description":"A being named Mithgarthsorm, revealed to be the true nature of a cat that Thor lifted in the house of Utgartha-Loki.","role_refs":["role

He urges Svava not to weep, but instead to prepare a bed for Hethin and give her love to the young hero. Svava replies that she vowed in her beloved home, when Helgi wooed her with rings, that if the warrior died she would not willingly embrace an unrenowned man. Hethin then asks Svava to kiss him and declares he will not return to Rogheim or Rothulsfjoll until he has avenged Hjorvarth's son, the noblest king. Gripir foretells that in Gjuki’s hall a marriage drink will be shared for both Sigurth and Gunnar, and that their outward forms will be exchanged while each retains his own mind. Sigurth asks whether this new kinship will turn out well. Gripir says Sigurth will keep silent, remember his oaths, and live in good wedlock with Guthrun, but that Brynhild will feel badly married and seek cunning vengeance. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l17159-l17282","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HELREITH BRYNHILDAR / BRYNHILDS HELL-RIDE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 17159-17282","start":"17159","end":"17282","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“After the death of Brynhild there were made two bale-fires, the one for Sigurth, and that burned first, and on the other was Brynhild burned, and she was on a wagon which was covered with a rich cloth. Thus it is told, that Brynhild went in the wagon on Hel-way, and passed by a house where dwelt a certain giantess.”","summary":"The introductory prose note situates the poem Helreith Brynhildar immediately after the short Sigurth lay in Codex Regius and discusses its dramatic unity, late (eleventh‑century) date, and near‑certain Christian influence, noting that Brynhild appears both as a Valkyrie and a swan‑maiden and that the poem is closely related to Sigrdrifumol but largely independent of the German heroic cycle. A brief prose bridge then explains that after Brynhild’s and Sigurth’s deaths two funeral pyres were made, Sigurth’s burning first, and Brynhild was burned on the other while placed on a richly covered wagon that travels along Hel‑way. As Brynhild rides toward Hel, she passes the house of a giantess, who calls out and tries to stop her. In the ensuing dialogue the giantess condemns Brynhild as fickle, blood‑stained, born for evil, a breaker of oaths, and responsible for the deaths of Gjuki’s children and the ruin of their house. Brynhild answers from the wagon, insisting she will seem better than the giantess when people judge them and explaining that Gjuki’s heirs forced her into joyless oath‑breaking by arranging her marriage. She recounts her earlier life: once known as Hild the helmed in Hlymdalir, associated with eight sisters whose swan‑robes a bold monarch took and placed under an oak, she swore oaths to a young king at age twelve. As a Valkyrie she gave victory to Autha’s brother and sent Hjalmgunnar, an old leader of the Goths, down to Hel, provoking Odin’s anger. Odin punished her by surrounding her with overlapping shields in Skatalund, encircling her south‑facing hall with leaping fire, and ordaining that only a fearless hero who brought the gold guarded by Fafnir could cross the flames and break her sleep. Sigurth, riding the horse Grani to his foster‑father’s land, is described as the best of men and a prince of the Danes. Brynhild tells how she and Sigurth then slept happily in one bed for eight nights as if they were siblings, without laying loving hands on each other. Later, Guthrun, Gjuki’s daughter, reproached Brynhild for sleeping in Sigurth’s arms, revealing that Brynhild had been betrayed in the choice of her spouse. In the final stanza Brynhild laments that men and women are born into long grief yet asserts that she and Sigurth will still live their lives together after death, and she commands the giantess to sink down.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the deaths of Brynhild and Sigurth, two bale-fires are made: one for Sigurth, which burns first, and one for Brynhild, who is burned while placed on a wagon covered with a rich cloth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Brynhild travels in a wagon on Hel-way after her cremation and passes by a house where a giantess dwells.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The giantess speaks from her dwelling, telling Brynhild she shall not travel further and that it would be more fitting for her to stay at her weaving than to follow another’s husband; the dwelling is described as ribbed with rocks across.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The giantess calls Brynhild fickle of heart, addresses her as a ‘gold-goddess’, and says she has washed heroes’ blood from her hands.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Brynhild replies from the wagon, telling the woman from the rocky walls not to chide her and claiming that she will seem better than the giantess when men know them both.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The giantess identifies Brynhild as Buthli’s daughter, says she was born for the worst of evils, accuses her of giving Gjuki’s children to death, and of laying their lofty house low.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Brynhild states she will tell the truth from the wagon and says that the heirs of Gjuki made her ever joyless and a breaker of oaths.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Brynhild says she was formerly named Hild the helmed in Hlymdalir by all who knew her.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild describes a bold monarch who took the swan-robes of eight sisters and placed them beneath an oak.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l18558-l18660","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / ATLAKVITHA EN GRNLENZKA / THE GREENLAND LAY OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 18558-18660","start":"18558","end":"18660","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Guthrun, Gjuki's daughter, avenged her brothers by killing Atli's sons and Atli himself, then burning his hall with his whole company; the following poem begins with Atli sending a rider named Knefrth to Gunnar at Gjuki's home, with benches around the hearth and sweet beer.","summary":"An editorial introduction discusses the two Atli poems (Atlakvitha and Atlamol) in the Codex Regius, their manuscript superscriptions mentioning Greenland, and scholarly arguments that they likely originated in the Norse Greenland settlement in the eleventh century. The note contrasts the shorter and less elaborated Atlakvitha with the longer and more romantic Atlamol, and analyzes their metre (Malahattr, with Atlakvitha mixing in Fornyrthislag) and Christian coloring, including Guthrun's readiness in Atlamol to die and go into another light and Atlakvitha's use of mythological names like Valhall and Hlithskjolf without clear grasp of their pagan context. The narrative material is described as largely South-Germanic, blending Attila and Burgundian legends as outlined in the Drap Niflunga, with Brynhild absent and Sigurth barely mentioned, though the atmosphere of Atlamol is said to be Norse. The editor suggests both poems rework older Atli material and notes the difficulty of translating Atlakvitha due to irregular metre, corrupt transmission, and rare words. A prose link to the poem recounts Guthrun, Gjuki's daughter and Atli's wife, avenging her brothers by killing Atli's sons, then Atli, and burning his hall with his whole company. Stanza 1 of Atlakvitha then shows Atli sending a keen-witted rider named Knefrth to Gunnar at Gjuki's home, described with benches around the hearth and sweet beer.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Codex Regius contains two Atli poems, the Atlakvitha (Lay of Atli) and the Atlamol (Ballad of Atli).","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the manuscript superscription of each Atli poem the word \"Greenland\" appears.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The editor states that this superscription indicates that around 1300 there was a tradition that the two poems originated in the Greenland settlement.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The two Atli poems narrate the visit of the sons of Gjuki to Atli's court, their deaths, and the subsequent revenge of their sister Guthrun, who is Atli's wife, on her husband.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Atlakvitha is described as shorter and telling the story with little elaboration.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Atlamol is described as longer, adding many details, some apparently invented, and giving the story a romantic, sentimental quality lacking in Atlakvitha.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Both Atli poems are distinguished from the rest of the collection by their use of the Malahattr metre; Atlamol employs it consistently and smoothly, while Atlakvitha mixes Malahattr lines with stanzas apparently in the older Fornyrthislag type.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Atlakvitha is dated to the first quarter of the eleventh century, and the Atlamol to roughly fifty years or more later.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In each case the poet is described as apparently Christian.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the Atlamol Guthrun is said, in stanza 82, to express her readiness to die and go into another light.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the Atlakvitha mythological names such as Valhall and Hlithskjolf are used with an evident lack of understanding of their relation to the older gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Greenland settlement grew rapidly after Eirik the Red's explorations (982–985) and flourished in the eleventh century.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Internal evidence, particularly for Atlamol, points to an origin remote from Iceland, Norway, and the Western Isles, and the editor concludes that both Atli poems probably originated in Greenland.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"William Hovgaard's \"Voyages of the Norsemen to America\" and Maurice Hewlett's \"Thorgils\" (based on the Floamannasaga) are cited for accounts of the Greenland settlement and the sufferings of early settlers.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"From the standpoint of narrative material there is said to be little that is distinctively Norse in either Atli poem; instead the story follows the prose Drap Niflunga, which is largely based on these two poems.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The story is described as representing a southern blending of Attila and Burgundian legends, and Atlakvitha actually uses the word \"Burgundians.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Brynhild is not mentioned in either Atli poem, and Sigurth's name appears only once, in Atlamol.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The general atmosphere, particularly in Atlamol, is described as essentially Norse despite the South-Germanic narrative basis.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Atlakvitha's metre is described as chaotic, with normal Malahattr lines frequently interspersed with lines and stanzas apparently of the older Fornyrthislag type.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"It is suggested that the composer of Atlakvitha reworked in Malahattr an older Atli poem in Fornyrthislag, and that both Atli poems were based on older poems, given the limited number of distinctively Norse traits in their material.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The translation of Atlakvitha is said to be difficult because of irregular metre, faulty transmission, and many words found nowhere else in Old Norse, leading to much guesswork about their meanings.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The notes indicate uncertainties in reconstructing defective stanzas and obscure passages without cataloguing all the varying suggestions made by editors and commentators.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"A prose summary immediately before the poem states that Guthrun, Gjuki's daughter, avenged her brothers, first slaying Atli's sons, then slaying Atli, and burning the hall with his whole company.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The prose summary identifies Guthrun as Gjuki's daughter.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The prose summary identifies those Guthrun avenges as her brothers.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The prose summary states that the hall was burned together with Atli's whole company.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"In stanza 1 Atli sends a keen-witted rider named Knefrth to Gunnar.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The rider Knefrth comes to Gjuki's home and to Gunnar's dwelling.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Gunnar's dwelling is described as having benches around the hearth and sweet beer.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Figure who has a court visited by the sons of Gjuki, sends a rider to Gunnar, and is eventually slain and burned in his hall by Guthrun as part of her revenge.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"Gjuki's daughter and sister to his sons, described as Atli's wife, who avenges her brothers by killing Atli's sons, then Atli, and burning his hall with his whole Manuscript issues such as line order and possible missing stanzas are noted, including the inference that Guthrun is already Atli's wife and that a lost stanza may have described Atli's treacherous invitation to the Gjukungs and the slaying of Hogni and Gunnar, as in Drap Niflunga. Another note recalls that in Volsungasaga Guthrun gives her brother a harp, with which he puts serpents to sleep, and connects this episode to the thirtieth Aventiure of the Nibelungenlied, where Volker plays Gunther's followers to sleep before the final battle. A further note explains that Geirmund, probably an ally or retainer (or brother) of Atli, lives at a home visited by Oddrun; the poet relocates Gunnar's death-place and Atli's dwelling to the island Hlesey, separated from Geirmund's home by a sound, despite earlier references to Hunland and the murky wood, illustrating heroic poetry's loose geography. Another variant tradition is cited in which Gunnar puts all serpents but one to sleep with his harp before a mighty adder bites his heart, killing him; the name \"Atli\" in one line may be a scribal error for \"of serpents.\" The kenning \"serpents-bed goddess\" is glossed as meaning a woman, specifically Borgny, based on a conventional association of women with gold and of gold with the \"serpents' bed.\" Finally, an editorial note suggests that one line may be a statement by the poet rather than part of Oddrun's content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l17996-l18100","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / GUTHRUNARKVITHA III / THE THIRD LAY OF GUTHRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 17996-18100","start":"17996","end":"18100","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The introductory prose explains that Guthrunarkvitha III is a short Norse lay preserved only in Codex Regius, composed in the early 11th century and chiefly concerned with an ordeal by boiling water, a practice introduced to Norway by St. Olaf and still regarded as foreign. The material is said to derive from North Germany, adapting a well-known story-type about a wife accused of faithlessness who proves her innocence through a boiling-water test, here attached to Guthrun and incorporating the names Guthrun, Atli, Thjothrek, and Herkja. A prose preface to the poem tells how Herkja, formerly Atli’s concubine and now his serving-woman, reports seeing Guthrun and Thjothrek together, angering Atli. In the verses Guthrun questions Atli about his sorrow, hears that Herkja has accused her of lying in bed with Thjothrek \"in lovers guise,\" and swears oaths by a sacred white stone that nothing improper occurred. She insists she never embraced Thjothrek; they only shared their sorrows in secret, and she recalls his arrival with thirty warriors, all of whom, along with her brothers and kin, have been killed by Atli. Guthrun laments the absence of her brothers Gunnar and Hogni and resolves to secure redress herself. She orders that Saxi, a southern king, be summoned to hallow a boiling kettle. Before a hall packed with seven hundred people, the queen thrusts her hand into the kettle, reaches the bottom, and brings up flashing stones, emerging unhurt and proclaiming herself cleared of sin by the kettle’s sacred boiling. Atli rejoices at her uninjured hand and commands that Herkja, who plotted Guthrun’s grief, undergo the same ordeal. Herkja’s hands are burned, and she is thrown into a foul bog, so that Guthrun’s grief is said to be requited.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introductory note states that Guthrunarkvitha III appears only in the Codex Regius, is complete, and free from serious interpolations.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poem is dated to the first half of the eleventh century, partly because it centers on an ordeal by boiling water introduced into Norway by St. Olaf, who died in 1030, and stanza 7 still treats this ordeal as foreign.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The material for the poem is said to have come from North Germany, and the note suggests the poet was not working from a fully formed narrative legend.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The introduction describes a story-pattern in which a wife accused of faithlessness proves her innocence by a test of boiling water; this story had long been current in Germany and elsewhere and had attached itself to various legendary women, but apparently not to Guthrun except in this poem.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The introduction remarks that including Thjothrek (Theoderich, Dietrich, Thithrek) in Atli’s court is anachronistic and indicates the relative lateness of the poem, because Theoderich legends reached the North only around the year 1000.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note characterizes Guthrunarkvitha III as a dramatic German story turned into a Norse narrative lay by a Norse poet, with the names Guthrun, Atli, Thjothrek, and Herkja incorporated for greater effect, and probably not originally part of the Sigurth and Atli tradition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A prose preface explains that Herkja was a serving-woman of Atli and had been his concubine; she told Atli she had seen Thjothrek and Guthrun together, which greatly angered Atli.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In stanza 1 Guthrun addresses Atli, asking about his sorrow, why his heart is heavy and he never laughs, and saying that it would better befit a warrior to speak with men while she looks on.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In stanza 2 Atli tells Guthrun that he is troubled by what Herkja has reported in the hall: that Guthrun lies in bed with Thjothrek beneath the linen in lovers guise.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In stanza 3 Guthrun declares that she will swear oaths by a sacred white stone to affirm that nothing occurred with Thjothrek that man or woman may not know.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In stanza 4 Guthrun states that she has never embraced Thjothrek; instead, they met in another way, secretly telling each other their sorrows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Stanza 5 says that Thjothrek came with thirty warriors, and none of those men now remains; Guthrun accuses Atli of murdering her brothers, his mail-clad men, and all the men of her race.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Stanza 6 relates that Gunnar does not come and Hogni is not greeted; Guthrun no longer sees her beloved brothers, and she declares that Hogni would avenge her sorrow with the sword and that she herself will now win payment for her woes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Stanza 7 has kettle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Stanza 8 describes how Guthrun reached the bottom of the kettle with her bright hand, brought up flashing stones, and proclaimed to the warriors that she was well cleared of sin by the kettle’s sacred boiling.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Stanza 9 reports that Atli’s heart laughed with happiness when he saw Guthrun’s unharmed hand; he then commands that Herkja, who had planned grief for Guthrun, come to try the kettle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Stanza 10 states that Herkja’s hands were burned by the kettle, that she was flung into a foul bog, and that Guthrun’s content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l19195-l19304","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / ATLAMOL EN GRNLENZKU / THE GREENLAND BALLAD OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 19195-19304","start":"19195","end":"19304","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A prose introductory note explains that the Atlamol follows the Atlakvitha in Codex Regius, was likely composed in Greenland around 1100, and is fairly well preserved. It outlines the story: Atli sends a message to the sons of Gjuki, who travel to his home; Hogni and Gunnar are slain, and Guthrun, bitter over her brothers’ deaths, takes bloody revenge on Atli. The note describes the poem as a Frankish blending of legends of the slaughter of the Burgundians and the death of Attila, and emphasizes that a South Germanic story was adapted for an eleventh‑century Greenland audience by adding characters such as Kostbera and Glaumvor, sea voyages, and episodes at the Thing, without changing the basic narrative. The poet likely knew older poems on Atli, possibly the Atlakvitha; some details, such as Hogni’s son aiding Guthrun, appear in other late versions. The poem is in Malahattr meter and was paraphrased faithfully in the Volsungasaga.\n\nStanzas 1–10 of the Atlamol depict secret plotting against the sons of Gjuki, Atli’s ill counsel and invitation to his kinsmen, a wise woman who senses danger yet cannot help and does not sail with them, the crafting and falsifying of runes by Vingi, the journey of Atli’s warriors to Limafjord, warm hospitality with ale, fires, gifts, and the kindness of Kostbera (Hogni’s wife) and Glaumvor (Gunnar’s wife). Gunnar and Hogni decide to go in response to the message. A feast with mead and many horns is held, the beds are prepared, and Kostbera, wise and skilled in rune‑craft, reads strange letters by firelight and later has a significant dream which she relates to the warrior when she wakes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Atlamol follows the Atlakvitha in the Codex Regius and is described as actually composed in Greenland.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poem is dated by most critics nearer 1100 than 1050 and is considered fairly well preserved, though with possible small gaps and minor interpolations or omissions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The narrative substance includes Atli’s message to the sons of Gjuki, their journey to Atli’s home, the slaying of Hogni and Gunnar, Guthrun’s bitterness over her brothers’ deaths, and her bloody revenge on Atli.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In bare outline the Atlamol is said to represent a Frankish blending of legends of the slaughter of the Burgundians and the death of Attila.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The poet added characters such as Kostbera and Glaumvor and introduced episodes with sea voyages and reproaches to Atli at the Thing in order to appeal to both men and women of the Greenland settlement.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note states that the story was brought from South Germanic lands to the North and adapted to the understanding and tastes of eleventh‑century hearers without materially changing the basic narrative.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Greenland poet likely knew older poems on Atli, possibly the Atlakvitha; Kostbera and Glaumvor are considered peculiar to the Atlamol, while Hogni’s son who aids Guthrun in slaying Atli appears under another name in other late versions.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The poem is in Malahattr meter throughout, its verse more regular than in the Atlakvitha, and the Volsungasaga compilers paraphrased it with considerable fidelity.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Stanza 1 describes how men of old gathered in secret counsel, plotted in ways that later harmed them, and deceived the trust of Gjukis sons.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Stanza 2 portrays fate growing for the princes so that they are given over to death; Atli’s ill counsel leads him to destroy his own strong support and send a message so his kinsmen should seek him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Stanza 3 introduces a wise woman who understands what is said in secret and wants to use her wisdom but does not know how to help; she remains behind while others are to sail the sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Stanza 4 relates that the woman fashions runes, but Vingi falsifies them before delivering them; Atli’s warriors then travel and arrive at Limafjord, the home of the kings.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Stanza 5 shows that at Limafjord the hosts are kind with ale and kindle fires, accept gifts from the guests, hang these gifts on the pillars, and harbor no fear or suspicion of craft from the visitors.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Stanza 6 depicts Kostbera, Hogni’s wife, and Glaumvor, Gunnar’s wife, coming forth kindly, welcoming the guests, and attending to their needs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Stanza 7 reports that Hogni is asked about his eagerness, that their guile would have been clear if they had been on guard, and that Gunnar promises to go if Hogni will, with Hogni answering according to Gunnar’s counsel.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Stanza 8 recounts that renowned figures bring mead and hold a fair feast with many horns until the men have drunk deeply, after which their mates prepare beds for them to rest, with some lines omitted in the text.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Stanza 9 describes Kostbera as wise and cunning in rune‑craft; she reads letters by the light of the fire, yet they seem so strange that her tongue cleaves to her palate and she cannot see their meaning.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Stanza 10 tells that Hogni soon seeks his bed; a ‘clear‑souled’ one dreams and does not keep the dream, speaking of it to the warrior when she awakens, with some lines omitted.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Leader whose ill counsel and message summon his kinsmen, the sons of Gjuki, to his home, where Hogni and Gunnar are slain; later the target of Guthrun’s bloody revenge.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sons of Gjuki (Gjukis sons / Gjukungs)","description":"Princes referred to as Gjukis sons, including Gunnar and Hogni, who are deceived by secret plotting, receive Atli’s message, journey to his home, and are ultimately slain.","role_refs":["role:3","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"Son of Gjuki and prince, later slain by Atli; husband of Glaumvor. In the poem he welcomes guests at Limafjord and promises to go to Atli if Hogni will also go.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hogni","description":"Son of Gjuki and prince, later slain by Atli; husband of Kostbera. He is asked about his eagerness, agrees to go following Gunnar’s counsel, and in other versions has a son who aids Guthrun in killing Atli.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10","ev:11","ev:3","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Guthrun","description":"Female relative (sister or wife in the broader tradition) introduction on origin and transmission of Atlamol","summary":"The introductory prose discusses the placement of Atlamol after Atlakvitha in Codex Regius, its composition in Greenland around 1100, its relatively sound preservation, and its narrative substance: Atli’s message, the journey of the sons of Gjuki, the killing of Hogni and Gunnar, and Guthrun’s revenge. It explains that the story is a Frankish blend of Burgundian and Attila legends brought from South Germanic lands to the North, and shows how the Greenland poet adapted it for his audience by adding characters such as Kostbera and Glaumvor, sea voyages, and Thing scenes, while preserving the basic narrative. It notes the use of Malahattr meter and that the Volsungasaga compilers paraphrased the poem faithfully.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3","fig:4","fig:5","fig:6","fig:7","fig:10","fig:11","fig:12","fig:13"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"scene:2","label":"Secret counsel plots against Gjukis sons and Atli’s fatal decision","summary":"Men of old gather in secret counsel and plot, deceiving the trust of Gjukis sons in a way that later harms them. Atli, by ill counsel, destroys his own strong support and sends a message summoning his kinsmen, initiating the chain of events leading to their journey and eventual deaths.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3","fig:4"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"scene:3","label":"Wise woman, runes, false Vingi, and voyage to Limafjord","summary":"A wise woman perceives the meaning of the secret plotting and wishes to use her wisdom but cannot find a way to help; she does not join the sea voyage. She fashions runes to convey a message, but Vingi, described as false and a speeder of hatred, alters them before delivering them. Atli’s warriors then set out and come to Limafjord, the home of the kings.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:8","fig:9"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Hospitality at Limafjord","summary":"At Limafjord the kings receive the visitors kindly, offering ale and kindling fires. They accept the gifts brought by the noble guest and hang them on the pillars, suspecting no craft or danger from the guests. Kostbera, Hogni’s wife, and Glaumvor, Gunnar’s wife, emerge, welcome the guests warmly, and see to their needs.","figure_refs":["fig:2","fig:3","fig:4","fig:6","fig:7"],"symbol_refs":["sym:1","sym:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"scene:5","label":"Gunnar and Hogni decide to travel","summary":"The guests or messengers question Hogni’s eagerness, noting that their guile would have been clear had the hosts been on guard. Gunnar declares he will go if Hogni will accompany him, and Hogni responds in agreement with Gunnar’s counsel, setting their departure in motion.","figure_refs":["fig:3","fig:4"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"scene:6","label":"Feast, rest, Kostbera’s rune reading and dream","summary":"A feast is held where renowned figures bring mead; many horns are used until the men drink deeply. Their mates prepare beds for them to rest. Kostbera, described as wise and skilled in rune‑craft, reads the letters by firelight but finds them so strange that she cannot understand them. Later, Hogni seeks his bed, and a clear‑souled person dreams and shares the dream with the warrior upon waking, suggesting an ominous warning.","figure_refs":["fig:3","fig:4","fig:6"],"symbol_refs":["sym:1","sym:3","sym:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:12","ev:13","ev:14"]}],"candidate_motifs":[{"id":"motif:1","label":"Deceptive invitation leads to fatal journey of heroic brothers","taxonomy_refs":["departure","sibling_pair"],"basis":"The prose outline states that Atli sends a message to the sons of Gjuki, they journey to his home, and Hogni and Gunnar are slain there. The opening stanzas depict secret plotting against Gjukis sons, Atli’s ill counsel and message to his kinsmen, and Gunnar and Hogni agreeing to travel. Although the deaths occur later in the poem, the passage establishes a fatal departure of a heroic sibling pair lured by a deceptive summons.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:5","ev:6","ev:11"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"The actual killing of the brothers is summarized in the prose note rather than shown in these stanzas; the motif identification relies on both summary and the initial narrative setup."},{"id":"motif:2","label":"Wise female figure uses runes and dreams as warnings","taxonomy_refs":["wisdom"],"basis":"A woman is called wise, understands secret plotting, and attempts to use her wisdom. She fashions runes to send a message, and later Kostbera is explicitly described as wise and cunning in rune‑craft, reading letters by firelight and experiencing a significant dream she tells to a warrior upon waking. These elements form a pattern of a wise woman employing esoteric writing and dreams to perceive and communicate danger.","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8","ev:13","ev:14"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"The text does not explicitly state that the unnamed wise woman and Kostbera are the same person, though the sequence and shared traits suggest continuity; this identification is kept implicit in the motif description."},{"id":"motif:3","label":"Hospitality, feasting, and gift exchange preceding betrayal","taxonomy_refs":["sacred_exchange"],"basis":"At Limafjord the kings show generous hospitality with ale and fires, accept and display gifts from the visitors, and their wives warmly care for the guests’ needs. A fair feast with mead and many horns follows. The prose note and surrounding narrative indicate that these hospitable exchanges occur in the lead‑up to the hosts’ eventual slaughter, suggesting a pattern where ritualized gift‑giving and feasting mask impending treachery.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:9","ev:10","ev:12"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The passage emphasizes social hospitality and exchange but does not explicitly mark these acts as ‘sacred’; mapping to a sacred_exchange motif extrapolates from the centrality of gift‑giving and feast customs in Germanic societies."},{"id":"motif:4","label":"Adaptation of foreign heroic legend into local poetic tradition","taxonomy_refs":[],"basis":"The note explicitly states that the Atlamol represents a Frankish blending of Burgundian and Attila legends, that the story was brought from South Germanic lands to the North, and that the Greenland poet adapted this imported narrative to the tastes of eleventh‑century Greenlanders by adding characters and episodes while preserving the basic outline. It also notes that later compilers paraphrased the poem faithfully in the Volsungasaga, showing ongoing transmission and adaptation.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"This motif concerns literary and cultural transmission rather than mythic plot elements; the taxonomy provided does not contain a specific category for adaptation or transmission, so no taxonomy_refs are assigned."}],"comparison_claims":[{"id":"claim:1","claim":"The passage explicitly describes the Atlamol as, in its bare outline, a Frankish blending of legends about the slaughter of the Burgundians and the death of Attila, indicating direct contact with and reworking of South Germanic and Frankish heroic traditions.","claim_level":"historical_contact","target":"Frankish and South Germanic heroic legends concerning the Burgundians and Attila","evidence_refs":["ev:2"],"counter_evidence_refs":[],"confidence":"high","limitations":"The note identifies the blended sources but does not detail specific shared narrative motifs beyond the general connection to Burgundian slaughter and Attila’s death."},{"id":"claim:2","claim":"The note observes that Hogni’s son who aids Guthrun in slaying Atli appears, under another name, in other late versions of the story, suggesting a common narrative pattern shared across multiple verse and prose traditions about Atli.","claim_level":"common_inheritance","target":"Other late verse and prose stories of Atli mentioned in the note","evidence_refs":["ev:3"],"counter_evidence_refs":[],"confidence":"medium","limitations":"The passage does not specify which texts or traditions these other versions are, nor does it describe the details of the overlapping episodes; the claim therefore remains general and confined to the stated character parallel."}],"evidence":[{"id":"ev:1","type":"summary","locator":"19195-19210 (Introductory note, opening)","quote_or_summary":"Explains that the Atlamol follows the Atlakvitha in Codex Regius, that its superscription indicating Greenland composition is generally accepted, mentions a polar bear reference and overall color supporting a Greenland origin, dates the poem near 1100, and notes its fairly good preservation despite some possible gaps and minor interpolations or omissions

A short prose preface then sets the narrative: Borgny, daughter of King Heithrek, cannot give birth until Oddrun, sister of Atli and beloved of Gunnar, arrives. The poem opens with Oddrun’s journey to Heithrek’s hall, her learning of Borgny’s secret lover Vilmund, her magical aid that enables Borgny to bear twin children, and Borgny’s thanksgiving invoking Frigg, Freyja, and other gods to bless Oddrun. Oddrun insists she is acting under an oath to help all who share warriors’ wealth, leading to a dispute with Borgny over loyalty and past words about Oddrun’s relationship with Gunnar. Oddrun then begins her own lament, recalling happiness in a hero’s hall, her father’s dying arrangements for her dowry and marriage to Grimhild’s son, and his designation of Brynhild as a helm-wearing wish-maid. The fragment concludes with Brynhild weaving in her bower, ruling lands and folk, and with the arrival of Fafnir’s slayer whose coming shakes earth and heaven and leads to a battle that destroys Brynhild’s city, after which she perceives her enemies’ evil wiles.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Oddrun is described as Atli’s sister and as having been beloved of Gunnar, son of Gjuki.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Heithrek is named as a king, and Borgny is identified as his daughter.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Vilmund is identified as Borgny’s lover and is called the heroes’ friend.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Borgny cannot give birth to a child until Oddrun comes to her, and she is said to lie in bitter pain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Oddrun learns of the maiden’s severe sickness, takes a black horse from the stall, saddles it, and rides over level ground to a loftily rising hall.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Inside the hall, a serving-maid informs Oddrun that Borgny lies in bitter pain and seeks Oddrun’s help.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The serving-maid tells Oddrun that Vilmund wrapped Borgny in bedclothes for five winters without her father’s knowledge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Oddrun goes to sit at Borgny’s knees and chants powerful magic charms to help her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After Oddrun’s chanting, a boy and a girl are born, described as the son and daughter of Hogni’s slayer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Once the twins are born and Borgny can speak, she invokes the holy ones, Frigg and Freyja and favoring gods, asking that they help Oddrun as Oddrun has saved her from sorrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Oddrun says she came not because Borgny had earned her aid but to fulfill an oath made long ago that she would bring aid to all when warriors shared their wealth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Borgny replies that Oddrun is wild and witless to speak with hatred, insisting she has followed Oddrun wherever she went, as if they had been born of brothers twain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Oddrun recalls an earlier evening when, after Oddrun gave a drink to Gunnar, Borgny said that no such deed had ever been done by a maiden except by Oddrun alone.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After this exchange, Oddrun, described as a sorrowing woman, sits down to tell the grief of her great troubles.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Oddrun recounts that she was once happy in a hero’s hall, loved by warriors and glad of her father’s gifts for five winters while he lived.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Oddrun reports that her dying father, the weary king, said she was to be dowered with red gold and wed in the South to Grimhild’s son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The same speech assigns Brynhild a helm to wear and calls her a bright wish-maid, stating that no nobler maiden would be born on earth if she is spared from death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Brynhild is depicted sitting at her weaving in her bower and having lands and folk.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"When Fafnir’s slayer sees Brynhild’s city, earth and heaven resound; a battle is fought with foreign swords, and the city Brynhild had is broken.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Soon after the battle, Brynhild becomes fully aware of the evil wiles directed against her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The introductory note states that Oddrun’s episode uses Gunnar’s death and implies that Atli’s vengeance on Gunnar and Hogni was due in part to his discovery of Gunnar’s love affair with Oddrun.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The note explains that the material forming the background of Oddrun’s story belongs to the German part of the legend and is closely paralleled in the Nibelungenlied, while Oddrun, Borgny, and Vilmund are Northern additions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The note observes that the geography of the Atli story in this poem is so chaotic that the original localization had lost significance when the poem was composed.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The manuscript heading is reported as ‘Of Borgny and Oddrun,’ and the poem is said to be well preserved, with clearly marked beginning and end.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Oddrun mentions warriors sharing wealth, suggesting a communal distribution of treasure among fighters in the hero’s hall.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11","ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Oddrun","description":"Sister of Atli and account of her past happiness and arranged marriage.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6","ev:9","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Borgny","description":"Daughter of King Heithrek and with Oddrun.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10349-l10450","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LAYS OF THE HEROES / VLUNDARKVITHA / THE LAY OF VLUND / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10349-10450","start":"10349","end":"10450","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Vlund promises to repair a broken piece of gold for Nithuth’s daughter Bothvild and then gives her beer until she falls asleep on the isle. He declares that he has almost completed his vengeance for the injuries he suffered at Nithuth’s hands and rises laughing into the air, while Bothvild weeps at his flight and her father’s expected wrath. At home, Nithuth’s wise wife enters the hall and finds Nithuth sleepless and joyless since the killing of his sons. Nithuth wishes to speak with Vlund and asks him what happened to the boys. Vlund first demands that Nithuth swear binding oaths by ship, shield, horse, and sword not to harm Vlund’s wife or bride, nor kill any wife or child he may have in Nithuth’s hall. Vlund then reveals that in the smithy Nithuth will find blood-sprinkled bellows and the hidden feet of his sons, whose heads Vlund struck off. Vlund explains that he set their skulls in silver and sent them to Nithuth, made gems from their eyes for Nithuth’s wife, and fashioned a brooch from their teeth for Bothvild, who is now pregnant with Vlund’s child. Nithuth responds in anguish, saying no words could wound him more, but admits that no one can bring Vlund down while he rides high in the clouds. Vlund rises laughing into the air and leaves Nithuth sitting in sadness. Nithuth then orders his thrall Thakkrath to summon Bothvild, adorned, to speak with him. He asks if it is true she was once on the isle with Vlund. Bothvild confirms she spent an hour of lust with Vlund there, regrets it, and says she had no power against such a man nor could she save herself from his strength.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Vlund promises to weld the break in a piece of gold so well that Bothvild’s father and mother The commentator explains cultural background: Yule-eve as a major new-year feast in the heathen North featuring feasting, vows, ghosts, witches, and especially powerful spirits; vows at the king's toast and a sacred boar consecrated to Freyr as integral Yule rites; and Hethin's terrible but unbreakable vow of vengeance for a troll-woman. Further notes describe duel customs on islands, time reckoned by nights, the fylgja as a female guardian spirit whose appearance foretells death and whose belief persisted into Scottish and Irish folklore, battlefields such as Wolf-Crag and Sun-Mountain, and Alf's victory attributed to a troll-woman's magic. The final prose note outlines an interpretive tradition in which Helgi Hjorvarthsson is reborn as Helgi Hundingsbane and Svava as Sigrun, explaining multiple contradictory accounts of Helgi's death, although the poems themselves do not mention such rebirths.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hrimgerth is said to refer to Svava, or to a protectress identified with her, as having saved Helgi and his ships from the vengeance of giantesses, though the stanza is metrically corrupt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A problematic passage is described as suggesting an identification of the Valkyries with the clouds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Atli and Helgi are described as holding Hrimgerth in conversation until sunrise, when the sun’s rays turn her into stone.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The note adds that in Norse tradition dwarfs rather than giants are normally the beings destroyed by sunlight, citing Alvissmol 16 and 35.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Yule feast in the heathen North is described as marking the new year and being a time of feasting, merrymaking, vows, ghosts, and witches, when spirits have their greatest power on Yule-eve.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Vows made as the king’s cup was passed at the Yule feast, called the king’s toast, are described as particularly sacred.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A sacred boar consecrated to Freyr is said to be an integral part of the Yule rites.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hethin’s vow, identified as enacting the vengeance of a troll-woman, is described as too sacred to be broken, even though he immediately realizes the horror of his oath.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Duels were commonly fought on islands, probably to avoid treacherous interference, giving rise to the term 'isle-going' for a duel.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A duel was generally fought three days after the challenge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Reckoning time by nights instead of days is described as a common practice among Germanic and Scandinavian peoples.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The fylgja is defined as a female guardian spirit whose appearance generally betokens death.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Belief in the fylgja or following-spirit is said to have been common throughout the North and to have survived into recent times in Scottish and Irish folklore.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Individuals and sometimes whole families could have following-spirits, but it was highly unusual for a person to have more than one.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Alf is identified as the son of Hrothmar, who killed Helgi’s grandfather and was later killed by Helgi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The battlefield name Frekastein (Wolf-Crag) appears several times in the Helgi lays as a designation for battlefields.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Alf is said to deserve no credit for a victory at Wolf-Crag, because it was due to the troll-woman’s magic rather than his own prowess.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Hethin will satisfy Svava’s vow by becoming famous as the slayer of Alf and declares that he will not return to Svava until he has won fame at places such as Rogheim (Home of Battle) and Rothulsfjoll (Sun-Mountain).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A scholar, Gering, is said to think that the reborn Helgi Hjorvarthsson was Helgi Hundingsbane and that Svava became Sigrun, based on an interpretive tradition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The annotator’s explanation is that because there were many stories about Helgi and the hero died in many irreconcilable ways, tradition had him born over again several times to account for his many deaths and avoid splitting him into several Helgis.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The note explicitly states that the poems themselves do not mention Helgi’s rebirth; the idea is attributed to the annotator, probably drawing on current tradition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The annotator’s identification of Svava as a Valkyrie and of the setting as Norway is described as largely imaginative and based on minimal textual hints.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Yule-eve is associated with ghosts, witches, and spirits whose power is considered greatest at that time.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Helgi Hjorvarthsson","description":"Hero of the lay
