Guthrun, dwelling on Hogni’s fate, urges Hogni’s son to seek vengeance; Atli is soon slain by Hogni’s son with Guthrun’s involvement. Mortally wounded, Atli awakens, realizes his injuries are fatal, and asks who has killed Buthli’s son. Guthrun openly admits her guilt and that of Hogni’s son; Atli accuses her of murderous betrayal. He recalls how he sought Guthrun’s hand, brought her home with a host of men, and describes former prosperity, abundant cattle, wealth, and generous bride-gifts (jewels, slaves, and handmaidens). He complains that Guthrun valued these as nothing, secretly prevented him from gaining the land left by Buthli, made his mother weep, and left him without marital joy. Guthrun counters that Atli lies, calling him cruel; she says his early quarrels with his brothers led to battles, sending half the sons of his house to hell and destroying all that should have done good.

Guthrun then recounts that she and her two brothers left their land and traveled with Sigurth, each steering a ship as they sought their fate until they came to the East. There they slew a king, seized his land, compelled princes to serve them out of fear, summoned men from the forest whom they hoped to find guiltless, and enriched many who were bereft. She says the Hun-king was slain and his young widow sat weeping, but that seeking Atli’s house brought even worse sorrow; her husband was a hero whose loss was hard. Guthrun describes Atli as never returning from the Thing as a victor in quarrels or battle, being yielding and lacking firm will, suffering in silence.

As Atli is dying, he again says Guthrun lies and urges her to be kind once for the honor of them both when he is borne forth. Guthrun promises to buy a ship and a bright-hued coffin, to wax the shroud to wrap his body, and to care for all as if they had always been dear. Atli dies, his heirs’ grief doubles, and Guthrun, described as wise, fulfills her promise regarding his burial. She then seeks death herself but must wait days before she dies. The notes interpret a reference to gold as Sigurth's treasure claimed by Atli, highlight Guthrun's indirect responsibility for Brynhild's death, and cite a Volsungasaga passage in which Hogni accuses Atli of breaking peace, imprisoning and murdering kin, and taking their wealth, implying the killing of Guthrun's mother Grimhild and a niece. They compare variants of a heart-cutting episode involving Hjalli, Beiti, and Hogni across Atlamol, Atlakvitha, and Volsungasaga, and mention a likely-lost stanza describing Gunnar's casting into a serpents' den. Gunnar's harp-playing with his toes while his hands are bound, and his death, are linked to Oddrunargratr and Atlakvitha. Later notes identify Guthrun as a 'wise one' and discuss her speech about guilt and requital, whose precise reference remains unclear.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Guthrun is described as having warlike deeds and ferocity of heart.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Guthrun is portrayed as a warrior who outdoes Brynhild in combat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Guthrun’s ferocity is devoted to the defense of her brothers.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Kriemhild in the Nibelungenlied is famed for cruelty and fierceness of heart but does no actual fighting.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Kriemhild’s ferocity is directed against Gunther and especially Hagene, for whose slaying she rather than Etzel is held responsible.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The commentator states that Kriemhild’s ferocity seems to have inspired the Atlamol poet to make Guthrun into a warrior surpassing Brynhild.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The mention of Atli’s brother in Atlamol is explained as a reminiscence of earlier tradition in which Etzel’s brother Bldelin (Bleda) is slain by Dancwart in the Nibelungenlied.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The two sons of Bera are identified as Snvar and Solar, and her brother as Orkning.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Atli is identified as ‘the warrior’, and the total of thirty warriors is noted as perhaps echoing Thjothrek’s thirty warriors.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Eighteen warriors are said to be killed by Snvar, Solar, and Orkning; Vingi is killed by the whole company, leaving eleven warriors, as Atli claims, although this leaves Gunnar and Hogni with no recorded kills.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Five brothers are sons of Buthli; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1604-l1630","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1604-1630","start":"1604","end":"1630","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Feridn, having reached the age of sixteen, descends from the mountain where he has been living and stays on the plain below. He asks his mother, Farnuk, why Zohk killed his father, and when she tells him the sad story, he resolves to take revenge on the tyrant. Farnuk urges him not to be rash, reminding him that he is young, alone, and without allies, while his enemy is ruler of the world and backed by armies. She advises that if he is destined to be king, he should wait until the Almighty provides him with the means. Feridn, displeased with her caution, insists that Heaven inspires him and that he will cast the tyrant down from his palace to the dust. His mother calls him imprudent and begs him to pause and not perish in a wild enterprise against imperial power. It is then recorded that Zohk’s fear of Feridn grows so intense that he becomes increasingly irritable and wastes away, while people of all ranks continually speak of the young invader and expect his arrival. Eventually Feridn comes, subdues Zohk, and extinguishes his power.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Feridn attains his sixteenth year and descends from the mountain to the plain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After descending, Feridn asks his mother why Zohk killed his father.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Farnuk tells Feridn the melancholy story of his father’s death at Zohk’s hands.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Upon hearing the story, Feridn resolves to take revenge on Zohk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Farnuk tries to divert Feridn from his determination, saying he is young, friendless, and alone, while Zohk is master of the world and supported by armies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Farnuk tells Feridn that if it is his destiny to become king, he should wait until the Almighty provides the means.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Feridn is displeased with his mother’s caution and replies that Heaven inspires him and that he will quickly bring the tyrant from his palace to the dust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Farnuk calls Feridn imprudent, questions whether he can contend against imperial provision.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Zohk","description":"A tyrant who killed Feridn’s father, described as master of the world and His mother frames his future kingship in terms of destiny, and he ultimately overthrows the tyrant, suggesting a pattern of a destined hero departing seclusion to claim or restore rightful rule.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:5"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The passage mentions destiny to become a king but does not narrate Feridn’s actual accession, so the royal_legitimacy aspect is implied rather than explicit here."},{"id":"motif:2","label":"Maternal warning and delay before dangerous heroic enterprise","taxonomy_refs":["wisdom","initiation","departure"],"basis":"Farnuk repeatedly warns Feridn that he is young, alone, and facing imperial power, urging him to avoid precipitate action and to wait until the Almighty grants him the means to fulfill his destiny. Zohk, the unjust killer of Feridn’s father, is eventually subdued and loses his power, fitting a pattern where a divinely guided hero carries out judgment against oppressive rule.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The narrative reports divine inspiration and destiny but does not explicitly depict a pronouncement of judgment or direct command from the deity; the judicial framing is interpretive."},{"id":"motif:4","label":"Tyrant weakened by fear of a widely spoken-of avenger","taxonomy_refs":["royal_legitimacy"],"basis":"Zohk’s dread of Feridn grows so intense that he becomes irritable and wastes away, while people of all ranks continuously talk about the young invader and expect his approach. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l156-l234","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Persian Literature, Volume 1 / PERSIAN LITERATURE / SPECIAL INTRODUCTION; lines 156-234","start":"156","end":"234","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage outlines the historical and literary context of Firdusi and his epic. After the Arab conquest of Persia and the fall of the Sassanian dynasty, Persian cultural and religious forms were outwardly replaced by Arabic language and Islamic names for the divine, yet the \"Persian spirit\" and memories of a glorious past endured in poetry and song, maintaining a sense of opposition to Arab dominance and preserving historical individuality. It describes earlier Zoroastrian and Persian sources of epic material in the Avesta, oral tradition, and written works such as the \"Zarer\" and \"History of King Ardeshir,\" culminating in Dihkan Danishwar’s \"Chodainameh\" (Book of Kings) in Pahlavi, which later provided material for Abu Mansur’s neo-Persian \"Shah Nameh\" and Dakiki’s versification. Firdusi, born in Tus in 935, is depicted as a poet whose name may mean \"garden\" and who gathered the imaginative \"flowers\" of his people into one epic \"garden.\" His life becomes intertwined with Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna and a brilliant court circle of poets and scientists. Firdusi labored on the Shah Nameh from 971, dedicated an early form in 999 to Ahmad ibn Muhammad of Chalandsha, and completed it in 1010 while serving effectively as court poet to Mahmud and composing panegyrics to him. A traditional tale recounts that Mahmud promised gold per verse but sent silver instead; Firdusi rejected this payment, distributed it, and left the court. A biting lampoon against Mahmud was allegedly bought off by a friend so the Sultan would not see it. The poet then wandered through various cities, wrote a more explicitly Islamic poem \"Yusuf and Salikha\" in Bagdad, and eventually returned to Tus around 1021/1025, where he died and was buried in his own garden because his views were considered unorthodox for burial in sacred ground. Another story says that Mahmud later repented and sent the long-promised gold, which arrived only after Firdusi’s funeral had passed another city gate; his daughter used the gold to build a hospice. The narrator treats these stories as pretty but partly uncertain, yet meaningful for understanding Firdusi’s fate and his relationship with Mahmud.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Arabs, inspired by the zeal of Mohammed, conquered Persia; Merv fell in A.D. 657 and the last Sassanian king, Yezdegird III, was killed, making the Arabs nominally supreme.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After the conquest, Turkish speech predominated at court and Arabic script became universal in Persia.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Despite political conquest, the \"temper\" of the old Arsacides and Sassanians and the Persian spirit continued to live on.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ormuzd was replaced by Allah and Ahriman by Satan in religious terminology.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Persians are described as having a glorious past that placed the conquered above the conqueror.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Persia’s past was kept alive in the myth-loving mind of the people, through the songs of poets and the lays of minstrels.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A continuous opposition of Persian to Arab existed despite their mingling in Islam; Persian Shiites oppose Sunnites of the broader Muslim world as a survival of racial antipathy.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The fall of the Umayyid caliphs at Damascus and the rise of separate dynasties in Spain, Sicily, Egypt, and Tunis encouraged Persians to preserve their historical individuality and ancient traditions.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Epic materials of Persia are said to be found in the Avesta and in traditions handed down orally from mouth to mouth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Some epic traditions were written in works such as the \"Zarer, or Memorials of the Warriors\" (A.D. 500), the \"History of King Ardeshir\" (A.D. 600), and various Chronicles of the Persian Kings.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Baisonghur’s preface to the \"Shah Nameh\" reports attempts by Farruchani, Ramin, and especially Dihkan Danishwar to compile a complete story of the nation’s history.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Dihkan Danishwar’s \"Chodainameh\" (Book of Kings) was written in middle-Persian using Pahlavi writing.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Abu Mansur, lord of Tus, had a \"Shah Nameh\" prepared in neo-Persian based on the \"Chodainameh\".","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In 980, a Zoroastrian poet named Dakiki versified a thousand lines of this neo-Persian Book of Kings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Firdusi (Abul Kasim Mansur or Ahmed) was born in the city of Tus in A.D. 935.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The narrator suggests that Firdusi’s name may derive from the Persian-Arabic word for \"garden.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Firdusi is likened to a gardener who gathered into one garden all the beautiful flowers blossoming in the fancy of his people through his great epic.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Firdusi’s life story has been elaborated by posterity, and his fortune is closely linked with the fame of Mahmud of Ghazna, the first to bear the title \"Sultan\" and to carry Mohammed and the prophets into India.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Mahmud of Ghazna is described as having a \"Round Table\" including poets like Farruchi, Unsuri, Minutsheri and scientists such as Biruni and Avicenna, with Firdusi among his intimates.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Before leaving Tus, Firdusi had essentially finished his epic in rough form and in 999 dedicated it to Ahmad ibn Muhammad of Chalandsha.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Firdusi had worked steadily on the epic since 971 and continued to refine it while serving almost as a court poet to Mahmud, who is portrayed as a patron of letters and the son of a Turkish slave.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"On February 25, 1010, Firdusi completed his epic, having inserted many verses in praise of Mahmud as his master.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"A traditional story relates that Mahmud promised Firdusi a gold dirhem for each line but instead sent sixty thousand silver dirhems, which Firdusi rejected, distributed in gifts, and then left Mahmud’s service.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Firdusi later wrote a lampoon full of bitter satire against Mahmud, whose praises he had formerly sung; this satire was reportedly bought by a friend for one thousand dirhems a verse so that Mahmud would not see it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"After leaving Mahmud, Firdusi wandered, spending time in Herat, Taberistān, and at the Buyide court in Bagdad.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"At Bagdad, Firdusi composed \"Yusuf and Salikha,\" described as a poem \"Mohammedan in spirit\" in contrast to the more Persian spirit of the \"Shah Nameh.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Around 1021 or 1025, Firdusi returned to Tus, where he died and was buried in his own garden Hearing that King Svafnir's daughter Sigrlin surpasses all others in beauty, he sends the jarl's son Atli to woo her. Atli's first mission fails despite a prior encounter in the woods with a speaking bird that tells him of Sigrlin and demands sacred offerings—altars and gold‑horned cattle—in exchange for helping Hjorvarth win her. Atli reports difficulties crossing high mountains and wading a river, and that Sigrlin is still denied. On a second expedition, Hjorvarth himself travels; from a mountain they see Svavaland burning. Camping by a stream, Atli discovers a house guarded by a sleeping great bird, kills it, and finds Sigrlin and Alof hidden inside. The bird is revealed to be the jarl Franmar, who has taken eagle form by magic to guard them from an enemy king, Hrothmar, who has slain Svafnir and ravaged the land. Hjorvarth takes Sigrlin as wife, and Atli takes Alof. Their son is a mighty, silent youth to whom no name clings. Sitting on a hill, he sees nine Valkyries ride by; the fairest, Svava, daughter of King Eylimi, speaks, names him Helgi, and tells him of a powerful serpent-marked sword lying at Sigarsholm that embodies fame, courage, and fear. Svava, a Valkyrie who rides air and sea, later shields Helgi in battle. Helgi rebukes Hjorvarth for allowing Hrothmar to keep the wealth that once belonged to their kin and for not avenging his maternal grandfather. Hjorvarth offers him a following; Helgi takes the named sword, goes with Atli, kills Hrothmar, and performs many great deeds. He also slays the giant Hati on a mountain. Later Helgi and Atli lie with their ships in Hatafjord; while Atli keeps the first watch, Hrimgerth, Hati's daughter, questions them. {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l12190-l12307","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR / CAPTURE OF THE BRAZEN FORTRESS; lines 12190-12307","start":"12190","end":"12307","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Isfendiyr, wanting to capture Arjsp's fortress, claims he once vowed to give a splendid banquet if Heaven favored him and invites the king and his troops. Disguised as a merchant, he arranges for the feast to be held on the lofty top of the fortress with a large fire. During the banquet Arjsp and his warriors become drunk on wine; Kherd then has a great pile of wood lit, and the smoke and flame rise as a prearranged signal. Bashtan, seeing this, attacks the fortress with two thousand horsemen, killing those he meets while using Isfendiyr's name. Arjsp, enjoying the wine and music, is suddenly warned that Isfendiyr has entered the fort, and he dispatches his son Kahram with fifty thousand horsemen to resist, while other forces defend the walls and his person.

At night Isfendiyr opens chests that conceal one hundred and sixty warriors, arms them and another hundred disguised as camel-drivers and servants, and leads this band to where Arjsp has taken refuge. They slaughter those defending the "sacred" area. Isfendiyr's sisters arrive and indicate Arjsp's chamber; Isfendiyr wakes the king from his drunken stupor, and the two fight fiercely until Isfendiyr splits Arjsp in two. Two wives, two daughters, and one sister of Arjsp are captured and entrusted to Isfendiyr's son to be taken home. Isfendiyr then exits the palace and kills many enemies at the fortress gates.

Meanwhile Kahram, hard pressed in battle with Bashtan, learns from watchmen that Arjsp has been slain and the garrison destroyed. He confirms the news at the fort, then leads his remaining troops against Isfendiyr and his two hundred and sixty warriors. Bashtan's force strikes from the rear, leaving Kahram nearly isolated. Isfendiyr challenges him to single combat, throws him, binds him, and beheads him, with verses reflecting on how a single blow removes a throne and how heads and crowns are trampled in battle.

After Kahram's death, Isfendiyr proclaims a full pardon for all who join him, noting that the land now has no king and likening the world without a governor to a headless trunk. The people submit, and he reassures them with gentle words befitting a generous and prudent ruler. He writes to his father about his victory, subdues surrounding provinces, executes those who remain hostile, and takes Arjsp's women into his service, giving their daughters to his own sons. A closing poem laments that no warrior of Chn or king of Trn remains, that Arjsp's former, mountainous realm is desolated and ruled by a stranger, and that all its treasures and royal pavilion have been seized, sharing the fate of Arjsp himself.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Isfendiyr tells the king that in a time of great Despite Zal’s prayers and careful upbringing of the child, Shughad is sent to the king of Kabul and marries his daughter. Later, Rustem’s harsh tribute collection in Kabul angers the king; Shughad, resentful of Rustem’s treatment of him, conspires with the king to kill Rustem by feigning a quarrel and luring him onto a road where deep pits bristling with swords are hidden. After a staged insult at a banquet, Shughad appeals to Rustem, who comes to Kabul, pardons the humbly-appearing king, and is lavishly entertained while the pits are dug. Invited to a hunting excursion, Rustem rides out on his horse Rakush; the horse senses danger and refuses to advance until beaten, then plunges into the concealed pits and, after seven falls and escapes, both horse and rider emerge mortally wounded. Realizing the treachery, Rustem rebukes Shughad, who replies that God has decreed this vengeance for Rustem’s past bloodshed; the king offers medicine and a matchless balm in feigned pity, but Rustem rejects it, denounces their treachery, and foretells that his son Fermurz will avenge him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Firdusi is race.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The prophecy causes horror and woe throughout Sistan and Iran, and Zal grieves the king then meets him barefoot in apparent humility, receives forgiveness, and offers lavish hospitality, only to invite him on a forest sporting excursion along a road where concealed sword pits have been prepared specifically to kill him.","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"This fits a wider pattern of treacherous feasts and deceptive invitations, but the passage only depicts this one instance without explicit moralizing about hospitality."},{"id":"motif:5","label":"Hero’s repeated descent into deep, dark pits that serve as his grave","taxonomy_refs":["hero_descent"],"basis":"Rustem and Rakush fall into a \"deep, dark, and perilous\" pit \"bristled o’er with swords\" that the narrative says will become his grave; they struggle out only to fall into additional pits, repeating this seven times before collapsing wounded at the edge of the seventh, effectively undergoing a multi-stage downward passage into man-made depths culminating in death.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The pits are engineered traps rather than a mythologized underworld, so the link to broader hero-descent motifs is structural and thematic rather than explicit."},{"id":"motif:6","label":"Divine vengeance repays a warrior for bloodshed","taxonomy_refs":["divine_judgment"],"basis":"As Rustem lies wounded, Shughad declares that \"for all the blood that thou hast shed, God has decreed this awful vengeance—now thy time is come,\" framing the hero’s death as a divinely ordered judgment for past violence.","evidence_refs":["ev:7"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"This interpretation of Rustem’s fate is voiced by the betrayer Shughad; the narrative does not explicitly confirm that God’s judgment is the true cause, so the attribution remains within the character’s speech."},{"id":"motif:7","label":"Animal companion senses danger but its warning is ignored","taxonomy_refs":["wisdom"],"basis":"On the way to the sporting ground, Rakush abruptly stops and refuses to advance along the planned route, only moving after Rustem angrily strikes him, at which point the horse leaps into the hidden pit; Isfendiyr refuses to go further and orders Rustem to accompany him to Iran, prompting Rustem to boast of his heroic feats and offer protection in exchange for being treated as an honored guest. Offended by Rustem’s pride and seating himself on the prince’s right hand, Isfendiyr retaliates by maligning Rustem’s lineage through a hostile account of Zal’s demon-like birth and fosterage by the Simurgh. Rustem counters with a genealogy linking both heroes to ancient royal ancestors and lists his many conquests of kings and demons, while Isfendiyr insists that Rustem remains a dependent of the Kais, claims his own Heft-khan and the capture of the Brazen Fortress as superior, and presents himself as a sovereign-prophet who has spread a Heaven-derived fire religion. Rustem replies that Isfendiyr undertook his trials with a great army, whereas Rustem faced his Heft-khan almost alone with only his horse Rakhsh and his sword, rescuing captives and slaying monsters in dark caves.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Bashtan tells his brother that their enemy Rustem had come into their power but was him home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Isfendiyr becomes indignant at Rustem’s boasting, restrains his impulse to attack him with a dagger, gives him a scornful content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l13730-l13825","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BAHMAN / HMAI AND THE BIRTH OF DRB / DRB AND DR / SIKANDER; lines 13730-13825","start":"13730","end":"13825","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Failaks, near death, crowns his son Sikander, appoints Arist (a disciple of Afltn) as vizir, and exhorts Sikander to humility, justice, and attentiveness to counsel. Sikander initially follows this advice. After his accession, the Persian king Dr demands the usual tribute from Rm, but Sikander reverses the demand and threatens to conquer Persia and even the whole world if refused. Dr raises an army as Sikander advances, and their forces meet on Persia’s frontier. Sikander then enters the Persian camp disguised as an envoy to assess the enemy. He tells Dr that Sikander has come not only to fight but to learn the empire’s history, laws, and customs and to travel through the world, asking for peaceful passage while declaring that Sikander does not fear war. Dr is struck by the envoy’s noble bearing and questions his identity, suspecting he may be Sikander, but the envoy denies it. At a banquet, Dr gives the envoy wine in a cup; the envoy drinks but keeps the cup, explaining that in his country an envoy retains any cup placed in his hands. Amused, Dr gives him additional cups, which he also keeps. During a later feast, someone recognizes Sikander and quietly informs Dr. Realizing the danger, Sikander grabs the four cups, flees the tent, mounts his horse, and escapes under cover of night despite a pursuit. Back in his own camp, he shows the four golden cups to Arist and his courtiers as trophies taken from Dr’s table and as proof that he has gauged the enemy’s strength, and he prepares for battle. The armies fight for seven days without decision; on the eighth day Dr is routed and pursued with heavy losses by the Rms to the Euphrates. Sikander occupies the capital. Dr rallies forces again but is defeated a second time. After this, Sikander seeks to win over the people; he tells them that Persia is his inheritance and that he is descended from Drb, promising just and paternal care, and the legions align with him, consolidating his rule.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Failaks, before his death, places the crown of sovereignty on Sikander’s head content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l13449-l13550","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF ISFENDIYR / THE DEATH OF RUSTEM / BAHMAN / HMAI AND THE BIRTH OF DRB; lines 13449-13550","start":"13449","end":"13550","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Queen Hma is praised as a just and generous ruler. She bears a son, secretly entrusts him to a nurse, but publicly declares he died. Fearing that the boy will one day displace her from the throne, she has him wrapped in rich garments, sealed in a box, and, via two trusted servants at night, cast into the Euphrates, reasoning that if God wills, he will survive elsewhere. The narrator likens the box to a little ark and reflects that human schemes are overruled by Heaven. A washerman finds the box, opens it, and discovers costly clothes, jewels, and a sleeping infant. Since their own child has just died, he and his wife see the baby as a gift from God; she suckles him, and they name him Drb. They keep the wealth, become prosperous, and move to another country to avoid discovery. As Drb grows, he excels other boys, especially at wrestling, but refuses to help with washing clothes, to his foster-father’s grief; verse describes his kingly spirit and noble origin. At school he surpasses his master, who praises his extraordinary intelligence and predicts a high future office. Drb longs for advanced training and a fine horse of Irk to learn warfare, but his foster-father is too poor, and the youth fasts in despair until his foster-mother sacrifices a valuable item to buy the horse. Drb devotes himself tirelessly to martial and intellectual training, then questions his origins. His foster-mother tells how he was found in the river-box, which relieves him of the shame of low birth and convinces him he is of higher lineage. She gives him two rubies from the box; he wears one and sells the other to fund travel. Meanwhile the king of Rm invades Irn. Hma orders her general Rishnawd to raise an army and invites ambitious young men to join. Drb eagerly enlists and is presented to Hma, who is struck by his royal appearance and briefly feels a mother’s instinct, thinking he must be of Kainian stock, though the feeling quickly passes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hma is described as a wise, generous, and just ruler under whose government even the poor become rich and no misfortune occurs.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After giving birth to a son, Hma entrusts him to a nurse to be raised secretly while publicly declaring that the child died the same day he was born.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When the boy is seven months old, Hma wraps him in rich garments, places him in a box, fastens the cover, and orders two confidential servants at night to throw the box into the Euphrates.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Hma reasons that if her son remains in the city he will end her authority and take the crown, so she decides to cast him into the river, leaving his preservation to God and hoping he might be reared in another country.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The narrative likens the box He converses with an earthen urn and remembers a potter, imagines spilled wine comforting the dead, likens the body to a tent and people to bubbles poured from the sky, and describes life as a phantom caravan from nothing to nothing. He seeks \"THE SECRET\" behind a veil, hints at an elusive Master who plays a cosmic drama, and contrasts rational theology and prophetic revelation with the immediate certainty of mortality. Wine and the grape appear as ministers, spouses, angels and warrior-kings that dispel fear, confound sectarian disputes, and offer joy in place of speculative hopes of paradise or fears of hell, while the Soul ultimately reports that it itself is heaven and hell.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker addresses a \"THEE IN ME\" who works behind a Veil and lifts his hands to seek a lamp amid darkness.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A responding voice \"from Without\" calls itself \"THE ME WITHIN THEE BLIND.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker leans to the lip of a \"poor earthen Urn\" to learn the secret of his life, and the urn tells him to drink while alive because once dead he will not return.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker thinks the answering vessel once lived and drank, and he kisses its passive lip, imagining how many kisses it has taken and given.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker recalls watching a potter thumping wet clay, which with its obliterated tongue seems to murmur, \"Gently, Brother, gently, pray!\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A story \"from of Old\" is mentioned about a clod of saturated earth cast by a Maker into human mould and passed down generations.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The text suggests that drops spilled from cups into the earth may sink down to quench the fire of anguish in some hidden eye far beneath and long ago.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A tulip is described as looking up from the soil for her morning drink of heavenly vintage, and humans are urged to do likewise until Heaven inverts them like an empty cup.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker advises no longer being perplexed with human or divine questions, casting tomorrow’s tangle to the winds, and playing with the \"Cypress-slender Minister of Wine.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"He observes that if the wine and lip end in the same \"Yes\" as everything else, one is today what one was yesterday and will be no less tomorrow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"An \"Angel of the darker Drink\" is described as shrink.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The soul is said to be able to fling the dust aside and ride naked on the air of heaven, and it is called a shame for it to remain crippled in a clay carcass.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The body is likened to a tent where a Sultan takes one day’s rest on the way to the {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14812-l14977","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM / THE RUBIYT; lines 14812-14977","start":"14812","end":"14977","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Wake! For the Sun, who scatter'd into flight
The Stars before him from the Field of Night,
Drives Night along with them from Heav'n, and strikes
The Sultan's Turret with a Shaft of Light.

...","summary":"A first-person speaker, in a series of quatrains, meditates on dawn, time, mortality, and the futility of trying to know ultimate origins or destiny. He invokes prophets, ancient kings, ruined palaces, and the growth of flowers and herbs from the bodies of the dead to illustrate the transience of worldly glory and human life. He contrasts promised paradises and theological debates with the immediate pleasures of wine, companionship, poetry, and the beauty of nature, urging a carpe diem attitude. The speaker recounts seeking wisdom from religious authorities and even describes a visionary ascent through seven gates to the throne of Saturn, yet he still cannot solve the "master-knot" of human fate and finds the ultimate door and veil of reality closed to him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Sun appears at dawn, scattering the Stars, driving Night from Heaven, and striking the Sultan's Turret with a shaft of light.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Before a false dawn fades, a Voice within the Tavern asks why the drowsy Worshipper nods outside when the Temple within is prepared.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"As the Cock crows, those standing before the Tavern call to open the door, saying they have little time to stay and may not return once departed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At the New Year, old desires revive and the thoughtful Soul withdraws to solitude, where Moses' white hand appears on a bough and Jesus breathes from the ground.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The city of Iram is said to have vanished with its Rose, and the location of Jamshid's seven-ringed Cup is unknown, yet a ruby still glows in the vine and many gardens bloom by the water.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"David's lips are locked in silence, while the Nightingale cries in lofty Pehlev for red wine to redden the Rose's sallow cheek.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker urges filling the Cup and throwing off the Winter-garment of repentance in the fire of Spring, noting that the Bird of Time has but a little way to flutter and is already on the wing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Whether in Nishapur or Babylon, and whether the Cup is sweet or bitter, the Wine of Life oozes drop by drop and the Leaves of Life fall one by one.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Each morning brings a thousand roses, but not the Rose of yesterday, and the month that brings the Rose will also take away Jamshid and Kai-Kobad.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker dismisses concern with Kai-Kobad, Kai-Khosru, Zal, Rustem, and Hatim, and offers peace to Mahmud while inviting a companion to walk along a narrow strip of herbage dividing desert from sown land where the names of Slave and Sultan are forgotten.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker imagines an ideal scene of a Book of Verses, a Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread, and a beloved companion singing in the Wilderness, which would make the Wilderness a sufficient Paradise.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Some people seek worldly glories and others long for the Prophet's Paradise, but the speaker recommends taking immediate cash and letting distant credit go, ignoring a distant drum.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A Rose "laughing" into the world tells the listener to tear off the silken tassel of the purse and scatter its treasure on the garden.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Those who hoarded golden grain and those who scattered it to the winds both become an earth that no one digs up again.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Worldly hope either turns to ashes or briefly prospers and then vanishes like snow on the dusty face of the desert.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The world is compared to a battered caravanserai whose portals alternate Night and Day, where many Sultans with pomp stayed their destined hour and then departed.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Lion and the Lizard are said to inhabit the courts where Jamshid once gloried and drank deeply, and a Wild Ass stamps over the head of the hunter Bahrām without breaking his sleep.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The speaker imagines that the reddest Roses grow where a buried Caesar bled, and that each Hyacinth in the garden fell into the earth from some once lovely head.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A tender green herb along the river bank is described as possibly springing from some once lovely lip beneath, so the listener is urged to lean on it lightly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The beloved is asked to fill a Cup that clears today of past regrets and future fears, for tomorrow the speaker may be with yesterday's seven thousand years.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Those the speaker loved, the loveliest and best, have drunk their cup and silently gone to rest, and the current merrymakers in the room will themselves descend beneath the couch of earth to make a couch for others.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The speaker urges making the most of what can still be spent before descending into dust, where people lie as dust under dust, without wine, song, singer, or end.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"A Muezzin from a Tower of Darkness calls both those who prepare for today and those who stare after tomorrow fools, saying their reward is neither here nor there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"All the Saints and Sages who wisely discussed the Two Worlds are mocked, their words scattered, and their mouths stopped with dust.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"In youth, the speaker frequently visited Doctor and Saint and heard great arguments about religious questions but always left with no more understanding than he entered.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The speaker says he sowed the seed of Wisdom with his own hand and worked to make it grow, but his harvest was the realization, "I came like Water, and like Wind I go."","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The speaker describes entering the universe without knowing why or whence, like water flowing, and leaving it like wind along the waste without knowing whither.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"He describes being hurried into existence without asking whence and hurried out without asking whither, calling this an insolence that must be drowned by many cups of forbidden wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The speaker claims to have risen from Earth's centre through the Seventh Gate, sat on the Throne of Saturn, and unravelled many knots along the road but not the master-knot of human fate.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"He describes a Door for which he found no key and a Veil through which he could not see; after some brief talk of "Me" and "Thee," there was no more of them.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"Earth, the mourning Seas, and rolling Heaven with its revealed and hidden signs are all said to be unable to answer the speaker's questions.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker / Narrator","description":"The first-person voice reflecting on time, death, pleasure, Isfendiyr angrily accuses Rustem of treachery; Rustem swears he is innocent and even offers to hand over his brother Zra, his son Fermurz, and his entire family to King Gushtasp for punishment, but Isfendiyr insists he will kill Rustem himself. The two champions fight with arrows: Rustem’s shafts do not harm Isfendiyr, while Isfendiyr’s arrows severely wound Rustem and his horse Rakush, who eventually flees riderless, leading Zra to discover his brother bleeding on the field. After an exchange of taunts and demands that Rustem submit to fetters, the opponents agree to postpone the fight until the next day; Isfendiyr sends the severed heads of his slain kinsmen to King Gushtasp with a letter and privately admits to Bashtan that Rustem seems superhumanly tough. Back in camp, Rustem’s father Zal tends his many wounds; Rustem describes Isfendiyr’s brazen, rock-like body and considers secretly withdrawing from the struggle. Zal warns that their family would then be enslaved and recalls the Simurgh’s promise to help if one of her feathers is burned in time of adversity; he burns the feather on a high place, the Simurgh appears, and after hearing of Rustem’s plight and seeing the wounded Rakush, she removes the arrows and heals the wounds with one of her content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14382-l14506","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"DRB AND DR / SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD; lines 14382-14506","start":"14382","end":"14506","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A series of editorial footnotes to Firdusi’s Shahnameh explaining cultural customs, lexical items, similes, and parallels to other literatures. Topics include the seclusion and influence of Eastern noblewomen, poetic imagery (moon, liver as seat of love, new moon simile), military practices and devastation, execution on a tree or stake (dar), royal correspondence on perfumed paper, multi-day feasting before journeys, kinship and command relationships among heroes, heroic boasting compared with Achilles, counsel of the veteran general Gudarz, metaphors of repentance involving ashes, descriptions of palace garden kiosks, coronation and festival customs of showering kings and people with gold, pearls, gems, and diamonds, golden slippers in battle array, the term sandurus, elephant banners indicating royal descent, and a note that a character is Rustem’s son-in-law.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Tahmineh tells Rustem that no one has ever seen her outside her private chamber or heard the sound of her voice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Women of rank in Persia and other parts of the East are described as living in seclusion (zenanas) that are comfortable and not considered a hardship, and Eastern women are said to have substantial influence and power despite their seclusion.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"An old song quoted from Sir Henry Wotton’s poem addresses the ‘meaner beauties of the night’ (stars) as common people of the skies who are overshadowed when the moon rises, and this is cited as containing a similar idea to a passage in Firdusi.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A kus is defined as a tymbal or large brass drum beaten in the palaces or camps of Eastern princes.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the Shahnameh, whenever an army was set in motion, the inhabitants and country—whether hostile or friendly—were given up to plunder and devastation and everything in the army’s progress was burnt and destroyed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sohrab is described in the original as being wounded in the liver.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Both Oriental and Greek and Roman poets are said to place the residence of love in the liver.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Letters from royal and distinguished personages in the East are usually written on perfumed paper covered with gold devices, scented here with amber, and the degree of embellishment is regulated according to the rank of the writer.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Four days of uninterrupted feasting are said to have been consumed before the commencement of an important undertaking or setting out on a journey, presented as an ancient practice.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Zura is identified as Rustem’s brother and as having immediate superintendence of the Zabul troops.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The phrase ‘punishment of the dar’ is explained as referring either to a tree upon which felons are hanged or, more generally, to breaking or tearing the body upon a stake.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In a speech, Rustem recounts to King Kaus the services he has performed, listing conquests in Egypt, China, Hamaveran, Rum, Sakasar, and Mazinderan; the editor compares this to Achilles’ boast of sacking many cities in the Iliad.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Gudarz is quoted as saying that kings ought to be endowed with judgment and discretion and that no advantage arises from impetuosity and rage.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Gudarz is described as one of the greatest generals of Persia, who conquered Judea, took Jerusalem under King Lohrasp of the first dynasty, and fought many wars against Afrasiyab under the kings of the second dynasty; his opinion is said to have considerable weight with Kaus.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Kaus acknowledges the violence of his disposition with the phrase ‘ashes fell into my mouth’ when Rustem departed in anger; a similar Hindustani metaphor is cited in which a person says ‘ashes have fallen into my meat’ to mean that happiness is gone after losing a friend’s favor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"One of Firdusi’s favorite similes is ‘My heart became as slender as the new moon.’","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Beautiful arbors or garden-pavilions within Eastern palace walls are fitted up fancifully and supplied with reservoirs, fountains, and flower-trees; in Turkey such romantic pavilions are called kiosks and are generally situated on an eminence near a running stream.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"At the coronation of Eastern kings it is said to have been customary to powder them with gold dust and seed-pearl; Firdusi describes a figure who ‘showered or scattered gems’; at festivals it is customary to throw money among the people, and Hafiz uses the term nisar in this sense; Clarke describes principal Sultanas of the Ottoman seraglio wearing richly jeweled garments with their hair powdered with diamonds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"In describing battle-array, Firdusi often mentions ‘golden slippers,’ though the translator has omitted them in the current passage.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The original term sandurus (sandaraca) properly refers to gum juniper, though the translator has rendered it as amber.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Banners adorned with the figure of an elephant are used to denote a warrior’s royal descent.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The text states that the person in question is also Rustem’s son-in-law.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Tahmineh","description":"Noblewoman in the Shahnameh who assures Rustem that no one has ever seen her outside her private chamber or heard her voice.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"Champion hero of AND DR / SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD; lines 14281-14380","start":"14281","end":"14380","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial footnotes describe the geography of Iran and Turan and the Oxus river as a boundary; the legendary hero Sam and his fiery war-beast Sohm; the ambiguous nature of the Simurgh and its fostering of Zal; a Persian reception custom (Istakbal) involving processions and a sweetmeat ritual reserved for the king; Mazindaran as a demon-occupied region; the mountain fortress Killah Suffeed; the vast army of Xerxes and a noose-using contingent; Alexander’s destruction of Persepolis; the Persian king Kai-Kaus, his appointment and elevation of Rustem, and his astronomical observatories; the Burgustuwan horse armor; and Rustem and the Arabian knight-errant Abu Mahommud Albatal as precursors of European chivalric single combat and knight-errantry.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Iran and Turan together are said to comprise all of Upper Asia except India and China, and are divided from each other by the great river known as Jihun or Amu (Oxus).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Every country beyond the Persian empire is described as being considered barbarous.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sam (Sm, Sam Suwr), son of Nariman, is said to have vanquished or tamed many animals and terrible monsters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"One particularly furious animal tamed by Sam was called Sohm because it was of the color and nature of fire.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sam made the fiery beast Sohm his war-horse in his engagements against demons.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Simurgh tells Zal that it has nursed him like a father.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The sex of the Simurgh is described as unclear, with the suggestion that it is probably neither male nor female, or both.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Simurgh is described as a biped and is likened by some to the Hippogriff or Griffin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"An alternative interpretation claims that the Simurgh story simply refers to a holy recluse of the mountains who nourished and educated a child abandoned by its father.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the Persian custom of Istakbal, horsemen and an assemblage on foot go out to meet an envoy, and a glass vessel filled with sweetmeats is thrown beneath the envoy’s horse as part of the ceremony.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The sweetmeat-glass-vessel ceremony is described as an honor shared with the king and his sons alone.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Two merchants of Shiraz, accompanied by the son of Mahomed Nebee Khan, incurred the envoy’s displeasure by not dismounting from their horses, contrary to the expected behavior of those of lower rank meeting a superior.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Mazindaran, on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea and known to the ancients as Hyrcania, is said to have been in the possession of demons at the period described.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The fort of Killah Suffeed lies about seventy-six miles northwest of Shiraz on a mountain, enclosing a level verdant area at the top watered by numerous springs, with an ascent of nearly three miles and an extremely difficult final approach that makes it almost impregnable.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The army of Xerxes at Thermopylae is reported as numbering 5,283,220 souls, including servants, eunuchs, and women.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Herodotus describes a people in Xerxes’ army who fight using cords of twisted leather with a noose to entangle a horse or man and then kill them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Istakhar, also called Persepolis and Chehel-minar (Forty Pillars), is said to have been laid in ruins by Alexander after his conquest of Darius.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Kai-Kaus is identified as the second king of Persia of the Kayanian dynasty and is described as a foolish and tyrannical prince.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Kai-Kaus appointed Rustem captain-general of the armies, combining this with the lieutenant-generalship and administration of the state under the title of \"champion of the world.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Kai-Kaus gave Rustem a golden crown, worn only by kings, and granted him the privilege of giving audience seated on a golden throne.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Kai-Kaus is said to have studied astronomy and to have founded two great observatories, one at Babel and one on the Tigris.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Burgustuwan armor is described as almost covering the horse and being usually made of leather and felt-cloth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"During a hunting excursion, Rustem is fully armed with spear, sword, shield, mace, bow, and arrows, and he is said seldom even to have slept unarmed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The note claims that single combat and the romantic enterprises of European chivalry may be traced to the East, and presents Rustem as a most illustrious example of piety, disinterestedness, and heroism in a chivalrous age.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Abu Mahommud Albatal is described as a famous Arabian knight-errant who wandered everywhere in quest of adventures and redressing grievances and was killed in the year 738.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sam (Sm, Sam Suwr)","description":"Son of Nariman who is said to have vanquished or tamed many animals and terrible monsters, including the fiery beast Sohm, which he used as a war-horse against demons.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Nariman (Narmn)","description":"Father of Sam (Sam Suwr).","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sohm","description":"A furious animal of the color and nature of fire, tamed by Sam and used as his war-horse in battles against demons.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Simurgh (Smrgh)","description":"A fabulous biped creature of ambiguous sex that tells Zal it nursed him like a father and is likened by some to the Hippogriff or Griffin.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Zal (Zl)","description":"A child said to interpretations.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Holy recluse of the mountains","description":"A holy recluse who, according to one interpretation, nourished and educated the abandoned child Zal in the mountains.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Envoy to Persia","description":"The envoy described by content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l16198-l16305","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DIVAN / XXIII / XLIII / LXIII; lines 16198-16305","start":"16198","end":"16305","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Three ghazals of Hafez are presented. In LXIII, the poet declares his heart weary of the world and devoted solely to a beloved friend, describes the beloved’s love as a fragrant garden that makes his heart burst its veil, rejects offering advice on the path of love, and tells a secluded zealot that he finds the mihrab’s arch in an eyebrow’s bow and sees no difference between the Ka'bah and the wine-house because the Divine is everywhere. He contrasts superficial Kalandars, who focus on hair, with the true Kalandar who gives his head on the path, identifying himself with this total self-giving. LXIX is a poem of intense praise and longing for Farrukh, whose beauty outshines trees, winds, and perfumes; the poet calls for wine, suffers physically from love, and vows service to any lofty soul who, like Hafez, serves Farrukh’s dark lock. LXXI describes springtime as the rose springs from Nothing into Being and the violet bows before it; the poet urges drinking wine with music and a charming cupbearer before the rose fades, likening its brief bloom to human life. Earth in spring rivals the Immortal Garden, but true immortality cannot be found here. The poem calls for Zoroaster’s worship to revive in the gardens while Nimrod’s fires live in tulips, urges the reader to drink wine served by a beauty of Christ-like breath and forget tales of punished tribes, likens the rose’s appearance to Solomon riding the wind and a bird’s song to David’s melodies, and ends by toasting the vizir Mahmud as support of the faith and relying on his enduring generosity.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poet says his heart has grown weary of the world and that the shrine of his affection contains no being but his friend.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"He describes his beloved’s love as a sweet garden whose fragrant breath would cause his heart, in joy, to burst its veil like a bud.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"He refers to a \"path of love,\" calls himself a fool, and says it would be like {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l15144-l15307","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM / THE RUBIYT; lines 15144-15307","start":"15144","end":"15307","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Heav'n but the Vision of fulfill'd Desire,
And Hell the Shadow from a Soul on fire ...

Ah, Love! could you and I with Him conspire
To grasp this sorry Scheme of Things entire,
Would not we shatter it to bits—and then
Re-mould it nearer to the Heart's Desire!","summary":"The passage from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam presents a series of quatrains reflecting on Heaven and Hell as projections of desire, human life as a shadow-play and a game controlled by a higher power, and fate as irrevocably written. The sky is likened to an inverted bowl, and creation is described as humanity being kneaded from earth's clay with the final reckoning predetermined. Ignorance of humanity’s origin and destiny leads the speaker to embrace wine, the tavern, and the vine as sources of meaning and even spiritual insight, contrasted with formal religious piety and the temple. The speaker questions divine justice, predestination, and punishment, invoking the Edenic snake and pleading for forgiveness. An extended allegory shows the poet in a potter’s house where clay vessels debate their purpose, their maker, and the prospect of being broken or cast into Hell. The poet then imagines his own burial intertwined with grape and leaf so that his ashes may ensnare passers-by in wine, and reflects on how wine and other “idols” have harmed his reputation yet remain precious. Seasonal images of Spring, the rose, and the nightingale express the poignant transience of youth and joy. The passage concludes with longing for a saving glimpse of a life-giving fountain in the desert, the wish for an angel to alter the roll of fate, and a final dream of conspiring with Love and God to shatter the flawed world-order and remake it nearer to the heart’s desire.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Heaven is described as the vision of fulfilled desire, and Hell as the shadow cast by a soul on fire into the surrounding darkness from which humans recently emerged and will soon expire.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Human beings are likened to a moving row of magic shadow-shapes that come and go around a sunlit lantern held at midnight by a "Master of the Show."","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Humans are called helpless pieces of a game played on a checker-board of nights and days, moved, checked, slain, and finally laid back one by one in a closet by a higher player.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A ball is described as making no decision about where to go, but simply moving where the Player strikes it, and the one who tossed people into the field is said to know everything about it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A "Moving Finger" writes and moves on, and no amount of piety, intellect, or tears can make it return to erase what has been written.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The sky is compared to an inverted bowl under which people crawl, live, and die, and it is said to be as impotent to help as any person, so lifting hands to it for aid is discouraged.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The poem states that with earth's first clay they kneaded the last man and sowed the seed of the last harvest, and that what the first morning of creation wrote will be read on the last dawn of reckoning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker claims that yesterday prepared today's madness, and tomorrow may bring silence, triumph, or despair; people are urged to drink because they do not know whence they came or why, nor why or where they go.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Astrological imagery describes Parwn and Mushtar being flung over the flaming shoulders of the foal of heaven when the speaker started from the goal, fixing his predestined plot of dust and soul.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the speaker's predestined plot, the vine struck a fibre to which his being clings; he accepts the dervish’s scorn and imagines that from his base metal a key may be filed to unlock a door at which the dervish howls outside.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker says that whether the one True Light kindles love or consumes him with wrath, a single flash of it caught in the tavern is better than losing it outright in the temple.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The poem questions the justice of provoking a conscious being out of senseless nothing only to impose a yoke of forbidden pleasure under threat of everlasting penalties, and of demanding pure repayment from a helpless creature made with alloyed dross.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"God is addressed as the one who set pitfalls and traps along the road the speaker had to wander, and the speaker protests that God will not enmesh him in predestined evil and then blame his fall as sin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"God is also addressed as the one who made man of baser earth and even devised the snake together with paradise, and is asked to give and receive forgiveness for all the sin that has blackened the face of man.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"At the close of Ramadan, personified as slinking away hunger-stricken, the speaker stands alone in a potter's house surrounded by shapes of clay of many sorts and sizes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Some clay vessels in the potter's house are described as loquacious and others as silent listeners.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"One vessel says its common earth was surely not taken and molded into its figure only to be broken or trampled back to shapeless earth again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A second vessel argues that no peevish boy would break the bowl from which he drank in joy, and concludes that the maker of the vessel will not destroy it afterward in wrath.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A more ungainly vessel, mocked for leaning awry, asks whether the potter's hand shook when he made it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Another talkative vessel asks who is really the potter and who the pot, while another reports that some say there is one who threatens to toss misshapen pots into Hell but dismisses the threat, asserting that he is a good fellow and all will be well.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"One vessel, whose clay is long dried with oblivion, hopes that if it is filled with the familiar juice of wine it might recover, and as the vessels speak the little Moon looks in and they whisper to each other about the potter’s approaching step.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The speaker asks for his fading life to be supplied with the grape, for his dead body to be washed with wine, and for his corpse to be wrapped in green leaves and laid by a frequented garden-side.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"He imagines that even his buried ashes will send up such a snaresome vintage into the air that no true-believer passing will escape being overtaken by it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The speaker calls the things he has loved "Idols" that have harmed his worldly reputation, drowning his glory in a shallow cup and selling his reputation for a song.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"He admits he has often sworn repentance but questions whether he was sober when he swore, and says that when spring came with rose in hand it tore his threadbare penitence apart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Wine is said to have played the infidel and robbed him of his robe of honor, yet he wonders what vintners ever buy that is half as precious as the wine they sell.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The speaker laments that spring vanishes with the rose, that youth’s fragrant manuscript closes, and that the nightingale which sang in the branches flies away to an unknown origin and destination.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"He wishes that the "Desert of the Fountain" would yield even one true, if dim, glimpse of water so that the fainting traveler might spring to it as trampled herbage springs back.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"He imagines a winged angel who might, before it is too late, arrest the still-unfolding roll of fate and make the stern recorder enter things differently or erase them entirely.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"In the final lines, he addresses Love, wishing that Love, he, and God together could grasp the whole "scheme of things," shatter it to bits, and remold it nearer to the heart’s {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l16667-l16805","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / SIGURTHARKVITHA EN SKAMMA / THE SHORT LAY OF SIGURTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 16667-16805","start":"16667","end":"16805","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A queen, already determined on death, speaks with Gunnar and others. Warriors are called to try to prevent her suicide, but Hogni refuses, saying she should not be held back from the "long road" and should never be born again, having been wicked from birth. Gunnar gloomily turns away as the queen divides her jewels and gazes on her wealth and the bodies of slain bond-women and slaves. She dons a golden byrnie, pierces herself with a sword, lies on a pillow wounded, and continues to think and speak. She summons her women to receive gold and garments, hoping some will follow her in death, but they refuse, saying enough have been slain. She resolves that none shall die unwillingly for her sake.

The dying queen then addresses Gunnar at length, prophesying the fate of his sister Guthrun and others. She foretells Guthrun’s grief over her dead husband, the birth of Guthrun’s daughter Svanhild, brighter than day or the sun, and Guthrun’s unhappy marriage to Atli, Buthli’s son and the queen’s brother. She recalls how she was treated and betrayed, predicts Gunnar’s frustrated desire to have Oddrun as wife and his secret love with her, and foretells that Atli will cast Gunnar into a den of snakes. She further prophesies that Atli himself will soon lose his life, wealth, and sons, as Guthrun, grim of heart, kills him with a sword in his bed.

The queen says it would better befit Guthrun to follow her husband in death, yet Guthrun will live and wander over the tossing waves to the realm of King Jonak, where she will bear him sons. Svanhild, the child she bore to Sigurth, will be sent far away and die because of the word of Bikki and the wrath of Jormunrek, leaving all of Sigurth’s race slain and increasing Guthrun’s sorrow.

Finally, the queen begs Gunnar for one last boon: to build a wide pyre in the field so there is room for all who are slain with Sigurth. She orders the pyre to be covered with shields, carpets, fair shrouds, and the bodies of fallen slaves, and asks to be burned beside the "Hunnish hero." She specifies that slaves richly adorned, as well as hounds and hawks, be burned at his head and feet. She asks that the keen steel lie between them as it once did when they shared a bed and were called wedded mates. She speaks of the grandness of the funeral procession and names the number of bond-women, thralls, and children who should follow him in death as gifts from Buthli. The lament is characterized as an early and central type of Germanic poetry, with traces seen in the Nibelungenlied, and as part of a basic German tradition with relatively few specifically northern additions. Brynhild is mentioned as Guthrun’s enemy and the cause of Sigurth’s death, while the three women who try to comfort Guthrun are viewed as poetic creations. A brief prose summary explains that Guthrun sits by the dead Sigurth, unable to weep though her heart is near bursting, while men and women attempt to console her; it is also said that she ate Fafnir’s heart and understands the speech of birds. The first thirteen stanzas then depict Guthrun’s grief: she thinks of dying as she sits by Sigurth’s body but cannot cry, even when warriors and their gold-adorned wives come and each woman recounts her own worst sorrow. Gjaflaug, Gjuki’s sister, tells of losing multiple husbands, daughters, sisters, and eight brothers, yet living on. Herborg, queen of the Huns, describes an even greater burden: seven sons and her husband fallen in battle in the south, her parents and four brothers drowned when waves smash their ship, her solitary work of decking and burying their bodies within half a year, and then her capture in war and enslavement by a jealous queen who beats her and makes her tie the queen’s shoes each morning. Despite these stories Guthrun still cannot weep for her dead husband. Finally Gollrond, Gjuki’s daughter, rebukes her foster-mother’s failure to comfort Guthrun and orders Sigurth’s corpse uncovered; Sigurth’s shroud is lifted, his head laid on Guthrun’s knees, and she is urged to look on and kiss him as if he still lived. Guthrun looks once, seeing his hair clotted with blood, his blinded eyes, and his breast pierced by a blade.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The First Lay of Guthrun (Guthrunarkvitha I) follows the remaining fragment of the long Sigurth
