Then Herborg, queen of the Huns, recounts greater sorrows: seven sons and her husband killed in southern battle, parents and four brothers drowned when waves smash their ship, her solitary work of decking and burying all their bodies within half a year without comfort, and finally her capture in war and enslavement by a monarch’s jealous wife who beats her and makes her bind the queen’s shoes. The shroud is lifted, Sigurth’s head is laid on Guthrun’s knees, and she is urged to look on him and kiss him as if he still lived. {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l6829-l6960","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB; lines 6829-6960","start":"6829","end":"6960","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""My light of life now fluttering sinks in shade,
Let vengeance sleep, and peaceful vows be made."

"Here ends the war! let gentle peace succeed,
Enough of death, I--I have done the deed!"","summary":"On the battlefield, the mortally wounded Sohrb halts the fighting with a dying plea for peace and mercy toward the Tartar host, accepting personal guilt for the war and revealing his long search for his father, Rustem. He laments that Rustem denied their kinship and has now, unknowingly, shed kindred blood. Rustem is devastated, declares the war ended, and sends his brother to announce peace, while blame for the tragedy is shifted onto the captive chief Hujr for concealing Rustem's identity. Rustem, in frenzy and remorse, is restrained from self‑destruction as the elder Gdarz reminds him that all humans are subject to death. Rustem then seeks from the King a sovereign balm said to heal all wounds and restore life, but the resentful King refuses to send it. Before Rustem can intervene, Sohrb dies. Overwhelmed by grief at having slain his own innocent son and fearing the mother's anguish, Rustem mourns, the Persian warriors bear Sohrb's body home on a bier, and Rustem burns his own martial splendor—pavilion, throne, bed, and weapons—leaving his warrior pride in dust and ashes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The army, urged by the Monarch to revenge the slain, rushes over the dusty plain to the site of the duel and finds Sohrb still breathing after the "unnatural" fight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sohrb, while dying, speaks to halt the fighting, saying his life is fading and asking that vengeance cease and peaceful vows be made, and that the King be asked to spare the Tartar host because they are guiltless and he led them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sohrb says he led the Tartar host, inflaming their souls with glory because of his mad ambition, and that he chose war to search for his father, whom he hoped to join in preventing a tyrant king from persecuting mankind.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sohrb recounts that he often sought his father, was delighted to find his mother's token, but was disappointed when Rustem denied their kinship and name; he says that despite this denial his affection clung to his father, and that fate has stained Rustem's hands with kindred blood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sohrb's breath fails and tears flow from his eyelids; Rustem is filled with horror and subdued by grief, while the Zbul bands, seeing his pale and haggard look, weep as Rustem declares that the war is ended, calls for peace, and admits that he has "done the deed" of killing Sohrb.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem, groaning, tells his brother Zra to go to the Tartar side and say that there should be no more war between them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zra goes to Hmn, the Turanian Chief, and reports the tragedy; Hmn, outwardly sorrowful, blames the captive chief Hujr, saying Hujr could have prevented the blow but denied Rustem's presence when Sohrb sought his father's banners, and therefore deserves vengeance.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Zra returns and tells Rustem of Hujr's alleged treachery; Rustem is ready to behead Hujr, whose headless trunk would have lain on the strand, but others' prayers and force restrain Rustem from killing the captive chief.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rustem turns again to his dying son, his remorse deepening; in a burst of frenzy he clenches his sword and attempts a desperate act, but the Persian chiefs restrain him and try to calm him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gdarz speaks to Rustem, saying that even if Rustem were to give himself a thousand wounds and die, it would not relieve Sohrb's suffering, and reminding him that all, high and low, are prey to death and that humans are victims of woe throughout life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Rustem instructs that the King be told of his desperate plight and asks that, if the King remembers Rustem's deeds, he send a sovereign balm said to heal all wounds and restore fleeting life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The King refuses to send the healing draught, calling Sohrb a shameless boy who had insulted him and threatened his throne, and arguing that reviving an enemy is foolish because it will only create future strife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Gdarz returns with the King's refusal, and although Rustem rises to go himself, Sohrb dies before Rustem can reach the throne.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After Sohrb's death, Rustem is tormented by anguish at having killed his own son; he sees his sword stained with filial blood, beats his chest, tears his hair, throws ashes on his head, and laments having slain his innocent son and the pain the boy's mother will suffer.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Persian warriors place Sohrb's body on a bier, cover his pale face, and carry him away from the battlefield in a long procession toward Rustem's home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Rustem, despairing and blaming himself as the source of the tragedy, burns his martial pomp—shield, spear, mace, pavilion, sparkling throne, and golden bed—so that his warrior's pride is consumed by fire and reduced to dust and ashes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sohrb","description":"A young warrior and leader of the Tartar host, mortally wounded in battle and revealed as Rustem's son, who delivers a dying plea for peace and acknowledges his own guilt in leading the enemy army.","role_refs":["role:1","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Rustem (the Champion)","description":"The mighty Persian Champion and father of Sohrb, who has unknowingly slain his own son, declares the war ended, struggles with guilt and frenzy, seeks a healing balm from the King, mourns his son's death, and burns his own martial splendor in grief.","role_refs":["role:2","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"The King (Monarch)","description":"The ruler who urges the army to seek revenge and who possesses a sovereign balm said to heal all wounds and restore life, but refuses to send it to save Sohrb because of resentment and fear of future strife.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Zra","description":"Rustem's brother, who acts as a messenger, carrying Rustem's message of peace to the Tartar side and reporting back the accusations against Hujr.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Hmn, the Trnian (Turanian) Chief","description":"A Turanian chief described as crafty, who hears Zra's report with feigned sorrow and blames the captive chief Hujr for concealing Rustem's presence from Sohrb.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Hujr","description":"A captive chief accused by Hmn of knowing that Rustem was present when Sohrb sought his father's banners and of denying it, thereby spreading ruin; Rustem nearly has him executed but is restrained.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Gdarz","description":"An elder Persian chief who restrains Rustem from a desperate act and offers group of Persian leaders who restrain Rustem from violent frenzy and attempt to calm his anguish.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Zbul bands","description":"Rustem's Zbul (Zabul) followers, who rejoice to see their chief but, realizing the cause of his distress, mourn and weep around him.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Tartar host","description":"The Tartar army led by Sohrb, whom he declares guiltless and for whom he begs the hands.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:9"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Dying hero and son","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Sohrb is mortally wounded, delivers a dying The King, enraged that Rustem has scorned his friendship and disobeyed his mandate, orders that Rustem be led away and impaled alive, and Ts receives the decree to break him and the Envoy Gw on the felon-tree. Cast from the King's side, Rustem mounts his horse and delivers a furious speech condemning Ks as an ungrateful tyrant, reminding him that Rustem saved his life in battle, fought in distant lands, bows only to God, could have taken the sceptre but refused, rescued Kai-kobd from Alberz mountain and placed the crown on his head, and defeated the White Demon and other foes. Rustem warns his friends of ruin, the coming conqueror and vultures that will gorge on all, declares Persia will no longer see its injured Chief, and withdraws from the court. The warriors, full of foreboding and lamenting the lack of a shepherd for the flock, look to Gdarz to soothe the frantic King and Rustem's wrath. Gdarz rebukes Ks for wishing to impale Rustem on an ignominious tree, recalls how Rustem saved him near the Caspian-wave by striking down savage foes and demons with his flaming brand, warns that no one can face Rustem or oppose invaders if he returns to Zbul wronged, and urges that wisdom rather than uncontrolled passion rule a monarch's soul. Ks, relenting, feels shame and fear instead of wrath and orders that Rustem's generous aid be implored and that the mighty Chief be restored to his King.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem nears the end of his journey and is met by Ts, Gdarz, and Gushwd, who honor him as their champion-friend and bring the \"shield of Persia\" to the anxious King.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The King, described as a senseless monarch swayed by foaming wrath because his friendship was scorned and his mandate disobeyed, orders that Rustem be led away and impaled alive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Gw the Envoy is astounded and shrinks from the order to impale such a true knight, but his resistance increases the King’s anger, and both Gw and Rustem are branded with revolt and shame; Ts receives the stern decree to break them on the felon-tree.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l6481-l6592","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB; lines 6481-6592","start":"6481","end":"6592","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this episode of the Rustem–Sohrb story, a denied filial claim plunges Sohrb into gloom as a narrow space is prepared for single combat between him and Rustem. Father and son fight fiercely with lances, swords, clubs, bows, and wrestling, until their armor is shattered and they are exhausted and parched. The narrator laments that animals know their own kind, but humans lack instinctive recognition, as father and son are driven to mortal strife. Rustem is shamed and astonished by the youth’s strength; Fate is said to forbid Sohrb’s blood from being shed, and Sohrb eventually wounds and stuns Rustem, urging him to cease fighting out of pity. Meanwhile, the legions clash; Sohrb ravages the Persian host like a wolf, and Rustem slays Trnians like a tiger. Rustem, grieved by Persian blood on Sohrb’s hands, calls on him to fight only with him, likening him to a wolf attacking a fold; they agree to resume their struggle in wrestling the next day as night falls and the stripling’s life is said to be hastening into shade. That night, Sohrb joyfully recounts his victories to Hmn, boasts that no Persian will survive the coming day, and calls for wine to strengthen hearts. Rustem and Gw sadly recall the slaughter; Rustem then seeks the mournful Monarch and describes Sohrb’s tremendous strength and his own inability to defeat him, saying that only Heaven knows who will be victorious since victory or death is given to man by Heaven. A messenger secretly carries the warning to the king, and during the night the governor, other heroes, and the warrior maid Gurd-afreed escape. At dawn Sohrb’s troops storm the fort, shatter the gates, and discover it empty. Disappointed that no chiefs resist him and that the warrior-maid he desires is gone, Sohrb broods over his love, describing himself as wounded and enchained by her charms. His visible distress is noticed by the stern Trnian chief Hmn, who concludes that Sohrb is enslaved by love. Hmn admonishes him that true heroes do not become the prey of love, reminds him of their bloody march from Trn and the great conquest before them, warns of the Iranian champions who will oppose them, and urges him to seek glory and empire first, promising that women will later flock to him. Rustem joyfully accepts. A Mobid secures the king's consent, and the monarch gladly gives his beloved daughter to the renowned warrior; the people celebrate the union with nuptial songs that bless the \"young moon\" of their marriage and wish for the destruction of enmity. Before morning fully shines, Rustem removes a bracelet from his arm, calling it a soul-ennobling charm, and gives it to Tahmneh with instructions that it be worn by any daughter or son born of their union, prophesying that their child will inherit Sam's strength, bravery in battle, and immortal fame. After affectionate embrace, Rustem rises at sunrise to depart; Tahmneh weeps and tries in vain to detain him. The king brings Rakush, Rustem mounts the fiery war-horse and rides toward Sistan, leaving wife and father behind. When he returns to Zabul, no one knows of the joys that had delayed him, though he often remembers the night with content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l20834-l20904","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HAMTHESMOL / THE BALLAD OF HAMTHER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 20834-20904","start":"20834","end":"20904","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Hamther and Sorli travel toward Jormunrek’s hall and see their sister’s son hanging on a bleak gallows-tree outside. Inside, Jormunrek and his Goths feast noisily until a horn announces armed visitors. Men report that helm-bearing warriors have arrived whose sister Jormunrek killed. The king, emboldened by wine, boasts that he would bind Hamther and Sorli and hang Gjukis’ heirs. A violent fight follows in the hall, with shattered cups and Goths’ blood on the floor. Hamther declares that Jormunrek now sees his own hands and feet flung into a hot fire. The king, likened to a roaring bear, orders his men to stone the sons of Jonak, since steel cannot wound them. Sorli rebukes Hamther for opening a figurative bag of harmful counsel and for courage without wisdom. Hamther regrets that they killed their keen brother Erp, saying the Norns drove him to slay a hero who would have been holy in battle. He warns against wolf-like strife between brothers and compares such quarrels to the greedy hounds of the Norns. Hamther then boasts that they stand over the fallen Goths like eagles on branches, that their fame is great even if they die soon, and that no one outlives the night once the Norns have spoken. Sorli sinks by the gable and Hamther falls at the back of the house. The poem identifies itself as the old ballad of Hamther.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hamther and Sorli are traveling on a road and encounter an ill way.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"They see their sister’s son hanging on a \"wind-cold wolf-tree\" west of the hall, his body described as Erp were alive, describing Erp as their keen brother whom they killed on the road and saying that the Norns drove him to slay the noble hero who should have been holy in battle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Hamther says it does not befit them to behave like wolves and strive among themselves, comparing such behavior to the spoken.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Sorli sinks beside the gable and Hamther falls at the back of the house, marking their defeat or death at the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7278-l7370","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7278-7370","start":"7278","end":"7370","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Prince Saiwush rejects Queen Sdveh’s advances. She fails to detain him, then tears her garments, screams, and falsely accuses him before King Ks of attempting an outrage. Ks, hearing that Saiwush preferred Sdveh to her daughter and plotted an abominable offence, considers death the only suitable punishment. To test the accusation he smells Saiwush’s hands and clothes, scented with rose-water, and contrasts them with Sdveh’s wine- and musk-scented garments, convincing him she lied. Though he contemplates her death, he spares her while acknowledging privately that Saiwush is innocent, ignoring her continued calls for his punishment. Ks then decrees an ordeal by fire to prove Saiwush’s innocence. The fearless youth, confident that truth will protect him, prays to the Almighty and rides, in golden helmet and white robe on a black horse, into a huge fire lit on the plain. Sdveh watches in terror yet also in passionate attachment; Ks falls from his throne in horror. Saiwush emerges from the flames unharmed, likened to the moon rising from the burning element. Ks rejoices and turns his anger on Sdveh, intending her death, but Saiwush intercedes for her. Sdveh nevertheless secretly persists in charms and incantations to destroy him. News then arrives that Afrsiyb has raised another army to invade Iran. Judging that Tartars cannot be bound by oath, Ks plans to lead a punitive campaign to Balkh, but Saiwush, seeking escape from Sdveh’s plots, petitions for the command and is supported by Rustem, who advises that the king need not go. Ks opens his treasury to equip the army, which marches toward Balkh. There Gerswaz, ruler of Balghar, joins the Tartar legions under Brmn; after three days of battle they are defeated by the Persians and abandon the fort. Afrsiyb, alarmed by this disaster, is further shaken by a terrifying dream: a serpent-filled forest, skies darkened by eagles, parched earth, a whirlwind toppling his tent and banners, rivers of blood, his army slaughtered, and himself captured and brought before Ks, where a brave youth stabs him in the loins. Waking in terror, he is told by Gerswaz that dreams mean the reverse of what they show, but remains unconsoled and consults his astrologers. They hesitate to interpret the dream until one, after receiving a promise of safety, agrees to reveal the ominous meaning.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Saiwush attempts to leave Sdveh’s presence quickly; Sdveh tries to cling to him to prevent his departure but fails, then tears her clothes, screams, and rushes out to accuse him before Ks, while her women raise loud lamentations.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sdveh tells Ks that Saiwush has preferred her to her daughter and contemplated an abominable offence against her, leading Ks to think that only death could atone for such a crime and to summon Saiwush.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"To test the accusation, Ks smells Saiwush’s hands and garments, which smell of rose-water, and then Sdveh’s garments, which smell strongly of wine and musk, convincing him that Sdveh’s accusation is false and prompting him to resolve on her death before later abandoning that plan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Although Ks declares himself sure of Saiwush’s innocence, he tells Sdveh to keep that fact concealed and disregards her continued insistence that Saiwush be punished.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ks decides to determine Saiwush’s innocence by an ordeal of fire, and Saiwush, unafraid, agrees to undergo the trial, telling his father not to be alarmed and stating that truth will carry him safely through the fiercest flames.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A tremendous fire is lit on a nearby plain; Saiwush, dressed in a golden helmet and white robe and mounted on a black horse, prays to the Almighty for protection and rides deliberately into the blazing conflagration.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"During the ordeal, Sdveh runs to the palace terrace and watches the scene; despite her accusation, she is so in love with Saiwush that she wishes she could share his fate, while Ks falls from his throne in horror at seeing Saiwush engulfed in flames.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Saiwush emerges from the fire unharmed, compared to the moon rising from the bursting element; Overcome with dread, the king closes the fragrant page and orders the warrior Gw to saddle his fastest horse and carry the country’s woes to Rustem without delay or rest. Gw rides swiftly to Zabul, where Rustem stands among his warriors dispensing honours. A sentinel announces a messenger from Persia, and Gw, described as the sacred envoy of the Persian king, privately delivers the message and unrolls the written page. Rustem marvels at reports of the youthful enemy champion, said to be of Sam’s excelling worth and to bear the same warrior bearing as Rustem, Sam, and Nariman. Remembering that Tahmneh of Samengan bore him an only child, whom he recalls as a daughter, Rustem briefly wonders if the champion could be his offspring before rejecting the thought. He then dismisses fear of the invader, arguing that all must eventually die, and invites Gw to join him at a palace feast before deciding on war. Using the image of fire that flutters and decays when storm-swollen ocean displays its wrath, he predicts that the youthful hero’s pride will soon be quelled. Despite Gw’s repeated reminders of the king’s grief, the champion’s prowess, and the land’s worsening woes, Rustem continues feasting with music and wine for days until he forgets Kai-Kaus. On the fifth morning, a trumpet’s clang carried on fragrant breezes ends the revelry; Rustem’s richly adorned horse bears him forth under victor banners, and Zra leads veteran troops from Zabul’s After his victory, Afrsiyb orders Krun to be pursued, but learns Krun has gone to protect the shubistn and has killed Brmn, which enrages Afrsiyb. Nauder’s reign lasts seven years, after which Afrsiyb becomes master of Persia.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Nauder discovers that content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8693-l8808","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU; lines 8693-8808","start":"8693","end":"8808","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a series of single combats between the Persian champion Rustem and Turanian/Tartar warriors, Rustem, fighting first on foot against the mounted Ushkabs, kills Ushkabs’s horse and then Ushkabs with powerful archery, standing afterwards like Mount Alberz as the enemy look on in awe. The Tartars bring Ushkabs’s body and the bloodied arrow to the Khakn of Chin, who marvels at the arrow’s force and pauses the battle. The leader then asks who will avenge Ushkabs; Kms volunteers, kills Rustem’s pupil Alwund, but is himself unhorsed when his kamund entangles Rustem’s horse Rakush and Rustem tears the line in two, then lassoes Kms, delivers him captive to the Persian army, and has him put to death. Kms’s death alarms the Turanian forces; Piran-Wisah urges retreat, but the Khakn persists, and the warrior Chingush challenges Rustem. After exchanging arrows, Chingush tries to flee, but Rustem pulls him from the saddle by his horse’s tail, kills him, wrings off his head, and casts his body to the vultures. Rustem calls for further challengers; none appear until Hmn comes, not to fight but to plead for an end to the destructive war. Rustem refuses, reciting Afrsiyb’s crimes, especially the murder of Saiwush, which he says cannot be forgiven. He withholds his name from Hmn and asks that Piran-Wisah be sent instead. Hmn concludes the unknown champion must be Rustem, likening him to predatory beasts and Iblis, and an old man laments that if Rustem is indeed present, the land faces fire, sword, and widespread Rustem tells Zra what to do if he is victorious and, if he dies, to lead the warriors home and gently inform his venerable father and mother that Heaven decreed his death, reflecting on the inevitability of mortality even for great heroes like Kirshsp, Sm, Narmn, and Jemshd. At dawn the warriors arm, and Sohrab, with his confederate Hmn nearby, is stirred by filial feeling and signs on his opponent’s person and horse; he suspects the warrior is Rustem and fears provoking his father's rage and shame, but Hmn denies that this is Rustem. Sohrab, described as soft-hearted yet fiery, smiles and proposes that he and Rustem sit together, seek heavenly forgiveness, feast, and become friends; he begs Rustem to reveal his name and whether he is Rustem. Rustem sternly rejects these overtures as delaying wiles and insists on the promised struggle. Calling him \"Old man,\" Sohrab laments Rustem’s refusal to heed prudent words and appeals to Heaven. They tether their horses to nearby rocks, gird themselves, test their strength, and wrestle fiercely until blood and sweat cover the plain. Sohrab seizes Rustem’s belt, throws him down, and straddles him like a lion over a wild ass, raising his sword to behead him. Rustem quickly claims a law that a chief must be twice overthrown before his blood may be spilled. Proud and trusting, the youth believes this deception, releases Rustem, and departs across the plain as if forgetting the fight. Hmn, horrified, likens the act to freeing a raging lion from a snare and warns Sohrab never to suspend the final blow nor trust a seemingly weak foe. Sohrab brushes off the complaint, declaring that the next day’s contest will decide Rustem’s {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l19306-l19474","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / ATLAMOL EN GRNLENZKU / THE GREENLAND BALLAD OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 19306-19474","start":"19306","end":"19474","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Kostbera reads runes sent by Hogni’s sister and warns him that they foretell death if he and his brother Gunnar travel to the king’s hall. Hogni dismisses the warning as women’s fearfulness and anticipates receiving gold. Kostbera reports a series of ominous dreams: their bed-covering and house burning, a bear breaking the house pillars and attacking people, and an eagle flying through the house sprinkling blood, which she fears is Atli’s spirit. Hogni repeatedly offers benign interpretations and affirms trust in Atli. 

Elsewhere, Gunnar’s wife Glaumvor wakes with similarly terrifying dreams about her husband: a gallows prepared for him, serpents eating his still-living flesh under the gods’ doom, a bloody sword and spear through his body with wolves howling at head and feet, a roaring river flooding the hall and washing over the brothers’ feet, and dead women in sad garments inviting Gunnar to their benches, beyond the help of the Norns. Gunnar acknowledges that their lives may be short but refuses to turn back from the journey.

At dawn five warriors and their followers, including Hogni, Gunnar, Hogni’s sons Snvar and Solar, and Orkning (Kostbera’s brother), prepare to depart, though they try half-heartedly to hold one another back and are described as lacking wisdom. The ‘fair-decked’ women follow them to the fjord, pleading in vain. Glaumvor questions Vingi, suspecting he repays their hospitality ill if evil follows his visit. Vingi swears glibly by giants and the gallows that he has not lied or harbored hostile thoughts. Bera then gives a gracious farewell, wishing them a safe and victorious voyage. Hogni urges his kin to have courage, saying words rarely bring one safely home when evil is strong. The men row so fiercely toward the home that once belonged to Buthli that the oar-loops and thole-pins break; they leave the ship without mooring it. On arrival, Hogni strikes the resounding gates, and Vingi utters a word described as better left unsaid, implying looming betrayal.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kostbera has read the runes that Hogni’s sister wrote and believes they warn that Hogni and He convenes wise men to benefit his people, and during his rule spinning, weaving, garment- and carpet-making, and the taming of hunting animals become established. Tahmers has a wise vizir who uses magic to capture a demon and bring it to the king. The demon’s brethren and allies, shamed by this, raise a demonic army of fire and smoke against Tahmers, who responds with his own army of brave warriors. Their leader, the demon Gh, is slain by Tahmers with a mace, and the remaining demons are captured and almost executed. They beg for mercy, offering to teach a marvelous art if spared. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l6962-l7089","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB; lines 6962-7089","start":"6962","end":"7089","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"His soul has travelled to some happier shore.\"","summary":"After Rustem has slain his son Sohrab, King Ks tries to console him by stressing the inevitability of death and the soul’s journey to a happier shore, even evoking world-destroying fire to emphasize that the past cannot be restored. Rustem, overwhelmed with grief, asks that Sohrab’s Tartar host be protected and allowed to return safely to their mountain home along the Jihun river, and the king ends the war and sends the Tartars away as the Persians mourn and then return to Iran. Rustem remains in Zabul to conduct extensive funerary rites, including the sacrifice of a thousand horses, a mourning procession through bowery groves, and repeated public viewings of Sohrab’s body, joined by Zal, Rudabeh, and the Persian community. A sepulchral mound shaped like a charger’s hoof is raised so that Sohrab’s fame will remain fresh and bloom through future days, and the story of his death spreads through Turan, Afrasiyab’s realm, and Samengan, extinguishing nuptial happiness. When Sohrab’s mother Tahmineh hears the news, she descends into frenzied grief, tearing her hair and face, addressing Heaven, calling her son a victim of unnatural strife between father and son, and lamenting that she did not guide him to Rustem or ensure he showed the recognition tokens that would have prevented his death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"King Ks tells Rustem that all humans must eventually yield their vital breath, worldly troubles end in death, and Sohrab’s soul has travelled to a happier shore.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"King Ks adds that even if Heaven were hurled against the earth or fire wrapped the world in crackling flames, what is past cannot be restored and grief brings no benefit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Rustem responds that Sohrab is gone and asks the king to protect Sohrab’s brave but unguided host, remove them from war and that detested place, and let them retrace their mountain-wilds along the distant waters of the Jihun under the guidance of his brother.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"King Ks agrees with Rustem’s request, ceases the war, and the Tartar legions return to their homes while Persian warriors gather around Sohrab’s body, grovel in dust shedding tears, and then follow the monarch back to beloved Iran.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Rustem remains among his native bands and continues rites of sacrifice, commanding a thousand horses to bleed and having torn drums scattered over the sand.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A mourning procession moves through Zabul’s deep and bowery groves, with the mighty Chief Rustem on foot preceding the bier and warrior friends assembled in grief as dismal cadences rise on the wind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zal hears the piercing wail, he and his kindred join the solemn train, hang around the bier and view the slain as the sorrowing father urges them to gaze on his glorious offspring dead, and the hoary sire shrinks back in surprise as tears of blood overflow his aged eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The funeral group enters Rustem’s rural palace gate in gloomy state.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rudabeh loudly bemoans the stripling’s doom, comparing Sohrab to a sweet flower drooping in the hour of bloom and recalling that his tender youth passed in distant bowers, sheltered in the soft prison of his mother’s arms, secure from danger and the world’s alarms.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Rudabeh laments that, flushed with generous pride, Sohrab sought his sire and thus unhappily died.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Rustem again opens the sacred bier, exposing Sohrab to public view as husbands, wives, and warriors old and young gather around the body, with rent garments and loosely flowing hair, filling the air with shrieks and clamours and crying that Sam the Champion slept thus and so sleeps Sohrab, then groaning and weeping.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A yellow robe is spread over Sohrab’s corpse, the aloes bier is closed upon the dead, and a sepulchral mound formed like a charger’s hoof is raised on the spot so that the hapless hero’s name and unblemished fame may remain fragrant, fresh, and blooming through succeeding days.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The narrator states that the story of Sohrab’s death has been told in every ear and that many tears have been shed at its recital throughout Turan, Afrasiyab’s wide realm, and Samengan, where nuptial bowers, beds, and all that promised happiness have fled.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"When Tahmineh hears the tale of woe she becomes distracted and wild, rushing from place to place, deforming her face with frenzied hands and tearing her musky locks from her polished temples, then flinging them on the ground and gazing in agony with eyes raised imploringly to Heaven.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Tahmineh cries that Sohrab, the sole comfort of her life, has been doomed as the victim of unnatural strife, and calls him her darling boy, her lost and murdered child, now defiled with dust and blood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Tahmineh recalls how, after Sohrab departed, He is said to be the first to bring fire out of stone and, on this basis, to found the religion of the Fire-worshippers, calling the flame the Light of the Divinity. A narrative describes how, while passing by a mountain with his retinue, he sees a terrifying monster; he throws a stone at it, which strikes a rock and produces sparks that ignite a fire, killing the creature. Hushang prostrates himself, praises the great Creator for this benefit to humanity, declares the fire to be Light from Heaven sent by God, and urges others to adore and worship it. That evening he lights a great fire, holds a royal feast, and names the celebration the Festival of Siddeh. Hushang is credited with discovering blacksmithing, organizing rivers and streams to supply towns and irrigate fields, introducing the use of certain animal furs for clothing, and teaching his people to make bread and cook their food; previously they lived on fruit and leaves and wore animal skins. The people eat their own bread, are grateful to him as benefactor, and mild laws are framed, bringing widespread cultivation and joy to the land. The world is said to remember Hushang’s virtues. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l18307-l18380","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / ODDRUNARGRATR / THE LAMENT OF ODDRUN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 18307-18380","start":"18307","end":"18380","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Oddrun, speaking in the first person, recalls earlier tragedies: Brynhild’s terrible vengeance in killing herself beside Sigurth. She then narrates her own love for Gunnar, likened to Brynhild’s love. Gunnar and his kin offer Atli, Oddrun’s brother, rich gifts—rings, many dwellings, and treasure once borne by Grani—as bride-price for Oddrun, but Atli refuses any marriage gold from Gjuki’s son. Oddrun and Gunnar nevertheless continue their love and are seen together by her kinsmen. Although Atli has trusted that Oddrun would never do wrong, he secretly sends his men to spy on her in a dark wood; they discover the lovers lying together under one cover. Oddrun and Gunnar try to bribe the warriors with rings to keep silent, but the men report everything eagerly to Atli while concealing it from Guthrun, who should have been told first. The narrative shifts to Atli’s vengeance: Gjuki’s sons ride, Hogni’s heart is cut out, and another heart is cast into a cave full of serpents. A ‘hero wise’ and ‘high-born king’ plays the harp in captivity, hoping Oddrun will help. Oddrun, away with Geirmund mixing a draught, hears the sorrowful harp-sound from Hlesey, gathers her serving-maids, and sails across a sound toward Atli’s home, intending to save the hero’s life. Atli’s crawling, evil mother arrives first and bites Gunnar’s heart so that Oddrun cannot help him. Oddrun calls herself a ‘serpents-bed goddess’, affirms her deep love for the warrior as for her own self, and concludes her lament, saying that her great grief has been witnessed by a listener and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7191-l7276","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7191-7276","start":"7191","end":"7276","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sudabeh, enamoured with the king Ks's son Saiwush, goes to the king and proposes that the youth choose a bride from among the damsels of royal lineage under her care in the harem. The king agrees and sends Saiwush to the shubistn, the sacred women's quarters. Saiwush, modest and suspicious of Sudabeh's motives, enters with fear and is struck by the splendor of the place, where Sudabeh sits on a splendid throne with coronet and flowing hair. She descends, embraces and kisses him, but he withdraws to sit among the other women, who place him on a golden chair and converse with him. He reports favorably to the king, who, recalling astrologers' prophecy that his son's marriage will produce a prince, urges him to choose a wife from the harem, despite Saiwush's reluctance to return to Sudabeh's apartments. On another day, the damsels leave Sudabeh alone with Saiwush. She recites verses praising his beauty and semi-supernatural ancestry, throws off the veil of modesty, embraces and kisses him, and declares herself wholly devoted, asking him to take her for himself when the king dies. Remembering Ks's past sufferings from the treachery of Sudabeh's father at Hmvern, Saiwush silently rejects the seduction as a demon's work and refuses to betray his father. To avoid further trouble, he offers instead to marry Sudabeh's daughter, which greatly pleases Ks, who opens his treasury in celebration. Sudabeh, however, continues to pursue her own design, reading incantations to secure success or punish the noncompliant youth. Later she summons Saiwush, confesses that for seven years she has lived in withered, unrequited love, begs him to bless her with affection, and threatens that his life will be in peril if he continues to refuse. {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l9011-l9097","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU; lines 9011-9097","start":"9011","end":"9097","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rustem, after reporting his previous successes to Kai-khosru through Frburz and receiving the king’s approval, undertakes further campaigns. He attacks Kafr, the cannibal king of Bidd who eats human flesh, especially beautiful young women, kills him, has his body given to dogs, and destroys his castle. Rustem then invades and ravages Khoten, recently held by Saiwush and dependent on Turan, which further alarms Afrsiyb. Afrsiyb secretly sends a spy to Rustem’s camp and, distressed by the report, consults the experienced Prn-wsah. Prn advises that former allies, Kms the Kashnian and the Khakn of Chin, have already been slain, and recommends seeking help from a neighboring giant-like king, Pladwund, renowned for his great stature and strength, who might by heaven’s favor defeat Rustem. Afrsiyb invites Pladwund, who eagerly joins him with his army, and together they march against the Persians.

In the ensuing battle, Pladwund uses his kamund to seize the warrior Gw. Rehm and Byzun rush to free him but are also captured; when the kamunds break, Pladwund draws his sword and wounds them. Their father Gdarz appeals to Rustem, who promptly comes, frees the captives, and engages Pladwund in fierce combat with clubs. Pladwund lands such a heavy blow on Rustem that its sound is heard by distant troops; Rustem, stunned and recognizing his opponent’s strength, prays to the Almighty for a favorable outcome, fearing Persia would be left without defense if he dies. When Pladwund attempts to finish him with his sword, the blade recoils from Rustem’s armor. Pladwund then proposes wrestling.

Both armies withdraw, leaving a farsang between them, with no assistance allowed to either champion. Afrsiyb instructs Pladwund to stab Rustem in the heart once he has him beneath him. In the wrestling match, however, Rustem seizes Pladwund, lifts him, and dashes him to the ground so violently that he appears dead. Believing him slain, Rustem leaves and remounts his horse Rakush. Pladwund has only feigned death; once free, he flees back to his own forces, tells Afrsiyb how he saved himself by pretending to be dead, and declares opposition to Rustem useless. When Rustem realizes the deception and pursues, the Tartars shower him with arrows. After his counterattack, Pladwund, terrified, abandons the field without even informing Afrsiyb.

Prn then advises Afrsiyb to flee to the remotest part of Tartary, as Pladwund’s flight has disheartened the Turanian troops and further resistance would be fruitless. Afrsiyb retreats so hastily that he leaves behind his standards, tents, horses, arms, and enormous treasure. Rustem sends the most valuable booty to the king of Iran and distributes a portion among the chiefs and soldiers. He then rides Rakush to Kai-khosru’s court, where he is welcomed with great honor and rejoicing. Kai-khosru opens his jewel chamber and showers Rustem with rich gifts: precious rubies, gold vessels filled with musk and aloes, splendid garments, a hundred beautiful crowned damsels with earrings, a hundred horses, and a hundred camels. Rustem returns to Zbul with the admiration and blessings of his country.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem communicates an account of his success to Kai-khosru through Frburz and receives strong marks of royal approval.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rustem undertakes new exploits by attacking Kafr, king of the city of Bidd, described as a cannibal who eats human flesh, especially the most beautiful young women of his While acknowledging that other Oriental civilizations like India and Arabia have produced great poets and heroes, the author notes that Persian figures such as Firdusi, Sa'di, Omar Khayyam, Jami, and Hafiz are far better known in the West. He attributes this to shared underlying cultural forces: a Hellenic love of beauty and a Semitic moral spirit that shaped both Persian civilization and the modern West. Persia, even in its early Iranian phase, was open to Semitic influence, and the Avesta’s religion is said to resemble that of the Old and New Testaments, making Zoroastrian Persians more intelligible to Westerners. Persian poetry is described as this-worldly, rich in imagery, and appealing to universally human concerns, which has allowed European writers like Goethe and others to \"re-sing\" Persian masterpieces for Western audiences. The author further characterizes Persian imagination as inherently gay and less stern than Semitic thought, delighting in chivalric tales and manifesting in the artistic decoration of palaces and manuscripts. Zoroaster himself was never deified, allowing storytellers to treat his deeds and those of ancient heroes with great imaginative freedom. Persian fancy is said to roam across the whole of national history, peer toward the hidden beginnings of all things, intertwine fact with fiction, and build both grounded narratives and airy imaginative constructions. Finally, the Shah Nameh (Book of Kings) is introduced as the greatest Eastern national epic, worthy of comparison with the Indian Nala, Homer’s Iliad, and the German Niebelungen. Rustem is summoned as the only champion able to deal with it. Guided by the peasant, Rustem hunts the creature for days; whenever he attacks with lasso, sword, spear, or arrow, the wild ass vanishes. Realizing it is the demon Akwn Dw, he continues until exhausted, then sleeps by a green spot near a spring while his horse Rakush grazes. Akwn Dw uproots the ground beneath the sleeping hero, carries him on his head, and offers to either throw him into the sea or abandon him on a desolate mountain. Knowing that such demons act by contraries, Rustem pretends to fear the sea and to prefer the mountain. The demon accordingly throws him into the deep sea, where Rustem kills attacking crocodiles, swims ashore, and thanks Heaven. Returning to the spring, he finds Rakush gone and eventually discovers him among Afrsiyb’s herd of horses. Rustem mounts his steed, drives off the entire herd, routs the pursuing keepers by declaring his identity, defeats Afrsiyb’s attack, and delivers the herd and four elephants to Kai-khosru. He then returns to the meadows and fountain near Akwn Dw’s dwelling, where he encounters the demon content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8495-l8583","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU; lines 8495-8583","start":"8495","end":"8583","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ts attacks a fort despite earlier royal warnings, leading to a deadly battle in which Ferd, the king's brother, is killed by Bhrm from ambush. Ferd's mother Glshaher, frantic with grief, rushes to her son's body and kills herself beside him. The Persians then force the gates and plunder the city. Bhrm rebukes Ts as responsible for the tragedy, prompting Ts to remain three days at the site and raise a scented monument to Ferd before continuing his campaign against Afrsiyb's forces. Afrsiyb sends large contingents under Nizd and Prn-wsah; Byzun distinguishes himself but is nearly captured and saved by his men. Prn-wsah, after losses to Gw, resorts to a shubkhn, a night attack, catching the Persians drunk and off guard and causing terrible slaughter. Ts realizes the scale of defeat at dawn. Kai-khosru, learning of this, writes to Frburz recalling his warning that Ts avoid Kullb because Ferd and his mother lived there and their residence should be sacred; he accuses Ts of causing their deaths and orders him bound and sent as prisoner while Frburz assumes command. Ts is confined and delivered to Khosru, who reproaches him and imprisons him in a dungeon. Khosru then writes to Prn, condemning the night attack as unworthy of a brave man and challenging him to open battle. Prn agrees to meet after a month, and the armies clash with arrows, swords, and javelins. Gw and Byzun press the enemy, who shift to attack Frburz so fiercely that he must shelter his remaining troops on the skirts of a mountain. Gdarz and Gw decide to stand firm or perish and send Byzun to ask Frburz either to join them or send the imperial banner. Frburz refuses to surrender the banner and calls on Gdarz to aid him. Byzun kills the standard-bearer, seizes the Derafsh Gvahn, and brings it to Gdarz, who raises it and leads a ferocious charge. The battle brings enormous casualties: most of Gdarz's sons and kin, many of the Ks family, and nine hundred relatives of Afrsiyb and Prn are killed, yet the Trnians win. Afrsiyb rewards his officers and urges them to eclipse the martial glory of Rustem and Khosru; Prn expresses confidence. Frburz escapes by night to Khosru's court, where the king mourns both the defeat and Ferd's death. Rustem is summoned to console him and save the empire. Khosru releases Ts and asks Rustem to lead the army against Prn, but Ts volunteers; Rustem agrees that Ts can oppose Prn, promising to fight if Afrsiyb appears. Khosru sends Ts and Gdarz with a large army against Prn. After seven days and nights of fighting, Hmn steps forward on the eighth day, kills several warriors in single combat, and then challenges Ts. Gdarz forbids Ts to accept and sends Gw in his place. Gw and Hmn fight fiercely, both wounded and exhausted, and return to their posts. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7876-l7975","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7876-7975","start":"7876","end":"7975","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rustem, continuing his vengeance, advances with the Persian army into Turan. In battle Fermurz captures Sarkh, son of Afrsiyb, and Rustem orders Sarkh to be executed by Ts in the same manner as Saiwush, despite Sarkh’s plea that he was Saiwush’s friend. Sarkh’s blood is collected in a dish and sent to Kai-khosru, and his head is displayed over the palace gate. Afrsiyb, learning of his favorite son’s death, assembles the entire Turanian army, described as so vast it darkens the sun, moon, and stars. Plsam, brother of Prn, ambitiously challenges Rustem and is promised Afrsiyb’s daughter and half the kingdom if he succeeds. After initial combat with Gw and Fermurz, Rustem intervenes, withstands a blow that breaks Plsam’s sword without harm, unhorses Plsam, drags him before Afrsiyb, and taunts the king, recalling his treachery to Saiwush. Afrsiyb and his warriors initially cower, then Afrsiyb fights Rustem; Rustem’s javelin kills the king’s horse, and Hmn rescues Afrsiyb, who flees. Rustem pursues, killing thousands, but the enemy withdraws into Chinese Tartary to secure Kai-khosru. Rustem then occupies Turan, ruling for about seven years with notable severity, executing anyone who mentions Afrsiyb’s name, rewarding Ts and Gdarz with rich gifts, while Zra ravages the land in revenge for Saiwush by burning and destroying everything, especially places associated with the prince. The whole realm is plundered, enriching the army. Rustem’s companions grow weary of life in Turan, call it exile in an ungenial climate, and remind him that Kai-ks has long been neglected. Rustem finally abandons the kingdom, and he and his warriors depart with the remaining jewels and gold, sending portions of the treasure to Zabul and Seistan and to the ‘king of kings’ in Persia.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem advances with the Persian army against Afrsiyb, continuing his vengeance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"As Rustem penetrates into Turan, the enemy sends thirty thousand men to oppose his progress.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the ensuing conflict Fermurz captures Sarkh, the son of Afrsiyb, as a prisoner.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem delivers Sarkh to Ts to be put to death precisely in the same manner as Saiwush.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sarkh declares himself a particular friend of Saiwush and begs to be pardoned on that account.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem has sworn that he will take his revenge without pity or remorse.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"S

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l18920-l19028","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ATLAKVITHA EN GRNLENZKA / THE GREENLAND LAY OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 18920-19028","start":"18920","end":"19028","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes to the Greenland Lay of Atli summarize the story of Guthrun’s marriage to Atli, arranged by her brothers Gunnar and Hogni, and the later slaying of Atli and his sons. The notes discuss specific words and stanzas, explaining references to Gunnar’s followers concealing their fear of the Huns in a hall called Valhall, the forest Myrkwood dividing Atli’s realm from that of the Gjukungs, and Gunnar arming his household for a journey. They explain the place Gnitaheith as the dragon Fafnir’s former lair and trace its ownership from Fafnir to Sigurth, then to the Gjukungs, and possibly to Atli as compensation for Brynhild’s death, with Atli later offering to restore it. The commentary mentions dragon-carved ship stems, the debated name Danp linked to a Gothic-Hunnish battlefield by the Dnieper, and genealogical connections among Kjar, Olrun, Authi, and Buthli, Atli’s father. One note describes Guthrun warning her brothers of Atli’s treachery by sending them a ring with a wolf’s hair, with an alternative version in which she sends runes. Other notes refer to a speech requesting drink for a possible ‘last feast’, Gunnar’s attitude toward a risky journey and return, Hogni’s sons Snvar and Solar accompanying him and dying, a younger son who stays behind, the land journey through Myrkwood (versus a partly boat journey in Atlamol), horses called ‘whip-fearers’, and watch-towers named with the same word as Othin’s watch-tower Hlithskjolf. The notes also touch on black bears and corpse-eating dogs, as well as various manuscript issues and textual variants.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Guthrun marries Atli at the instigation of her brothers Gunnar and Hogni.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Atli and his two sons, Erp and Eitil, are slain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In Atlamol there are two messengers, one named Vingi and one unnamed, but in Drap Niflunga the annotator combines the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8269-l8388","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 8269-8388","start":"8269","end":"8388","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"At the Persian court, Ts and Gudarz argue over the succession: Ts declares loyalty to king Ks and his heir Frburz, while Gudarz insists that the murdered eldest son Saiwush should be appeased by elevating Kai-Khosru (Khosru), whom nobles consider worthy of empire. They trade insults, with Ts scorning Gudarz’s blacksmith ancestry and Gudarz proudly invoking his kinship with Kavah the blacksmith, who tore up the fiend Zohak’s name-roll, freed Persia from devouring serpents, raised a banner of freedom, and secured Feridn’s virtuous rule. Ts boasts of superhuman martial power. Ks stills their anger; Gudarz proposes a fair test between Frburz and Khosru, and Ks affirms a father’s equal love for his children while seeking to prevent disunion. Ks then describes a nearby demon fortress, Bahmen, from which fire continually issues, and decrees that each prince shall attack it with an equal army; the conqueror will be sovereign of Persia. Frburz, supported by Ts, goes first but finds the ground aflame and a universal fire with furnace-like winds; many warriors die, and the fortress appears in mid-air without gate or door. After a week of fruitless searching and heavy losses, they return scorched and discomfited. Ks then sends Khosru with Gw and Gudarz. Recognizing the blazing, sky-reddening fortress as sorcery wrought by demon spirits, Khosru recalls a heavenly dream that taught him how to break magicians’ charms. He writes the name of God on his javelin; Gw displays it on the fortress’s magic walls while praying for Almighty aid. The fires suddenly cease and darkness falls; following Khosru’s orders, the troops shoot clouds of arrows from ten thousand bows at the enchanted tower, killing many demons. Light returns as mist rolls away, revealing fleeing fiends and the fortress’s great gate. The victors enter, seize its wealth, and Khosru builds a lofty temple to commemorate his victory before returning triumphantly to Ks, whose heart rejoices at the news.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ts sends an envoy to Gdarz suggesting that hostile proceedings be suspended until information is content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l19476-l19610","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / ATLAMOL EN GRNLENZKU / THE GREENLAND BALLAD OF ATLI / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 19476-19610","start":"19476","end":"19610","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"For your safety I sought that at home ye should stay; / None escapes his fate, so ye hither must fare.\"","summary":"In this portion of Atlamol, Gunnar and Hogni confront Atli after being lured into a trap. They kill Vingi, once of Atli's host, and a fierce battle breaks out between the Niflungs and Atli's mail‑clad warriors. Inside the hall, a thrall reports the fighting to Guthrun, who casts away her jewelry in grief, then arms herself, joins the battle, and kills two warriors including Atli's brother. The struggle is famous for its ferocity, with the sons of Gjuki and their allies slaying many foes before falling. Atli, enraged by his losses, blames his wife for bringing slaughter on his kin, while Guthrun answers that he first wronged her by murdering her mother and starving her niece. Atli then orders Hogni's heart cut out and Gunnar bound to a gallows and cast to serpents. Hogni accepts his fate bravely. Atli's steward Beiti proposes substituting the terrified thrall Hjalli, a cook, who begs piteously to do any menial work rather than be killed.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker tells opponents to go far from the house because its entrance is false and threatens that they will soon be burned while a gallows is fashioned for them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The threatening speaker says the opponents were invited fairly but deceit was concealed beneath the invitation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hogni answers that he fears nothing in his fate and warns the speaker that further threatening words will only worsen the speaker's fate.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Gunnar and Hogni kill Vingi with axes and the text says they sent him to hell.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Atli summons his men, who hasten in mail-coats, and a courtyard lies between the two sides.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Atli's side declares that they have long planned how soon they might slay their opponents.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hogni replies that their enemies wait unarmed, that Vingi has already been killed, and then fighting begins with arrows shot and shields raised in defense.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Inside the house a thrall reports that heroes are fighting in front of the hall.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"On hearing the thrall's report, Guthrun becomes grim with grief and throws off her fair necklaces and silver rings so that the rings burst apart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Guthrun goes out, flings open the doors, fearlessly welcomes the guests, and gives the Niflungs a last greeting, speaking openly and at length.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Guthrun says she sought the Niflungs' safety by trying to keep them at home, declares that none escapes his fate, and attempts to speak wisely for peace, but they all refuse to listen.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Seeing how hard the battle is, Guthrun throws off her mantle, takes a naked sword, and fights fiercely to guard the lives of her kin.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Guthrun kills two warriors, including Atli's brother whose feet she cuts off, and she sends another man to hell without trembling.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The battle is said to have wide fame and to be the greatest deed of the sons of Gjuki, who as Niflungs fight mightily, cutting mail-coats and hewing helmets with fearless hearts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The heroes fight from morning until midday, and also through dusk and dawn; when the battle ends the field flows with blood and, before they fall, eighteen enemies are slain by the two sons of Bera and Bera's brother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"A warrior speaker says that there were once thirty thanes ready for battle but only eleven remain, and he calls this reduction evil to see and the fault of the person he addresses.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The same speaker recalls that there were five brothers when Buthli died, says that Hel now has half of them and two lie smitten there, and laments that from a wife who brings slaughter he can win little joy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The warrior says that since his wife was given to him they have seldom lain together, that his kin are gone and his gold taken, and that worst of all she sent his sister to hell.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Guthrun answers that Atli committed the first evil by taking her mother and murdering her for gold and by starving her sister's daughter in a prison; she treats his sorrow as a jest and says she is glad that grief comes to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Atli orders his warriors to increase the grief of the beautiful woman Guthrun so that she will weep and lose her happiness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Atli commands his men to seize Hogni, cut out his heart with knives, and to bind grim-hearted Gunnar on the gallows and cast him to serpents.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Hogni tells Atli to do as he wishes, says he gladly awaits what is to come, and recalls that they held Atli at bay while they were whole, but now they are wounded and exhausted so Atli can work his will.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Beiti, described as Atli's steward, proposes seizing Hjalli and sparing Hogni, calling Hjalli a sluggard who has lived too long and is fit for death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Hjalli, Buthli's cook and pot-watcher, is terrified, runs about and climbs into corners, complains that it is bad for him if he must die for others' fierceness, and says it is sad to die leaving his swine and fine food.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Hjalli is seized as Buthli's cook, howls in fear as the knife approaches, and offers to dung the courtyard and do the basest work if only his life is spared.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"War leader who summons his men, speaks of long planning to slay his foes, quarrels with Guthrun about mutual wrongs, and orders the torture of Hogni and the death of rebukes Atli for his earlier crimes.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"One of the Niflung sons of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l10287-l10372","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAI-KHOSRU / AKWN DW / BARZ, AND HIS CONFLICT WITH RUSTEM / SSEN AND AFRSIYB; lines 10287-10372","start":"10287","end":"10372","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Afrsiyb challenges Kai-khosru to single combat, invoking God to grant victory to the more deserving. Kai-khosru wishes to accept and avenge the blood of Saiwush, but Rustem and the warriors restrain him, warning of Afrsiyb’s prowess. The king insists that a monarch who does not fight is unworthy of the crown until Barz dramatically begs him not to go, even threatening suicide; Kai-khosru relents, recognizing Barz as descended from Rustem. Barz kisses the ground before the king and rides out to face Afrsiyb. Afrsiyb, feeling betrayed by one he had reared and trained, denounces Barz as an ingrate of demon-birth. Barz replies that he faithfully served Afrsiyb when he “ate his salt,” but now eats the salt of Kai-khosru and owes allegiance to him. In the ensuing duel Afrsiyb wounds Barz with an arrow and rejoices at the sight of his blood. Barz attempts to close with his mace but cannot reach Afrsiyb and turns to archery; both show great skill. When Afrsiyb exhausts his arrows and takes up his mace to finish Barz, Hmn and Prn dissuade him from risking himself against a low-status opponent and order a general attack instead, urging the army to kill Barz as a threat. Barz is surrounded and badly wounded, but Rustem and Fermurz charge to his aid, killing many enemies. The battle becomes a noisy, tumultuous slaughter, likened to an armorer’s workshop and a stormy sea, with the field reddened by blood. Kai-khosru brings further forces, routs the Trnians, and Afrsiyb escapes in the confusion. When the king wants to pursue, Rustem counsels that their defeat is sufficient. Near Sstn, Rustem, now four hundred years old, asks leave to return home for rest and suggests Fermurz and Barz as his successors. Kai-khosru agrees, rewards his champions, allows Zl and Rustem to go to Sstn, and himself returns to his capital.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Afrsiyb rides into the middle of the plain and challenges Kai-khosru to single combat, saying God will give triumph to the one who merits it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Kai-khosru prepares to accept the challenge by dismounting from his elephant and mounting a horse, but his warriors seize his bridle and prevent him from fighting.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Kai-khosru declares that he will personally avenge the blood of Saiwush.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem warns Kai-khosru that Afrsiyb is highly skilled in all the arts of war and recalls that Afrsiyb escaped from being pinned in wrestling only by great dexterity, urging the king to let his warriors fight in his stead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Kai-khosru asserts that a monarch who does not fight for himself is unworthy of the crown, which angers him when his champions restrain him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Upon hearing the king’s words, Rustem weeps metaphorical “tears of blood.”","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Barz grasps the king’s stirrup, strikes his forehead against it, and threatens to kill himself if the king goes into single combat, saying that his own blood will be upon the king’s neck.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Barz’s eloquent speech persuades Kai-khosru to relent, and the king remarks to Rustem that there can be no doubt Barz is descended from him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Barz kisses the ground respectfully before the king, mounts his horse with agility, and rides to the central space where Afrsiyb awaits.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Afrsiyb internally laments that he has nurtured and instructed Barz only for Barz to shed his blood, calls him demon-born and ignorant of his father’s name, and reproaches him for ingratitude.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Barz replies that although Afrsiyb protected him and he served faithfully while eating his salt, he now eats the salt of Kai-khosru and owes allegiance to the Persian king.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In battle, Barz rushes at Afrsiyb like a demon; Afrsiyb warns him not to approach like a furious elephant and then wounds Barz with an arrow that pierces his armor and side, causing bleeding that delights Afrsiyb.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Barz tries to close with his mace but cannot reach Afrsiyb because of his enemy’s agility, and he is forced to switch to using his bow; their arrows are skillfully blocked or exchanged until Afrsiyb empties his quiver and takes up his mace intending to finish Barz.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Hmn and Prn advise Afrsiyb not to risk himself in single combat with Barz, arguing that Barz is of no account compared to Kai-khosru and that Afrsiyb’s death would doom Trn; they direct the Trnian troops to begin a general attack and prioritize killing Barz.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Trnian warriors surround Barz and inflict many wounds on him until Rustem and Fermurz charge to his aid, killing many enemies and causing great carnage as the Persian army advances.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The noise of battle is likened to an armorer’s workshop and the field to a tumultuous sea, with the ground crimsoned by the blood of slain heroes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Kai-khosru himself rushes to assist Barz with a powerful force that turns the battle and puts the Trnians to flight; Afrsiyb escapes in the confusion.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"When the king wishes to pursue the fleeing enemy, Rustem advises that their defeat and dispersion are sufficient.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"After the battle, near Sstn, Rustem asks permission to return home because he is four hundred years old and needs rest, proposing that Fermurz and Barz take his place.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Kai-khosru consents to Rustem’s request, distributes rewards to his distinguished warriors, leaves Zl and Rustem to travel The Persian troops flee, leaving Tus and Frburz to be captured, bound, and placed under Hmn’s guard. Afrsiyb rejoices at the news, while Kai-khosru grieves. Rustem’s wrath is stirred and he sets out with Gustahem at night. Mistaking Afrsiyb’s pavilion for Barz’s tent, he sees Afrsiyb enthroned with Barz and Piran beside him and Tus and Frburz standing in chains. Afrsiyb tells the captives they will be executed next day as he slew Saiwush, then departs. Rustem thanks Heaven his friends live, waits until the watchman is inattentive, kills him, frees Tus and Frburz from their chains, and returns them to Kai-khosru.

At dawn Afrsiyb learns a Persian champion has killed the watchman and rescued the prisoners; Piran concludes it must be Rustem. Afrsiyb angrily sends Barz to attack and challenge Rustem. Rustem answers that if Barz calls for Rustem, he himself comes in Rustem’s place to cast him down. Barz replies that though he is young and Rustem is aged and experienced, if Rustem is fire, he is water and can quench him. They fight with bows, then with maces until the maces bend, then wrestle. Barz finally smashes Rustem on the head with his mace so that Rustem feels as if a mountain had fallen on him and one arm is disabled, yet Rustem conceals the wound. Barz marvels that such a blow had so little apparent effect. Rustem suggests finishing the combat the next day, and Barz agrees.

Barz reports to Afrsiyb that Rustem and his horse seem as hard as flint and that his own strength had little effect; he is unsure of the outcome of the renewed duel. Rustem shows his wounded arm to Kai-khosru (Khosru), says he has escaped but wonders who can now face Barz; he judges that only his son Fermurz, away fighting in Hindustan, can do so, and proposes summoning him while delaying the duel. The sorrowful king permits his departure and even offers to fight Barz himself, but Gdarz insists the king must not be risked and says that Gw, Byzun, and other chiefs should successively face the enemy.

Back in his tent, Rustem tells his brother Zra to prepare a litter so he can go to Sistan to obtain a remedy for his wound from the Simurgh.
