Receiving no answer, Sohrab topples the royal pavilion, terrifying the king, who orders that Rustem be summoned. Ts finds the mighty champion, reports Sohrab’s deeds, and with other nobles helps arm Rustem. Hearing the tumult, Rustem interprets it as a demonic, world-ending conflict led by Ahirmun, then arms himself, mounting Rakush and riding out with dragon-emblazoned banners borne by Zra. Seeing the powerful and handsome youth Sohrab, Rustem calls him aside, and Sohrab proposes that the two of them decide the battle by single combat away from both armies. Rustem admires the youth, speaks of his own age and experience and past victories over demons, yet expresses compassion and reluctance to kill such a brave young warrior. Moved by these words, Sohrab asks if he is Rustem, whose fame is universal. The appended footnotes explain various symbolic terms used elsewhere in the Divan, including Magians as spiritual teachers, the cypress as a symbol of freedom, magical vessels of kings, the punishment of Korah, inscriptions invoking the Opener of the gates, the gatekeeper of Paradise and the thornless lote-trees with rivers in the Garden of Delight, and cosmological images such as the poisonous cup of Heaven, ruby gems lit by the sun, and zodiacal light.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker addresses an unlearned person and urges them to attempt the quest of love, saying one who has not trodden the path cannot guide others on the way.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The addressee is grade.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Slumber and food are said to have kept the addressee far from Love’s exalted good, and they are advised to abstain from content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l5516-l5646","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB; lines 5516-5646","start":"5516","end":"5646","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Grd-afrd, a Persian 'warrior-dame,' is moved by news of conflict and a hero's shame. She arms herself, hides her hair beneath a helm, and rides from the fort disguised as a man to challenge the bravest enemy. The young champion Sohrb accepts the challenge, mocks her as easy prey, and they fight fiercely; he wounds her and eventually strikes off her helmet, discovering she is a beautiful woman. He lassoes and captures her, but she reveals her face and uses beauty and persuasive argument about his honour and the spoils of victory to sway him. Overcome with love, he allows her to ride back to the castle gate. Inside, her father and the Persian warriors greet her joyfully and thank heaven. From the walls she urges Sohrb, addressed as a warrior of Trn and Turk, to abandon the attack, warning that when King Ks and Rustem come, his host will be destroyed. Shamed and vengeful at losing his \"prey,\" Sohrb has the suburb-town pillaged and vows to return the next day to burn the fort, then withdraws to await battle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Grd-afrd, described as a 'peerless warrior-dame,' hears of the conflict and a hero's shame, reacts with groans and tears of anger, and quickly arms herself and mounts a foaming horse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Grd-afrd puts on burnished mail, hides her clustering locks beneath a helm, and is so fully accoutred in a manly guise that no eye could discern her sex.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Leaving the fort 'like a lion,' Grd-afrd rides into the midst of the foe and boldly demands, in a haughty tone, the bravest chief to try the chance of fight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sohrb, already an armed champion, returns to the battle, scornfully calls his new opponent 'another deer' and 'another prize,' and has a noose spread for her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Seeing the insidious noose, Grd-afrd attacks with arrows that whizz around Sohrb's head; the narration notes that in forest sports no bird escaped when she touched the bowstring, emphasizing her exceptional archery.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sohrb, burning with fury, raises his buckler to ward off the storm of arrows, charges forward, while Grd-afrd slings her bow, takes up a lance, and continues the mounted fight with persevering courage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"During the combat, Sohrb throws a javelin that passes through Grd-afrd's girdle belt, glances down her polished armour, almost unhorses her, but she cuts the spear in two, draws the fragment from her side, regains her seat, and urges her steed onward.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sohrb overtakes Grd-afrd, strikes off her helm, and sees that his opponent has a woman's face, described as radiant with blushes and commanding grace; he exclaims in admiration that she is a woman from the Persian host and comments that if Persian damsels fight so, who can resist Persian warriors.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Sohrb draws a noose from his saddle thong, throws the twisted loop around Grd-afrd's waist, and tells her not to seek escape, calling her an 'unthinking maid' and remarking that such beauty seldom appears among their captives.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The narration states that in this desperate situation Grd-afrd, expert in wiles and 'siren-art,' exposes her blooming face, raises her bright black eyes, and appears in the full blaze of her charms before Sohrb.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Grd-afrd addresses Sohrb as a brave warrior and argues that if both hosts see her tresses and know he has fought and been resisted by a woman, his honour will be imperilled; she urges him to keep their struggle unknown, not to expose a helpless maid, and promises that the fort, treasure, chief, and garrison will obey him and reward his toil, granting him the honours of the day.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sohrb is described as raptured by Grd-afrd's smiles, swept into 'ungoverned love'; her face is likened to a paradise, with fawn-like eyes and rosy cheeks, and he is said to be vanquished and lost, struggling only with his amorous flame as he rides behind her, letting her gain the castle gate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Once inside the fortress, Grd-afrd stands safe among her friends, smiling; her father clasps her to his heart with tearful pleasure, the warriors crowd around her, and they offer grateful prayers to favouring heaven.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"From the walls, Grd-afrd, with majestic air, calls Sohrb 'warrior of Trn' and urges him to forbear, not to demand useless strife, and to return in peace to his native land.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Sohrb replies by calling her a 'beauteous tyrant' devoted to betray, and warns that when the walls are laid in ruins and she is a captive maid, repentance and sorrow will soften her disdainful heart.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Grd-afrd answers that over Persia's fertile fields the savage Turk's sword is vain, and that when King Ks hears of the invasion and mighty Rustem appears in arms, destruction will cover the plain and not one man of Sohrb's host will remain; she laments that such bravery must meet certain defeat and urges him to avert content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l16646-l16712","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CXXXV / CXLVI / CXLIX / CLVII; lines 16646-16712","start":"16646","end":"16712","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two poems attributed to Hafiz: the first invites a companion to cast off a deceitful ascetic robe, exchange convent revenues for wine, confront Fate, and speak of the other world and Rizvn's green glade with ghilmn and houris, ending with a warning against boastfulness and overstepping one's rug. The second poem declares the speaker a slave of Love free from both worlds, recalls an origin in Highest Heaven and descent by Adam to a lonely cloister, contrasts paradise pleasures with the beloved's street, questions his birth star and Mother Earth's plant, describes service in Love's house of wine with grief, and dwells on the loved one's Alif-form, lock of hair, and the poet's tear-drops.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker addresses \"Sfi\" and proposes that they remove from their limbs a dress associated with cheating and draw a blotting line through this emblem of deceit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker says they would sacrifice the convent's revenues and alms for wine and draw a dervish-robe of guile through the vintry's fragrant flood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker imagines becoming intoxicated, rushing forth, bearing off a feasting foe's wine, and then by force drawing his charmer out of doors.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fate is described as concealing her mystery within a hiding pale, while the speakers, acting as drunken men, will draw the veil from Fate's face.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker urges that they shine by noble deeds so they will not appear ashamed when starting for the other world and drawing their spirit's gear from here.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The poem mentions Rizvn's green glade and says that if \"they\" refuse to make it theirs, the speakers will draw the ghilmn from their halls and the houris from their bowers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The poem asks where \"her winking brow\" can be seen so that, like the new moon of old, they may at once draw the celestial ball as with a bat of gold.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The poem addresses Hafiz, saying it does not become him to put forth boastful claims or to draw his foot beyond the limits of his rug.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The later poem states aloud, with a glad heart, that the speaker is Love's slave and free from both worlds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker calls himself a bird of sacred gardens and says he fell into a net of chance.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker says his place was the Highest Heaven, that he was born an angel, and that he came by Adam to a lonely cloister.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"He says that sweet houris, Tb's shade, and the Fountain's brink fade from his mind when he thinks of \"thy street.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The speaker claims that no astrologer knows his star of birth and addresses the Lord, asking under what plant Mother Earth bore him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"He explains that since, with ringed ear, he has served Love's house of wine, grief's gratulations have come to him each hour.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"He says that \"my eyeball's man\" drains his heart's blood because he placed his trust in \"man's own darling.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker says that his loved one's Alif-form stamps all his thought and that, apart from that, his master has taught him no other letter.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"He prays that Hafiz's tear-drops may be dried by \"thy lock\" so that he does not perish in their rushing tide.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Hfiz","description":"Named figure whose claims, rug boundary, and tear-drops are mentioned and who appears to be the speaking voice of the poems.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:17","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Sfi","description":"Companion addressed at the beginning of the first poem and invited to join mystery in a hiding pale and has a veil on her face.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Feasting foe","description":"Opponent described as having rich stores and wine that the intoxicated speakers plan to seize.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Charmer","description":"Attractive figure belonging to the feasting foe, whom the speakers intend to draw out of doors by force.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Ghilmn","description":"Group of figures residing in halls at Rizvn's green glade, whom the speakers say they will draw from those halls.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Houris","description":"Group of As Rustem enters the city, Rakush’s loud neighing is heard by the blind, imprisoned monarch Ks, who rejoices that his misfortunes are ending, though his people think him mad or dreaming until Rustem appears. Ks, his warriors, and companions such as Gdarz, Ts, Bhrm, Gw, and Gustahem welcome Rustem, but Ks and his warriors are still blind under the Demons’ spells. Ks warns Rustem to conceal Rakush from the sorcerers, since the White Demon would otherwise rally an overwhelming army, and urges him to storm the cavern of the Demons beyond the Seven Mountains, defeat their gigantic chief the White Demon in a deep and horrible recess, and use warm blood from the White Demon’s heart, dropped into the eyes, to restore the sight of the king and warriors. Rustem, after warning his friends to stay alert, sets out guided by Ald to the Haft-koh (Seven Mountains), finds numerous companies of Demons and a cavern crowded with them, waits until the sun is hot when most Demons sleep, binds Ald to a tree, and then rushes among the sleeping Demons, slaughtering them until the survivors flee. Later, when Gw intends to fulfill an oath to stain the earth with Prn’s blood, Ferangs recalls Prn’s past kindness in saving her and Kai-khosru from Afrsiyb after Saiwush’s death and pleads for mercy; Afrasiyab wishes to kill him immediately, but is dissuaded first by his followers and then by the warrior Pilsam, so the prince is fettered and taken back to the splendid palace he himself had built. There, Afrasiyab's daughter Ferangis, Saiwush's wife, pleads passionately for his life, insisting on his innocence and warning her father of earthly disgrace and torment in hell for unjust bloodshed, recalling earlier punished tyrants and naming Iranian heroes who might avenge such a crime. Afrasiyab feels temporary compunction but then imprisons Ferangis and orders his brother Gersivaz to have Saiwush beheaded in such a way that his blood does not touch the earth. Gersivaz delegates the task to Karzura; as the executioner seizes him, Saiwush prays that a son may be born to vindicate his name and avenge his murderer, then is beheaded. The blood is caught in a golden vessel, yet a few drops fall to the ground, from which a wondrous tree later grows, known as the Saiwush tree; at the same time a tremendous storm and darkness cover the earth, and the people of Khoten curse Afrasiyab and cherish Saiwush's memory. Ferangis is frantic with grief, and a proverb is recalled that it is better to be in hell than under Afrasiyab's rule; hearing of her sorrow, the king orders Gersivaz to have her secretly killed so there will be no child from her marriage, but his counselor Piran protests, condemning the unnatural murder of daughter and unborn infant and warning of lasting infamy and punishment after death. him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Saiwush attempts to flee but is overtaken when Gersivaz pursues him, his horse is killed in {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8410-l8493","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU; lines 8410-8493","start":"8410","end":"8493","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Upon Kai-Khosru's accession, Zal and Rustem rejoice and travel to court with gifts to pay homage. Khosru warmly receives them, immediately asks Rustem's help to avenge the murder of his father Saiwush by Afrasiyab, and Rustem agrees. King Kai-Kaus hosts a royal banquet, then transfers command of the imperial army to Khosru, who vows he will find no happiness on the throne until he has taken vengeance. The army is organized under various commanders, including Friburz, Tus, Gudarz, Gustahem, and a guard under Byzun.

As the forces march, Khosru instructs Friburz and Tus to avoid molesting his brother Ferd, another son of Saiwush who dwells with his mother Gulshaher in a strong fort called Kullab on their route, telling them to bypass his lands. Friburz obeys, but Tus prefers a more pleasant, cultivated route that leads directly toward the fort. Ferd, hearing that Tus approaches with an armed force, assumes hostile intent. Although Tus sends his son-in-law R as envoy to explain he only wishes to pass peacefully, Ferd distrusts the message, fights, and kills R. Tus then besieges the fort. Ferd sallies out, skillfully shooting arrows that kill the horses of Tus, then the warrior Gw, and then Gw's son Byzun, who nevertheless rises on foot and challenges Ferd. After a brief spear combat, Ferd retreats into the fort and hurls stones from the walls, badly wounding Byzun, who withdraws. Tus, enraged by these setbacks, vows that none within the fort will be left alive the next day.

At this point, Ferd's mother, the daughter of Wisah, dreams that the fortress is engulfed in flames and all its inhabitants are burned to death. She reports this ominous dream to her son. Ferd responds by declaring that he does not fear death, that no man is immortal, and that his goal is to win a bright and spotless name in war. When Gw (Giv) reaches the rapid, dangerous river with Kai-khosru and his mother Ferangs, the ferrymen, acting under these orders, refuse ordinary payment and instead demand Gw’s black horse, the woman, the youth’s crown, or Gw’s armor; Gw refuses to surrender any of them. Recalling the example of Kavah the blacksmith, who once crossed a stream in armor while rescuing Fereidun, and trusting in an auspicious omen and the protection of the Almighty, Kai-khosru rides his horse into the boiling torrent, followed by his mother and Gw; all three safely reach the opposite bank, to the amazement of the ferrymen. Afrsiyb arrives just as they land but, dissuaded by Hmn from attempting a risky crossing with few troops, turns back to Trn in grief and anger. Once inside Persian territory Gw thanks God and informs King Ks of their safe arrival; the king rejoices, sends Gdarz to meet Kai-khosru, welcomes the youth with tears and kisses, seats him on a throne identical to his own, and commands the assembled nobles to obey him. All consent except Ts, who leaves in disgust, declaring he will only pay homage to Frburz, son of Ks, and will not accept a child of the Trnian line. When a second assembly is called to formalize allegiance, Ts again refuses, despite Gw’s attempts to persuade him. Gdarz, enraged by this defiance, musters twelve thousand troops and his seventy-eight kinsmen, together with Gw, to enforce the royal command, but Ts, though prepared for conflict, inwardly resolves not to draw the sword and cause Persian bloodshed, saying that such blood should only be shed in a just war against foreign (Tartar) content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l9207-l9307","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU / AKWN DW; lines 9207-9307","start":"9207","end":"9307","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"It is a spot beyond imagination / Delightful to the heart, where roses bloom, / And sparkling fountains murmur ... in that retreat / Which blooms like Paradise\"","summary":"Rustem is taunted by the demon Akwn Dw, ensnares him with a lasso, beheads him, and sends the severed head as a trophy to Kai-Khosru, who honors Rustem before the hero returns to Zabulistan with a royal escort. Later, the people of Armn petition Kai-Khosru to relieve them from destructive wild boars. While the king is feasting with warriors, wine, music, and bewitching damsels, the young hero Byzun volunteers to exterminate the boars despite objections that he is too young. Accompanied by the veteran Girgn, Byzun travels to the border region, hunts and kills many boars, burns the forest and cultivation to destroy their sustenance, and cuts off their heads and tusks as proof for the king. Girgn, envious of Byzun's success, tries to prevent him from sending the trophies and then, over wine and lavish praise, entices him with a description of a garden of perpetual spring visited by Manjeh, the beautiful daughter of Afrsiyb. Girgn proposes they encamp among the maidens and seize virgins for the king. Byzun eagerly goes with him to the garden, approaches Manjeh's summer-tent, and Manjeh, seeing him, falls deeply in love and sends her nurse to learn his identity and origin.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Akwn Dw taunts Rustem, questioning whether he has risen from death, escaped monsters of the deep, and whether his body is made of flint, brass, or iron, or can raise a battle storm like a demon.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rustem responds to Akwn Dw's taunt by preparing for combat, casting his kamund so that the demon is ensnared, and then striking such a blow with his sword that he severs the demon's head from its body.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Rustem sends the severed head of Akwn Dw as a trophy to Kai-Khosru.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Kai-Khosru views the demon's head with amazement because of its hideous expression and vast size.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After killing Akwn Dw, Rustem pays his respects to Kai-Khosru, is received with honor and affection at court, enjoys the court's hospitality for some time, and then returns to Zabulistan, accompanied part of the way by Kai-Khosru and a crowd of valiant warriors.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The people of Armn petition Kai-Khosru to remove a grievous calamity: their land is overrun with herds of wild boars that destroy fields, orchards, and gardens and make it dangerous to go abroad.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the petition from Armn arrives, Kai-Khosru is at a banquet among his warriors, drinking wine and listening to music and the songs of bewitching damsels, with verse praising beauty, music, and wine.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On hearing of the Armnians' plight, Kai-Khosru refers the matter to his counsellors and nobles so that a remedy may be applied.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Byzun, filled with youthful enthusiasm, offers to undertake the extermination of the wild boars himself after learning what is required and the king's disposition.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gw objects to Byzun taking on the task, arguing that Byzun is too young and that a hero of greater experience is needed for such an arduous enterprise.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Byzun argues that although he is young he is mature in judgment and discretion, trusting the king's liberal decision; Kai-Khosru ultimately permits him to go on the expedition accompanied by the veteran warrior Girgn.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Byzun and Girgn set off on the perilous expedition and, after several days' journey, arrive at a place between Iran and Turan where the wild boars are most destructive.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Byzun and Girgn hunt down and kill many wild boars, and Byzun sets fire to the forest and reduces the cultivated land to ashes to destroy the depredators' sustenance, freeing the country from the destructive visitation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"To provide incontestable proof of his exploit, Byzun cuts off the heads of the wild boars and removes their tusks to send to Kai-Khosru.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After witnessing Byzun's boldness and his intention to send trophies to Kai-Khosru, Girgn becomes envious of the youth's success and fears for his own reputation.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Girgn first attempts to dissuade Byzun from sending the trophies; when he fails, he resolves to get Byzun out of the way and manipulates him skillfully, praising him beyond all other warriors while Byzun is warmed with wine.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Girgn tells Byzun about a nearby beautiful place, a garden of perpetual spring visited each spring by Manjeh, the lovely daughter of Afrsiyb.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The garden is described as full of blooming roses, sparkling murmuring fountains, many-colored flowers, musk-laden breezes, hyacinths and lilies, trees with branches weighed down by golden fruits, a stately pheasant, a singing bulbul, and love-inspiring damsels; it is said to bloom like Paradise.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Girgn proposes that they go to this garden, encamp among the groups of maidens, and secure a bevy of fair virgins there as gifts for the king.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Excited by Girgn's description, Byzun promptly goes with Girgn to the romantic retreat of the princess Manjeh.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Byzun and Girgn approach so close to Manjeh's summer-tent that she sees Byzun clearly, becomes deeply enamoured of him, and sends her nurse to inquire who he is and from whence he came.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"Heroic warrior who defeats the demon Akwn Dw, sends its severed head to Kai-Khosru, is honored at court, and returns to Zabulistan with a royal escort.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Akwn Dw (Akvan Div)","description":"Demon who taunts Rustem about his resilience and is ensnared and beheaded in battle.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Kai-Khosru","description":"King who receives the severed head of Akwn Dw, honors Rustem, feasts with warriors and bewitching damsels, hears the petition of the people of Armn, consults counsellors, and authorizes Byzun's expedition against the wild boars.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Valiant warriors of Kai-Khosru","description":"Group of warriors who accompany Kai-Khosru, attend his banquet, and partly escort Rustem on his return to Zabulistan.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"People of Armn (Armnians)","description":"Subjects whose land is devastated by wild boars and who petition Kai-Khosru for protection and relief.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Byzun","description":"Youthful hero who volunteers to exterminate the wild boars, travels with Girgn, hunts and burns them out, prepares heads and tusks as trophies, is plied with wine and praise by Girgn, and is enticed to visit Manjeh's garden, where he is seen and admired by the princess.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Gw","description":"Older hero or counsellor who objects that Byzun is too young and maidens.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Wild boars","description":"Herds of fierce boars that devastate fields, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7481-l7554","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7481-7554","start":"7481","end":"7554","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Saiwush, a Persian prince, is lavishly honored at Afrsiyb’s court in Turan and, on the advice of the general Prn-wsah, marries the lovely Glshaher. Later Prn arranges a second, politically motivated marriage between Saiwush and Ferangs, Afrsiyb’s daughter; Glshaher selflessly approves, and Afrsiyb rewards the couple with the sovereignty of Khoten and great wealth. While Kai-ks in Persia grieves over Saiwush’s flight and Rustem leaves the court in anger, Saiwush in Khoten commissions Prn to find an ideal residence site, builds a paradise-like mountain palace adorned with portraits of Persian and Turanian kings and champions, yet remains sorrowful over his estrangement from home; meanwhile Glshaher, staying in her father’s house, bears a son named Ferd.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Saiwush is placed on a golden throne next to Afrsiyb, and a magnificent banquet with music and the songs of beautiful women is held in his honor.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"At the banquet, singers praise Saiwush for being of the line of Kai-kobd, for his faith and honor, and for his extraordinary beauty that wins universal admiration.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Afrsiyb’s favorable feelings toward Saiwush persist and increase, and he treats Saiwush with all the respect and honor due to his royal birth.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After a year, Prn-wsah, one of Afrsiyb’s generals, advises Saiwush that since he is favored by the king, far from Persia, and his father is old, it would be better for him to marry and reside in Turan for life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Saiwush accepts the advice, meets the lovely Glshaher (also called Jarra), and they immediately marry by mutual consent, expressing their love with many kisses.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Some time after the first union, Prn proposes another alliance for Saiwush with Ferangs, the daughter of Afrsiyb, to strengthen his own political interests and power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Saiwush, deeply devoted to Glshaher, first consults her about the proposed second marriage, though he feels unable to refuse because of Afrsiyb’s hospitality and affection.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Glshaher is called a heroine and willingly sacrifices her feelings, saying she would rather be Ferangs’s handmaid than compromise Saiwush’s happiness and prosperity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The second marriage between Saiwush and Ferangs takes place, and Afrsiyb, pleased with the match, grants them the sovereignty of Khoten along with abundant gold, horses, camels, and elephants.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Saiwush and his new bride soon travel to take up their rule in Khoten.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In Persia, Ks suffers intense distress and sorrow when he hears of Saiwush’s flight into Turan.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rustem, angered by the conduct of King Ks, abruptly leaves the court without permission and retires to Sstn.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ks, finding himself in an embarrassed situation, recalls Ts and the army from Balkh and abandons further hostilities against Afrsiyb.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After arriving in Khoten, Saiwush orders that a beautiful site be selected for his residence, and Prn searches all the surrounding provinces, hills, and valleys to fulfill this request.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Prn discovers a site about a month’s journey away on a mountain, with rich and varied scenery, fresh green trees, birds singing, clear rivulets, a mild climate, healthy inhabitants, and breezes filled with music and perfume, likened to the imagined charms of Paradise.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Saiwush builds a palace and garden-temples at the mountain site and has pictures painted of notable contemporaries and portraits of ancient kings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The palace walls are decorated with likenesses of Kai-kobd, Kai-ks, Poshang, Afrsiyb, Sm, Zl, Rustem, and other champions of Persia and Turan.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The completed retreat is described as so splendid that its sight could restore youthful vigor even to the aged.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Despite the beauty of his new residence, Saiwush is unhappy, and tears come to his eyes whenever he thinks of his estrangement from home.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Glshaher, remaining in her father’s house, bears a son who is named Ferd.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Saiwush","description":"Persian prince of the line of Kai-kobd who becomes an honored guest at Afrsiyb’s court in Turan, marries Glshaher and later Ferangs, is granted sovereignty over Khoten, builds a splendid mountain palace, yet remains sorrowful over his separation from home.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:5","role:8","role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Afrsiyb","description":"King of Trn (Turan) who warmly receives Saiwush, favors him, allows his marriages, and grants him and his daughter Ferangs the sovereignty of Khoten along with great wealth; his portrait also appears among ancient kings in Saiwush’s palace.","role_refs":["role:3","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Prn-wsah (Prn)","description":"One of Afrsiyb’s generals who advises Saiwush residence.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Glshaher (Jarra)","description":"Described as a lovely woman and a heroine, she is Saiwush’s To Rustem...","summary":"As Rustem lies mortally wounded, he asks Shughad to string his bow so he can stand as a scarecrow to keep wolves and wild animals from his corpse. Shughad, secretly rejoicing at Rustem's condition, complies, but Rustem grasps the bow with unexpected strength. Terrified, Shughad hides behind a tree, yet Rustem shoots an arrow that pierces both the tree and Shughad, killing him. Rustem thanks the Creator for allowing him to avenge himself on his murderer and dies. His followers, including Zra, have previously perished in pits dug by a traitor-king of Kabul and the traitor-brother. Only one survivor escapes and carries the news to the aged veteran Zl in Sistan. Zl is overwhelmed with grief, tearing his white hair and garments, and lamenting that he was not there to die in Rustem's place. Zl then sends Fermurz with a large force to Kabul to retrieve Rustem's body. The king of Kabul retreats with his army to the mountains, but Fermurz devastates the land, finds only the skeletons of Rustem and Zra—whose flesh has been eaten by beasts of prey—gathers their bones, returns home, and buries them amid public lamentation. Afterwards he returns to Kabul, defeats and captures the king, brings him to Sistan, and has him put to death. In a brief notice, the narrative adds that the aged king Gushtsp, now infirm, bequeaths his empire to Bahman and then dies after a reign of 108 {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l11933-l12025","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR; lines 11933-12025","start":"11933","end":"12025","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Presently from the mountain there rushed down
  A furious storm of wind, then heavy showers
  Of snow fell, covering all the earth with whiteness,
  And making desolate the prospect round.
  Keen blew the blast, and pinching was the cold;
  And to escape the elemental wrath,
  Leader and soldier, in the caverned rock
  Scooped out by mouldering time, took shelter, there
  Continuing three long days.","summary":"Isfendiyr, on the fifth stage of his Heft-Khan, travels with a small army until he reaches the region of the Smrgh (Simurgh). He prepares a bladed machine drawn by horses; the great bird descends from the mountain, injures herself on the hidden weapons, and Isfendiyr then leaps out and cuts her in two, while her young flee. His ally Bashtan and the army marvel, while the demon-guide Kurugsar is shaken. Kurugsar warns that the next danger will be a deadly snowstorm against which no one can prevail, since it would mean contending with the elements and the Almighty; he urges Isfendiyr to turn back, and the people, recalling the companions of Kai-khosru who perished in snow, initially agree. Isfendiyr refuses, offering to proceed alone, and the men renew their loyalty. On the sixth stage he reaches a mountain with a running stream, makes camp, and is then caught in a violent storm of wind and deep snow that lasts three days, forcing men and beasts to shelter in caverned rocks and suffer from hunger. Isfendiyr and his warriors uncover their heads, prostrate themselves, and pray to the Almighty, after which Heaven shows compassion and the storm ceases, allowing them to emerge. Isfendiyr declares the sixth labor complete, but Kurugsar warns that forty farsangs still remain before the Brazen Fortress of Arjsp, including three farsangs of burning sand as hot as fire with no water and air so deadly that no creature can survive, and he again advises the hero to abandon the attempt as beyond human Kai-khosru at first allows Shydah to depart and sends word that his answer to Afrasiyab will go by Krun, but Shydah insists on fighting, and the king’s honor leads him to agree to a duel the next day. That night Kai-khosru composes a letter to Afrasiyab demanding that he surrender crown, mace, kingdom, and army, declaring that strength and victory come from God and Heaven and that Afrasiyab’s throne will soon be his. He instructs Krun to first tell Shydah that he is doomed to die in battle, that his finery will be his shroud, and that his father will weep blood as Kai Kaus once wept for Siyavush. In the morning Kai-khosru and Shydah meet apart from their armies and agree to wrestle. The joyful young prince cannot move the king, who lifts and throws him, then leaps on him like a lion and kills him with a dagger thrust to the heart. Kai-khosru orders Shydah’s body washed with musk and rose-water, buried, and honored with a tomb. When Krun arrives at Afrasiyab’s court with the peace answer, news of Shydah’s death has already reached the king, who in anguish ignores the message, sounds the war drums, and marches with a great army. The Turanians, enraged by the prince’s death, fight with reckless fury. A verse reflection describes two sovereigns driven by revenge—one for a father, the other for a son—while thousands die and blood flows like a tide to gratify human hate and pride. The Turanians are defeated and flee; the people seize Afrasiyab’s horse’s bridle and force him to follow his routed forces. Kai-khosru sends news of victory to Kaus and relentlessly pursues Afrasiyab across many lands to the borders of Chin. The Khakn of Chin, alarmed, sends rich gifts to placate him, but Kai-khosru declares he seeks only Afrasiyab and threatens to devastate the land if he is harbored. Rustem, having avenged the murder of Saiwush, has also arranged a search for the hidden prince Kai-khosru. The old warrior Gudarz dreams of the young prince, who reveals his location and indicates that only Gudarz's son Gw is destined to restore him to the world and to his birthright. Gudarz sends Gw on this mission. Gw travels through remote regions, repeatedly hiring guides and killing them to keep his quest secret. He endures great hardship, eats only wild ass, wears its skin, and traverses mountains and forests, often tempted to turn back but pressed on by honor. In a desert he meets men sent by Piran-wisah to find Kai-khosru; concealing his purpose under the pretext of hunting, he learns their direction and then continues alone. Gw eventually finds a youth by a fountain and assumes he is Kai-khosru. Each immediately recognizes the other: Gw declares the youth to be Saiwush's son, and the youth recognizes Gw from knowledge of portraits of the Iranian champions. To confirm his identity, the youth shows a hereditary bodily mark of the race of Kai-kobad, which convinces Gw that he has found the prince. Gw explains his mission, mounts Kai-khosru on a horse, and walks beside him as they travel first to the abode of Kai-khosru's mother, Ferangis. Piran's searchers arrive too late and report to Piran that a Persian horseman has carried the youth away. Ferangis joyfully recovers her son, urges immediate departure, and directs Gw to a meadow with Afrasiyab's horses, including Behzad, formerly Saiwush's horse that her father has kept in good condition. Gw lassos Behzad and another horse, and the three set out for Iran. When Afrasiyab hears of Kai-khosru's escape, he sends Kulbad with three hundred horsemen in pursuit. Near Bulgharia, Kulbad overtakes them while Kai-khosru and his mother sleep. Awake and vigilant, Gw arms himself, mounts Behzad, and charges the pursuers alone. Trusting a prophecy that Kai-khosru will become king of kings, he fights with confidence and routs Kulbad and his three hundred horsemen. Returning to the camp, he informs Kai-khosru, who regrets not sharing in the battle. Gw replies that he did not wish to disturb the prince's sleep and attributes the victory to Kai-khosru's good fortune and auspicious star. The three then continue their journey through barren, pathless wilderness and forests toward content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l7556-l7645","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 7556-7645","start":"7556","end":"7645","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"I go, surrounded by my enemies;\nThe hand of merciless Afrsiyb\nLifted against me.\"","summary":"Afrsiyb, pleased with reports of Saiwush, sends his brother Gerswaz with valuable gifts and news of a grandson’s birth. Jealous of Saiwush’s growing power, Gerswaz feels slighted by the prince’s lack of customary respect and observes his military and administrative diligence with resentment. Returning to Afrsiyb, he portrays Saiwush as proud and ambitious, warning that he and Afrsiyb’s daughter Ferangs intend to overthrow Turan and join it to the Persian empire. Although Afrsiyb initially defends Saiwush’s loyalty as a former refugee under his protection, Gerswaz persuades him that Saiwush now knows Turan’s strengths and weaknesses and, aided by Rustem, could conquer it if allowed to return to Iran. On Gerswaz’s advice, Afrsiyb sends a friendly-seeming letter meant to lure Saiwush from Khoten and secure him. Saiwush gratefully resolves to obey at once, but Gerswaz privately urges delay, arguing that such meekness ill suits his noble lineage and military resources. Gerswaz’s persistent counsel leads Saiwush to postpone his departure, using Ferangs’s feigned illness as an official pretext in a dispatch to Afrsiyb. Gerswaz carries this dispatch back, making Saiwush appear disobedient. Byzun refuses to retreat to safety and insists on joining Rustem’s planned assault on the tyrant Afrasiyab. That night they infiltrate Afrasiyab’s palace, kill guards, and terrify the king into flight, seizing his harem women and treasures as spoils. The next day Afrasiyab’s much larger army attacks but is routed by Rustem’s valor, forcing the king to flee back to Turan. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8921-l9009","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH / KAI-KHOSRU; lines 8921-9009","start":"8921","end":"9009","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rustem demands that the Khakn of Chin surrender his elephants, ivory throne, crown, and golden chain as trophies for Kai-khosru, threatening to capture him alive. The enraged Khakn orders a massive arrow assault, prompting Gdarz to send Rehm and Gw to Rustem’s aid. Rustem, worried that his horse Rakush may tire, declares he will fight on foot if necessary, trusting in Heaven and vowing to kill many foes and send captives and spoils to Khosru. He charges into battle, denouncing the Turks as allied with the devil, praying to God, and using his kamund to slaughter many. Seeing the losses from his white elephant, the Khakn sends a messenger, who claims the kings of Ind and Chin never harmed Saiwush and that Afrsiyb’s spells compelled them to fight, asking for peace. Rustem insists that only the surrender of the Khakn’s crown, throne, elephants, and treasure will bring peace. The Khakn answers with abuse, and Rustem lassos him from his elephant, binds him, and kills him, taking his crown and ending his rule. A reflection follows on the ways of Heaven and fate, which alternately raise and cast down people, giving some kingship and wealth and others poverty, stressing the world’s deceitfulness. Prn-wsah, seeing the Khakn captured and the confederate banners overthrown, urges his forces to flee. Rustem celebrates the victory with a banquet for his warriors. When news of the deaths of Kms and the Khakn and the rout of their armies reaches Afrsiyb, he is stricken with distress, vows revenge and the extermination of the Iranians, and opens his treasury to raise a new army of a hundred thousand men.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem demands that the Khakn surrender his elephants, ivory throne, crown, and chain of gold as trophies for Kai-khosru, Persia’s king, and threatens to capture him alive if he refuses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Khakn, angered by Rustem’s words, warns Rustem to guard himself and orders his troops to attack with a tremendous him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem tells Rehm he fears his horse Rakush is growing weary and says he will attack the Khakn of Chin on foot even against a countless army.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Rustem declares that if Heaven continues his friend he will kill many enemies, take many prisoners, and send the captives and spoils of Chin to Khosru.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem advances roaring like a tiger toward the Khakn, calls the Turks allies of the devil, slaughter.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"From the back of his white elephant, the Khakn sees the extent of his losses and orders a warrior who knows the language of Iran to request a cessation of hostilities.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The messenger says that the kings of Ind and Chin never injured Saiwush, for peace, stating that the Khakn came for plunder and now asks for peace in vain until these are surrendered.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Upon hearing Rustem’s conditions, the Khakn bursts into loud reproaches and abuse, whereupon Rustem casts his kamund, drags the Khakn from his white elephant, binds his hands behind his back, and with a stroke deprives him of his crown, throne, and life.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The narrator reflects that since time began, Heaven’s decrees raise some men and deceit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Prn-wsah, seeing the Khakn of Chin delivered over to Ts, his death, and the overthrow of the confederate banners, declares celebrates his triumph by giving a banquet to his warrior friends.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"When Afrsiyb learns of the overthrow and death of Kms and the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l12027-l12095","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR; lines 12027-12095","start":"12027","end":"12095","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In the seventh stage of his quest, Isfendiyr hears of new dangers but his warriors pledge to follow him even unto death. Distrusting his demon-guide Kurugsar, he re-chains him as they proceed to a region reputed to be burning sand. When they arrive, the sand is cool because of heavy snowfall, which Kurugsar interprets as a sign that Isfendiyr is under the Almighty’s protection. Isfendiyr rebukes him for frightening the troops with false terrors and hastens the company across the sands, soon reaching a great river in spite of Kurugsar’s earlier claim that there would be no water for forty farsangs. Confronted, Kurugsar confesses that, resentful of being doubted and held in irons despite six days of accurate guidance, he exaggerated the final day’s dangers hoping Isfendiyr would turn back and release him. Isfendiyr forgives him, strikes off his chains, treats him kindly, and renews a promise to reward him with the government of a kingdom after victory. Grateful, Kurugsar again admits his deception, promises safe passage, and guides the party successfully across the river until they camp one farsang from the Brazen Fortress. There Isfendiyr asks about the stronghold; Kurugsar describes it as unimaginably strong and impregnable. Isfendiyr then vows to reach Arjsp, cleave the oppressor who murdered his grandsire Lohursp, slay the bravest heroes of Turan, carry their wives and children captive to Iran, and lay Arjsp’s realm waste. Offended by this cruel intent, Kurugsar angrily calls down a curse on Isfendiyr, wishing him calamity, malignant stars, a life of sorrow, a bloody death, and a lonely grave in the desert. Enraged, Isfendiyr immediately kills him with a single stroke, cleaving him in two. After nightfall, Isfendiyr and some warriors secretly reconnoitre the Brazen Fortress and find it constructed entirely of iron and brass, three farsangs high and forty wide, with no accessible point of attack and unlike anything ever seen by man.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The episode occurs during the \"Seventh Stage\" of Rustem throws Sohrb down and delivers a deadly thrust, and the narrator reflects on Destiny as a power that marks victims for death. Dying, Sohrb tells Rustem that fate, not Rustem, is to blame, laments that he has never seen his father, whom he sought using a sign from his mother, and warns that his father Rustem will avenge him anywhere. Rustem is horrified, reveals that he is Rustem, and demands proof. Sohrb, shocked that Rustem did not recognize him when he earlier claimed him as father, asks him to remove his armor and see the gold bracelet on his arm, a mystic token his mother gave him as his father’s sign when he went to war. When the mail is loosened, Rustem sees the bracelet, realizes he has killed his own son, and collapses in grief, tearing his hair as the sun sets in gloom. Rustem’s legions, noticing his absence and his riderless horse Rakush, spread the rumor to King Ks that Rustem is dead. {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l11547-l11643","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF AFRSIYB / THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT; lines 11547-11643","start":"11547","end":"11643","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Isfendiyr, reconciled with his father King Gushtsp, advances with a great army against Arjsp. Arjsp sends his son Kahram and the demon-born gladiator Kurugsar to oppose him. Kurugsar wounds Isfendiyr with an arrow that pierces his mail but does not seriously injure him. Isfendiyr abandons using the sword against the frenzied opponent, instead casting a noose (kamund) around Kurugsar’s neck, dragging him from the saddle, binding him, and displaying him as a prisoner before the Persian ranks. Isfendiyr then slaughters large numbers of enemy warriors, routes Kahram’s division, and cuts down many richly armed foes. As he attacks the center where Arjsp commands, Arjsp’s men explain that Isfendiyr is almost invulnerable, with a body like brass and the strength of an elephant; their weapons cannot harm him while his sword easily cleaves armored warriors. Arjsp is forced to flee. The Iranian troops pursue the routed Trnian forces, killing many in revenge for Lohursp’s death. In despair, the remaining Trnians dismount, put straw in their mouths as a sign of extreme misfortune, and cry for quarter. Isfendiyr is moved to compassion and ends the battle. When he appears before Gushtsp, his armor is bristling with so many arrows it resembles a field of reeds; about a thousand arrows are removed. Gushtsp kisses him, blesses him, holds a great banquet, and the city of Balkh rejoices over the victory.

Some days later, a new campaign is planned to free Isfendiyr’s imprisoned sisters. Gushtsp wishes to relinquish rule, offer Isfendiyr the crown and throne, and retire from worldly cares to serve God in a hermit’s cell. In verse, he declares this intention. Isfendiyr answers in verse that he desires no throne or diadem, wishes only for his father’s long and blessed life, and regards devoted service to him as his duty. He prefers to wield his sword in the king’s service, seeks vengeance on Arjsp, and aims to free his sisters from slavery. Gushtsp, smiling, blesses him and invokes Heaven to be his refuge and guide him to victory.

Isfendiyr then tells his father that Kurugsar, his captive, repeatedly begs that his case be laid before the king, arguing that killing him would bring no benefit and that, if spared, he can be very useful. Gushtsp is inclined to mercy on condition that Kurugsar swears a solemn oath to be wholly loyal and faithful. Kurugsar swears, is unbound and released. Gushtsp entertains him with wine, states that he has pardoned him at Isfendiyr’s special request, and commands him to be grateful and obedient to Isfendiyr. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l11444-l11545","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DEATH OF AFRSIYB / THE DEATH OF KAI-KHOSRU / LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT; lines 11444-11545","start":"11444","end":"11545","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Gushtsp, having imprisoned his son Isfendiyr in a mountain-prison, travels to Sistan to visit Zal and Rustem and to convert them to the religion of Zerdusht. Rustem welcomes him and publicly adopts the new faith, which he spreads in his own lands, though reportedly out of fear of Gushtsp. While Gushtsp is away, Bahman, Isfendiyr's son, abandons his post in grief over his father's imprisonment and goes to Balkh. The enemy king Arjsp, hearing that Isfendiyr is confined and Balkh is undefended, sends his son Kahram with a huge army against the city. The old king Lohursp, living in religious retirement at Balkh, is forced by the frightened people to lead a small force of about a thousand horsemen against Kahram's hundred thousand and is killed in the defeat. Kahram triumphantly enters Balkh, enslaves the people, destroys the Gubers' places of worship, kills the keeper of the altar, and burns the Zendavesta, described as containing their doctrinal formulary. One woman of Gushtsp's household escapes and reaches Sistan to inform him of his father's death, the fall of Balkh, and the capture of his women and daughters. Gushtsp prepares in haste to march out and invites Rustem to join him, but Rustem refuses on the plea of illness. Kahram, joined by Arjsp and his demon-legions, meets Gushtsp in a great battle described as earth-shaking and merciless, where kin fight kin and warriors submit to chance, fate, or heavenly decree. Gushtsp is defeated and takes refuge in a mountain-fort. He consults Jamsp about the stars, and Jamsp foretells that only Isfendiyr can restore his fortunes. Gushtsp, repentant, sends Jamsp with a letter to Isfendiyr, claiming he was deceived by treacherous enemies, promising to execute them, and to restore the royal crown. He chains Gurzam, the counselor who first inflamed his anger. Jamsp reaches the prison and urges Isfendiyr to help, but the prince bitterly recalls his father's disdain and unjust imprisonment stirred by Gurzam's hatred. After Jamsp describes the many kinsmen slain and Gushtsp's peril, Isfendiyr finally yields. A blacksmith removes his chains so painfully that he faints. On recovering, he is taken to his father, who embraces him, begs forgiveness, restores the throne, and appoints him commander of the imperial armies. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l10375-l10466","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"AKWN DW / BARZ, AND HIS CONFLICT WITH RUSTEM / SSEN AND AFRSIYB / THE EXPEDITION OF GDARZ; lines 10375-10466","start":"10375","end":"10466","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Kai-khosru, seeking to weaken his Turanian rival, sends Gudarz with a great army, including Giv, Tus, and Byzun, while Faramarz is ordered to subdue Hindustan and then join him near China to capture Afrasiyab. On the Turanian side, Homan and then Piran are appointed with large forces; Byzun kills Homan in battle, and after a two-year war a great engagement ends with the death of the venerable counselor-warrior Piran and the destruction of his army, achieved without Rustem, who remains in Sistan despite royal requests. Afrasiyab, devastated by Piran’s death, laments the loss of his friend and guide and vows vengeance, while Kai-khosru advances rapidly, crossing the Jihun and passing through Samarkand and Bokhara. Afrasiyab digs up hidden treasure to raise a prodigious army and appoints his son Shydah-Poshang over a vast cavalry force; Kai-khosru counters by appointing his young relative Lohurasp, asking Rustem to advise him because of his inexperience. Afrasiyab then sends Shydah as an ambassador with generous peace terms involving a hostage son and troops, but privately instructs him to demand single combat between the kings or between Shydah and Kai-khosru, promising to surrender Turan if Shydah is slain. Shydah eagerly accepts this mission. Kai-khosru treats the offer as a sign of weakness and declares he will not make peace until he has avenged Saiwush’s death; when Shydah arrives and delivers the message, the king prepares for combat but Rustem and the assembled nobles warn him that Afrasiyab is deceitful and that the embassy is a trick to draw him into solitary combat.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kai-khosru, after the earlier overthrow of the sovereign of Turan, appoints Gudarz to command a new expedition against his rival, saying that Rustem has already performed his duty with extraordinary gallantry and wisdom in repeated campaigns.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gudarz departs toward Turan with an immense army accompanied by Giv, Tus, and Byzun.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Faramarz is instructed first to invade and conquer Hindustan, then to march to the borders of Chin and Machin to join large force to oppose him and gathers another reserve army under Piran.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the first major conflict, Byzun attacks Homan; Homan is killed in their combat, and his defeated army retreats and joins the rear of Piran’s legions, increasing the enemy’s strength.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Because of the strengthened Turanian forces, Gudarz’s side informs Kai-khosru, who promptly sends reinforcements and writes to Sistan requesting Rustem’s aid.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The war continues for two years with both armies being regularly recruited until a Kai-khosru appoints his young relative Lohurasp with eight thousand horsemen and, passing through Sistan, asks Rustem to give Lohurasp sound counsel because of his tender age and inexperience.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After learning of Lohurasp’s appointment and Rustem’s involvement, Afrasiyab increases Shydah’s command by another hundred thousand men but sends him first as an ambassador to Kai-khosru to offer terms of peace.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Afrasiyab instructs Shydah to promise peace by offering one of his sons as a hostage, additional troops for Kai-khosru’s service, and a sacred pledge never to break his engagements again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Privately, Afrasiyab tells Shydah that if Kai-khosru refuses peace, he must propose that the kings decide the issue by single combat; if Kai-khosru refuses to fight Afrasiyab, Shydah is to fight in his place, and Afrasiyab promises to surrender the kingdom of Turan and retire from the world if Shydah is slain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Afrasiyab orders Shydah to present the terms fearlessly and without the least sign of apprehension, and Shydah responds content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l16492-l16518","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LXXXVII / LXXXVIII / CXXIX / CXXXIV; lines 16492-16518","start":"16492","end":"16518","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A first-person speaker describes an adored but faithless fourteen-year-old youth, called a child, idol, and young friend, whose beauty is compared to the moon, a rose, milk-scented breath, and sugary lips, but whose black, roguish eyes metaphorically shed blood. The youth playfully makes war on the speaker’s heart and is expected to bring about the speaker’s cruel death, yet the law will not object. The speaker resolves to guard his heart from this youth, who does not know good from evil, but laments that the heart has gone off in search of a \"new-born rose\" and has been lost for many days. The speaker says the young friend owns his heart and can break his very center, so that a Pasha would make the youth a lifeguard for such power. Finally, the speaker declares willingness to sacrifice his life in thanks if a \"pearl of sheen\" would take up serene rest in the shell of Hafiz’s eye.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The beloved is described as having a moon-like cheek on which delight and beauty glow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker states that there is neither constancy nor love in the person with the moon-like cheek and asks the Lord to bestow these qualities.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A child is said to make war against the speaker’s heart and, in playful sport, will one day put the speaker to a cruel death, with the law offering no objection.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker considers it best to guard his heart from this person, saying and sweet idol of fourteen years of age.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The idol’s earrings and soul are poetically linked with the image of the full moon of fourteen days.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The beloved’s breath is compared to the sweet smell of milk, and the lips are called Zerdusht urges Isfendiyr to subdue kingdoms so the new religion and the sacred book Zendavesta may spread everywhere. Isfendiyr invades Rm, Hindstn, Arabia, and other countries, where rulers and peoples welcome him, adopt the faith of Zerdusht, and accept the Zendavesta, proudly declaring the new worship, even described as the worship of Isfendiyr. Isfendiyr reports his successes to his father by letter and asks for further commands. Gushtsp rejoices and holds a great banquet. A favoured warrior, Gurzam, secretly hostile to Isfendiyr, slanders him to Gushtsp, alleging that Isfendiyr is over-ambitious, hated by the army, and plans to seize Balkh and imprison his father. Disturbed by these accusations, Gushtsp drinks wine for three days and then sends his minister Jamsp with a letter summoning Isfendiyr. When Jamsp arrives, Isfendiyr says he has dreamt that his father is angry; Jamsp confirms the anger is real. Isfendiyr protests that he has tirelessly spread the Zendavesta and conquered distant kingdoms for his father, and asks why he is called in anger. Jamsp replies that a son does wrong to disobey his father and that a father's wrath is kindness; he advises Isfendiyr to go regardless, because Gushtsp is both king and father. Isfendiyr agrees, appoints his eldest son Bahman to command the army, and takes his other three sons with him. Before Isfendiyr reaches Balkh, Gushtsp has already arranged to imprison him under a show of justice. At court, Gushtsp accuses him of excessive ambition and implies that he has made himself a great king. Isfendiyr insists he remains his father's servant. Gushtsp asks his courtiers what should be done with a son who usurps his father's authority and eclipses him; they reply that such a son should be broken on the \"felon tree\" or bound in chains, or he will ruin king and kingdom. Isfendiyr offers to resign his honours, but this is ignored. Gushtsp orders him confined in a tower-prison on an adjacent mountain and chained. He is bound to four iron columns fixed deep in the earth and reaching to the sky. A supernatural voice, heard by nearby soldiers and their leader Rishnawd, repeatedly commands the arch to stand firm because the sleeper is Bahman’s son, destined for the Persian throne. When Rishnawd investigates, Drb is found asleep under the rent arch; once he is moved away, the arch collapses. Rishnawd learns Drb’s history, summons a washerman and his wife who confirm it, recognizes a ruby on Drb’s arm, and concludes he is Bahman’s son whom Hma had ordered cast into the Euphrates. Convinced of his identity, Rishnawd honors him, seats him at his right hand, and gives him high command. In battle against the Rms, Drb in the vanguard displays extraordinary valor, cutting through the enemy and nearly reaching the emperor Kasar before night intervenes. The Rms, disheartened that a youth with a small force can defeat them while the Persian sovereign is a woman whose general remains largely inactive, consider retreat. Kasar insists on renewing the battle, but after another day of heavy fighting the Persians again prevail. Kasar then acknowledges his aggression and offers tribute; Rishnawd agrees to terms, and the emperor returns home. Rishnawd sends news of the victory and Drb’s valor to Hma, along with the ruby. Hma recognizes the token, recalls her earlier instinctive affection when Drb enlisted, and rejoices that her son is being restored. She goes to the Atish-gadeh (Fire-altar), makes an offering, orders a great fire lit, and distributes large sums in charity. Then, with a splendid retinue, she travels to meet Drb, embraces and kisses him, and on an auspicious day transfers the crown and throne to him after a reign of thirty‑two Rustem recalls how he and his father supported Lohursp’s accession when Kai-khosru gave him the crown, despite warriors preferring Frburz, son of Ks. He protests that Gushtsp, the current king, now seeks ungratefully to bind him hand and foot, and remembers once rebuking Ks in his court without any chief daring to oppose him. Isfendiyr replies that his courage surpasses Ks’s and that he has come personally to fetter Rustem. He tests Rustem’s strength by wringing his hand, then proposes they drink wine together that day and fight with weapons the next, intending to bind Rustem and show him in fetters to his troops. Rustem instead offers to carry Isfendiyr to Zl, seat him on an ivory throne, crown him with gold, open the treasury, and lead troops for him as warrior-chief so that Isfendiyr may rule the world as king.

Isfendiyr complains of vain boasting and calls for food. At the ensuing feast, Rustem eats and drinks prodigiously, emptying many dishes and flagons of wine, astonishing Isfendiyr and the assembled chiefs. As Rustem prepares to leave, Isfendiyr tells him to consult his father about submitting to bonds, while Rustem tells Isfendiyr to consult his own brethren and friends and either be his guest or meet him at sunrise to decide their quarrel in battle. Isfendiyr, eager for combat, insists that he will easily bind Rustem and must do so to avoid disgrace in his father’s eyes.

Rustem reflects that the many men and demons he has fought are nothing compared to his present concern over reputation in this conflict. He states that killing Isfendiyr would be like cutting off a lovely branch from the illustrious tree of the Kainian princes, and fears being cursed for such a deed, especially since Isfendiyr’s father is old and the prince is near his coronation. He asserts that he has offered allegiance and devotion and accuses the king, Gushtsp, of a treacherous plot to push his son toward an untimely death to ease his own fear, despite Rustem’s long support of crown and throne and undefeated record in battle. Isfendiyr counters that Rustem seeks to keep a spotless name at the expense of his own and insists again that Rustem must go in fetters. Rustem warns that death is approaching Isfendiyr if he persists. The prince rejects the warning, telling Rustem to bring his father, brother, and friends to witness his downfall and lament his fate in the battle. He devises a deceptive plan: at a grand banquet he publicly praises Isfendiyr and offers him the crown and throne, but announces that first Isfendiyr must go to the champion Rustem—who had previously refused Gushtsp aid and now holds extensive territories—and either kill him or bring him back in bonds. Gushtsp declares that once this is done he will have no enemies left and will retire, leaving Isfendiyr the crown. He swears on the Zendavesta that he will relinquish power when Rustem is subdued and grants his son the full resources of the empire.

Isfendiyr responds bitterly, recalling that after he first defeated the enemy king Arjsp, the intrigues of Gurzam led to his imprisonment in chains. Even now, after slaying Arjsp and his son and conquering their empire, he has not received the promised reward. He laments the horrors of his earlier Heft-khan: slaying wolf, lion, and dragon, punishing a sorcerous enchantress, enduring a deadly snowstorm, and crossing a vast unfathomable deep to seize treasure that now belongs to the king, while he is left with sorrow. He accuses Gushtsp of breaking solemn promises, contrasting his own treatment with that of Gushtsp's youth in Rum, when Gushtsp slew a dragon and a wolf and was immediately rewarded by his father Lohursp with crown and throne.

Gushtsp acknowledges the justice of the rebuke but insists that as king he must expect from his son at least as much service as Zal and Rustem once gave to Kai-khosru, noting that nearly half of Iran lies under Rustem's control. He emphasizes Isfendiyr's "form of brass" and great valor, asserts that the hero of the Heft-khan need not fear Rustem, and again offers crown, throne, army, and treasure on the condition that Rustem be subdued. Isfendiyr replies that he does not fear Rustem but is unwilling to fight him, since Rustem has long been mentor and friend to their royal house and once hosted Gushtsp for two years with generous hospitality.
