content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l13021-l13142","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR / CAPTURE OF THE BRAZEN FORTRESS / THE DEATH OF ISFENDIYR; lines 13021-13142","start":"13021","end":"13142","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"I die, pursued by unrelenting fate, / The hapless victim of a father's hate.\"","summary":"In this passage Rustem and the prince Isfendiyr confront each other in battle. Isfendiyr scorns his brother's advice and accuses Rustem's father Zl of sorcerous healing. Rustem claims invulnerability, offers hospitality and immense wealth, and swears by God, Zerdusht, the Zendavesta, the sun, and the moon to go peacefully to Isfendiyr's father if left unfettered. Isfendiyr refuses, insisting that he must bring Rustem bound before the king to secure the crown and throne. The two begin combat. Rustem prays to God to guide his charmed forked arrow into Isfendiyr's eyes while sparing him punishment for the involuntary deed, then shoots and blinds him, casting him into darkness and knocking him down. Bahman, Isfendiyr's son, Bashtan, and the Iranian troops mourn as they remove the arrow, apply medicine, and carry him to his tent. Rustem returns to Zl, who reports that wise men and astrologers foretell that whoever slays Isfendiyr will soon die; Rustem declares himself guiltless. Visiting the wounded prince, Rustem and Zl hear Isfendiyr attribute his misfortune to fate and an all-ruling power. Isfendiyr entrusts his son Bahman to Rustem's guardianship, asking him to teach kingship and warfare; Rustem vows to seat Bahman on the throne. Isfendiyr then tells Bashtan that death approaches quickly, that he will need only a winding sheet and grave, and sends messages to his father and mother, declaring himself the victim of his father's hate and unrelenting fate. After his death, his body is carried on a bier to Irn amid public lamentation. Rustem takes Bahman to Sstn, despite his brother Zra's warning that raising the son of his slain enemy will lead to future vengeance; Rustem insists he must honor the dying request and that events are written in Heaven's dispensations.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Isfendiyr treats his brother's suggestion with scorn and rides on horseback to confront Rustem.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Isfendiyr observes that Rustem's severe arrow wounds from the previous day have disappeared and attributes this healing to the sorcery of Rustem's father Zl.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Isfendiyr declares that the wounds he inflicted could only be closed by magic art and sorcery.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rustem claims that even a thousand arrows would fall harmless to the ground if shot at him and predicts that Isfendiyr will ultimately fall by his hands.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Rustem invites Isfendiyr to be his guest and promises to go with him unfettered to Isfendiyr's father so the king may do with him as he wishes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem swears by the Almighty, by Zerdusht, by the Zendavesta, and by the sun and moon to guarantee his offer to accompany Isfendiyr.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Isfendiyr insists that Rustem must be fettered and rejects Rustem's request not to bind his arms.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rustem offers Isfendiyr a thousand jewels, a thousand imperial diadems, a thousand damsels, and all his family wealth gathered by Narmn, Sm, and Zl.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Isfendiyr rejects Rustem's treasures, saying he may have wandered from the way of Heaven but must obey the king's commands so that his father will surrender the crown and throne to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Rustem tells Isfendiyr that in hopes of a crown and throne he is willing to sacrifice himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Isfendiyr seizes his bow to begin the combat, and Rustem likewise prepares with a forked arrow placed in his bow-string.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rustem turns his face toward Heaven and prays to God to direct his arrow into Isfendiyr's eyes while not punishing him for an involuntary deed, stating that he desired reconciliation and would have given his treasures to avoid conflict.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Isfendiyr shoots an arrow forcefully at Rustem, but Rustem evades it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Rustem shoots a charmed forked arrow that lodges in Isfendiyr's eyes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After being struck in the eyes, darkness covers Isfendiyr's sight, his bow drops from his weakened hand, and he sinks down upon the sand.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Rustem comments that Isfendiyr previously discharged many arrows at him in vain and has now been overthrown by a single arrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Bahman, Isfendiyr's son, loudly laments when he sees his father bleeding on the ground.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Bashtan and the Irnian troops approach with deep sorrow visible on their faces.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The fatal arrow is drawn from Isfendiyr's wounded eyes, medicine is applied, and he is mournfully conveyed to his own tent.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Rustem returns with his army to Zl, who has remained in anxious suspense about the outcome of the conflict.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Zl rejoices at Rustem's victory but reports that wise men and astrologers have predicted that whoever slays Isfendiyr will soon meet a fatal end, and he prays God to protect Rustem.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Rustem replies that he is guiltless and that Isfendiyr's blood is upon Isfendiyr's own head.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Rustem and Zl visit the wounded Isfendiyr the next day to offer sympathy and condolence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Isfendiyr states that he does not ascribe his misfortune to Rustem but to an all-ruling power, saying that fate would have it so.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Isfendiyr entrusts his son Bahman to Rustem's care and guardianship, asking Rustem to instruct him in grave.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Isfendiyr asks Bashtan to tell his father that the wish of his heart has not been breathed in vain and that the doom he desired for his son has been sealed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"Isfendiyr instructs Bashtan to bear the mournful tidings to his mother in a kindly tone and to soothe her grief for her lost warrior son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"Isfendiyr groans and declares that he dies pursued by unrelenting fate as the hapless victim of a father's hate.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"After life departs, Isfendiyr's body is placed upon a bier and conveyed to Irn amid the tears and lamentations of the people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"Rustem takes charge of Bahman according to Isfendiyr's dying request and brings him to Warned, Minchihr gathers his courtiers and addresses his son Nauder. He advises Nauder not to set his heart on the crown because the world is fleeting, recounts his own long reign of sorrows and joys, his battles fought under Feridn’s commands, his vengeance on the tyrant brothers Slim and Tr for killing Irij, and his building of cities and transforming a poisonous tree into one bearing wholesome fruit. He resigns the ancestral kingdom, originally belonging to Feridn, to Nauder and exhorts him to remain faithful to the worship of God as taught by Moses and to the path of holiness. Minchihr then prophesies that Nauder will face peril from an invading enemy from the wild mountains of Trn, son of Poshang, and instructs him to seek the aid of Sm, Zl, and a \"young branch just blossoming\" to defeat this foe. Father and son weep, and Minchihr again warns Nauder not to trust this unstable world, comparing human life to a caravan passing from city to city at an appointed time and stating that his own time has come and he must travel the destined road. Allowed to return with the booty via the road of the Heft-khan, he revisits the place of a former winter storm and recovers property he had previously lost under the snow. He reaches his father’s court, is warmly welcomed, and a royal feast is held; king and son drink so much wine that they become intoxicated. Gushtsp asks for a detailed account of Isfendiyr’s adventures on the road of the Heft-khan, but Isfendiyr refuses to narrate them while drunk, promising to speak when sober. The next day, with Gushtsp on his throne and Isfendiyr seated before him on a golden chair, the prince recounts his triumphant progress by the Heft-khan. Gushtsp expresses pleasure, yet envy and suspicion secretly move within him, and he delays fulfilling his promise to make Isfendiyr sovereign of Iran after the overthrow of Arjsp. Noticing his father’s changed disposition, Isfendiyr privately appeals to his mother Kitabun, reminding her of Gushtsp’s solemn promise to grant him the crown once he had slain Arjsp and freed his captive sisters, and asking her to admonish the king in the name of faith and honor. Kitabun prudently counsels silence and patience, warning that he could again be imprisoned in chains, and telling him that he is the rightful successor, favored by the army, while his father is old and infirm, so he will become King of Persia in due time. Unsatisfied and suspecting that his mother will speak to the king, Isfendiyr later addresses Gushtsp as if under the influence of wine, reminding him of his unparalleled deeds, including overthrowing his greatest enemy and supporting his honor, and demanding that he fulfill his promise. Gushtsp outwardly tells him not to be impatient and assures him that the throne is his, but inwardly feels deep irritation. Afterwards, Gushtsp consults Jamsp to learn what the stars foretell for Isfendiyr. Jamsp prophesies that Isfendiyr is of exalted fortune and will overcome all enemies and finally gain sovereignty over the heft-aklm, the seven climes. This favorable prediction intensifies Gushtsp’s resentment, and he asks with bitter curiosity about his son’s death. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l594-l657","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE DIVAN / THE SHH NMEH / FIRDUSI / INTRODUCTION; lines 594-657","start":"594","end":"657","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A critic describes James Atkinson's nineteenth-century English translation and abridgment of Firdusi's Shah Nameh, especially the episode of Sohrab. The piece compares Atkinson's freer, stylistic approach to literal translations, argues that epic poetry expresses universal human passions that can survive translation, and notes the work's influence on English literature. Atkinson's blend of prose summary and occasional verse is praised for bringing the spirit and setting of an extinct Persian society within reach of modern readers, in a way likened to Pope's Homer, Tennyson's use of Malory, and a Horatian metaphor about prose and poetry.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"About a hundred years before the introduction was written, a physician employed by the East India Company in Bengal and Calcutta published an English heroic-couplet translation of the 'Story of Sohrab' from the Shah Nameh.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The 'Story of Sohrab' is called the most pathetic episode in the Shah Nameh, and the English poem is compared with Jules Mohl's literal French translation of the Persian epic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"James Atkinson is said to stand in relation to Firdusi much as Pope does to Homer, implying a freer, stylistic mode of translating an epic.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The author remarks that it would be absurd for an English translator to imitate Persian idiom or attempt a literal rendering of Persian tropes, asserting that a poet's manner cannot be faithfully reproduced in translation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The introduction claims that what is really valuable and affecting in an epic poem survives when transferred into the natural idiom of another language, because epic action hinges on fundamental human passions whose 'alphabet' is universal.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The publication of Atkinson's 'Sohrab' is described as the revelation of a new world to London literary coteries and as influencing the Persian pastorals of Collins and the oriental poems of Southey and Moore.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Atkinson's metrical 'Sohrab' is the only complete episode of the Shah Nameh included in the collection being introduced.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Persian original of the Shah Nameh is said to consist of about one hundred and twenty thousand lines, and a literal rendering of the whole is described as too bulky for the general reader.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Atkinson provides a prose résumé of the chief episodes of the Shah Nameh, occasionally including passages of verse described as running through the narrative like golden threads in a storied tapestry.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The translator's literary style is praised as admirable, and his description of the tent of Manjeh is said to be as simple and direct as Homer's depiction of the palace of Alcinous.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The language given to Sohrab in Atkinson's version is said to recall the pathos of Virgil's Nisus and Euryalus and the paternal love and despair of Dante's Ugolino.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rustem's tears of anguish and sorrow are described as vanishing like morning dew in the excitement of fresh adventure, and Firdusi's portrayal of human feeling is said to lack the refined gradations and intensity seen in Dante.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Atkinson's versification is characterized as belonging to Queen Anne's time rather than resembling the poetry of Browning and Tennyson.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Tennyson is said to have treated Sir Thomas Malory much as Atkinson treated Abul Kasim Mansur (Firdusi), by bringing the essential features of an extinct society within the range of modern vision and sympathies.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The introduction asserts that everything of value in Firdusi for contemporary readers is found in Atkinson's version, while philologists and antiquarians can consult the Persian original or faithful French translations.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Atkinson's Firdusi is described as a translation and abridgment that has become a British classic, placed alongside Collier's 'Marcus Aurelius,' Leland's 'Demosthenes,' and Cotton's 'Montaigne.'","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The work is said to embalm the genuine spirit and life of an Oriental poem in the simple yet tasteful form of English narrative.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The blending of verse and prose in Atkinson's book is praised; using a metaphor attributed to Horace, the critic says Atkinson alternately trudges on foot and rises on the wings of verse, so that the reader feels they have been reading a Persian poem and forgets it is in English.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"James Atkinson","description":"An English physician in the employ of the East India Company who translated and abridged Firdusi's Shah Nameh, including the heroic-couplet 'Story of Sohrab.'","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Firdusi (Abul Kasim Mansur)","description":"The Persian epic poet, author of the abridgments.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Jules Mohl","description":"A French translator whose literal content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l1384-l1512","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HSHENG / TAHMERS / JEMSHD / MIRTS-TZ, AND HIS SON ZOHK; lines 1384-1512","start":"1384","end":"1512","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The princess, Jemshd's wife and King Greng's daughter, pleads with her father not to betray or kill the fallen king and offers her own life, invoking the Day of Judgment and the shame of a lasting bad name. Her grief persuades her father to abandon his plan and promise Jemshd treasure, an army, and protection, but Jemshd distrusts him, learns that the vizirs plan to secure him to avert Zohk's threatened invasion, and flees. Wandering first toward Chin and then to Ind, Jemshd laments his miserable fate, rests in the shadow of a tower, and falls asleep. A passing envoy of Zohk with troops recognizes the sleeping fugitive, chains him, and sends him back as a prisoner. Moral reflections stress that the world offers no rest and that Jemshd's former glory has turned into bondage. Brought before Zohk in heavy chains, Jemshd is mocked for his lost throne and laws; Zohk offers him a choice of deaths, but Jemshd submits without fear. Zohk then has him fastened between planks and sawn in two. Further reflections condemn attachment to the fleeting world. News of Jemshd's gruesome death reaches Zabulistan, and his wife wastes away in grief before killing herself with poison. Jemshd's sisters Shahrnaz and Arnawz, previously seized into Zohk's harem, are later freed by Feridun. Zohk's tyranny continues: he constantly sheds blood, while serpents are fed on human brains and daily sacrifices of youths, warriors, and slaves are made.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The damsel hears cruel words from her father, groans, and weeps before him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The damsel implores her father not to be accessory to the murder of \"such a king,\" saying that wealth and kingdoms pass away but a bad name remains until the day of doom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"She urges her father to abandon his dreadful intention, to save Jemshd's blood, to avoid domestic crime against friends and kindred, and to fear the giver of life, so that on the Day of Judgment he will not be dismayed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"She declares that if her father is determined to separate her from Jemshd, he should first cut off her head and let his daughter die.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The princess's intense and continuous grief softens her father, who abandons his previous resolution and promises to supply Jemshd with possessions, treasure, and an army, planning to meet him in his garden the next morning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The damsel quickly goes to tell Jemshd the good news of her father's promised support.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The next day King Greng meets Jemshd in the garden, showing him favor and affection, but Jemshd cannot trust his assurances and wishes to escape.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Jemshd privately learns that King Greng's vizirs are discussing how to secure him, fearing that Zohk will invade and devastate the country if Jemshd's refuge is discovered, so he takes flight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Jemshd travels first toward Chin and then into Ind; after going a great distance through a beautiful country, he comes to a tower and rests in its shadow, troubled by his melancholy condition.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Jemshd laments that he may perish forlorn and mingle with the dust, calls upon Almighty God, describes his fate as uniquely sad, and wishes he had never drawn the breath of life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Overwhelmed by sorrow, Jemshd eventually falls asleep at the tower.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"At the same time, Zohk sends an envoy with troops to the Khakn of Chin; passing by the tower, the envoy sees a man sleeping on the ground, recognizes him as Jemshd, binds his feet with chains, mounts him on a horse as a prisoner, and sends him to Zohk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The narrator comments that the world offers no place of rest, warns mortals not to fix their hearts on earthly life and pleasures, and notes Jemshd's fall from glory that reached the heavens to being bound in fetters with justice in the hands of slaves.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Zohk, upon hearing of Jemshd's capture, orders that he be brought before the throne in order to enjoy the triumph.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In Zohk's court, everyone stares at Jemshd, who stands oppressed with shame, loaded with chains and heavy fetters from neck to feet, compared to a narcissus bent with heavy dew.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Zohk greets Jemshd with a scornful smile and asks where his diadem, throne, kingdom, sovereign rule, and laws are now, remarking on the change fate has wrought upon him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Jemshd replies that he has been unjustly brought in chains before Zohk, betrayed and insulted by him, and accuses Zohk of pretending to feel his wrongs.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Angered by Jemshd's defiant words, Zohk offers him a choice of deaths, asking whether he shall be beheaded, stabbed, impaled, or shot through the heart with an arrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Jemshd answers that since he is in Zohk's power, Zohk may do as he wishes; he does not fear the utmost vengeance nor seek to avoid a moment's bodily pain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Zohk decides on a particularly horrible revenge: two planks are brought, Jemshd is fastened between them, and his body is sawn the whole length, producing two figures of Jemshd from one.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The narrator reflects that people wrongly place their affections on the fleeting world, where only wickedness is refreshed, deathly sounds are constant, and expresses a desire for Heaven to end continual sorrow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"News of Jemshd's brutal death reaches Zabulistan; his wife, the princess, pines away in inconsolable grief and finally takes poison to free herself from unbearable affliction.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"It is stated that Jemshd has two sisters, Shahrnaz and Arnawz, who are seized and taken to Zohk, kept for some time in the king's harem, and later released by Feridun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Zohk's tyranny is described as intolerable; he is constantly shedding blood and committing every kind of crime.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Serpents are still fed on human brains, two youthful victims bleed every day, the sword is always ready and thirsting to strike, and both warriors and slaves are sacrificed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Princess (Jemshd's wife and King Greng's daughter)","description":"The damsel or princess who pleads with her father to spare Jemshd, is described as heart-alluring, and later wastes away from grief and takes poison after learning of Jemshd's death.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"King Greng","description":"Father of the princess who had resolved on a fatal course regarding Jemshd but whose heart is softened by his daughter's grief; he promises Jemshd treasure, possessions, and an army and meets him in his garden.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Jemshd","description":"A king whose former glory is said to have reached the heavens; he becomes a fugitive from King Greng's court, wanders through Chin and Ind, is captured asleep at a tower by Zohk's envoy, brought in chains before Zohk, mocked, offered a choice of deaths, and finally sawn in two between planks.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Zohk","description":"A tyrant cruelty and bloodshed in which serpents are fed on human brains and daily human sacrifices Zohk.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Khakn of Chin","description":"A ruler in Chin to whom Zohk sends an envoy with an escort of {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l12494-l12588","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LOHURSP / GUSHTSP, AND THE FAITH OF ZERDUSHT / THE HEFT-KHAN OF ISFENDIYR / CAPTURE OF THE BRAZEN FORTRESS; lines 12494-12588","start":"12494","end":"12588","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this passage a speaker in verse rejects the idea of reigning if it brings guilt, preferring seclusion. King Gushtsp then appoints his son Isfendiyr as his successor, granting him the crown and throne and commanding him to march to war. Isfendiyr withdraws in anger, but after Gushtsp sends his minister Jamsp to him, the prince consents to obey his father's orders. Isfendiyr's mother Kitabn, deeply distressed, comes to warn him that the enterprise—subduing Rustem—is hopeless and unjust, recalling Rustem's previous conquest of the White Demon and vengeance for Saiwush's death by Afrsiyb, and cursing a throne and country that repay good with evil. Isfendiyr replies that he does not fear Rustem but cannot dishonor such a hero with bonds, yet his pledged word obliges him to follow his fortune.

The next morning he departs with a vast army and treasure. On the road, a leading camel lies down and refuses to move; Isfendiyr orders it killed, while the people regard the event as a bad omen and advise turning back, which he refuses, lest the king see it as a pretext. Near Sistan he sends his eldest son Bahman with a flattering message to Rustem, requesting a deputation to receive him. Bahman hesitates to respond until Rustem's father Zl urges Rustem to uphold their loyalty to the Kainian dynasty and welcome the prince. Rustem goes out, dismounts from his horse Rakush, respectfully embraces Isfendiyr, and invites him home, but Isfendiyr, bound by strict paternal commands, declines to delay.

Instead, Isfendiyr brings Rustem to his own quarters and asks to bind him hand and foot in chains in order to present him fettered to the king, who wishes to see him once in bonds before freeing him. Rustem hesitates, proposing that Isfendiyr first be his guest as Gushtsp once was, after which he will comply, but Isfendiyr insists that accepting his bread and salt would make it dishonorable to fight or force Rustem. The two discuss guest-right: Rustem likewise cannot eat Isfendiyr's bread and salt and then oppose him. As a compromise, Isfendiyr suggests that Rustem merely drink wine, "his own pure ruby," without sharing food; Rustem agrees, and they each drink their own wine together. Later Rustem seeks permission to consult his father Zl and, on returning home, praises Isfendiyr as wise and possessing a body like brass fit for battle, saying his gifts derive from Feridn.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker in verse warns that a resolved decision will quickly shroud royal glory in a gloomy cloud and declares a preference to remain sequestered and free from crime rather than aspire to reign.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gushtsp tells Isfendiyr that he is appointed as his successor and that the crown and throne are his, ordering him to march to the scene of action and accomplish the object of the war.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"On hearing his father's words, Isfendiyr retires sullenly to his own house, indicating anger or displeasure.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Perceiving Isfendiyr's angry mood, Gushtsp instructs his minister Jamsp to ascertain the prince's state of mind and whether he intends to proceed to Sistan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Jamsp visits Isfendiyr, and when asked for advice as a friend, replies that a father's commands must be obeyed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After Jamsp's visit, the king is informed that Isfendiyr consents to undertake the expedition, and further discussion ceases.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kitabn, deeply affected by news of the expedition, immediately goes to her son to represent the hopelessness of the enterprise he has agreed to conduct.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Kitabn describes a mother's counsel as a golden treasure and warns that Rustem, the champion of the world, will never allow himself to be confined in bonds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Kitabn recalls Rustem's conquest of the White Demon and his terrible revenge that filled the world with blood after Saiwush was cruelly slain by Afrsiyb.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In her speech, Kitabn curses the throne and the country that return evil for good and spurn their benefactor, urging Isfendiyr to restrain his steps and not engage in a war that cannot honor him, since Rustem can still conquer all the world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Kitabn speaks while shedding ceaseless tears, emphasizing her anxiety and grief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Isfendiyr answers that he does not fear Rustem or his prodigious power and skill but cannot place ignominious bonds on so great a hero, while insisting that his faithful word has been pledged and he must follow where his fortune leads.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The next morning Isfendiyr takes leave of the king and begins his march towards Sistan with a vast army and immense treasure.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"On the march, one of the camels in advance lies down and, despite being beaten, cannot be made to stand.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Seeing the camel's obstinacy, Isfendiyr orders the animal to be killed before proceeding.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The people interpret the camel's behavior and death as a bad omen and urge Isfendiyr not to continue the journey.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Isfendiyr disregards the people's interpretation, reasoning that the king would regard turning back as a mere pretence, and continues his journey.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Approaching Sistan, Isfendiyr sends his eldest son Bahman to Rustem with a flattering message, requesting that the champion honor him with an istakbal, or deputation, to receive him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"On arriving, Bahman hesitates and delays, reluctant to give a direct answer to Isfendiyr's request.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Zl intervenes, reminding Rustem that they have always been devoted to the Kainian dynasty and urging him to wait upon the prince, bring him home, tender allegiance, and entertain him suitably at their mansion.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Rustem goes out to welcome Isfendiyr, dismounts from his horse Rakush, and respectfully walks on foot to embrace the prince.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Rustem invites Isfendiyr to his house, but the prince says that his father's commands are so strict that, after seeing Rustem, he is not permitted to delay his departure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Despite Rustem's urging, Isfendiyr refuses to remain and instead artfully conducts Rustem to his own quarters.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"In his own quarters, Isfendiyr proposes that if Rustem will allow himself to be bound hand and foot in chains, he will convey him to the king, whose humor is to see Rustem once in fetters and then release him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Rustem initially remains silent in response to Isfendiyr's proposal to bind him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Isfendiyr tells Rustem that if he is unwilling to comply with the demand to be bound, he should go his way.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Rustem answers that Isfendiyr should first be his guest, as Gushtsp once was, and that afterwards he will conform to the prince's will.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Isfendiyr explains that his father visited Rustem under different circumstances and says that if he eats Rustem's bread and salt and Rustem then refuses acquiescence, he must resort to force, which would be dishonorable against a host.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Isfendiyr argues that if he becomes Rustem's guest, he cannot in honor fight with him, and if he fails to take Rustem bound into his father's presence as commanded, he will have no answer for the king.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Rustem replies that for the same reason he cannot eat Isfendiyr's bread and salt.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"Isfendiyr suggests a compromise in which Rustem will not eat his bread and salt but will only drink wine, specifically "his own pure ruby," thus avoiding full guest-right while sharing drink.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"Rustem agrees to the proposal, and the two drink wine together, each his own.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"After a short time, Rustem expresses a wish to consult his father Zl and, when allowed to depart, returns home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"Back at home, Rustem describes Isfendiyr in strong terms of admiration, praising his personal Ks hears that this king has a daughter of extraordinary beauty, Sdveh, and, enamored by the description, sends a messenger to ask for her hand. The defeated king, who values only his daughter and his property, reluctantly agrees because Ks is his powerful conqueror. Sdveh readily consents, and within a week she is sent in a splendid procession with many animals and female attendants. On arrival, Sdveh’s beauty enchants Ks, and they are married without delay according to local law. The King of Hmvern, still dissatisfied and desiring both his daughter back and revenge, invites Ks as his guest. Sdveh warns Ks not to trust the invitation, but he ignores her counsel and travels with her and his famous warriors to the city. They are lavishly entertained for seven days with banqueting, Ks sitting on a gorgeous throne. On the following night, soldiers suddenly attack amid trumpets and war-cries; Ks and his principal warriors are seized and carried to a remote fortress on a high mountain, where they are imprisoned under heavy guard. Ks’s tents are plundered and his treasures taken. Sdveh is inconsolable and rejects her father’s pleas, preferring death to separation from her husband, so she is sent to the same dungeon to share his captivity. The passage concludes with a reflection on the falsity of the world, noting that treachery disregards friendship and kinship, and asking who can be safe in such a world of strife and sorrow.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The disaffection of the King of Hmvern, allied with the King of Misser and Shm and the still content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l4912-l5017","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS; lines 4912-5017","start":"4912","end":"5017","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rustem, Gdarz, and Ts hear that their king, Ks, has fallen into misfortune after attempting to discover the secrets of the heavens. Gdarz rebukes the king for his repeated follies and urges him to accept his lot and obey God; the king repents, secludes himself for forty days in shame, and then resumes just and generous rule, rivaling the glory of legendary kings Feridn and Jemshd. Later, Rustem hosts a seven-day feast with his warriors and they decide to mount a pretended hunting expedition into the sporting grounds of Afrsiyb, who responds by assembling a large Trnian army to capture Rustem and overthrow Ks. Confident in himself, his horse Rakush, and his seven companions, Rustem advances to battle, routs the larger Trnian force, slays notable champions, and sends the enemy into flight. In pursuit, he urges Rakush on poetically, nearly captures Afrsiyb with a noose, but the king escapes across a boundary-stream, leaving heaps of dead behind and experiencing a bitter reversal of fortune likened to a cup of pleasure turned to poison.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rustem, Gdarz, and Ts learn of the king Ks's misfortune and set out to assist him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gdarz says that Ks has brought three calamities on himself, including disasters at Mzindern and Hmvern and his current punishment for attempting to discover the secrets of the heavens.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Gdarz tells Ks he is fitter for a mad-house than a throne and exhorts him to be satisfied with his lot and obedient to God, \"the creator of all things.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ks is moved to tears, acknowledges his folly, and after being brought back to his palace, shuts himself up for forty days in unseen shame and repentance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After forty days of seclusion, Ks recovers his spirits and resumes ruling with liberality, clemency, and justice, almost rivaling the glory of Feridn and Jemshd.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rustem makes a splendid feast at which he and his brother warriors Gw, Gdarz, and Ts drink wine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"During the feast it is decided to form a pretended hunting party and go to the sporting grounds of Afrsiyb.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The feast lasts seven days, and on the eighth day preparations are made for the march, with an advance party sent to reconnoitre the enemy.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Afrsiyb, upon learning of Rustem's movements, assembles a Trnian army of thirty thousand veterans to occupy positions around the sporting grounds, hoping to capture Rustem and his seven champions so that Ks will cease to be sovereign of Persia.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"As the Trnian army approaches with great noise and dust that darkens the sky, Rustem smiles and declares to Garz that he does not fear the king of Trn even if alone with Rakush, his armor, and battle-axe, and that each of his seven companions equals five hundred Trnian heroes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Rustem says that if Afrsiyb crosses the boundary-river, the contest will show that he has sought his own defeat.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"At Rustem's signal the cup-bearer brings goblets of the red wine of Zbul; Rustem pledges his royal master in loyalty, and Ts and Zra join in this demonstration of attachment to the king.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Rustem, arrayed in his armor (buburiyn), mounts Rakush and advances toward the Trnian army, accompanied by Ts, Gdarz, Gurgn, Gw, Bhrm, Berzn, and Ferhd.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Afrsiyb is amazed and disheartened by Rustem's terrible strength and the presence of the Persian champions; Rustem's drums and trumpets sound and a fierce battle begins with daggers, swords, and javelins.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Fearing the destruction of his army, Afrsiyb offers to give a diadem, his throne, and his kingdom to any warrior brave enough to oppose and subdue Rustem.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Plsum attempts to earn Afrsiyb's promised reward but fails, and Alks, described as the bravest of the Trnian warriors, is killed when Rustem pierces his brain with a javelin, causing him to fall dead from his saddle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Trnians, terrified by Rustem's killing of Alks and the success of the seven Persian champions, make a final effort but are forced to choose between destruction and flight, and they attempt to flee.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Seeing the enemy flee, Rustem urges Rakush forward in pursuit, addressing the horse affectionately as his valued friend and urging it to speed so he can kill the despot and flood the plain with the blood of foes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Rakush races across the plain so swiftly he seems to fly, and Rustem reaches Afrsiyb's side and throws a noose that binds the king for a moment before the bond is broken.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Afrsiyb, described as the Tartar-monarch and despot, escapes from Rustem's noose, leads his legions across the boundary-stream, leaves countless heaps of dead behind, and is said to have quaffed pleasure's cup that has now become poisoned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Rustem","description":"Persian champion hero who aids Ks, hosts the feast, leads the pretended content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l13933-l14037","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BAHMAN / HMAI AND THE BIRTH OF DRB / DRB AND DR / SIKANDER; lines 13933-14037","start":"13933","end":"14037","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sikander (Alexander) approaches Ind and demands King Kaid’s submission. Kaid replies that he will obey but claims four incomparable possessions: a beautiful daughter, a wise minister, a skilful physician, and a priceless goblet. Sikander insists on receiving all four, and Kaid reluctantly sends them; Sikander treats the minister and physician with honor, celebrates a feast, marries Kaid’s daughter, drinks from the goblet she offers, and Kaid then comes personally to acknowledge Sikander’s authority. Sikander next summons Far, king of Kanj, who proudly refuses to submit. Facing Far’s army with many elephants, Sikander’s philosopher Aristtals and other counsellors devise iron horse-and-rider engines filled with combustibles that explode in battle, burning many elephants and routing the enemy; Sikander kills Far and rules Kanj. Afterward he goes to Mecca with rich offerings, then to another city where he is honored and told of two wondrous speaking trees, one male (speaking by day) and one female (by night), which grant people’s wishes. Sikander visits them hoping for a long life; a terrible sound issues from the tree, which a priest interprets as meaning fourteen years of life remain. When Sikander asks if he will see his mother and children in Rūm again, the oracle declares he will die at Kashn and never see them, and he departs in sorrow. In another city the people complain of two man‑eating demons or giants, Yajuj and Majuj (Gog and Magog); Sikander has a huge barrier built which they cannot scale, freeing the inhabitants from fear. Continuing on, he comes to a place of countless people and a lofty mountain reaching to the stars; at its foot a terrifying guardian‑dragon waits with open jaws, but Sikander faces it without fear and slays it.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kaid writes to Sikander that he possesses four unique things: a daughter beautiful as an angel of Paradise, a wise minister, a skilful physician, and a goblet of inestimable value.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Kaid states he will submit to Sikander’s authority but says he cannot relinquish his four unique possessions.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sikander replies by letter and peremptorily demands that Kaid send him the daughter, minister, physician, and goblet immediately.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Kaid, not daring to refuse or evade, complies and sends the daughter, minister, physician, and goblet to Sikander.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sikander receives the minister and physician with great politeness and attention.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At a splendid evening feast, Sikander marries Kaid’s beautiful daughter and, taking the goblet from her hands, drinks the wine it contains.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Afterward, Kaid personally attends upon Sikander and acknowledges his authority and dominion.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sikander writes to Far, king of Kanj, demanding that he submit to Sikander’s power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Far replies haughtily that Kaid of Ind is a coward to obey, that he Far descends from a race of matchless warriors, and that he will not submit to a Greek.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sikander’s force is described as eighty thousand men: thirty thousand Iranians, forty thousand Rūms, and ten thousand Inds.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Far’s army is described as sixty thousand horsemen and two thousand elephants.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sikander’s troops are greatly terrified at the sight of Far’s many elephants.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Aristtals and other ingenious counsellors are asked to devise a way to counter the war elephants and suggest constructing an iron horse with an iron rider on wheels, drawn by horses, both filled with combustibles.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The plan includes a soldier in iron armor following the machine, his hands and face smeared with combustible matter, who at a signal will pierce the iron horse and rider so that the combustibles ignite, causing a tremendous explosion and blaze in the air.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Sikander approves the invention and gathers blacksmiths and artisans to build a thousand such machines as quickly as possible.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In battle, Far advances with his two thousand elephants; Sikander’s explosive machines are fired by the Rūms, many elephants are burned and destroyed, the rest flee with the troops, and Sikander then fights and kills Far and becomes ruler of Kanj.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After conquering Kanj, Sikander travels to Mecca with rich presents and offerings, then proceeds to another city where he is received with great homage by the leading people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"In that kingdom there are two remarkable trees, one male and one female; a voice comes from them, the male tree speaking by day and the female by night, and people visit them to have their wishes granted.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Sikander goes to the trees hoping inwardly that much of his life remains; when he comes under the tree, a terrible sound arises in his ears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"An attendant priest interprets the sound as meaning that fourteen years of Sikander’s life remain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Sikander weeps at this prophecy and asks whether he will return to Rūm and see his mother and children before he dies; the answer given is that he will die at Kashn and will not see his family again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Sikander departs from the trees in sorrow and continues his journey toward Rūm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"In another city, the inhabitants tell Sikander that two demons or giants named Yajuj and Majuj, also called Gog and Magog, assail them at night and devour men, goats, and whatever they encounter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Sikander orders a barrier to be built five hundred yards high and three hundred yards wide; when completed, Yajuj and Majuj are unable to scale it, and the inhabitants live without fear of them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Sikander continues onward to a place crowded with countless inhabitants and sees in the distance a lofty mountain reaching to the stars.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"At the foot of the mountain there is a terrifying guardian-dragon with open jaws ready to crush its victim; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l13827-l13931","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BAHMAN / HMAI AND THE BIRTH OF DRB / DRB AND DR / SIKANDER; lines 13827-13931","start":"13827","end":"13931","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Dr, a Persian king, laments the disaffection of his army and warns his remaining loyal friends that their families will be enslaved by Sikander. A small loyal force fights again but is defeated, and Dr flees with three hundred men into the desert. Sikander captures Dr's wife and family but magnanimously returns them. Despairing, Dr asks Sikander for refuge within his own dominions, offering the buried treasure of his ancestors; Sikander instead invites him to come and promises to restore him to his throne, but Dr refuses to submit or acknowledge Sikander's authority and seeks aid instead from Far, a king of Ind. Sikander learns of this correspondence and arranges to intercept him. Astrologers have foretold that Dr will soon fall into Sikander's hands; his ministers Mahiyr and Jamsipr decide to kill him themselves to gain favor with the conqueror. At night, while the escort soldiers are scattered, they stab Dr as they ride beside him and send word to Sikander. At dawn Sikander hastens to the scene, dismounts, places Dr's wounded head on his lap, and weeps over him. Dr, mortally wounded, tells him remedies are too late, blesses him, and commends his reign to Heaven. Sikander protests that he never wished to see Dr in this state and declares that, according to his mother, they share the same father; he calls this brotherly affection and vows vengeance on the murderers. Dr is comforted and makes a final request: that Sikander preserve his family's honor by marrying his daughter Roshung, dearer to him than life; that any son born of this union be named Isfendiyr and zealously propagate the sacred doctrines of Zerdusht and the Zendavesta, celebrate the Nu-rz tide festival, light the Holy Fire at the altar, and spread the faith of Lohursp everywhere as the true religion. Sikander promises to fulfil these wishes. Dr places the palm of his brother's hand on his mouth and soon dies. Sikander mourns, has the body placed on a golden couch, and attends it in sorrow to the grave. After the burial, the traitorous ministers Jamsipr and Mahiyr are brought near the tomb and executed on the dar, described as just vengeance for their king's blood. With no rival left, Sikander begins his rule over Persia, maintaining existing customs and ranks and delighting his subjects with justice and liberality. Remembering his promise, he writes to Roshung's mother, who sends her daughter with gifts. Sikander marries Roshung, who adopts the empire's customs and laws. He loves her greatly and remains in Persia for some time before deciding to march into Ind to conquer that land of enchanters and enchantment.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Dr's army is described as universally disaffected, and he tells his remaining personally devoted friends that Sikander's skill has deluded his subjects and that their wives and children will be enslaved by the conquerors.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A small number of troops remain faithful to Dr and insist on making another effort against Sikander; Slim urges striking first, and the two brothers rapidly gather armies from their kingdoms and march on Iran. Feridn, comparing them to game coming to a hunter, has his forces wait. Minchihr asks to begin the battle, and Feridn assigns commanders; the renowned warriors assemble under heavy arms, with the sacred banner of the blacksmith at their front. Krun brings a hundred thousand troops; Minchihr takes the center, with Kabd, Garshsp, and Sm commanding other divisions. The brothers, called ‘shedders of a brother’s blood,’ array their own legions. Tr rides forward to taunt, questioning Minchihr’s status as a ‘new king’ and alluding to Heaven giving Irij a daughter. Kabd rebukes Slim and Tr for murdering someone who sought their protection, declares that all will curse them until the day of doom, and that those who die in Minchihr’s righteous cause will go to Heaven with their sins forgiven. Minchihr laughs at Tr’s boasting, declares he fights only for vengeance for slain Irij, but postpones battle for a day and feasts that night. At dawn a fierce battle turns the plain into a ‘sea of blood,’ yet Minchihr’s army is victorious, aided by his skill and Heaven’s favor. That evening Slim and Tr plan a massive night attack, but Minchihr’s spies discover it. Minchihr leaves Krun in charge of the main army, takes thirty thousand men into ambush, and strikes Tr’s hundred thousand as they advance. In the clash he unhorses Tr with a javelin, beheads him with a dagger, leaves the body for beasts of the field, and sends the severed head to Feridn before going after Slim. After the confederate army’s defeat, Slim retreats into a fort, which Minchihr besieges. During the siege, a warrior named Kak sallies out and hurls a javelin at Minchihr but misses; Minchihr seizes Kak by the girdle, throws him from the saddle, and Kak dies from spear and sword wounds on content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14142-l14279","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"DRB AND DR / SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD; lines 14142-14279","start":"14142","end":"14279","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents Firdusi's satirical and reproachful address to Sultan Mahmud, emphasizing the transience of earthly power, the need to fear God, and the poet's own steadfast faith and heroic literary achievement. Firdusi recalls Mahmud's sentence to have him trampled by elephants, asserts that he fears God alone, and claims his fame rests on God and the Prophet rather than on Mahmud. He denounces Mahmud's cruelty and low ancestry using images of unchangeable vice and inherent goodness, and contrasts this with the noble heroes of his Book of Kings, which he describes as a thirty-year labor that will endure and inspire heroic deeds, even though Mahmud has cheated him of his promised reward. Editorial footnotes then discuss the character of Persian love poetry, comparing it to English \"metaphysical\" poets and citing Hafez's imagery, and identify the Turanians with the Scythians of Greek historians.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Firdusi addresses Mahmud as a tyrant and declares that earthly state and power are transient, urging him to fear God.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Firdusi commands Mahmud not to afflict humankind and adds that even the weak and small ant should not be harmed because life is sweet to all.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Firdusi describes his own temperament as firm, stern, and bold, and mentions his blood-dropping sword as an emblem of his fearsome character.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Firdusi recalls being sentenced by Mahmud to be trodden on and crushed to death by elephants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Firdusi compares himself to a lion inured to blood, claiming he makes the impious and base his food and could grind Mahmud’s limbs and scatter them as far as the Nile’s dark waters bear treasure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Firdusi declares that he fears not man but God alone, bows only to God’s Almighty throne, and that God inspires his verses and guards him from earthly foes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Firdusi states that he passes his days in the pride of song, offering gratitude and praise to Heaven.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Firdusi asserts that Mahmud is free from sense and feeling and asks what will become of him after death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Firdusi imagines Mahmud tearing him limb from limb and casting his dust and ashes to the blast, yet insists that he would still live because his hopes of fame rest on God and the Prophet rather than on Mahmud’s name.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Firdusi recounts that Mahmud would hurl him under the tread of a wild elephant until dead, but declares that, roused by such insult, he would become an elephant in power and seal Mahmud’s doom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Firdusi reminds Mahmud that many warriors and kings of illustrious and humble, imperial birth, including Tur, Salm, Jemshid, and Minuchihr, have died and that nothing could save them from the common doom; kings perish and all human things return to dust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Firdusi claims that Mahmud’s father was a blacksmith of Isfahan and that Mahmud lacks high, ennobling ancestry.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Firdusi rhetorically asks whether goodness can spring from vice or mercy from a tyrant king, using images such as water bowers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Firdusi contrasts the bitter tree and bad heart with streams of milk in Eden whose sweetness increases as they flow, using content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l3433-l3545","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"DEATH OF MINCHIHR / NAUDER / AFRSIYB MARCHES AGAINST NAUDER / AFRSIYB; lines 3433-3545","start":"3433","end":"3545","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Zal joins Mihrb of Kabul to resist Afrsiyb’s generals Shimass and Khazervn, defeating them in battle and killing Khazervn, while Rustem lies ill with smallpox. Shimass flees and his forces are routed. On hearing of this defeat, Afrsiyb, in rage, releases his captive Nauder from fetters only to kill him. Afrsiyb then seeks to seize the brothers Ts and Gustahem, but they flee Iran and take refuge with Zal in Sistan, along with Krun and Nauder’s former supporters. Zal shelters them but deems Ts and Gustahem too young to rule and himself unfit for kingship because he is not of the Kais’ blood. He first turns to Afrsiyb’s younger brother Aghrras, a virtuous governor of Ra, and offers to support him as king of Persia, but Afrsiyb intercepts Aghrras near Babel; after a tense exchange in which Aghrras rebukes him and invokes God, Afrsiyb kills his brother. Zal interprets this fratricide as a crisis that will topple Afrsiyb’s tyrannical throne and vows revenge, seeking instead a ruler from the line of Feridn. The narrative recalls how Tahmasp, son of Slim, once fled to an island and died there, leaving a son Zau. Zal sends Krun, son of Kavah, to summon Zau, who accepts, comes to Persia, and is enthroned with public prayers and a shower of gold and jewels. Zau subdues the country, forces Afrsiyb to retreat for lack of allies, and rules Persia for five years before dying and being succeeded by his son Garshsp.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Afrsiyb sends Shimass and Khazervn with thirty thousand men against Kabul and Zabul.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"On hearing of the invasion, Zal unites with Mihrb, chief of Kabul, and raises a large army in Sistan to confront the two Tartar generals.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Zal arms himself for war, mounts his horse, and leads his soldiers into the shield.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Zal, wielding his father’s mace, strikes Khazervn in the head with such force that he kills him and stains the ground with blood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At the time of this battle, Rustem is confined at home with smallpox and does not take part in the fighting.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After Khazervn’s death, Shimass seeks revenge but retreats in fear when Zal raises his mace, and his squadrons flee with him, compared to herds scattered by a tempest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Zal pursues the fleeing enemy forces and kills many of them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When Afrsiyb learns of the defeat of his generals, he releases Nauder from fetters and immediately kills him with a single deadly blow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Afrsiyb then plans to seize Ts and Gustahem, but on learning of his intent the two brothers leave Iran and go to sovereignty.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Aghrras is described as Afrsiyb’s younger brother, endowed with valor, prudence, and humanity, and appointed by negotiates with Afrsiyb, who accuses him of rebellious conduct and ambition beyond the country of Ra; Aghrras rebukes Afrsiyb, saying that God did not give him power to injure men, especially his kin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Afrsiyb, angered by Aghrras’s rebuke, draws his sword and kills his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l14619-l14701","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SIKANDER / FIRDUSI'S INVOCATION / FIRDUSI'S SATIRE ON MAHMUD / THE RUBIYT OF OMAR KHAYYM; lines 14619-14701","start":"14619","end":"14701","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Critical introduction to Omar Khayyam's Rubaiyat, emphasizing its form as independent quatrains, its rich sensual imagery of roses, nightingale, wine, feasts, and love, and its dominant tone of melancholy, misanthropy, and fear of death. Omar is described as both a great Persian poet and the greatest mathematician of his day, whose precise analytic mind produces exquisitely finished verse. The commentator highlights Omar's revolt against religious bigotry, his longing for knowledge of the invisible combined with foreboding that the grave is the end of life, and his pantheistic yet skeptical views of the power behind existence. Omar is portrayed as a man of science whose rationalism distances him from religion, similar to figures like Darwin. The passage argues that Omar's twelfth-century pessimism and spiritual \"heart-sickness\" resemble the religious doubt and despair of nineteenth-century Europe (Byron, Spencer, Darwin, Schopenhauer), explaining the modern popularity of Fitzgerald's translation.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Rubaiyat is described as a poem that cannot be easily classified within European standards such as elegy or epigram.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poem consists of a string of quatrains, each with complete and independent significance, rather than a sustained train of connected imagery and reflection.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Each quatrain has the concentrated character of an epigram but lacks the expected lightness of epigrammatic style.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Omar Khayyam named his book simply Rubaiyat or Quatrains, leaving readers to classify it more precisely if they chose.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Edward Fitzgerald's English version of the poem is praised as one of the most masterly translations ever made from an Oriental classic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Omar, like Hafiz, is called one of the most Persian of Persian writers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The volume is said to contain all the gorgeousness of the East and the luxury of refined civilization.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Omar's bowers are described as always full of roses, and the notes of the nightingale are said to tremble through his stanzas.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Images of wine, the bright eyes of lovely women, feasts, revels, joys of love, and satisfied appetite are listed as grosser elements in Omar's song.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Despite sensual imagery, the prevailing note of Omar's poetry is described as deep and settled melancholy, sometimes breaking into misanthropy and despair.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The intensity of Omar's style is said to be inspired by an ever-present fear of death and a constant sense of approaching Fate, even in his most genial moments.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Passages in the Rubaiyat often combine thrilling sweetness with endings that strike a note of dejection and anguish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Omar Khayyam is described as the greatest mathematician of his day, possessing a fine and analytic mind.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The exactness of Omar's mind is reflected in the exquisite finish, subtle wit, and delicate descriptive touches in his quatrains.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The verses of the Rubaiyat are compared to gems of the purest water, exquisitely cut and clasped by \"jacinth work of subtlest jewelry.\"","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The general tone of the quatrains content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l4717-l4801","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KAI-KOBD / KAI-KS / THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB; lines 4717-4801","start":"4717","end":"4801","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"News of Ks's imprisonment encourages rival states to seize Iran, and Afrsiyb invades from Trn, conquering the country in three months. Survivors reach Zbulistn and inform Rustem, who assembles troops to free his captive sovereign and sends a threatening letter to the king of Hmvern, recalling his earlier victories over the White Demon and the magician-monarch of Mzindern. When the king replies defiantly, Rustem departs Zbulistn, travels by land and water to Hmvern, and battles the king, who summons the rulers of Berberistn and Misser so that three kings and their armies face Rustem alone. Confident that Heaven is on his side, Rustem routs their forces, captures the kings of Misser and Berberistn, and forces the king of Hmvern to sue for peace by offering to release Ks, his warriors, and the plundered royal treasure; Rustem agrees, saying he seeks only his sovereign's liberty.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The imprisonment of Ks becomes widely known and encourages various inferior states to attempt to seize control of Irn.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Afrsiyb, described as the most powerful aspirant to the throne, gathers an immense army, invades Irn from Trn, and conquers the country in about three months, leaving ruin and desolation behind him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Some survivors from the battlefield flee to Zbulistn and inform Rustem about the misfortunes and imprisonment of Ks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Considering it necessary to liberate his sovereign, Rustem assembles troops from various quarters in preparation for action.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Rustem sends a messenger to Hmvern with a letter demanding the release of the prisoners and threatening that the king will suffer the same fate as the White Demon and the magician-monarch of Mzindern if he refuses.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The king of Hmvern is alarmed by Rustem's threat but replies arrogantly, saying that if Rustem wants to share Ks's situation, he is welcome to come.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In response to the defiant reply, Rustem leaves Zbulistn and undertakes an arduous journey by land and water to reach the confines of Hmvern.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Roused by the noise and bold aspect of Rustem's invading army, the king of Hmvern draws up his own forces and engages in battle, but he cannot withstand Rustem's courage, and his troops flee in confusion.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In near despair, the king of Hmvern requests help from the chiefs or rulers of Berber and Misser, who promptly send assistance so that three kings and their armies stand against Rustem alone.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The combined forces of the three kings are described as each bringing their strongest troops, likened poetically to an \"eagle of valour\" flapping its wing.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"When the king of Hmvern sees Rustem's imposing, strong, and commanding person, he is filled with fear and hides behind his own troops.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Rustem declares that even if a hundred thousand men oppose him, numbers are useless because Heaven is on his side as a friend and will cause the foe to be reduced to dust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Rustem has the trumpets sounded, charges the enemy mounted on his horse Rakush, and kills many opponents, with the narrative emphasizing numerous severed heads and streams of blood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The chief of Hmvern and his legions are the first to retreat from the fighting; the King of Misser, ashamed of their cowardice, advances to punish Rustem but, after receiving one heavy blow to the head, turns to flee.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Rustem quickly pursues the fleeing King of Misser, casts a kamund or noose around his loins, drags him from his horse, and delivers him bound into the hands of Bhrm, who keeps him at his side.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Rustem then attacks the troops of the Shh of Berberistn, and, aided valorously by Zra, he defeats and kills them, afterwards charging the Shh himself and taking him and forty of his principal chiefs prisoner.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Seeing the scale of the carnage and the failure of his expectations, the King of Hmvern sends a messenger to Rustem requesting a suspension of hostilities and offering to release Ks and all his warriors and to return the royal property and treasure taken from him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The troops of the three kingdoms plead for quarter and protection, and Rustem accepts the proposed terms of peace.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Rustem states that he asks for nothing more than Ks's liberty and the release of his chiefs, declaring that he came only for his sovereign and claims no other prize.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The action spans multiple regions, including Irn, Trn, Zbulistn, Hmvern, Berberistn, and Misser, indicating a wide geographic and political stage for the
