content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l6229-l6358","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SEVEN LABORS OF RUSTEM / INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB; lines 6229-6358","start":"6229","end":"6358","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Untold, a secret is a jewel bright,\nYet profitless whilst hidden from the light;\"","summary":"Sohrb surveys the Persian camp from a distance, asking the captive Persian Hujr to identify the richly decorated tents and their commanders. Hujr names several chiefs—Ts, Gdarz, Gw son of Gdarz, Frburz son of the Persian king, and Gurz—while Sohrb is especially struck by a green pavilion bearing a dragon standard and a majestic horse, where the greatest warrior sits enthroned. Fearing for Rustem, Hujr lies about this champion’s identity and origin, and repeatedly claims ignorance, while Sohrb, remembering the identifying tokens his mother gave him and feeling intense grief, still fails to confirm the truth about his own birth. He keeps his lineage secret as well, and the narrator comments on fate and the sorrows of the world. Sohrb presses again for news of Rustem, refusing to believe that such a champion would stay away from battle, and offers rich rewards if Hujr will speak. He describes tears greater than Noah’s flood that cannot erase the beloved’s image from his heart, offers his broken heart in a bargain, and explains that Love has bent his nature toward wine. The poems counsel striving after truth so an inner sun rises, denouncing a false dawn, and encourage readiness to sacrifice one’s head and heart. Hafiz mentions yearning for mountains and plain, an unloosed chain, an ant reproaching Saf over Jem’s lost signet, and the faithlessness of the fair likened to a withered plant in a garden. contrasted with the beloved’s purity, the passing of Majnn (Majnun) and each lover’s turn, Love’s ample realm of joy, his willingness to sacrifice himself and his heart for his friend’s weal, the It emphasizes his unusually joyful and harmonious character, portraying his life as a happy pilgrimage animated by an inner sense of divinity and pantheism. His poetry is described as magically attractive, deeply earnest yet persistently gay, and cherished by both Europeans and Asiatics; his tomb at Shiraz is visited as a kind of Mecca for literary pilgrims, and his verses are memorized by educated Persians. The text notes his birth in Shiraz in the early fourteenth century, his death in 1388, and explains that the name \"Hafiz\" (“the man who remembers”) reflects his role as a professor of Mohammedan scriptures who memorized the Koran. His unconventional lifestyle drew disapproval from dervishes at the monastic college, whom he satirized, though the broader Mohammedan world—including kings and rulers—celebrated his lyrics. Hafiz once set out for India at the invitation of a Southern prince, but hardships at sea caused him to return to Shiraz. At his death, his pantheism and conduct led ecclesiastical authorities to deny him burial in consecrated ground, but they reversed the decision after opening his book at random and reading a passage predicting his admission to Paradise despite sin. He was then buried in a sacred cemetery at Shiraz, depicted as a beautiful enclosure with nightingales, ever-blooming roses, doves, and white stones. Kai-khosru grows up among peasants, showing exceptional prowess that reveals his royal nature. Piran then deceives Afrsiyb by claiming the boy is an idiot and coaching Kai-khosru to feign madness. Appearing before Afrsiyb in royal attire, Kai-khosru answers incoherently; the king, feeling shame yet believing him harmless, sends him back with gifts to his mother. The narrative then shifts: Kai-ks (Kai Kaus), on learning of his son Saiwush’s fate, grieves deeply along with his warriors. The king then rises to meet Rustem, confesses that his naturally wayward temper led to an outburst of wrath that shrank his heart, praises Rustem as the boast of his army and source of his regal power, and begs to restore their fellowship. The king orders a day of rejoicing and, beside a crystal spring in a flowered bower, holds a splendid banquet with music, dancing women, gifts of gold for the warriors, and abundant wine. The Turanian legions, startled by the endless Iranian host, show it to Sohrb; he mounts the fort and surveys them without fear while his companion Hmn grows pale with terror. The note situates the poem in manuscript tradition and relates it to Voluspo and Thrymskvitha. In the poem, the gods and goddesses hold council about Baldr’s baleful dreams. Odin rides his horse Sleipnir down to Niflhel and Hel’s hall, where he uses magic to raise a dead wise-woman (volva) from her grave. Under questioning (and despite reluctance), she prophesies that Baldr will soon die in Hel, slain by Hoth with a famous branch, and that a newborn son of Rind and Odin, Vali, will avenge him by burning Baldr’s slayer. She also alludes to weeping maidens who will raise sail-yards, recognizes Odin’s true identity, and predicts that no man will consult her again until Loki is freed from his bonds and the destroyers come to the final battle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"“Baldrs Draumar” is preserved in the Arnamagnan Codex and in various late paper manuscripts under the title “Vegtamskvitha,” and consists of fourteen stanzas apparently in good condition.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The introductory note states that the subject-matter and style of Baldrs Draumar link it closely with the Voluspo, and that four of the five lines of stanza 11 appear almost unchanged in Voluspo stanzas 32–33, with the whole poem elaborating that episode.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note suggests that Baldrs Draumar and Voluspo may share an author, and that stylistic similarity between Baldrs Draumar and Thrymskvitha supports a conjecture of common authorship for those two poems, with Baldrs Draumar likely taking shape by the first half of the tenth century.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The note remarks that in both Baldrs Draumar and Voluspo a volva foretells the fall of the gods, and that in this poem she prophesies the first incident of that fall, the death of Baldr; in both texts she is associated with rising from the grave.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The note characterizes Baldrs Draumar as essentially dramatic rather than narrative, summarizing a story assumed to be familiar to its audience.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The gods and goddesses assemble in council to discover why Baldr is having baleful dreams.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Odin, described as an old enchanter and father of magic, rises, saddles his horse Sleipnir, and rides down to Niflhel, where he encounters a hound from hell that is bloody on its breast and howls at him from afar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Odin’s ride makes the earth resound until he reaches Hel’s high house.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Odin rides to the eastern door where he knows the wise-woman’s grave to be, speaks magic and mighty charms, and causes her to rise spell-bound and speak though still dead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The wise-woman says an unknown man has forced her calls himself Valtam’s son, and asks the wise-woman to speak of hell, saying he already knows of heaven; he asks for whom benches bright with rings and gold-bedecked platforms have been prepared.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The wise-woman answers that mead—the shining drink—has been brewed for Baldr, with a shield laid over it, and that the mighty gods have lost their hope; she says she has spoken unwillingly and would now be silent.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Odin repeatedly presses the wise-woman to continue, seeking to know who will become Baldr’s bane and steal the life of Odin’s son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The wise-woman declares still.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Odin asks who will win vengeance for Baldr’s slaying or bring Baldr’s killer to the will neither wash his hands nor comb his hair until he brings Baldr’s slayer to the flames, after which she repeats her unwillingness to speak.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Odin asks which maidens will weep and toss the yards of the sails to the whose union with a woman begins a higher life; Gilgamesh as a judge assimilated to Shamash; the hero’s wanderings into increasing darkness; the Deluge interpreted as an annual river overflow and the Assyrian creation story as drying of primeval waters with world creation in spring; a month named for destruction and another called the \"Mission of Ishtar\" tied to Ishtar’s disappearance and mission to the lower world; the flood survivor Zi-u-gd-du/Zi-u-su-du and his Akkadian counterpart Ut-napishtim whose names relate to lengthened life; and an extended discussion of the twin-brother motif, including Gilgamesh–Enkidu as twins or brothers and further companion or primeval pairs such as Abraham–Lot, David–Jonathan, Achilles–Patroclus, Eteokles–Polyneikes, Yama–Yami, and their Iranian equivalents.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Enkidu’s union with a woman is described as the beginning of a higher life for blessing.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In contrast to the Deluge, an Assyrian creation story describes the drying up of primeval waters, the earth’s appearance Rig comes striding from a grove, teaches Jarl runes, claims him as a son, and bids him hold wide ancestral heritage. A warrior journey through dark forest and frosty crags leads to battles where land is won, and Jarl comes to hold eighteen halls and distribute wealth and rings. Jarl’s messengers travel by wet ways to Hersir’s hall to seek the wise maiden Erna, who marries Jarl; they live happily and have many sons, including Kon. The sons grow up taming beasts and learning weapon craft, but Kon the Young learns everlasting runes of life, gaining powers to shield warriors, dull swords, still seas, lessen flames, quiet minds, and calm sorrows, with great strength. Kon shares runes with Rig-Jarl, surpasses him in craftiness and wisdom, and wins the right to be called Rig. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l2429-l2589","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 2429-2589","start":"2429","end":"2589","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of Hovamol, a first‑person divine speaker addresses Loddfafnir with repeated counsel about listening to wise elders, treating guests and the needy well, and using natural and magical remedies. The speaker then recounts hanging for nine nights on a windy, mysterious tree, wounded by a spear and offered \"myself to myself\" to Othin, without food or drink, until he seized the runes and fell. He gained nine mighty songs from the son of Bolthorn and drank mead from Othrrir, after which he thrived and increased in wisdom. The passage explains that powerful runes and signs were made by Othin and other beings for gods, elves, dwarfs, giants, and men, and it urges measured sacrifice and prayer according to one’s gain. Finally, the speaker lists a series of secret songs with diverse powers: healing, blunting weapons, breaking bonds, stopping arrows, turning back curses, quenching fire, reconciling hatred, calming wind and sea for ships, exposing house‑riders, protecting comrades in battle, making a hanged man on a tree go forth and speak, safeguarding a young thane sprinkled with water, and naming and knowing all gods and elves.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker repeatedly addresses Loddfafnir, urging him to hear and learn his counsel, promising profit and great gain if he does so.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker warns not to scorn the gray-haired singer, saying that old people often speak good and that skillful counsels can come from shriveled skin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker advises not to curse a guest or drive him away, but to deal well with a man in want.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage states that a strong beam must be raised to give entrance to all and that it should have a ring, or else grim consequences will follow for the owner.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When drinking ale, one should seek the might of earth, and various cures are listed: earth cures drink, fire cures ills, oak cures tightness, the ear cures magic, rye cures rupture, the moon cures rage, grass cures scab, and runes cure sword-cut; the field absorbs the flood.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The preceding sayings are identified as Hors’s words spoken in the hall, described as kind for the kin of men and cursed for the kin of giants, with blessings wished for speaker, learner, and listener.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker recounts hanging on a windy tree for nine full nights, wounded by a spear and offered to Othin, describing this as \"myself to myself,\" on a tree whose root none may know.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"During the hanging, no one gave the speaker bread or drink; he looked down, seized the runes with a shriek, and immediately fell back.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker obtained nine mighty songs from the son of Bolthorn, who is named as Bestla’s father.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker drank goodly mead poured from Othrrir, after which he began to thrive, grow, and gain wisdom, with each word leading to another word and each deed to another deed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage declares that runes and fateful signs, colored by the king of singers and made by the mighty gods, are very strong and mighty, and written by the ruler of gods.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Othin wrote runes for the gods, Dain for the elves, Dvalin for the dwarfs, Alsvith for giants and all mankind, and the speaker says he has written some himself.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The speaker asks whether the listener knows how to write and read runes, how to tint them, test them, ask, offer, send, and sacrifice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The passage asserts that it is better to make no prayer or sacrifice than to make offerings that are too large, advising that gifts be measured by one’s getting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"It is said that Thund wrote these teachings of old, before the race of men began, when he rose on high upon coming home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The speaker claims to know songs that kings’ wives and ordinary men do not know; the first song, called help, can bring relief in sorrow, pain, and sickness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A second song is said to be needed by those who wish to practice leechcraft or medicine, though its detailed effects are omitted in the text.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The third song enables the speaker to blunt his enemy’s blade so that neither sword nor staff bites.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The fourth song causes bonds and fetters fastened on the speaker’s legs and hands to spring off and break, allowing him to go free.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The fifth song allows the speaker to stop an arrow flying against the folk, provided he sees it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The sixth song turns back harm sent with a sapling’s roots, so that the hostile hero who sends it must taste the ill before the intended victim.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The seventh song can quench a fire that burns the hall over the heads of the speaker’s comrades.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The eighth song enables the speaker to set right hatred that has grown among heroes’ sons.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The ninth song shelters the speaker’s ship on the flood by calming the wind on the waves and putting the sea to sleep.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The tenth song affects house-riders flying high in the air, causing them to go wildly, show their true shapes, and return to their own homes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The eleventh song is sung in the shields when the speaker must lead his long-loved friends to battle, so that they go to the fight whole, return from it whole, and come home whole.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The twelfth song is used when the speaker sees a hanged man swinging high on a tree; by writing and coloring runes, he causes the hanged man to go forth and speak to him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The thirteenth song involves sprinkling a young thane thoroughly with water so that he will not fall when he goes among the host or sink beneath the swords.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The fourteenth song enables the speaker to name the mighty gods and to know well about the gods and elves, knowledge that Loki responds by insulting Heimdall’s role as the watchman of heaven. Skathi predicts that the gods will bind Loki on rocks with the entrails of his frost-cold son; Loki boasts of his role in Thjazi’s death and hints that Skathi once invited him to her bed. Sif approaches with a crystal cup of mead, claiming Loki knows her to be blameless among the gods, but Loki drinks and accuses her of unfaithfulness, calling himself crafty in lies. Beyla announces Thor’s imminent arrival as the mountains shake and says Thor will silence the slanderer of gods and men; Loki responds by abusing Beyla. Thor then appears and repeatedly calls Loki \"unmanly,\" threatening to silence him with the hammer Mjollnir, to cleave his shoulder from his neck, to hurl him eastward where men will not see him, to break his bones, and to send him to hell and the gate of death. Loki taunts Thor by recalling future events in which the wolf will swallow Sigfather and by mocking Thor’s past humiliations involving a giant’s glove and Skrymir’s wallet. Loki finally declares that he will now leave, acknowledging Thor’s fighting skill, and threatens Aegir (here called gir) that no more feasts will be held because flickering flames will burn everything in the hall and scorch his back. A prose epilogue relates that Loki hides in Franang’s waterfall in the form of a salmon but is caught by the gods, who bind him with the bowels of his son Vali while his other son Narfi is changed into a wolf. Skathi suspends a poisonous serpent above Loki’s face so its venom drips on him. Loki’s wife Sigyn sits by him holding a shell to catch the poison, but whenever she must empty it the drops fall on Loki, who struggles so violently that the earth shakes; this shaking is explained as the origin of earthquakes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Heimdall tells Loki he is drunk and that excessive drinking leads men to lose control of their tongues, calling Loki’s deeds mad.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Loki tells Heimdall to be silent and says that long ago an evil fate was fixed for Heimdall, requiring him to stand with a stiff back as the warder of heaven.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Skathi tells Loki that although he is lively, the gods will bind him on the rocks using the torn bowels of his frost-cold son, limiting his freedom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Loki replies that even if the gods bind him on rocks with the bowels of his frost-cold son, he was first and last at the deadly fight where Thjazi was caught.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Skathi answers that if Loki was first and last at the fight where Thjazi was captured, then a cold counsel will always come to him from her dwellings and fields.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Loki reminds Skathi that she spoke more lightly with Laufey’s son when she asked him to come to her bed, suggesting that such mutual sins should be acknowledged.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Sif comes forward, pours mead for Loki into a crystal cup, greets him, and says that he knows her alone among the gods to be blameless.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Loki takes the drinking vessel, drinks, and claims that Sif is not alone in shunning men, saying he knows someone who took her from Hlorrithi’s arms and calling himself crafty in lies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Beyla announces that the mountains shake and believes Hlorrithi is coming from his home to silence the man who is slandering both gods and men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Loki tells Beyla to be silent, identifies her as Byggvir’s wife, accuses her of being steeped in sin and filth, and calls her a shame to the gods.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Thor comes and repeatedly addresses Loki as an unmanly one, threatening to close Loki’s mouth with the hammer Mjollnir, to cleave his shoulder from his neck, to hurl him eastward where men will not see him, to break all his bones with Hrungnir’s slayer, and to send him to hell and the gate of death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:9","ev:11","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Loki greets Thor as the son of Earth, questions why Thor threatens loudly, predicts that Thor will be less fierce when fighting the wolf that will swallow Sigfather, and mocks Thor for hiding in the thumb of a glove and failing to get meat from Skrymir’s wallet, suffering hunger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:10","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Loki says he expects to live a long time despite Thor’s hammer threats and later declares he has spoken his thoughts to the gods and their sons, and now will leave in front of Thor alone, since Thor fights well.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12","ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Loki tells gir that although he has brewed ale, he will hold such feasts no more, for flickering flames will play over everything in the hall and gir’s back will be burned with content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l4391-l4441","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 4391-4441","start":"4391","end":"4441","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes on Grimnismol explain that a sequence of stanzas, as transmitted and quoted by Snorri, consists largely of a catalogue of Othin's many names, whose meanings are often uncertain due to oral transmission and variant manuscripts. The notes gloss numerous epithets that depict Othin as a hooded wanderer, ruler, warrior, deceiver, shape‑changer, wise being, thunderer, father of victory and of the slain, helper of sailors, god of wishes, shouter, wand‑bearer, and more. They mention the tripartite form Har, Jafnhar, and Thrithi in Snorri's Edda, suggest possible Christian influence on this triad, and briefly refer to episodes now largely unknown—such as Othin's address to Geirrth, an episode involving Sokkmimir son of Mithvitnir, and the identification of Ygg with Othin and of the \"maids\" with the three Norns.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The editor states that the condition of stanzas 46–50, quoted by Snorri, is uncertain, that catalogue‑type lines and whole stanzas shifted freely during oral transmission, and that many of the names occur nowhere else and have meanings that are largely guesswork.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The notes remark that Othin appears in disguise in nearly every episode, so the number of his names is almost limitless.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In note 46 Othin is given names including Grim ('The Hooded'), Gangleri ('The Wanderer'), Herjan ('The Ruler'), Hjalmberi ('The Helmet-Bearer'), Thekk ('The Much-Loved'), Thrithi ('The Third'), Helblindi ('Hel-Blinder' or 'Host-Blinder' in variant manuscripts), and Hor ('The High One'), while the meanings of Thuth and Uth are said to be unknown.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Snorri's Edda is described as telling stories in the form of answers to questions, with Har, Jafnhar, and Thrithi as speakers; the \"tripartite form of Othin\" created by these three figures has been widely debated, and the editor suggests the line may show muddled influence of early Christianity.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Note 47 glosses further names of Othin: Sath ('The Truthful'), Svipal ('The Changing'), Sanngetal ('The Truth-Teller'), Herteit ('Glad of the Host'), Hnikar ('The Overthrower'), Bileyg ('The Shifty-Eyed'), Baleyg ('The Flaming-Eyed'), Bolverk ('Doer of Ill'), Fjolnir ('The Many-Shaped'), Grimnir ('The Hooded'), Glapsvith ('Swift in Deceit'), and Fjolsvith ('Wide of Wisdom').","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Note 48 adds names referring to Othin's appearance and functions: Sithhott ('With Broad Hat'), Sithskegg ('Long-Bearded'), Sigfather ('Father of Victory'), Hnikuth ('Overthrower'), Valfather ('Father of the Slain'), Atrith ('The Rider'), and Farmatyr ('Helper of Cargoes', interpreted as 'god of sailors').","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Note 49 states that nothing is known of Asmund, of Othin's appearance as Jalk, or of the occasion when he rode in a sledge as Kjalar ('Ruler of Keels?'); the meanings of Thror and Vithur are uncertain, while other names are glossed as Oski ('God of Wishes'), Biflindi (with widely varying manuscript forms), Jafnhor ('Equally High'), Omi ('The Shouter'), Gondlir ('Wand-Bearer'), and Harbarth ('Graybeard').","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Note 50 remarks that nothing further is known of the episode mentioned there, that Sokkmimir is presumably Mithvitnir's son, and that Snorri quotes only the names Svithur and Svithrir, omitting the rest of the stanza.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Note 51 says that the poem returns to direct action with Othin addressing the terrified Geirrth, that the manuscripts show no lacuna in this stanza, and that some editors add a second line from paper manuscripts: 'Greatly by me art beguiled.'","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Note 53 identifies Ygg as Othin ('The Terrible') and explains that 'the maids' in the stanza are the three Norns.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Note 54, described as possibly misplaced and more or less corrupt, glosses more names: Thund ('The Thunderer'), Vak ('The Wakeful'), Skilfing ('The Shaker'), Vofuth ('The Wanderer'), Hroptatyr ('Crier of the Gods'), Gaut ('Father'), and refers Ofnir and Svafnir back to stanza 34.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Othin (Odin)","description":"Chief god of the poem, referred to by many epithets depicting him as hooded wanderer, ruler, warrior, deceiver, shape‑changer, wise being, thunderer, father of victory and of the slain, helper of sailors, god of wishes, shouter, wand‑bearer, and more; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l5706-l5840","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HYMISKVITHA / THE LAY OF HYMIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 5706-5840","start":"5706","end":"5840","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The introductory note describes the poem Hymiskvitha as a late and comparatively inferior work, likely compiled in Iceland from various fragments about Thor, notable for its skaldic-style diction. It discusses manuscript placement, scholarly debates about its composition and dating, and explains skaldic kennings with an example from Egil's saga, noting that Snorri Sturluson treats related material in the Prose Edda. The note states that the poem’s vigor lies in two Thor stories: his expedition to obtain Hymir's great kettle and his fishing trip where he caught the Midgard serpent. The poem then begins: the gods feast and seek drink, test blood, and decide they need a large kettle to brew ale. A mountain-dweller host and a \"word-wielder\" figure are involved; the latter arranges that Sif’s mate (Thor) should bring a kettle. The gods cannot find a suitable vessel until Tyr advises Thor to seek one from his giant father Hymir, who lives east of the rivers Elivagar at the end of heaven and owns a mighty kettle a mile deep. Thor and Tyr travel from Asgard to Egil’s home and on to Hymir’s hall. There they encounter Tyr’s terrifying many-headed grandmother and a fair, gold-adorned, bright-browed giantess who brings beer to her son and hides Thor and Tyr beneath a kettle, warning that Hymir is wrathful toward guests. Hymir, a harsh and misshapen giant, returns from hunting with his beard frozen and icicles rattling. The giantess greets him, announcing the arrival of their son and Thor, described as foe of Hroth and friend of mankind, called Veur. Hymir’s glance breaks a beam and shatters a pillar, causing eight objects to fall from a ledge; only the hard-hammered kettle remains whole. Thor and Tyr emerge; Hymir regards them grimly, foresees sorrow at seeing Thor, and has three steers brought in to be boiled.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hymiskvitha is preserved complete in two manuscripts, placed after different poems in Regius and the Arnamagnæan Codex.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Snorri Sturluson does not quote Hymiskvitha in the Prose Edda, though he recounts the main story found in the poem.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The poem is described as a distinctly inferior and composite work, based on narrative fragments pieced together.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Scholars disagree whether Hymiskvitha was formed by splicing three distinct poems or composed as a new poem based on now-lost earlier works.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The compiler is said to have combined various prose and verse material about Thor to impress hearers greedy for wonders.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hymiskvitha is considered one of the latest poems dealing with the gods, probably composed in Iceland, possibly in the first half of the eleventh century or even later.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The note mentions a \"nine hundred headed\" person in Hymir’s home as an example of the poem’s extravagant imagery.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Skaldic poetry is described as lyric verse with complex diction and a special vocabulary of kennings, often with named authors.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Snorri wrote a section of the Prose Edda to explain skaldic kennings.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"An example from Egil’s saga describes a sword with kennings such as \"halo of the helm,\" \"wound-hoe,\" \"blood-snake,\" uses numerous skaldic circumlocutions and is saved from mediocrity by two main Thor stories: the expedition for Hymir’s kettle and the fishing trip where he caught Mithgarthsorm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In stanza 1, the gods make a feast together and seek drink before they are Hlorrithi.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Tyr states that his father Hymir, described as wise and fierce, lives to the east of Elivagar at the end of heaven and owns a mighty kettle a mile deep.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Thor asks Tyr whether they can win the \"whirler of water\" (the kettle), and Tyr replies that they can if they are cunning.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Thor and Tyr travel swiftly from Asgard to Egil’s dwells.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The youth (implicitly Tyr) finds his grandmother, whom he greatly loathes, and she has nine hundred heads.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Another woman, described as fair, gold-adorned, and bright-browed, comes forth and brings beer to her son.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The bright-browed giantess, called a kinsman of giants, hides Thor and Tyr beneath a kettle, warning that her dear-loved content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1516-l1627","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOLUSPO / THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1516-1627","start":"1516","end":"1627","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Bellows’s notes to Voluspo stanzas 50–65 explain the identities and roles of various beings and images involved in Ragnarök and the subsequent renewal of the world. He identifies Hrym as leader of the giants and helmsman of the ship Naglfar, the world-serpent Mithgarthsorm encircling the earth from the sea, and the giant Hrsvelg as an eagle at heaven’s edge who makes the winds. He describes invasions by the people of Muspell over the rainbow bridge Bifrost and the people of Hel by ship under Loki, the fire-ruler Surt, and the wolf Fenrir, along with Frigg’s grief, Freyr’s slaying of the giant Beli, Vithar’s survival, and Thor’s death after killing the serpent. The notes mark the end of the destruction and the beginning of a new world, where gods gather at Ithavoll, recover golden tables, Baldr and his brother Hoth return as symbols of peace, Hnir gains prophetic power, and blessed halls such as Gimle are contrasted with a hall for the dead. A possibly spurious stanza introduces an unnamed lawgiving ruler and raises questions about Christian influence and later interpolation.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hrym is described as the leader of the giants and the helmsman of the ship Naglfar.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Naglfar is a ship made out of dead men’s nails to carry the giants to battle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The serpent Mithgarthsorm, one of Loki and Angrbotha’s children, was cast into the sea where it completely encircles the land and is called the girdler of earth.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The giant Hrsvelg sits at the edge of heaven in the form of an eagle and makes the winds with his wings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The people of Muspell come over the bridge Bifrost, the rainbow, which breaks beneath them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The people of Hel arrive in a ship steered by Loki.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Fenrir is identified simply as \"the wolf\" in this context.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Loki is described as the brother of Byleist.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Surt is called the ruler of the fire-world.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The poetic expression \"scourge of branches\" is explained as meaning fire.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Hlin is apparently another name for Frigg, who is Othin’s wife.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l8144-l8258","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / RIGSTHULA / THE SONG OF RIG / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 8144-8258","start":"8144","end":"8258","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“The Rigsthula is a definitely cultural poem, explaining, on a mythological basis, the origin of the different castes of early society… Men say there went by ways so green of old the god, the aged and wise, mighty and strong did Rig go striding.”","summary":"An editorial introductory note explains that Rigsthula survives only in the incomplete Codex Wormanius of Snorri’s Prose Edda and that the poem, unlike other Eddic works, is a cultural myth tracing the origin of thralls, peasants, warriors, and ultimately a king, functioning as praise of the royal estate and probably composed in Denmark in honor of a specific monarch. The poet is described as a wandering Norse singer strongly influenced by Celtic speech and literary spirit, though the poem’s style is still Norse. A late medieval annotator identifies the figure Rig with the god Heimdall, but the editor argues the poet likely had Othin in mind, aiming to derive royal estate from the chief of the gods. A short prose frame then reports old stories that the god Heimdall walked along a seashore, came to a dwelling, and called himself Rig. The opening stanzas depict Rig as an aged, wise, mighty god walking on green and midmost ways to a house where a fire burns on the floor and two hoary people, Ai and Edda, sit by the hearth in old dress. Rig speaks wise words, sits between them, and Edda serves coarse bread, broth, and boiled calf’s flesh. After more wise speech, Rig lies down in their bed with Ai and Edda on either side.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rigsthula is preserved only in Codex Wormanius, an incomplete manuscript of Snorri’s Prose Edda, and the poem’s end is missing.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poem is described as explaining on a mythological basis the origin of thralls, peasants, and warriors in early society.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The note states that from the warriors there finally springs one destined to become a king, and the poem is characterized as a song in praise of the royal estate.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The editor argues that Rigsthula was not composed in Iceland and was probably written on the Continent, most likely Denmark, in praise of a particular king.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The manuscript breaks off just before the connection between the mythical Young Kon and the historical monarch is established.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note suggests that the poem was probably composed in honor of either Gorm the Old or Harald Blue-Tooth, with Harald Fair-Haired also proposed but considered less likely.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The poet is described as probably a wandering Norse singer who had spent much time in Celtic-inhabited western islands and visited the court of a Danish king.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The note states that the poet had picked up Celtic speech, that the name Rig is almost certainly of Celtic origin, and that he had absorbed elements of Celtic literary spirit.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The introductory note emphasizes extensive contact between Norsemen of Norway and Iceland and Celts of Ireland and the / THE BALLAD OF SKIRNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 4822-4942","start":"4822","end":"4942","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Commentary on Skirnismol describing the Vanir deities Njorth, Freyr, and Freyja and their attributes; the sun as lethal 'Elfbeam'; the mountain-giant Gymir, his wife Aurbotha, and their daughter Gerth; Freyr's gift of his sword to Skirnir and Freyr's later weaponless battles with Beli and the fire-demon Surt; the symbolic apples of Ithun and magical rings Draupnir and Andvaranaut; Skirnir's curse on Gerth empowered by a magic staff; the cosmic Eagles hill at the end of heaven overlooking hell where the giant Hrsvelg in eagle form makes the winds; the frost-giant Hrimnir and the watchman god Heimdall; and references to multi-headed giants and the wise race of the Wanes, along with textual notes and cross-references to other Eddaic poems and Snorri's prose.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Njorth begat two children in Noatun: a son named Freyr and a daughter named Freyja, described as fair of aspect and mighty.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Freyr is called the noblest of the gods and is said to rule over rain, sunshine, and the fruitfulness of the earth, as well as wealth for mankind; people call on him for plenty and welfare.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Freyja is called the noblest of the goddesses; when she rides to a fight she has one-half of the slain while Othin has half.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When Freyja goes on a journey she rides in a cart drawn by two cats, and she likes love-songs and is invoked in love matters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Hlithskjolf is identified as Othin's watch-tower.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Skathi is named as Njorth's wife in the manuscripts mentioned by the editor.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"'Elfbeam' is explained as a name for the sun, whose rays are said to be fatal to elves and dwarfs.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Gymir is described as a mountain-giant, husband of Aurbotha, and father of Gerth, who is called fairest among women.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"An inferred missing stanza in Freyr's speech is reconstructed as ordering Skirnir to bring the maiden to Freyr and lead her home whether her father wills it or not, with a promise of good reward for Skirnir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Freyr gives his sword to Skirnir.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the last battle Freyr is attacked by Beli, whom he kills bare-handed while weaponless.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Later the fire-demon Surt slays Freyr when he is weaponless.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The phrase 'brother's slayer' is suggested to refer to Beli, slain by Freyr, while Skirnir is noted as never having killed anybody.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Apples are said to be a symbol of fruitfulness and of eternal youth.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The goddess Ithun has charge of apples which the gods eat whenever they feel themselves growing old.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The ring Draupnir was made by dwarfs for Othin and had the power to create gold.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Othin laid the ring Draupnir on Baldr's pyre when Baldr's corpse was burned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Baldr later sent the ring Draupnir back to Othin from hell.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Andvari's ring, Andvaranaut, is said to have a similar power of creating gold.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"By stanza 26 Skirnir's bribes and threats have failed, and he begins a curse which, through his magic staff, is to fall on Gerth if she refuses Freyr.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Eagles hill is described as a hill at the end of heaven overlooking hell.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The giant Hrsvelg sits on Eagles hill in an eagle's guise and makes the winds with his wings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Hrimnir is identified as a frost-giant.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Heimdall is described as the watchman of the gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Giants with three heads and giants with numerous heads are mentioned in related poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The Wanes are referred to elsewhere as 'wise Wanes.'","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Stanza 13 of Skirnismol is said to be almost exactly like many stanzas in the first part of the Hovamol and may have been a separate proverb.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Njorth","description":"Deity who begat Freyr and Freyja in Noatun and is mentioned At evening a wedding feast is held for the giants, where Thor alone consumes an ox, eight salmon, all the delicacies set for the women, and three tuns of mead. Thrym, leader and king of the giants, is astonished at the bride’s enormous appetite and drinking. A wise serving-maid sitting nearby twice explains these alarming signs, saying that Freyja has fasted from food and gone without sleep for eight nights because of her longing for Jotunheim. When Thrym looks beneath the bride’s veil to kiss her, he recoils in fear at her terrifying eyes, which seem to burn with fire. The giants’ luckless sister then arrives and asks boldly for a bridal fee of rings of red gold in exchange for her willing love and welcome. Thrym orders that the hammer Mjollnir be brought in to hallow the bride and laid on the maiden’s knees so that the hand of the goddess Vor may bless them both. Seeing his hammer, Hlorrithi laughs inwardly and then kills Thrym, king of the giants, and slays all the giant folk. He also kills the giants’ old sister who had asked for the bridal fee, giving her a blow instead of shillings, and using the hammer’s might in place of many rings. The passage closes by noting that Othins son thus obtained his hammer.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Thrym is described as owning {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l5842-l5985","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HYMISKVITHA / THE LAY OF HYMIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 5842-5985","start":"5842","end":"5985","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""The venomous serpent swiftly up
To the boat did Thor, the bold one, pull;
With his hammer ... he smote from above."
(Hymiskvitha, st. 24)","summary":"Thor visits the giant Hymir, eats two of his oxen, and insists on going out to sea to fish. Using the head of a black ox as bait, Thor hooks a venomous earth-girdling serpent, hauls it toward the boat, and strikes its head with his hammer, shaking the earth before the serpent sinks back into the sea. Returning, Thor carries the boat home on his shoulders. Hymir then tests Thor by asking him to break a treasured drinking cup; with advice from the giant's fair beloved, Thor smashes the cup against Hymir's skull, destroying it. Hymir offers his huge brewing kettle as a prize if they can carry it out of his house: Tyr fails, but Thor lifts it onto his head and departs. Hymir and a throng of many-headed beings pursue from eastern caves, but Thor fights with his hammer and slays the sea-monsters. Elsewhere, one of Thor's goats is lamed by Loki's deed, and a wilderness-dweller gives both his children as compensation. Thor finally brings Hymir's kettle to the gods' council, enabling them to drink ale joyfully in girs hall at autumn.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Thor, called the husband of Sif and Hlorrithi, eats two of Hymir's oxen alone before going to spoil.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Thor (called Veur and slayer of giants) is eager to row on the sea and needs bait, which he seeks from the hook.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A venomous serpent, named as foe of the gods and girdler of all the earth beneath, gapes at the bait and takes it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Thor pulls the venomous serpent up swiftly toward the boat and strikes the "hill of the hair" of the brother of Fenrir with his hammer from above.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The monsters roar, rocks resound, and all the ancient earth is shaken; afterwards the fish sinks back into the sea.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"On the return, Hymir rows back joylessly, sits speechless at the oars, and uses the rudder to seek a second bailer, and all home to the giant's house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Hymir, described as stubborn, says that none should be called truly strong unless he content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l3660-l3765","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / GRIMNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF GRIMNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 3660-3765","start":"3660","end":"3765","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Introductory prose to Grimnismol describes the poem as largely a catalogue of mythological names overlaying a dramatic story in which Othin, disguised as Grimnir, is mistakenly tortured by King Geirrth between two fires, uses the ordeal to display his wisdom to the king’s kind young son Agnar, and finally reveals his true names, causing Geirrth to fall on his sword and die. The note explains that such prose narratives before and after poems are common in Eddic manuscripts, likely written in the 12th–13th century by a compiler and reflecting an underlying oral prose tradition on which the poems are based. It argues that early Norse verse rarely served for direct storytelling and suggests broader implications for the development of ballad and epic poetry.\n\nThe attached prose narrative tells how King Hrauthung’s sons Agnar and Geirrth are blown out to sea while fishing, wrecked on a shore, and spend the winter with a poor peasant and his wife. The housewife cares for Agnar, while the peasant cares for Geirrth, teaches him wisdom, and in spring gives him a boat and secret counsel. Geirrth returns home to find his father dead, becomes king, and is renowned. Later Othin and Frigg sit in Hlithskjolf looking over all the worlds; Othin comments that Agnar, Frigg’s fosterling, is begetting children with a giantess in a cave, while Geirrth, his fosterling, rules as king. Frigg replies that Geirrth is miserly and tortures guests when he thinks too many come, and she and Othin wager over this claim. Frigg sends her maid Fulla to warn Geirrth that a magician is in his land, marked by the fact that no dog will leap at him. Geirrth, despite the description of the charge as slander, orders the stranger whom the dogs will not attack to be seized. The man, in a dark-blue mantle, calls himself Grimnir and refuses to say more. Geirrth has him placed between two fires to force him to speak, and he sits there eight nights. Geirrth’s ten-year-old son, named Agnar after his father’s brother, takes pity on Grimnir, brings him a full horn to drink, and says the king does wrong to torment him without cause. Grimnir drinks; the fires burn his mantle, and he begins to speak, leading into the poem proper.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In both Codex Regius and the Arnamagnan Codex, Grimnismol follows Vafthruthnismol, and Snorri quotes more than twenty of its stanzas.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Grimnismol is described as largely encyclopedic, consisting chiefly of proper names and lacking dialogue form.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Underneath the catalogue of mythological names in Grimnismol there is a consecutive and dramatic story involving Othin and King Geirrth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Othin, concealed under the name Grimnir, is mistakenly tortured by King Geirrth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Bound between two blazing fires, Grimnir begins to display his wisdom for the benefit of King Geirrth’s little son Agnar, who has been kind to him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Grimnir gradually works up to a final moment when he declares his true names to King The note comments on their limited poetic and mythological value and on the textual history involving Snorri and later copyists.\nIn the verses, Freyja wakes her sister Hyndla, who lives in a hollow cave, so they can ride to Valhall to seek favor from Heerfather (Odin), described as a generous god who gives gold, armor, weapons, triumph, wisdom, skill in words, fair winds, artistic talent, and courage. Freyja honors Thor and asks that he show Hyndla favor. She asks Hyndla to bring forth a wolf from her stall to run beside Freyja’s slow boar on the road of the gods. Hyndla accuses Freyja of secretly bringing her lover, Ottar the young son of Instein, along the way of the slain. Freyja denies this, identifying the gleaming boar with golden bristles as Hildisvini, made by the dwarfs Dain and Nabbi. Freyja proposes that they dismount and discuss the lineage of two heroes, explaining that Ottar and Angantyr have made a wager in foreign metal and that Ottar’s claim to his father’s wealth must be protected. She recounts Ottar’s devotion: he built her a stone shrine whose rock has become glass, often reddened with the blood of beasts, and he has consistently trusted in the goddesses. Freyja asks Hyndla to recite the ancient names and races of noble families (Skjoldungs, Skilfings, Othlings, Ylfings, free-born, and high-born men in Midgard). Hyndla begins by tracing Ottar’s patrilineal and maternal ancestry through named forebears, then evokes renowned heroes such as Ali and Halfdan of the Skjoldungs, describing Halfdan’s famous battles, his slaying of Sigtrygg with an ice-cold sword aided by Eymund, and his marriage to Almveig, who bore him eighteen Short example stanzas illustrate each form, including a scene where Vingthor (son of Jorth) wakes and finds his mighty hammer missing, a proverb-like stanza about early rising versus the idleness of a wolf and a sleeping man, and a stanza about a wise woman who understands others' secret plans to sail yet does not go with them.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The translator states that three verse-forms—Fornyrthislag, Ljothahattr, and Malahattr—are used in the Eddic poems and that all normally organize lines into four-line stanzas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fornyrthislag lines are sharply divided by a caesural pause into two half-lines; each half-line has two accented syllables and two or sometimes three unaccented ones, and the two half-lines are bound together by alliteration of two or three accented syllables.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Fornyrthislag example stanza shows Vingthor waking, discovering that his mighty hammer is missing, shaking his beard, his hair bristling, and beginning to grope or search.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Ljothahattr, the first and third lines of each stanza follow syllables.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Ljothahattr example gives a didactic statement that one who wishes to obtain another’s blood or goods must go forth early, and that an idle wolf will get little meat and a sleeping man little success.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Malahattr is described as a younger verse-form alliteration works as in Fornyrthislag.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Malahattr example portrays a wise woman eager to use wisdom, who understands what others go.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Poems in Fornyrthislag are normally titled with the suffix -kvitha, rendered as \"lay\" in the translation, whereas poems in existed.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The translator keeps the number of lines per stanza and the number of accented syllables from the Norse originals, allows GROUGALDR / GROAS SPELL / II. FJOLSVINNSMOL / THE LAY OF FJOLSVITH; lines 9748-9913","start":"9748","end":"9913","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Svipdag questions Fjolsvith about a hall surrounded by magical flames, its makers, a healing mountain called Lyfjaberg, and the maidens who sit at Mengloth's knees and aid those who bring offerings. Fjolsvith explains that Lyfjaberg heals sick women who climb it, that the maidens protect men in return for offerings, and that only Svipdag may sleep in Mengloth's arms, for the sun-bright maid is destined to be his bride. Svipdag reveals his identity and demands the gates be opened. Fjolsvith calls Mengloth, noting fawning hounds and the house bursting open. Mengloth initially threatens Fjolsvith with ravens on the gallows if he lies, but then questions the newcomer. Svipdag names himself Solbjart's son and says he came by wind-cold ways, acknowledging the inevitability of Urth's words. Mengloth joyfully welcomes him, saying she has long waited on Lyfjaberg for him, and declares that their longed-for meeting is the greatest joy and that they will live their lives together.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A hall is described as being encompassed by flickering magic flames.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The hall is called Lyr and is said to tremble on the tip of a spear-point, known as a noble house though mankind knows little more of it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fjolsvith names Uni, Iri, Bari, Jari, Var, Vegdrasil, Dori, Ori, Delling, and Loki as those who made the hall.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Svipdag asks which of the gods has made the hall he beholds within.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A mountain on which a lovely maid lies is called Lyfjaberg.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Lyfjaberg is said to be a joy to the sick and sore, and every woman who climbs it will grow well even if she has long been ill.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Maidens are described as sitting gladly together at Mengloth's knees.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The maidens at Mengloth's knees are named Hlif, Hlifthrasa, Thjothvara, Bjort, Bleik, Blith, Frith, Eir, and Aurbotha.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Svipdag asks whether these maidens bring aid to all who give offerings, if there is need.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Fjolsvith says the maidens quickly aid all who give offerings on the holy altars and that they guard the sons of men from danger and ill.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Svipdag asks whether there exists any man who may seek to sleep in Mengloth's arms.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Fjolsvith replies that no man may sleep in Mengloth's arms except Svipdag, and that the sun-bright maid is destined to be his bride.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Svipdag orders that the gates be flung back and the gateway widened, declares that Svipdag himself is present, and asks that Mengloth be sought to see if she will give him gladness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Fjolsvith calls to Mengloth that a man has come and urges her to see the guest, noting that the hounds are fawning, the house bursts open, and he thinks Svipdag is there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Mengloth threatens that hungry ravens will soon pluck out Fjolsvith's eyes on the gallows if he lies about the hero having come to her hall.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Mengloth asks the newcomer whence and how he came, and what name and race his kinsmen call him, saying she must know these as a sign that she is destined to be his bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Svipdag identifies himself as Svipdag, Solbjart's son, says he came by wind-cold ways, and states that no man may war with the words of Urth, though her gifts be unearned.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Mengloth welcomes Svipdag, saying she has long waited for him, promises him a welcoming kiss, and declares that the longed-for meeting of two who love is the greatest content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l241-l332","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THIS VOLUME IS ENDOWED IN PART BY CHARLES S. PETERSON OF CHICAGO / ACKNOWLEDGEMENT / GENERAL INTRODUCTION / WHAT IS THE POETIC EDDA?; lines 241-332","start":"241","end":"332","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Their history is strangely mysterious. We do not know who composed them, or when or where they were composed; we are by no means sure who collected them or when he did so; finally, we are not absolutely certain as to what an Edda is.\"","summary":"The passage is a scholarly introduction explaining what the Poetic Edda is, outlining the mysterious and uncertain history of the Eddic poems, the nature of the Prose Edda attributed to Snorri Sturluson, the traditional (but incorrect) ascription of an Edda to Sæmund the Wise, Arngrimur Jonsson’s correction of this view, and Bishop Brynjólfur Sveinsson’s 1643 discovery of a manuscript (later called Codex Regius) containing many mythological and heroic poems. It describes how these poems, supplemented by a few others from different manuscripts, have come to be grouped under the modern label “Poetic Edda,” emphasizes that this is a somewhat haphazard anthology with some lost components, and reviews competing and unsatisfactory etymologies for the word “Edda,” including proposals that it means “Poetics” or “great-grandmother.”","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poems of the so-called Edda have a \"strangely mysterious\" history: their composers, dates, places of composition, and collectors are all unknown.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The meaning of the word \"Edda\" itself is uncertain, and the best current guess at its meaning is considered misleading when applied to the collection of poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A prose work preserved in manuscripts of the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries contains a large collection of mythological stories, explanations of Norse poetic diction, and a treatise on metrics.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"This prose work is clearly a handbook for poets and has been known as the Edda of Snorri Sturluson, also called the Prose Edda, Snorri’s Edda, or the Younger Edda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A copy of the prose Edda in the Uppsalabok manuscript, written about fifty or sixty years after Snorri’s death in 1241, contains the heading: \"This book is called Edda, which Snorri Sturluson composed.\"","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Icelandic tradition persisted in ascribing either Snorri’s Edda or a similar work to Sæmund the Wise (1056–1133).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the early seventeenth century Arngrimur Jonsson argued that Snorri Sturluson, and no one else, must have been responsible for the prose Edda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Because Snorri’s prose Edda quotes many poems as sources for its mythological stories, scholars inferred that Sæmund the Wise must have written or compiled a verse Edda on which Snorri’s work was largely based.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In 1643 Brynjólfur Sveinsson, Bishop of Skalholt, discovered a manuscript, written as early as about 1300, containing twenty-nine poems, some of which include lines and stanzas used by Snorri.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Scholars identified this manuscript as at least part of the long-sought Edda of Sæmund the Wise, and the bishop labeled it Sæmund’s Edda, the Elder Edda, or the Poetic Edda.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The discovered manuscript, now in the Royal Library in Copenhagen and known as the Codex Regius (R2365), has served as the basis for all published editions of the Eddic poems.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Most modern editions of the Poetic Edda, including this translation, contain thirty-four poems, twenty-nine preserved in the Codex Regius and several additional similar poems from other manuscripts.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A shorter manuscript in the Arnamagnæan collection (AM748) contains fragmentary or complete versions of six Codex Regius poems and one additional poem, Baldrs Draumar, not found in Codex Regius.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Four other poems—Rigsthula, Hyndluljoth, Grougaldr, and Fjolsvinnsmol (the last two often combined as Svipdagsmol)—from various manuscripts closely resemble the Codex Regius poems in subject matter and style and are often included in the Poetic Edda.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Snorri’s Edda contains one complete poem, Grottasongr, which many editors add to the poetic collection, although it is omitted from this translation because an English version is already available in Brodeur’s rendering of Snorri’s work.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Poetic Edda, as currently defined, is described as a more or less haphazard collection of separate poems dealing with Norse mythology or with hero cycles not tied to traditional history.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The author notes that other similar poems, now lost, must once have existed in medieval Icelandic collections, but only thirty-four such poems are known to be preserved, twenty-nine in a single manuscript.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"An early assumption interpreted the word \"Edda\" as meaning \"Poetics,\" a sense that fits Snorri’s treatise but lacks philological support and does not suit the collection of poems.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Jacob Grimm identified the word \"Edda\" with a word in the poem Rigsthula that he conjectured meant \"great-grandmother,\" Project Gutenberg text of Bellows translation."},{"id":"ev:2","type":"summary","locator":"256-270","quote_or_summary":"The passage describes a prose work preserved in thirteenth- and early fourteenth-century manuscripts that contains a large collection of mythological stories, explanations of important figures and tropes in Norse poetic diction, and a treatise on metrics. It is clearly a handbook for poets and is known as the Edda of Snorri Sturluson, also called the Prose Edda or Younger Edda. Brodeur appeared in 1916.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Public domain; Project Gutenberg text of Bellows translation."},{"id":"ev:3","type":"summary","locator":"271-290","quote_or_summary":"Icelandic tradition continued to ascribe either Snorri’s Edda or a similar work to Sæmund the Wise (1056–1133). In the early seventeenth century Arngrimur Jonsson demonstrated that Snorri must have been responsible for the prose Edda. Because Snorri’s book quotes poems as sources for its mythological stories, scholars inferred that Sæmund must have written or compiled a verse Edda on which Snorri’s prose work was largely based.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Public domain; Project Gutenberg text of Bellows translation."},{"id":"ev:4","type":"summary","locator":"291-305","quote_or_summary":"In 1643 Brynjólfur Sveinsson, Bishop of Skalholt, discovered a manuscript, apparently written as early as 1300, that contained twenty-nine complete or fragmentary poems, some of them including lines and stanzas used by Snorri. Scholars rejoiced, believing this to be at least part of Sæmund the Wise’s long-sought Edda, and the bishop labeled the manuscript Sæmund’s Edda, the Elder Edda, or the Poetic Edda.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Public domain; Project Gutenberg text of Bellows translation."},{"id":"ev:5","type":"summary","locator":"306-320","quote_or_summary":"The discovered manuscript is now in the Royal Library in Copenhagen, known as Codex Regius (R2365), and serves as the basis for all published editions of the Eddic poems. Later editors added a few similar poems from other sources, so that most editions, including this translation, now contain thirty-four poems. A shorter manuscript, AM748, preserves parts of six Codex Regius poems and one additional poem, Baldrs Draumar. Four further poems—Rigsthula, Hyndluljoth, Grougaldr, and Fjolsvinnsmol (the last two often combined as Svipdagsmol)—resemble the Codex Regius poems in subject and style and are usually included. Snorri’s Edda also contains the complete poem Grottasongr, which some editors add, though it is omitted here because an English version already exists in Brodeur’s translation of Snorri’s work.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Public domain; Project Gutenberg text of Bellows translation."},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"321-332","quote_or_summary":"The author concludes that the Poetic Edda is not a clearly delimited work but a more or less haphazard collection of separate poems dealing with Norse mythology or hero cycles outside traditional history.
