{"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l11030-l11249","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HELGAKVITHA HJORVARTHSSONAR / THE LAY OF HELGI THE SON OF HJORVARTH / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / OF HJORVARTH AND SIGRLIN; lines 11030-11249","start":"11030","end":"11249","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"At night by a fjord, the giantess Hrimgerth threatens King Helgi's ships and men, trading insults with the watchman Atli. She reveals that Helgi earlier slew her giant father Hati. Hrimgerth demands to lie one night with Helgi as recompense, but Helgi rejects her and suggests the giant Lothin as a more fitting mate. Hrimgerth accuses him of favoring a gold-decked, magic-working maiden who scanned the harbor and, with a host of helmed maidens on horseback, used supernatural power to hold the fleet fast; their horses shook dew and hail that became human harvest. At dawn Helgi uses runes of death so that Hrimgerth dies and stands forever as a stone harbor mark.

In a later prose episode, Helgi seeks and wins the hand of King Eylimi's daughter Svava; they exchange vows, love one another deeply, and Svava remains a Valkyrie while staying with her father as Helgi fights abroad. Helgi's brother Hethin, living with their father King Hjorvarth in Norway, encounters a troll-woman riding a wolf with serpents as a bridle on Yule-eve. When he refuses her company, she curses him, saying he will pay at the king's toast. That evening at a Yule feast the sacred boar is brought in and men swear great vows upon it; under this influence Hethin vows to have Svava, his brother's beloved, and is then overwhelmed with grief and wanders until he finds Helgi.

Hethin confesses the vow. Helgi tells him not to grieve, insisting their beer-oaths must stand, and notes that he is going to an island for a battle in three nights from which he may not return. The narrator explains that Helgi foresaw his own death because his following-spirits had met Hethin when he saw the wolf-riding woman. King Alf son of Hrothmar has arranged a battle at Sigarsvoll, and Helgi declares that the wolf-riding woman knew that Sigrlin's son (Helgi) would fall there. A great battle follows in which Helgi is mortally wounded. He sends Sigar to summon Eylimi's only daughter swiftly if she wishes to see her lover alive, and Sigar conveys the message to Svava that Helgi wants to see her before he dies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker addresses Hrimgerth as a corpse-hungry giantess, curses her to sink nine miles deeper down, and says a tree may grow tall on her bosom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Hrimgerth identifies herself as the daughter of the giant Hati, described as the mightiest of giants, who carried off many women from their homes before Helgi killed him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Atli says that Hrimgerth lay in front of the ship and before the fjord, intending to give the rulers’ men to Ron, but a spear stuck in her flesh and thwarted her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Hrimgerth claims that her mother lay by the leaders’ ships and that she herself slew Hlothvarth’s sons on the sea.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Hrimgerth and Atli exchange coarse insults and threats; Hrimgerth invites Atli to come ashore to Varin’s cove to test his might, while Atli refuses to leave the ship until the warriors awaken and insists on guarding his chief.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Hrimgerth calls on Helgi to compensate her for the death of her father Hati by allowing her to sleep a single night beside the prince, saying that would requite all her ills.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Helgi refuses Hrimgerth’s request, saying that the giant Lothin, the worst of wild-dwellers, is a fitting mate for her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hrimgerth accuses Helgi of loving a gold-decked maid who scanned the harbor among the men the previous night; she says this maid bore magic when she came from the sea to land and held the fleet fast, preventing Hrimgerth from killing the monarchs’ men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Helgi asks Hrimgerth to tell the truth about how many figures guarded the ships, asking whether there was a single protector or many together.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hrimgerth reports that there were thrice nine maidens, with one helmed maid of white hue riding first; their horses quivered and from their manes fell dew into the deep dales and hail on the high woods, from which men obtain their harvest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Atli tells Hrimgerth to look eastward because Helgi has struck her down with runes of death, and he states that the prince’s fleet and the monarchs’ men are safe in harbor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Helgi declares that it is now day, praises Atli for holding Hrimgerth until then, and pronounces that she must lose her life and stand forever as a stone harbor mark at which men will mock.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The prose states that King Helgi goes to King Eylimi and asks for the hand of Eylimi’s daughter Svava; Helgi and Svava exchange vows and love each other greatly.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Svava remains at home with her father while Helgi is in the field, and she is explicitly described as still being a Valkyrie as before.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Hethin, living with his father King Hjorvarth in Norway, walks home alone from the forest on Yule-eve and encounters a troll-woman riding on a wolf with snakes used as a bridle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The troll-woman asks Hethin for his company; when he refuses, she says he shall pay for this at the king’s toast.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"That evening, at a feast, the sacred boar is brought in, the men lay their hands on it, and they take great vows at the king’s toast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"During the vow-taking, Hethin vows that he will have Svava, Eylimi’s daughter and the beloved of his brother Helgi; afterward great grief seizes him, and he travels on wild paths southward over the land until he finds Helgi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"When Hethin meets him, Helgi greets Hethin and asks what news he brings from Norway and why he left his land to come alone to them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Hethin tells Helgi that he has done an evil deed: at the king’s toast he chose the king’s child, Helgi’s bride, for himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Helgi tells Hethin not to grieve and insists that the words they both swore by the beer shall hold; he says he plans to go to an island, expects to arrive there in three nights, and doubts that he will return, depending on fate.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Hethin reminds Helgi that Helgi once said Hethin was a very good friend and gave him gifts, and he says it would be more fitting for Helgi to redden his sword than to give friendship to a foe by yielding his bride.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The narrator explains that Helgi spoke as he did because he foresaw his own death, since his following-spirits had met Hethin when he saw the woman riding on the wolf.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The narrator notes that King Alf, son of Hrothmar, had arranged a battle-place with Helgi at Sigarsvoll after a delay of three nights.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Helgi says that at dusk a woman rode on a wolf, wanting him to follow her, and that she knew Sigrlin’s son would fall at Sigarsvoll.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"A great battle takes place at Sigarsvoll, where Helgi receives a mortal wound.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"After being mortally wounded, Helgi sends Sigar riding to seek out Eylimi’s only daughter and asks that she come swiftly if she would find her lover alive; Sigar conveys to Svava that Helgi wishes to see her before the nobly-born life leaves him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Hrimgerth","description":"A corpse-hungry giantess, daughter of the giant Hati, who attacks Helgi’s ships and men, demands to sleep with Helgi as recompense for her father’s death, and is finally slain by Helgi’s runes and made into a stone harbor mark.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"A warrior on Helgi’s ship who stands watch at night, exchanges insults and threats with Hrimgerth, refuses to leave the ship until the warriors wake, and helps delay Hrimgerth until dawn.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Helgi","description":"A king and mighty warrior, referred to as Sigrlin’s son, who earlier slew the giant Hati, rejects Hrimgerth’s demand, commands the defense of his ships, uses runes of death against Hrimgerth, wins Svava as his beloved, foresees his own death, fights King Alf at Sigarsvoll, is mortally wounded, and sends for Svava before dying.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5","ev:7","ev:8","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Hati","description":"A giant, father of Hrimgerth, described as the mightiest of giants and a ravisher of women, who was slain by Helgi.","role_refs":["role:14"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Ron","description":"A being to whom Hrimgerth would have given the rulers’ men if she had not been wounded by a spear; presented as receiving drowned men of the sea.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Hrimgerth’s mother","description":"An unnamed giantess whom Hrimgerth says lay by the leaders’ ships and whose actions are connected to the slaying of Hlothvarth’s sons on the sea.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Hlothvarth’s sons","description":"Men said by Hrimgerth to have been slain on the sea near the leaders’ ships.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Lothin","description":"A giant, described as the worst of the wild-dwellers and called wise, whom Helgi proposes as a more suitable mate for Hrimgerth.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Gold-decked helmed maid","description":"An unnamed maiden whom Hrimgerth describes as gold-decked and magical, scanning the harbor and coming from sea to land, who held Helgi’s fleet fast and led a host of helmed maidens whose horses’ manes shed dew and hail that became men’s harvest.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Host of maidens on horseback","description":"A group of thrice nine maidens riding horses, led by a helmed maid white of hue; {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1115-l1217","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOLUSPO / THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1115-1217","start":"1115","end":"1217","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly notes to Völuspá (The Wise-Woman's Prophecy) explaining the opening stanzas: the status of the völva and Odin, the phrase \"holy races,\" Heimdall and the term \"Heimdall's sons,\" the title Valfather and Valhall, the nine worlds and the world-ash Yggdrasil, the primordial giant Ymir and Ginnunga-gap, Bur's family and Mithgarth, the leek as a symbolic and magical plant, Mundilferi as father of sun and moon, Ithavoll as the gods' meeting-place, the identification of giant-maids with the Norns and their comparison to \"three fates,\" the dwarf-name catalogue (including giants Brimir and Blain, directional and descriptive dwarf names, Durin, Regin), and Dvalin's runes and wandering dwarfs such as Lofar.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Völva is a wise-woman called upon by Othin, belongs to the race of the giants, speaks unwillingly, and is compelled to answer by Othin's magic power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The phrase \"holy races\" is glossed as probably referring to mankind in general.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Heimdall is described as the watchman of the gods, and mankind is referred to as \"Heimdall's sons,\" though the reason for this phrase is uncertain and has caused perplexity.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Rigsthula, Rig appears as the ancestor of the three great classes of men, and a fourteenth-century annotator identifies Rig with Heimdall, although the Rig of the poem seems more like Othin.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Valfather (Father of the Slain) is a title of Othin, chief of the gods, used because slain warriors are brought to him at Valhall (Hall of the Slain) by the Valkyries (Choosers of the Slain).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The cosmology is described as having nine worlds: Asgarth (world of the gods), Vanaheim (world of the Wanes), Alfheim (world of the elves), Mithgarth (world of men), Jotunheim (world of the giants), Muspellsheim (world of fire), Svartalfaheim (world of the dark elves), Niflheim (world of the dead), and a ninth world, presumably that of the dwarfs, perhaps Nithavellir, though the ninth world is uncertain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The tree mentioned is the world-ash Yggdrasil, which symbolizes the universe.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ymir is a giant out of whose body the gods made the world.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The phrase Ginnunga-gap or \"Yawning gap\" designates the primordial void and is sometimes used as a proper name.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Bur's sons are Othin, Vili, and Ve; Bur's wife is Bestla, who is the daughter of Bolthorn.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Mithgarth, meaning \"Middle Dwelling,\" is defined as the world of men.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The leek was often used as a symbol of fine growth and was also believed to possess magic power.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The sun and moon are regarded, in other Eddic passages, as the daughter and son of Mundilferi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ithavoll is mentioned as the meeting-place of the gods and appears only in this poem (here and in stanza 60) and in no other connection.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The poem refers to a game called \"tables,\" but the exact nature of this game is uncertain.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The term \"giant-maids\" in the stanza may refer to the three great Norns, which are said to correspond to the \"three fates,\" although this identification is uncertain and possibly affected by missing text.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Other passages describe the Norns as three throngs instead of simply three, and indicate many lesser Norns belonging to various races; in some places they are spoken of as giant-maidens.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Jotunheim is the world of the giants.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A section of the poem appears to be an interpolated catalogue of dwarfs, running through stanza 16, and Snorri quotes nearly the entire section with the names in somewhat changed order.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Brimir and Blain are named as giants about whom nothing is known; they may both be names for Ymir, with Brimir later appearing in connection with the home of the dwarfs, and some editors treat these words as common rather than proper nouns.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Few of the dwarfs named in the catalogue are mentioned elsewhere, Durin is singled out as authority for the list for no clear reason, and repetitions in the names suggest that not all stanzas of the catalogue come from the same source.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Many dwarf names seem to have definite meanings, such as Northri, Suthri, Austri, and Vestri (North, South, East, and West), Althjof (Mighty Thief), Mjothvitnir (Mead-Wolf), Gandalf (Magic Elf), Vindalf (Wind Elf), Rathsvith (Swift in Counsel), and Eikinskjaldi (Oak Shield), though in many cases the interpretations are guesswork.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Regin in the dwarf list is probably not identical with Regin the son of Hreithmar known from other poems.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"In Hovamol, Dvalin is said to have given magic runes to the dwarfs, which probably accounts for their skill in craftsmanship, and in Fafnismol he is mentioned as the father of some of the lesser Norns.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Snorri's Edda mentions, without explanation, that some dwarfs left the rocks and mountains to find a new home on the sands, and that Lofar was descended from these wandering dwarfs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Völva (wise-woman)","description":"The wise-woman in stanza 1, belonging to the race of giants, called upon by Othin and compelled by his magic to speak.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Othin (Odin)","description":"Chief of the gods, who calls on the Völva, uses magic to compel her, and is titled Valfather, Father of the Slain, receiving dead warriors in Valhall.","role_refs":["role:2","role:3","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Heimdall","description":"Watchman of the gods; mankind is called \"Heimdall's sons,\" and a later annotator identifies him with Rig, ancestor of human classes.","role_refs":["role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Rig","description":"A figure in Rigsthula described as ancestor of the three great classes of men, identified by a fourteenth-century annotator with Heimdall but said to resemble Othin more closely in the poem.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Valkyries","description":"Female beings called \"Choosers of the Slain\" who bring slain warriors to Othin at Valhall.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"\"Heimdall's sons\" (mankind)","description":"A phrase used for mankind in general, referring to humans as \"Heimdall's sons\" though the justification for it is unclear.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Yggdrasil","description":"The world-ash, a cosmic tree that symbolizes the universe.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Ymir","description":"A primordial giant out of whose body the gods made the world.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Bur","description":"Father of Othin, Vili, and Ve, and husband of Bestla.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Vili","description":"One of Bur's sons, brother of Othin and Ve.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Ve","description":"One of Bur's sons, brother of Othin and Vili.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Bestla","description":"Wife of Bur and daughter of Bolthorn.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Bolthorn","description":"A figure identified as the father of Bestla; by implication a giant.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Mundilferi","description":"A figure elsewhere described as the father of the sun (daughter) and moon (son).","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Ithavoll","description":"A field mentioned as the meeting-place of the gods, appearing only here and in stanza 60.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Norns","description":"Fate-like beings who may appear as three great Norns corresponding to the three fates, or as three throngs and many lesser Norns of various races; sometimes described as giant-maidens.","role_refs":["role:11","role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Giant-maids","description":"Giant-maidens mentioned in the stanza, possibly to be understood as the three great Norns.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Asgarth","description":"World of the gods, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:19","name_or_label":"Vanaheim","description":"World of the Wanes, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:20","name_or_label":"Alfheim","description":"World of the elves, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:21","name_or_label":"Mithgarth","description":"\"Middle Dwelling,\" the world of men, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:22","name_or_label":"Jotunheim","description":"World of the giants, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:23","name_or_label":"Muspellsheim","description":"World of fire, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:24","name_or_label":"Svartalfaheim","description":"World of the dark elves, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:25","name_or_label":"Niflheim","description":"World of the dead, one of the nine worlds.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:26","name_or_label":"Nithavellir","description":"A possible name for the ninth world, presumed to be the world of the dwarfs, though this identification is uncertain.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:27","name_or_label":"Brimir","description":"A little-known giant named in the dwarf catalogue, possibly another name for Ymir and later connected with the home of the dwarfs; some editors treat the word as a common noun.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:28","name_or_label":"Blain","description":"A little-known giant named in the dwarf catalogue, possibly another name for Ymir; some editors treat the word as a common noun.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:29","name_or_label":"Dwarfs (collective)","description":"A race listed in an interpolated catalogue; their names often have interpretable meanings, they are skilled craftsmen associated with magic runes, and some traditions say certain dwarfs wandered from rocks and mountains to settle on sands.","role_refs":["role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:30","name_or_label":"Durin","description":"A dwarf singled out as authority for the list of dwarfs, though the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l8850-l8922","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HYNDLULJOTH / THE POEM OF HYNDLA / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 8850-8922","start":"8850","end":"8922","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"And all are thy kinsmen, Ottar, thou fool!\"","summary":"A speaker recites an extensive genealogy of noble and heroic lineages—royal families, berserk warriors, and legendary figures such as Sigurth and the Volsungs—insisting that all of them are kinsmen of Ottar and emphasizing both the antiquity and length of his line. The passage includes mention of berserkers likened to fire over land and sea and of Jormunrek's sons being given as offerings to the gods in death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Several noble families (Skjoldungs, Skilfings, Othlings, Ynglings), described as the noblest of men dwelling in Mithgarth, are said to be connected to Ottar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage repeatedly states that all the named noblemen and heroes are Ottar's kinsmen, addressing him directly as \"thou fool.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Many individuals are linked through parent-child and marital relationships (for example, Hildigun as mother, Thora as mother of Dag's sons, Ketil as \"mothers-father,\" Nanna as daughter of Nokkvi), forming a long lineage.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The refrain \"It is much to know, wilt thou hear yet more?\" presents the genealogical information as significant were in the household of Hrolf the Old.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The sons of Arngrim and Eyfura, born in the east in Bolm, are described as causing and \"Fafnir's slayer.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A hero is said to be from the seed of the Volsungs, while Hjordis is of Hrauthung's race and Eylimi {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l10186-l10346","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LAYS OF THE HEROES / VLUNDARKVITHA / THE LAY OF VLUND / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 10186-10346","start":"10186","end":"10346","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of Vlundarkvitha, three maidens connected with swans live with three men, embracing Egil and Vlund, and one of them wears swan-feathers. After seven winters their longing returns and they depart for a murky wood to follow their fate, leaving Egil, Slagfith, and Vlund to seek them. Vlund remains alone in Ulfdalir, fashioning red-gold rings with gems and stringing them on bast ropes as he waits for his wife’s possible return.

King Nithuth, lord of the Njars, learns that Vlund is alone and sends armed men by night to his hall. They enter by the gable wall, see hundreds of rings on bast ropes, and take all but one. When Vlund comes home from hunting, he roasts bear flesh over a fire, rests on a bearskin, and counts his rings. Missing one, he assumes Hlothver’s daughter has taken it and returned. Falling asleep, he wakes bound in chains and fetters and is confronted by Nithuth, who questions how he obtained these treasures in Ulfdalir. Nithuth’s wise wife comments that Vlund looks unkind; Nithuth gives the stolen ring to his daughter Bothvild and keeps Vlund’s sword. The queen says Vlund’s eyes glow like snakes and that he gnashes his teeth when the sword or ring are shown; she advises that his sinews be cut and that he be set on an island called Svarstath. His knee sinews are cut, and he is confined on this island near the mainland, where he smithies precious objects for the king. Only Nithuth dares visit him. Vlund laments that Nithuth wears the sword he forged and that Bothvild has the golden ring that once belonged to his bride.

Vlund continues to hammer and fashion wonders for Nithuth. Two boys, Nithuth’s sons, come to look through his door into Svarstath and ask for the keys to a chest. When they look inside, they see gold and precious stones. Vlund invites them to return alone the next day, promising them gold and instructing them not to tell anyone of their visit. The brothers eagerly return to see the rings; Vlund opens the chest, then cuts off their heads and hides their feet under the sooty straps of his bellows. He takes their skulls, sets them in silver, and sends them to Nithuth; he makes fair gems from their eyes for Nithuth’s wise wife, and fashions a brooch from their teeth to send to Bothvild. Later Bothvild boasts of her ring, confesses that she has broken it, and says she dares tell no one but Vlund.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hlathguth and Hervor are named as Hlothver’s children, and Olrun is described as the wise The narrative frame then states that Thor, returning from a journey in the East, comes to a sound where a ferryman with a boat stands on the far side. Thor and the ferryman exchange insults as Thor asks to be ferried across, offering food as payment. The ferryman predicts the death of Thor’s mother, mocks Thor’s poverty and appearance, and names the boat’s owner Hildolf, a wise hero. Thor reveals his divine identity and lineage as Othin’s son, Meili’s brother, and Magni’s father, but the ferryman, calling himself Harbarth, still refuses and taunts him. They trade threats and boasts: Harbarth claims to be fiercer than any foe since the giant Hrungnir’s death, while Thor recounts slaying Hrungnir, whose head was of stone. Harbarth then boasts of spending five winters with Fjolvar on an island, fighting, killing men, seeking much, and ‘mastering maids,’ prompting Thor to ask how they succeeded with women.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poem Harbarthsljoth is preserved complete in the Codex Regius and partially in the Arnamagnan Codex.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Harbarthsljoth predominantly uses the Malahattr metre, a conversational verse-form, but employs other metres as well, and parts of it appear to be prose, resulting in metrical confusion.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The poem is characterized as a contest of abuse between Thor and Othin, with Othin appearing in the disguise of the ferryman Harbarth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The poem consists mainly of boasting and references to disreputable events in the lives of the disputants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Some editors interpret the poem symbolically as a conflict seriously.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Verse-form and linguistic features, including suffixed articles, suggest that the poem in its present form dates to about the East when he came to a sound where a ferryman with a boat was on the opposite shore, and Thor called out to him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Thor calls across the water asking who the man is on the farther shore of the sound.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The ferryman responds by asking what kind of peasant is calling across the bay.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Thor asks to be ferried over the sound, promising to feed the ferryman in return and mentioning a basket of good food on his back, including herrings and porridge he has eaten.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The ferryman says Thor does not know his future and that Thor’s homecoming will be doleful because his mother is dead; Thor replies that the death of his mother is the greatest grief.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The ferryman mocks Thor’s status and appearance, saying he does not have three good dwellings, stands barefoot, wears a beggar’s dress, and lacks hose.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Thor tells the ferryman to steer the boat over and asks whose craft it is; the ferryman says thieves.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Thor gives his name and lineage, saying he is Othin’s son, Meili’s brother, Magni’s father, and a strong one of the troublesome to wade across and get wet, but that he will pay Harbarth’s mocking words well if he comes across the sound.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Harbarth and asks what Harbarth was doing at the time.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Harbarth says he spent five full winters with Fjolvar on an island called Algron, They supply genealogical information on Hogni, Sigrun, Hring, Helgi, Sinfjotli, Sigmund, the Volsungs, Yngvi, Halfdan the Old, the Ynglings/Ylfings, Sigurth, and their claimed descent from Othin rather than Freyr. The notes interpret \"wound-givers\" as Valkyries and explain wolves as steeds of giantesses and corpse-eaters, and point out an apparent error in naming Hringstathir as a conquest from Granmar's sons though it was earlier given to Helgi by his father.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The gloss \"Fire-beasts\" is explained as dragons, before line 2, and many editors suspect line 3 of being spurious.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Lines 4–5 of stanza 53 are possibly the remains of a separate stanza.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Reginthing (The Great Council) is described as the council-place for the whole country, distinct from the local council 3.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sparinsheith (Sparin's Heath) is mentioned as a place about which nothing more is known of Sparin or his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l13227-l13310","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY NOTE / GRIPISSPO / GRIPIRS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 13227-13310","start":"13227","end":"13310","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A modern introductory note explains the poem Gripisspo, situating it after the prose Fra Dautha Sinfjotla in Codex Regius and describing it as a late, probably Icelandic Eddic poem composed around 1200. The poem is framed as a dialogue between youthful Sigurth and his uncle Gripir, summarizing Sigurth’s entire career as known in Iceland in the later twelfth century. The note then reviews scholarly views on the origin and spread of the Sigurth (Siegfried) story: it developed among the Franks of the Rhine country, reached the North from Germany, and became especially popular in Norway and Norwegian settlements through commercial and cultural contact between Franks and Norwegians between 600 and 800. The author emphasizes the scarcity of early sources, the tendency of popular heroes to attract unrelated stories, and the blending of history and fairy tale in early medieval sagas. Sigurth’s origin is said to be unknown, but he is characterized as an early traditional Frankish hero whose legend already included tales of his strength and valor, his winning of a great treasure, his wooing of a somewhat supernatural bride, and his death at the hands of his kinsmen.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Gripisspo immediately follows the prose Fra Dautha Sinfjotla in the Codex Regius and is contained in no other early manuscript.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gripisspo is described as one of the latest poems in the Eddic collection, probably composed not much before the year 1200, and possibly the latest of all.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The author of Gripisspo appears to have had written copies of other Sigurth-cycle poems and may be the same person who compiled and annotated the Codex Regius.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In form, Gripisspo is a dialogue between the youthful Sigurth and his uncle Gripir, and in substance it condenses Sigurth’s whole career as told piecemeal in the older poems.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The writer of Gripisspo is said to be skillful in handling verse but lacking inspiration, with characters devoid of vitality and speeches full of conventional phrases.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The poem Gripisspo is almost certainly Icelandic and provides a brief summary of Sigurth’s story as it existed in Iceland in the latter half of the twelfth century.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The introduction notes that the question of the origin, growth, and spread of the Sigurth story is immensely complex and has generated a large volume of critical literature.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"It is stated that the elsewhere.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"There was considerable commercial and other contact between the Franks of northwestern Germany and the Norwegians, but Historical evidence shows considerable commercial and other contact between Franks of northwestern Germany and Norwegians, but not Swedes or Danes, from 600 to 800, including finds of Charlemagne’s coins and other indications of an interchange of ideas and goods. The introduction outlines how Odin (Othin), chief of the gods, summons a wise-woman (volva) to recount the creation of the world, the origins of dwarfs, the first man and woman, the world-ash Yggdrasil, the first war between the gods and the Vanir, Odin’s own secret lore and search for knowledge, and finally the destruction of the gods at Ragnarok and the subsequent renewal of the world with Baldr’s return and spontaneously fertile fields. The editor argues that the poet was a tenth-century heathen, probably Icelandic, yet influenced by Christian ideas through contact with converted Celtic neighbors. The poem’s opening stanzas then show the wise-woman addressing the ‘holy races’ and Heimdall’s sons at Odin’s request, recalling the giants who once fed her, the nine worlds in a tree with deep roots, the primordial void before earth, sea, or heaven existed, the raising of land and the making of Midgard by Burr’s sons, the early aimlessness of sun, moon, and stars, and the gods’ council to name times of day and the moon’s phases to number the years.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introduction states that Odin, chief of the gods, summons a volva or wise-woman, presumably from the grave, to relate past events, including creation and early mythic history.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The volva’s narrative is described as including the creation of the world and the beginning of years, the origin of the dwarfs, the first man and woman, the world-ash Yggdrasil, and the first war between the gods and the Vanir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The introduction notes that later in the poem the volva reveals some of Odin’s own secrets and details of his search for knowledge, after which Odin rewards her and she begins the main prophecy of the final destruction of the gods.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The final battle is described as one in which fire and flood overwhelm heaven and earth while the gods fight their enemies; Valkyries bring slain warriors to support Odin and the other gods, Baldr is slain through the wiles of Loki, the enemies of the gods gather, Odin is killed, and fire leaps high about heaven itself.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the destruction, a new and beautiful world is said to rise from the ruins; Baldr returns, and fields that have not been sown bear ripe fruit.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The introduction asserts that the poet of Voluspo was heathen and a vigorous believer in the old gods, yet that the poem shows striking evidences of Christian influence, likely derived from contact with already-converted Celtic neighbors.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The editor suggests the poet probably lived mainly in Iceland (or possibly the Western Isles) in the middle of the tenth century, among roving Norsemen who were in close contact with Christian Celtic races.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The introduction emphasizes that Voluspo was transmitted orally before being written down, that some interpolations (such as a dwarf-name catalogue) and errors exist, but that the overall order of stanzas in Codex Regius appears logical and that the poem is composed of a series of vast mythic ‘pictures’ rather than a continuous narrative.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In stanza 1, the wise-woman says she asks for hearing from the holy races, Heimdall’s sons, both high and low, and that Odin (Valfather) wishes her to relate well the old tales she remembers of men long ago.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In stanza 2, the wise-woman remembers the giants of old who gave her bread in former days, and states that she knew nine worlds, the nine in the tree with mighty roots beneath the ground.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In stanza 3, she describes an ancient time when Ymir lived, before sea, cool waves, sand, earth, or heaven existed; there was only a yawning gap and no grass anywhere.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In stanza 4, she says that Burr’s sons lifted up the level land and made mighty Midgard; the sun from the south warmed the stones of earth, and the ground became green with growing leeks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In stanza 5, the sun, described as the sister of the moon, casts her right hand from the south over heaven’s rim; the sun did not know where her home should be, the moon did not know his might, and the stars did not know their stations.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In stanza 6, the gods seek their assembly-seats, hold council, and give names to noon, twilight, morning, the waning moon, night, and evening in order to number the years.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Odin / Othin / Valfather","description":"Chief of the gods, conscious of impending disaster and eager for knowledge, who summons the wise-woman and rewards her; Gothmund rebukes him for lying and accuses Sinfjotli of eating wolves’ entrails, killing his brothers, sucking wounds, and lurking in rocky dens. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l7120-l7282","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / THRYMSKVITHA / THE LAY OF THRYM / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 7120-7282","start":"7120","end":"7282","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An editorial introduction describes the Thrymskvitha as an early, well-preserved Eddic poem found only in the Codex Regius, praises its artistic quality, and notes possible stylistic connections and shared authorship with Skirnismol, Lokasenna, and Baldrs Draumar. The poem then begins: Thor (Vingthor, also called Hlorrithi, son of Jorth and of Othin) wakes to find his mighty hammer missing and becomes fiercely angry. He tells Loki the hammer is stolen, and they go to Freyja, asking to borrow her feather-dress so Loki can search for it. Freyja readily agrees; Loki dons the feather-dress, flies from the gods’ home to the realm of the giants, and reaches Thrym. Thrym, seated on a mound, tending his gold-leashed dogs and horses, questions Loki about the state of gods and elves. Loki replies that gods and elves fare ill and asks about the hammer. Thrym admits he has hidden Hlorrithi’s hammer eight miles deep in the earth and will not return it unless he is given Freyja as his wife. Loki flies back to the gods’ realm, meets Thor in the courtyard, and reports that Thrym keeps the hammer and demands Freyja as his bride. Thor and Loki go to Freyja; Thor tells her to put on a bridal veil so they can hurry to the giants’ home. Freyja becomes wrathful, snorts so fiercely that the gods’ dwelling shakes and her Brising necklace breaks; she refuses, saying she would seem extremely lustful if she went to the giants. The gods and goddesses then convene a council to devise a way to win back Hlorrithi’s hammer. Heimdall, described as the whitest of the gods and knowing the future like the Wanes (Vanir), proposes that Thor himself be dressed as a bride, wearing the Brising necklace, keys, a woman’s dress, gems on his breast, and a cap. Thor objects that the gods would call him unmanly if he let himself be veiled as a bride. Loki, son of Laufey, tells him to be silent, warning that otherwise the giants will dwell in Asgarth if the hammer is not brought home. The gods then dress Thor in the bridal veil and Brising necklace, with keys, dress, gems, and cap, while Loki declares he will accompany him as a maid-servant to the giants’ home. Thor’s goats are driven home to the hall and harnessed; as Othin’s son travels toward Jotunheim, the mountains burst and the earth burns with fire. Meanwhile Thrym orders the giants to put straw on the benches and prepare, for Freyja, daughter of Njorth from Noatun, is being brought to be his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1219-l1311","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOLUSPO / THE WISE-WOMANS PROPHECY / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 1219-1311","start":"1219","end":"1311","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes to Voluspo discuss the dwarf Andvari and his cursed treasure, the role of Loki in robbing him, and the resulting deaths in later legends. They explain the apparent break in the poem before the creation of the first humans, Ask and Embla, whom three gods—Othin, Hnir, and Lothur—make from trees. The notes describe Hnir (including his survival of a great destruction and his later prophetic role) and Loki/Lothur, emphasizing Loki’s treacherous nature, adoption by Othin, and probable origin as a fire-god whose heat animates the first human pair. Yggdrasil is identified as the world-ash kept green by healing water from Urth’s well, and the three Norns—Urth, Verthandi, and Skuld—are explained as Past, Present, and Future, carving runes on wood that control human destiny. The first war between the gods and the Wanes (Vanir) is outlined, along with their eventual treaty, exchange of hostages (including Hnir and Njorth), and joint worship. Gollveig/Gold-Might is presented as a Vanir figure whose mistreatment sparks the war, with some suggestion that she is identical with Freyja and that gold and fire imagery symbolize refining and the dangerous power of gold. The name Heith is linked to wise-women and prophetesses, possibly including the Volva narrator. The notes also summarize the Wanes’ victory, the gods’ decision to grant them equal worship, and the later story of Asgarth’s rebuilding by a giant who demands the sun, moon, and Freyja as payment. Loki delays the builder by a trick so he fails to earn his reward, whereupon Thor kills the enraged giant. The gods’ violation of their oaths to the builder is said to incur the lasting hatred of the giants, who become enemies of the gods in the final battle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Andvari is described as a dwarf whose wealth is treacherously robbed by the god Loki.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After being robbed, Andvari lays a curse on his treasure that later brings about the deaths of Sigurth, Gunnar, Atli, and many others.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Reginsmol is identified as the poem that tells the story of Loki’s robbery of Andvari and the curse on the hoard.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The editor states that the poem resumes its course at stanza 17 after an interpolated section, and that something may have been lost between stanzas 8 and 17.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"There is said to be no apparent connection between the three giant-maids in stanza 8 and the three gods Othin, Hnir, and Lothur in stanza 17, possibly due to confusion over the word ‘three.’","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In stanza 17, the three gods Othin, Hnir, and Lothur go forth to create man and woman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ask and Embla are explained as names meaning ‘ash’ and ‘elm’ and are given as the first man and woman, made by the gods out of trees.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hnir is a god who appears in poems together with Othin and Loki.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hnir survives ‘the destruction’ and in the new age receives the gift of prophecy.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hnir was given by the gods as a hostage to the Wanes in exchange for Njorth after their war.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Lothur is said to be apparently an older name for Loki.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Loki is characterized as the treacherous but ingenious son of Laufey, with his status as a god considered somewhat doubtful by Snorri.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Loki was adopted by Othin, who later regretted this adoption.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Loki is described as probably combining two originally distinct figures, one being an old fire-god, which explains his gift of heat to the newly created human pair.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Yggdrasil is identified as the world-ash.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Urth, meaning ‘The Past,’ is named as one of the three great Norns.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The world-ash is kept green by being sprinkled with marvelous healing water from Urth’s well.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The three maidens mentioned are identified as the Norns; some editors read their dwelling as a ‘sea’ while Snorri’s prose suggests a ‘hall’ or ‘home.’","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The three Norns are named Urth, Verthandi, and Skuld, glossed as Past, Present, and Future.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Magic signs or runes that control the destinies of men are described as being cut on pieces of wood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The editor judges that lines 3–4 of this Norn stanza are probably interpolations from another account of the Norns.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The ‘first war’ mentioned in the poem is explained as the war between the gods and the Wanes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The cult of the Wanes is said to have originated among seafaring peoples of the Baltic and North Sea coasts and to have spread into Norway in opposition to the worship of the older gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Ultimately the two types of divinities, the gods and the Wanes, came to be worshipped together, and the war ended with a treaty and an exchange of hostages.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Njorth and his children Freyr and Freyja are identified as chief among the Wanes and later conspicuous among the gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The Wanes are described as having been originally water-deities.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The phrase ‘I remember’ is taken to refer to the Volva’s own memories, despite manuscript variants reading ‘she remembers.’","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Gollveig (‘Gold-Might’) is presented as apparently the first of the Wanes to come among the gods, and her ill-treatment is said to be the immediate cause of the war.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Müllenhoff is cited as maintaining that Gollveig is another name for Freyja.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Lines 5–6 of the relevant stanza are said to seem to symbolize the refining of gold by fire, though one or both may be interpolated.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"Hor (‘The High One’) is glossed as Othin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"Heith (‘Shining One?’) is described as a name often applied to wise-women and prophetesses.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"The editor notes that applying this stanza to Gollveig is unclear and that it may instead refer to the magic and destructive power of gold.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"Bugge is said to argue that the stanza applies to the Volva reciting the poem and to place it first in a reordered sequence of stanzas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:35","text":"One stanza describes a battle and the victory of the Wanes; afterward the gods hold council to debate whether to pay tribute to the Wanes or to admit them to equal rights of worship, ultimately choosing equal worship.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:36","text":"After the war, Asgarth is described as having been destroyed by the Wanes and then rebuilt by the gods with the help of a giant builder.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:37","text":"The giant builder demands as his payment the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freyja as his wife; the gods, alarmed at his rapid progress, compel Loki—who advised the bargain—to delay the builder by a trick so that the work is not finished in time.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:38","text":"When the builder fails to receive his payment he becomes enraged and threatens the gods, and Thor kills him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:39","text":"Freyja is identified as the bride of Oth, who is otherwise only known from Snorri’s note that he was a man who went on long journeys.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:40","text":"Thor is described as the thunder-god, son of Othin and Jorth (Earth).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:41","text":"The gods are said to have violated their oaths to the giant who rebuilt Asgarth, thereby arousing the undying hatred of the giants’ race and making the giants their enemies in the final battle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Andvari","description":"A dwarf whose wealth is treacherously robbed by Loki

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l12986-l13061","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HELGAKVITHA HUNDINGSBANA II / THE SECOND LAY OF HELGI HUNDINGSBANE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 12986-13061","start":"12986","end":"13061","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes discuss several stanzas and the prose ending of Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II. Note 38 suggests that one stanza derives from a lost passage featuring a contest of words between Helgi and Hunding and was mistakenly inserted as an example of power granted to Helgi by Othin. Note 39 identifies the final section as describing Sigrun visiting the dead Helgi in his burial hill, and explains the phrase ragna rk as 'doom of the gods', critiquing its Anglicization to 'ragnarok' and confusion with a word for 'darkness'. Other notes gloss terms such as 'sword-tracks' (wounds), discuss perplexing plurals like 'brides' and 'loves' in relation to Helgi, and suggest that Helgi’s ghostly following might also have been visited by wives before the women return home. Note 48 explains Wind-helm as the sky, identifies the bridge as Bifrost the rainbow, and equates Salgofnir (Hall-Crower) with the cock Gollinkambi who awakens gods and warriors for the last battle. Note 49 connects 'Meeting of dreams' (Dream-Thing) with sleep and mentions that the speech may belong to the maid. The prose commentary then criticizes belief in human rebirth as 'old wives' folly, describes a theory of the hero Helgi’s rebirth devised to unify multiple stories of his death, and outlines connections among the lost Lay of Kara (Karuljoth), Helgakvitha Hundingsbana II, and Hromundar saga Greipssonar. In that saga, Helgi Haddingjaskati is protected by the Valkyrie Kara, who flies over him in swan form, but he accidentally wounds her in battle with Hromund; Hromund then beheads Helgi. This is described as Helgi’s third recorded death (after Alf and Dag). content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l8260-l8402","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / RIGSTHULA / THE SONG OF RIG / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 8260-8402","start":"8260","end":"8402","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Rig, a wise wandering guest, spends three nights in succession at three households of increasing status. After he leaves the first home, the woman Edda gives birth nine months later to a son named Thrll, an ugly but strong laborer who marries Thir; their many children perform menial tasks and are said to give rise to the race of thralls. Rig then visits the hall of Afi and Amma, who host him with a simple but decent meal; nine months after his three-night stay, Amma bears Karl, a sturdy farmer who manages oxen and plows and later marries Snr, a key-bearing bride. Karl and Snr have numerous children, from whom the yeomen’s race is said to descend. Finally, Rig is lavishly received in a fine hall by Fathir and Mothir; nine months after his three-night visit, Mothir bears Jarl, a silk-wrapped blond boy with bright cheeks and eyes described as grim like a snake’s.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After Rig has remained in a household for three nights, he continues on the \"midmost way,\" and nine months later Edda bears a son named Thrll, whose hair is covered with a cloth and who is sprinkled with water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Thrll is described as having wrinkled, rough skin on his hands, knotted knuckles, thick fingers, an ugly face, a twisted back, and big heels.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"As he grows, Thrll gains strength and uses it to bind loads with bast, carry burdens, and bring home faggots all day long.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A woman named Thir comes to Thrll’s home; she has crooked legs, stained feet, sunburned arms, and a flat nose, and she sits in the middle of the room beside the son of the house as they whisper and make the bed, sharing it until day is through.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thrll and Thir have many sons and daughters, whose names are listed; they care for the house, dung the ground, guard swine, tend goats, and dig turf, and the poem states that from them the race of thralls has arisen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Rig walks straight along the road to a hall owned by Afi and Amma, where a door hangs and a fire burns on the floor, and he goes inside.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Afi and Amma sit working: the man hews wood for the weaver’s beam, with trimmed beard, a curl over his brow, and close-fitting clothes; the woman works at the distaff and weaving, wearing a headband, a smock, and a kerchief fastened with clasps.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rig, described as knowing wise words to speak, sits in the middle of the room with Afi and Amma on either side; Amma sets vessels full of food before them, including boiled calf’s flesh, and afterward Rig rises from the board, makes ready for sleep, and lies in the bed with the other two on either side for three nights.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After Rig’s three-night stay and departure, nine months pass and Amma gives birth to a son named Karl, who is sprinkled with water, wrapped in a cloth, and described as ruddy-faced with flashing eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Karl grows and gains strength, managing oxen, preparing plows, building houses and barns, making carts, and handling the plow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Karl’s bride Snr is brought home wearing goatskins and carrying keys; she sits beneath a veil, and together she and Karl prepare a home, exchange rings, deck the bed, and make a dwelling.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Karl and Snr have numerous sons and daughters, whose names are listed, and the poem states that from them the yeomen’s race has arisen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Rig continues along the road to a third hall whose doors face south; the portal stands open with a ring on the posts, and the floor inside is strewn.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Inside the third hall, Fathir and Mothir gaze into each other’s eyes and play with their fingers; Fathir winds strings for a bow and shapes shafts and bows, while Mothir examines her arms and smooths and fits the sleeves of her blue gown, wearing a gay cap and clasps on her breast, and she is described as having bright brows, a shining breast, and a neck whiter than new-fallen snow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Mothir spreads a bright linen cloth on the board, lays thin wheat loaves upon it, and then brings silver-covered vessels with browned meat, well-cooked birds, and wine in plate cups; she and Fathir drink and talk with Rig until day is gone, after which Rig lies in the bed with them on either side for three nights.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"After Rig’s three-night stay in the third hall and departure, nine months pass and Mothir bears a son named Jarl, who is wrapped in silk, sprinkled with water, has blond hair and bright cheeks, and whose eyes are described as grim like a snake’s.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The phrase \"Rig knew well wise words to speak\" is repeated when he sits with Afi and Amma and again in the hall of Fathir and Mothir, highlighting his skill in speaking wisely.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"In each of the three households Rig visits, his three-night stay in the bed with the resident couple is followed, nine months later, by the birth of a son who is given a name (Thrll, Karl, Jarl) in a scene that includes sprinkling the newborn with water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6","ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Rig","description":"A traveling, wise-speaking guest who follows the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1782-l1947","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 1782-1947","start":"1782","end":"1947","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of gnomic verses advises on wise versus foolish conduct. Themes include the sluggard who tries to avoid danger yet cannot escape old age, the fool whose behavior at feasts and in conversation reveals his ignorance, and the benefits of travel for gaining wisdom. The sayings urge moderation in drinking and eating, proper timing and restraint in speech, and avoiding mockery and quarrels at feasts. They commend visiting friends but not overstaying as a guest, value owning even a poor hut over begging, and recommend always carrying weapons on the road. Further verses discuss using one’s wealth rather than hoarding it, the exchange of gifts (especially weapons and clothing) as the basis of friendship, appropriate reciprocity toward friends and enemies, cautious dealings with only partly trusted people, the delight of companionship for the solitary wanderer, and the superiority of brave and generous living over cowardice and stinginess.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A sluggard believes he will live forever if he avoids facing a fight, but old age will not give him peace even if spears spare his life.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"At a feast, a fool gapes and either stammers or sits silent, and once he drinks it becomes clear what his mind is like.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Only someone who has wandered widely and traveled far is truly aware of how great a guiding mind a person with much wisdom can have.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The verses advise not to shun mead but to drink in moderation, to speak briefly to the point or remain silent, and note that a person will not rightly be blamed for rudeness if he seeks his bed early.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A greedy man with a vague mind will eat until he is sick, and a vulgar man is scorned by the wise because of his overeating.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Herd animals know when to go home from the grass, but a foolish man never knows the proper measure of his belly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A paltry, poor-minded man mocks everything and does not realize that he himself is not free from faults.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A witless man lies awake all night thinking of many things, and when morning comes his cares and woe are unchanged.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A foolish man counts as friends all those who laugh at him and fails to notice when wise people openly express hatred of him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When the foolish man comes to a council, he discovers that few people will speak in his favor.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"An ignorant man sitting alone in a corner thinks he knows everything, but he does not know what answers to give when others question him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A witless man is advised to remain silent among others so that no one discovers his ignorance, whereas talking too much reveals that he knows nothing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A man seems wise if he can ask questions well and answer well; nothing that people say among humankind is fully concealed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Someone who is never silent often speaks words that gain no trust, and a babbling tongue without restraint brings harm upon its owner.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A man at a feast should not be mocked merely for attending; he may seem wise if no one questions him and he sits safely without getting wet or otherwise exposed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"A wise guest leaves quickly after making mockery, but a man who laughs at a feast and mocks in the midst of his foes knows little.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Many men are friendly in mind until they begin to mock their friends while feasting, and strife among guests is said to be a bane to humankind.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"One should often eat an early meal and not arrive fasting at a feast, otherwise one sits chewing as if choking and can hardly ask for what one wants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The road to an enemy is described as crooked and far even if his house is on the highway, while the way to a friend is wide and straight even if he lives far away.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"A man should not remain as a guest in one place forever, because love turns to loathing if one sits too long at another’s hearth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"It is better to have one’s own house, even a hut, and to be master at home; a pair of goats and a patched roof are better than begging, and having to beg for food makes a man’s heart bleed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:21","ev:22"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"A man should never walk a step in the open field without his weapons, since he never knows when he will need a spear on the distant road.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:23"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"If a man has wealth he should not let himself suffer in need, since he may save for a foe what he intended for a friend, and many plans go worse than hoped.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:24"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"No one is so generous with gifts or food that he will not gladly accept a gift, and no one is so lavish with wealth that he does not resent a lack of recompense.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:25"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Friends should gladden one another with weapons and garments as they are able, and friendships of gift-givers last longest, if fate allows.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:26"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"A man should prove a friend to his friend and repay gifts with gifts, and should answer mockery with mockery and fraud with falsehood.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:27"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"A man should be a friend to his friend and to his friend’s friend, but he should never form friendship with his enemy’s friend.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:28"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"With a fully trusted friend from whom one seeks good, a man should share thoughts, give gifts, and visit frequently.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:29"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"With someone one hardly trusts yet wishes to benefit from, a man should speak fairly but think falsely and repay fraud with falsehood.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:30"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"With someone whose mind is unknown and whom one hardly trusts, a man may laugh outwardly but should not reveal his own mind, and should give similar gifts to those he receives.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:31"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"The speaker recalls being young and wandering alone without knowing the road, feeling rich when he found a comrade, since one man is a delight to another.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:32"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"The lives of brave and noble men are said to be best and seldom focused on sorrow, whereas a coward fears everything and a stingy man is reluctant to give.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:33"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Foolish or witless man","description":"A recurring human type described as sluggard, fool, witless, ignorant, paltry, greedy, or vulgar, whose ignorance, anxiety, and bad conduct at feasts and in life bring ridicule and trouble.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12","ev:14","ev:15","ev:16","ev:17","ev:18","ev:33"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Wise man","description":"A human type presented as aware through travel, able to ask and answer well, moderate in drinking, prudent in speech, and skilled in navigating social relations.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:12","ev:13","ev:14","ev:16","ev:19","ev:20","ev:22","ev:24","ev:26","ev:29","ev:30","ev:31","ev:32"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Brave and noble man","description":"A man whose life is described as best, seldom feeding on sorrow, contrasted with the fearful coward and the stingy man.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:33"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Coward","description":"A man who fears all things and is contrasted with the brave and noble
