content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l3432-l3491","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / VAFTHRUTHNISMOL / THE BALLAD OF VAFTHRUTHNIR / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 3432-3491","start":"3432","end":"3491","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"The wolf shall fell the father of men,\nAnd this shall Vithar avenge;\"","summary":"In this portion of Vafthruthnismol, maidens of giant-kin are foretold to pass over Mogthrasir's hill in three groups and to protect the dwellers on earth. Othin, emphasizing his wide travels and knowledge, questions Vafthruthnir about who will rule the gods after the fires of Surt have sunk. Vafthruthnir answers that Vithar and Vali will dwell in the gods' home, while Mothi and Magni will possess Mjollnir when Vingnir falls in battle. Othin then asks what doom will bring his own death when the gods go to destruction. Vafthruthnir prophesies that a wolf will kill the \"father of men,\" but that Vithar will avenge him by tearing apart the wolf's terrible jaws and slaying it. Finally, Othin asks what he himself spoke into his son's ear before the son burned in the bale-fire. Vafthruthnir admits that no man can tell what Othin said, notes that he has recounted ancient tales and the fated fall of the gods, and concedes that although he has striven with Othin in knowledge, Othin is wiser.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Maidens pass over Mogthrasir's hill in three throngs and are said to protect the dwellers on earth, even though they come of the giants' kin.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The maidens are explicitly identified as being of the giants' kin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The dwellers on earth are described as needing or receiving protection from the passing maidens.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Othin says he has fared much, found much, and gained much from the gods, and he asks who will rule the realm of the gods when the fires of Surt have sunk.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The fires of Surt are associated with a time after which rule of the realm of the gods must be determined.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Vafthruthnir replies that in the gods' home Vithar and Vali shall dwell when the fires of Surt have sunk.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Vafthruthnir further says that Mothi and Magni shall have Mjollnir when Vingnir falls in fight.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Othin asks what will bring the doom of death to Othin when the gods go to destruction.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Vafthruthnir answers that a wolf shall fell the \"father of men\" and that Vithar will avenge this by tearing apart the wolf's terrible jaws and slaying the wolf.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The death of the \"father of men\" is linked to the wolf, and the wolf is depicted as having terrible jaws that can be torn apart by Vithar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Othin asks what Othin himself spoke in the ears of his son before the son burned in the bale-fire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Vafthruthnir states that no man can tell what Othin spoke in his son's ears and that he has told his old tales and the fated fall of the gods with a \"fated mouth.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Vafthruthnir says he has striven in knowledge with Othin and concludes that Othin is ever the wiser.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The gods are described as going to destruction, and their fall is part of The notes describe Baldr as the best and noblest of the gods, son of Othin and Frigg, whose death is caused by a mistletoe weapon thrown by blind Hoth at Loki’s instigation, and who will return among the survivors after the final battle. They outline Loki’s monstrous offspring with the giantess Angrbotha (Hel, Fenrir, Mithgarthsorm) and his role in the destruction of the gods, as well as Sleipnir’s unusual parentage from Loki and the stallion Svathilfari. Hel is said to rule a murky underworld, Niflhel, for unhappy dead, with differing traditions on who goes there. Othin appears as god of magic and travels in disguise under the name Vegtam, concealing his divinity from a wise-woman of the giant race whom he questions. Rind is named as a goddess who bears Vali to Othin; Vali is begotten specifically to avenge Baldr and kills Hoth the day after his birth. Another note interprets maidens who weep for Baldr as Ægir’s daughters, the waves, whose tempestuous grief tosses ships skyward. Finally, Loki’s escape and connection with the gods’ destruction and the wise-woman’s possible future counsel to him are content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l14111-l14290","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / REGINSMOL / THE BALLAD OF REGIN / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 14111-14290","start":"14111","end":"14290","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage recounts how Sigurth comes to King Hjalprek's stud and chooses the horse Grani. Regin, a dwarf and son of Hreithmar, arrives at Hjalprek's home, becomes Sigurth's foster-father, and tells him of his family and the story of the cursed gold. The gods Othin, Hnir, and Loki visit Andvari's waterfall, where the dwarf Andvari lives in the form of a pike and Regin's brother Otr fishes as an otter. Loki kills Otr with a stone, the gods strip his skin, and that evening they are seized by Hreithmar, who demands that the otter skin be filled and covered with gold as ransom. Loki borrows Ran's net to catch Andvari, questions him about his identity and the fate of liars in Vathgelmir's waters, and forces him to yield his gold and a ring. Andvari curses the treasure to bring death to two brothers and harm to heroes. The gods pay Hreithmar with the gold, covering even a single whisker with the ring Andvaranaut. Loki warns that the gold will be the bane of Hreithmar's sons and foretells that a maid will cause kin-strife and hatred among future heroes, but Hreithmar dismisses the warning. Fafnir and Regin later demand a share of the gold, Hreithmar refuses, and Fafnir kills him in his sleep and takes the entire hoard. Their stylistic features and textual history suggest a late origin, and a connecting prose or verse narrative between them may have been supplied orally by reciters rather than preserved in the manuscripts. The central narrative is described as a love story between Svipdag and Mengloth, whose tale is otherwise unknown in the Poetic Edda and unmentioned by Snorri. Groa appears here as Svipdag's mother, while Snorri elsewhere calls her a wise woman, wife of Orvandil, who uses magic charms to help Thor. The note states that the core of the story is a hero winning a bride who is surrounded by flames, a motif likened to parts of the Sigurth–Brynhild traditions. It comments on scholarly attempts to read the story as a nature or solar myth, suggesting such an interpretation is unnecessary. Finally, it notes that the Svipdag–Mengloth story later became popular throughout the Nordic countries, inspiring many ballads that help reconstruct the broader narrative around the dialogue The author explains that the poems were composed by many different men over time, circulated orally for generations, and that most mythological poems are pre-1000 due to their heathen character, though linguistic evidence suggests they did not take near-final form before the ninth century. Heroic-cycle poems largely belong to the period 950–1050, with some later. The legends behind the poems, especially heroic ones like those of Helgi, Vlund, Sigurth/Siegfried, Brynhild, the sons of Gjuki, Atli/Attila, and Jormunrek/Ermanarich, are often of Danish or German origin. Nothing definite is known about the poets themselves, but the poems show high artistic craftsmanship by both composers and audiences. The geographic origin of the poems is debated among Norway, Iceland, Greenland, and the Western Isles, with evidence of Celtic influence on some poems. Iceland is described as the true center of the Scandinavian island world and the chief place of preservation for the Eddic content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l1949-l2115","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 1949-2115","start":"1949","end":"2115","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This section of Hávamál (stanzas 49–81) presents a series of gnomic sayings about appearance, friendship, hospitality, work, wisdom, speech, wealth, mortality, and reputation. It contrasts the seeming heroism of clothed carved poles with the worthlessness of a naked man, likens an unloved man to a dying fir tree, warns against false friends, and praises the power of even small gifts to win friendship. Several stanzas insist that humans are only half-wise, that each person should have some but not too much wisdom, and that knowing one’s fate brings sorrow; people are known by their speech, rash words bring harm, and silence is often safest. The verses commend early rising, hard work, and prudent provisioning, advise modesty about appearance, and describe the insecurity of social status and wealth. They affirm that life is better than death even with disability, that sons and kinsmen honor the dead with memorial stones, and that wealth is fleeting while a noble name and the fame of deeds endure. Runes made by the gods and shaped by a master poet are said to give certain knowledge, and the passage ends by urging that days, people, and things should only be praised after they have been fully tested.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man gives his garments in a field to a pair of carved poles, which then look like heroes when dressed, while the naked man is said to be nothing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A fir tree dying on a bleak hillside, with its needles and bark useless, is compared to a man whom no one loves and whose life will not be long.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The friendship of false friends is described as burning hotter than fire for five days, but cooling on the sixth so that all love ends.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Small gifts, such as half a loaf of bread and a half-filled cup, are said to be enough to win a firm friend.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The minds of men are said to be small, and although men differ in wisdom, all are described as only half-wise.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Each man is said to have a measure of wisdom but is warned not to know too much; excessive wisdom brings unhappiness, and seeing one’s own fate in advance is said to increase sorrow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A brand is kindled from another brand and fire from fire, and similarly a man is known by his speech, while stupidity is linked with a certain kind of silence.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Those who wish to gain another’s blood or goods, or who have few workers, are urged to rise early and seek their work, while idle wolves and sleeping men are said to win little meat or success.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A man is advised to know in advance how many seasoned shingles, strips of bark, and how much wood he will need for his thatch and fuel over a month or half-year.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"People are told to go to council washed and fed, but not to care too much about their clothes, shabby shoes, or poor horse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"An eagle that comes to the ancient sea droops and hangs its head, and this is likened to a man in a crowd who finds few to speak for him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Those who wish to be known as wise should be ready both to question and answer, but are told to share thoughts with only one person, because what three know becomes common knowledge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A warning states that for the words one speaks to others, one may receive only an evil return.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Arriving too early or too late to a gathering can mean that the beer is either already drunk or not yet brewed, and a man who is loathed finds little; hosts would invite a guest who needed no food or who hung up more hams than he had eaten.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Fire, the power to see the sun, health, and a life not stained with sin are presented as the finest gifts for men.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"No man is entirely wretched even when very sick, because he may find joy in his sons, in kinsmen, in wealth, or in worthy works.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"It is said to be better to live than to be a corpse, since a living man can catch a cow; disabilities such as lameness, missing hands, deafness, or blindness still allow usefulness, whereas no good can come from a corpse.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A late-born son is valued, and memorial stones beside the road are said to be set up when kinsmen honor their kin after death.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Wealth is portrayed as swift and unreliable: people who once had well-stocked flocks can be reduced to carrying a beggar’s staff, and wealth is called the falsest of friends.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Cattle, kinsmen, and oneself are all said to die, but a noble name and the fame of a dead man’s deeds are said never to die.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:22"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Runes are described as a certain source of what is sought from them, made by great gods and shaped by a master poet, yet the passage concludes that silence is safest and best.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:23"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"An unwise man whose fortune changes by gaining a woman’s love or wealth becomes prouder but no wiser, and proceeds in conceit.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:24"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"People are advised to praise a day only in the evening, a woman on her pyre, a tested weapon, a maiden at her wedlock, ice after it has been crossed, and ale after it is drunk.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:25"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Generic men and women","description":"References to \"man\" and \"men\" as generalized human beings who receive advice about wisdom, work, friendship, wealth, and mortality.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8","ev:17"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Gods","description":"Unspecified gods who are said to have made the runes.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:23"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Master-Poet","description":"A master poet who is said to have painted or shaped the runes made by the gods.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:23"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Sons and kinsmen","description":"Relatives who bring joy to sick men, honor the dead, and raise memorial stones by the road.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:17","ev:19"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Prudent or wise person","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The text describes people who manage a proper measure of wisdom, avoid knowing too much of their fate, moderate their might, and are ready to ask and answer questions.","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:8","ev:11","ev:14"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Unwise or foolish person","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Men are called half-wise, stupidity is associated with certain forms of silence, and an unwise man grows proud rather than wiser when he gains love or wealth.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:9","ev:24"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Friend, host, or guest","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Men are depicted as false friends or loyal friends, as hosts who offer beer and food, and as guests whose manner of eating and giving affects how welcome they are.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:16"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Kinsman or son","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Sons and other kinsmen bring joy to the sick and honor the dead by erecting memory stones.","evidence_refs":["ev:17","ev:19"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"Maker and shaper of runes","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:3"],"basis":"The runes are said to have been made by the gods and painted or formed by the master poet.","evidence_refs":["ev:23"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Fire","literal_form":"Fire, burning brands, and flames, including fire kindled from fire, friendship burning like fire, fire as a prime gift, and flames from a rich man’s pyre.","associated

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l15648-l15718","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SIGRDRIFUMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE VICTORY-BRINGER / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 15648-15718","start":"15648","end":"15718","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes on Sigrdrifumol discuss stanzas 20–37: the fragmentary dialogue between Brynhild and Sigurth, Brynhild’s warnings about the dangers of Sigurth swearing loyalty to her, and a paraphrased conclusion in Volsungasaga where they mutually choose each other and bind their union with oaths. The notes explain a later section of numbered counsels resembling Loddfafnismol in Hovamol, gloss kennings such as \"Tree\" for warrior, \"Wolf of his word\" for oath-breaker, \"Silver of kinship\" for bride-price, and \"Race of wolves\" for the family of a slain foe, and interpret interpolated lines advising on silence, taunts, and killing a liar, as well as preferring battle to being burned to death at home. Further comments treat textual transmission from Regius and paper manuscripts and suggest that Brynhild’s speech of advice and its concluding warning once existed fully in verse.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The editor states that in the lost intervening stanzas between 20 and 21 Brynhild warned Sigurth about the perils that would follow if he swore loyalty to her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The gloss \"Tree, etc.\" is explained as referring to a warrior.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A paraphrase from Volsungasaga reports Sigurth saying that nowhere can one find anyone wiser than Brynhild, that he swears to have her for his own, and that she is his heart’s desire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the same paraphrase Brynhild answers that she would rather have Sigurth even if she might choose among all men, and the two bind this commitment between them with oaths.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The editor notes that with stanza 22 begins a list of numbered counsels closely resembling Loddfafnismol (Hovamol 111–138), which is here attributed to Brynhild but probably was not originally connected to her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The gloss \"Wolf of his word\" is defined as meaning an oath-destroyer or oath-breaker.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The editor interprets a chaotic interpolated stanza as warning that keeping silent too long may lead men to think one a coward, and advising that if someone falsely taunts one for silence, one should not argue but kill him the next morning to prove he is a liar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"\"Silver of kinship\" is explained as a marriage-price for which a bride was bought.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The note on stanza 31 says it means that it is better to go forth to battle than remain at home and be burned to death; many Norse warriors died in house-burnings, with the burning of the house in Njalssaga cited as a famous instance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The gloss \"Race of wolves\" is given as referring to the family of a slain foe.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The editor suggests that certain lines may come from an old Sigurth–Brynhild poem and may have formed part of a stanza of warning preceding Brynhild’s speech, and notes that in Volsungasaga they are paraphrased at the end of Brynhild’s long speech of advice.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The editor infers that paper manuscripts likely preserve all of the Sigrdrifumol from the lost section of Regius, except 20","quote_or_summary":"Stanzas 20–21 are all that remains of a dialogue between Brynhild and Sigurth from an earlier poem. In the lost intervening stanzas Brynhild evidently warned Sigurth of the perils that would follow if he swore loyalty to her. The gloss \"Tree, etc.\" is given as \"warrior.\" The manuscript does not indicate the speaker, and Volsungasaga names Sigurth before stanza 21.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:2","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 21","quote_or_summary":"The editor suggests that the original poem likely concluded with two stanzas paraphrased in Volsungasaga: Sigurth says that nowhere is anyone wiser than Brynhild, swears that he shall have her for his and that she is his heart’s desire; Brynhild answers that she would rather have him though she might choose among all men; and this they bind between them with oaths. Stanzas 22–37 may have been introduced early but probably were not part of the original poem.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:3","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 22","quote_or_summary":"With stanza 22 begins a list of numbered counsels, closely resembling Loddfafnismol (Hovamol 111–138), which is here attributed to Brynhild. The editor argues that it is highly improbable that this counsel section originally had anything to do with Brynhild.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:4","type":"quote","locator":"Note on stanza 23","quote_or_summary":"\"Wolf of his word: oath-destroyer, oath-breaker.\"","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:5","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 25","quote_or_summary":"Stanza 25 is described as a chaotic and obscure interpolation. The editor interprets it as meaning that it is dangerous to keep silent too long, as men may think one a coward; but if anyone taunts one falsely because of the silence, one should not argue with him, but the next morning kill him as proof that he is a liar.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 28","quote_or_summary":"The gloss \"Silver of kinship\" refers to a doubtful passage, but apparently means the marriage-price for which a bride was bought.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 31","quote_or_summary":"The meaning of stanza 31 is explained as that it is better to go forth to battle than to stay at home and be burned to death. Many Norse warriors met their death by being burned in their houses; the burning of the house in Njalssaga is cited as the most famous instance.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:8","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 35","quote_or_summary":"Lines 3–4 of stanza 35 are probably interpolated. The phrase \"Race of wolves\" is glossed as meaning the family of a slain foe.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:9","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 37","quote_or_summary":"Lines 3–4 of stanza 37 may derive from the old Sigurth–Brynhild poem, like stanzas 24 and 20–21, and may have been inserted here in place of two lines with which the eleventh counsel originally ended. They perhaps formed part of the stanza of warning that evidently preceded Brynhild’s speech in stanza 20. In Volsungasaga these lines are paraphrased at the end of Brynhild’s long speech of advice (stanzas 20–37), immediately followed by the prose passage cited in the note on stanza 21. The editor concludes that the paper manuscripts probably preserve all of the Sigrdrifumol contained in the lost section of Regius, possibly excepting two concluding stanzas, which may have been given only as a prose note, though they almost certainly once existed in verse form.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."},{"id":"ev:10","type":"summary","locator":"Note on stanza 29","quote_or_summary":"Line 1 of stanza 29 comes at the end of the thirty-second leaf of Regius, and whatever further material was contained there has vanished with a lost eight-leaf folio. The rest of stanza 29 and stanzas 30–37 are added from later paper manuscripts, which were undoubtedly copied from an old parchment, though probably not from the complete Regius. Volsungasaga paraphrases these additional stanzas.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","rights_note":"Project Gutenberg text; public domain."}],"confidence":{"extraction":"medium","motif_candidates":"medium","comparison_claims":"high","notes":"The passage is predominantly editorial and philological; motifs are inferred from glosses and paraphrased narrative rather than full poetic stanzas, so narrative reconstruction is tentative even where lexical meanings are clear."},"reviewer_status":{"status":"needs_review","reviewer":"","reviewed_at":"","notes":""},"extracted_by":"atlas-automated-gpt","extracted_at":"2026-07-18","notes":"Motif and symbol identifications rely on editorial glosses and Volsungasaga paraphrases referenced in the notes; the underlying verse is fragmentary or lost, so some scene and motif reconstructions may need adjustment after checking the full poetic and saga contexts."}

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l2117-l2278","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES / HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE; lines 2117-2278","start":"2117","end":"2278","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Othin (Odin) speaks a series of wisdom sayings about practical conduct, trust, and love, warning against many unreliable people, animals, and objects. He reflects on how love can bind even the wise and tells of his own failed attempt to meet Billing's daughter, who deceives him. He then recounts how he entered Suttung's hall, used Rati to bore through stone, obtained drinks of the marvelous mead from Gunnloth, brought the vessel Othrrir to humankind, narrowly escaped the giants' land with her help, and yet broke an oath sworn on a ring, betraying Suttung and leaving Gunnloth in grief while questioning who can trust his troth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Othin advises chopping wood when the wind is strong and going to sea when the weather is fair.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"He suggests playing with maidens at dusk, noting that many eyes watch by day.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"He says that from a ship one should seek swiftness, from a shield protection, from a sword cutting ability, and from a maiden kisses.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Othin recommends drinking ale by the fire and skating over ice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"He advises buying a lean horse and a tarnished sword, then fattening the horse at home and keeping a hound in one’s dwelling.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Othin says a man should not trust a maiden’s oath or a woman’s words.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"He describes women’s hearts as fashioned on a whirling wheel and their breasts as fickle in form.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Othin lists a breaking bow and a burning flame among things in which one should not place trust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"He includes a ravening wolf, a croaking raven, a grunting boar, and a tree with its roots broken among dangerous or unreliable things.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"He adds billowy seas and a bubbling kettle to the catalogue of things not to trust.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"He mentions a flying arrow, falling waters, new-formed ice, and the folds of a serpent as hazards.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"He warns against relying on a bride’s bed-speech, a broken sword, the sport of bears, and the sons of kings.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"He counsels skepticism regarding a sick calf, a stubborn thrall, a flattering witch, and a newly slain foe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"He warns not to trust a brother’s slayer, a half-burned house, or a swift horse with an injured leg, concluding that no one has trusted all such things.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Othin advises not to hope too confidently for an early harvest or to trust a son too soon, noting that fields need good weather and sons need wisdom, which are often denied.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"He compares the fickle love of women to risky undertakings such as riding an unshod horse on ice, steering a rudderless ship in a storm, or hunting reindeer while lame on slippery rocks.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Othin acknowledges that men can be false to women, saying that when they speak fairest they may think most falsely and act against wisdom with deceit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"He advises that a suitor who seeks a maiden’s love should speak soft words, offer wealth, and praise her beauty, claiming that the one whose wooing is best wins.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Othin says no one should fault another for loving, since even the wise are often fettered by beauty while fools go free.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"He notes that powerful love can turn wise men into witless fools and affects many people.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"He states that only a person’s own head knows what is near their heart, and that for the wise no sickness is worse than lacking the joy they long for.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Othin relates that he once sat among reeds for a long time awaiting a maiden he loved as his life but never obtained.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"He identifies the maiden as Billing’s daughter, whom he found lying asleep on her bed, shining like the sun, and whose absence made an earl’s estate seem empty to him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Billing’s daughter tells Othin to come again at evening if he wishes to win a woman and insists that others must not learn of their intended meeting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Othin says he hastened away, hoping for great joy and disregarding wise counsel, believing he would soon enjoy measureless joy with the maiden.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"When Othin returns at night, he finds all the warriors awake with burning lights and waving brands, which thwart his approach.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Returning in the morning when all are sleeping, Othin finds a dog bound on the maiden’s bed in place of Billing’s daughter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"From this experience Othin concludes that many fair maidens are false to lovers; he describes the maiden as crafty and says he received foul scorn and gained nothing from her despite his wiles.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Othin advises that even a man who is glad at home and merry with guests should be wary and wise, ensuring his speech is fair.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"He says a man who cannot say anything in company is called a fool, which is typical of the witless.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"Othin recounts that he found an old giant and went to Suttung’s hall, where he spoke many words to achieve his will, finding that silence brought little gain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"He says that the mouth of Rati gnawed through the stone to make a passage for him, with the giants’ paths lying above and below, so that he rashly risked his head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"Othin says that Gunnloth, sitting on a golden stool, gave him drinks of the marvelous mead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"He admits that he repaid Gunnloth harshly for her heroic heart, troubling her spirit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:35","text":"He states that he fully enjoyed Gunnloth’s beauty and that Othrrir, the vessel of the mead, has been brought up into the midst of the men of earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:36","text":"Othin notes that he would hardly have come home and left the giants’ land alive without Gunnloth’s help and her arms around him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:37","text":"On the following day, frost-giants come into Hor’s hall seeking some word of Hor and asking whether Bolverk has returned among the gods or been slain by Suttung.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:38","text":"It is said that Othin swore an oath on his ring, yet he sought Suttung’s betrayal through drink and left Gunnloth in grief, leading the speaker to ask who can now trust his troth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Othin (Odin)","description":"First-person speaker who offers wisdom sayings, recounts his failed attempt to meet Billing’s daughter, and narrates his risky acquisition of the marvelous mead from the giants.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:7","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11","ev:13","ev:14","ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Billing’s daughter","description":"Maiden whom Othin loves, who invites him to a secret evening meeting but deceives him so that he finds only a dog bound on her bed.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gunnloth","description":"Maiden in Suttung’s hall who sits on a golden stool, gives Othin drinks of the marvelous mead, helps his escape from the giants’ land, and is left sorrowful by his harsh repayment and departure.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14","ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Suttung","description":"Giant associated with a hall and with the marvelous mead; Othin speaks many words in his hall, seeks Suttung’s betrayal in gaining the mead, and the frost-giants later wonder if Suttung has slain Bolverk.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:13","ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Rati","description":"Figure or tool described as having a mouth that gnaws through stone to create a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-poetic-edda-bellows-gutenberg-l2765-l2877","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/poetic-edda-bellows.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOVAMOL / THE BALLAD OF THE HIGH ONE / INTRODUCTORY NOTE / NOTES; lines 2765-2877","start":"2765","end":"2877","translation":"The Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes to Hávamál stanzas (mainly 104–143) summarizing how Odin steals the magic mead of poetry from the giant Suttung by shape-shifting and seducing Gunnloth, spills some mead so that humans gain poetry, and breaks a sacred ring-oath. The notes introduce Loddfafnir as a wandering singer quoting Odin’s counsel near the Wells of Urd, explain formulaic advice lines, and describe imagery about mixed good and evil in humans, old age, and the dangers of excessive hospitality. They then outline the confused rune section titled in some manuscripts “Odin’s Tale of the Runes,” where Odin hangs on the ash Yggdrasil and wounds himself with his own spear to win the runes, learns nine magic songs from an uncle (perhaps Mimir) descended from his grandfather Bolthorn, uses them to gain the magic mead in the vessel Odrerir, and is called king of singers in a lost poem where runes are carved in wood and colored red.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Suttung is described as an old giant who possesses a magic mead, a draught of which grants the gift of poetry.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Odin, wishing to obtain the magic mead, changes himself into a snake.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In snake form Odin bores his way through a mountain into Suttung’s home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Odin makes love to Suttung’s daughter Gunnloth, and with her connivance drinks up all the magic mead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After drinking the mead, Odin flies away in the form of an eagle, leaving Gunnloth behind.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"While staying with Suttung, Odin assumes the name Bolverk, meaning ‘Evil-Doer.’","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Rati is identified as the gimlet with which Odin bores through the mountain to reach Suttung’s home.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Othrrir (Odrerir) is used here as the name of the magic mead itself and elsewhere as the name of the vessel containing it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"While flying over the earth pursued by Suttung, Odin spills some of the magic mead from his mouth, and this spilled portion gives mankind the gift of poetry, which he had not intended to share.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The name Hor is another name for Odin, and some frost-giants, kinsmen of Suttung, do not realize that Odin and Bolverk are the same being.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Odin is said to have sworn an oath to Suttung that there was no such person as Bolverk among the gods, which may explain the giants’ ignorance of his alias.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Odin is described as keenly conscious of having violated his most sacred oath, one sworn upon his ring.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Loddfafnir is characterized as a wandering singer who, seated on his chanter’s stool, recites verses he claims to have received from Odin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Wells of Urd are mentioned, and Urd (‘the Past’) is identified as one of three Norns.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The phrase translated ‘the speech of Hor’ (Háva mál) serves as the title of the entire poem Hávamál.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In the Loddfafnismol section, Odin uses a repeated formula at the start of his counsels to Loddfafnir, and except in two stanzas Loddfafnir presents himself as simply quoting Odin’s words.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A late paper manuscript preserves two lines stating that the sons of men always bear both evil and good mingled in their breasts.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"One stanza compares an old man’s wrinkled skin to dried skins and bellies of animals hanging inside an Icelandic house.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A stanza is explained as warning against too much hospitality: the door-beam or bolt, constantly lifted to admit guests, becomes weak and needs a ring to help keep the door closed, otherwise the host becomes a victim of his own generosity.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Stanzas 139–146 are described as a confused group related to runes, with some paper manuscripts labelling the section ‘Odin’s Tale of the Runes.’","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Within this rune section, Odin is said to have hung himself on the windy tree, the ash Yggdrasil, as an offering to himself and wounded himself with his own spear in order to win the magic runes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Yggdrasil is described as an ash tree called ‘the Horse of Odin’ because of the story of Odin hanging on it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Stanza 141 identifies Bolthorn as Odin’s grandfather and Bestla as his mother; it also mentions an unnamed uncle, speculated to be Mimir, from whom Odin learns nine magic songs.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The nine magic songs learned from Odin’s uncle are said to have enabled him to win the magic mead contained in the vessel Othrrir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The rune stanzas 143–144 are thought to derive from a lost poem on the authorship of the runes, and in this context Odin is called ‘king of singers.’","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Runes are described as magic signs commonly carved in wood and then colored red.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Stanza 141, about Bolthorn’s son and nine magic songs, is said to interrupt the account of Odin’s winning of the runes and appears to be interpolated from some version of the magic mead story.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The editor notes that certain lines in the rune stanza have presumably been borrowed from the poem Svipdagsmol, stanza 30.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The rune section precedes the Ljothatal, a list of charms associated with runic knowledge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Odin (Othin, Hor, Bolverk, king of singers)","description":"Chief god referred to under several names, who steals the magic mead of poetry from Suttung using shape-shifting and seduction, swears and breaks a ring-oath, gives counsels to Loddfafnir, hangs himself on Yggdrasil and wounds himself with his spear to win the runes, learns nine magic songs from an uncle, and is titled ‘king of singers’ in a rune poem.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3","role:4","role:6","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Suttung","description":"An
